pericopes.text: And now I, Moroni, proceed to give an account of those ancient inhabitants which were destroyed by the hand of the Lord upon the face of this north country.
And I take mine account from the twenty and four plates which were found by the people of Limhi, which is called the Book of Ether.

And as I suppose that the first part of this record, which speaketh concerning the creation of the world, and also of Adam, and an account from that time even to the great tower, and whatsoever things transpired among the children of men until that time, is had among the Jews,

therefore I do not write those things which transpired from the days of Adam until that time; but they are had upon the plates; and whoso findeth them, the same will have power that he may get the full account.
But behold, I give not the full account, but a part of the account I give, from the tower down until they were destroyed.
And on this wise do I give the account. He that wrote this record was Ether, and he was a descendant of Coriantor;

provenance.other: The English Bible has two ascending genealogies and they are formally distinct. The Chronicler's is appositional and verbless — 1 Chronicles 6:33-38, 'Heman a singer, the son of Joel, the son of Shemuel', running up to 'the son of Levi, the son of Israel'; Ezra 7:1-5 is the same shape. Luke 3:23-38 is the only one built on a repeated relative clause, and “which was the son of” occurs in exactly 16 KJV verses, every one of them in that pericope. Ether 1:6-32 is neither: it is a chain of finite clauses, 'and Moron was the son of Ethem', twenty-five of them. “was the son of” occurs in exactly 23 KJV verses and no KJV passage repeats it as a chain.
provenance.significance: What Ether 1 shares with Luke 3 is not wording but direction, and direction is the rarer thing. Every genealogy in the Hebrew Bible that means to establish descent runs forward and begets: Genesis 5, Genesis 11:10-26, Ruth 4:18-22, the whole first nine chapters of Chronicles. Luke alone reverses the current and runs from the man in front of the reader back through thirty-odd names to the boundary of the world — Adam, and the son of God. Ether 1 does exactly that, from the writer of the record back through thirty names to Jared, and then over the edge of the record into Genesis 11. Moroni's frame makes the point himself at 1:3-5: the part of the account that runs from Adam to the tower is 'had among the Jews' and he will not copy it, so his list stops precisely where Luke's keeps going. Two ascending genealogies, one running up into Genesis and the other running up out of it, meeting at the great tower.
provenance.alternative: A writer producing a backwards list of invented names needs no model at all, and the Chronicler supplies the ascending 'son of' chain without the Lukan relative clause. What tips the balance is 1:32, where the chain switches into Luke's exact formula at the one name Luke's own genealogy contains.

links.note: 'He that wrote this record was Ether, and he was a descendant of Coriantor.' From here to 1:32 the chapter is a single ascending genealogy of thirty names, and the ascent is the argument. The KJV's genealogies overwhelmingly beget forward; the two that climb are the Chronicler's appositional lists and Luke 3:23-38, and only Luke's climbs as its whole rhetorical point — to plant a named man at the end of a chain and then walk the chain back to the origin of things. Ether 1 takes the same walk and stops one generation short of Genesis, handing the reader to Genesis 11 at 1:33. Recorded as structural because there is almost no shared wording to weigh: the case rests on form, direction and terminus, which is what the `figural` category is for.
links.whyNot: Genealogy is a form, not a text, and a list of fathers can be written backwards by anyone who wants to reach a founder. Nothing here is verbally distinctive except at 1:32, and a reader who called this the Chronicler's ascending chain with a different verb would be taking a defensible line.
links.text: And Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, which was the son of Heli,

pericopes.text: Coriantor was the son of Moron;
and Moron was the son of Ethem;
and Ethem was the son of Ahah;
and Ahah was the son of Seth;
and Seth was the son of Shiblon;
and Shiblon was the son of Com;
and Com was the son of Coriantum;
and Coriantum was the son of Amnigaddah;
and Amnigaddah was the son of Aaron;
and Aaron was a descendant of Heth, who was the son of Hearthom;
and Hearthom was the son of Lib;
and Lib was the son of Kish;
and Kish was the son of Corom;
and Corom was the son of Levi;
and Levi was the son of Kim;
and Kim was the son of Morianton;
and Morianton was a descendant of Riplakish;
and Riplakish was the son of Shez;
and Shez was the son of Heth;
and Heth was the son of Com;
and Com was the son of Coriantum;
and Coriantum was the son of Emer;
and Emer was the son of Omer;
and Omer was the son of Shule;
and Shule was the son of Kib;
and Kib was the son of Orihah, which was the son of Jared;

provenance.other: “which was the son of Jared” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “the son of Jared” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — the same one. The 1830 reading is 'and Kib was the son of Orihah, which was the son of Jared'; 1920 changed 'which' to 'who', which erases the agreement, so the six-word run is visible in the first edition and not in the current text (CONVENTIONS §8).
provenance.significance: Twenty-five verses of this genealogy read 'X was the son of Y' with a finite verb. At the last link in the chain, and only there, the sentence changes gear into the appositive relative — 'Orihah, which was the son of Jared' — which is Luke 3's formula and no one else's in the English Bible. The clause it produces is a KJV singleton, and the name it lands on is the name that made it one. Luke's Jared is the antediluvian son of Mahalaleel and father of Enoch, five generations before the flood; Ether's Jared is the man who walks away from Babel after it. The two lists share a formula, a name, and a direction of travel, and they use them at opposite ends of the same primeval history — Luke passing Jared on the way up to Adam, Ether stopping at Jared because that is where the Jewish record he declines to copy takes over.
provenance.alternative: The clause could be produced mechanically: any ascending genealogy in KJV English that contains a Jared will generate 'the son of Jared'. That is the honest deflation, and it is why this is moderate rather than high.

links.note: 'And Kib was the son of Orihah, which was the son of Jared.' The genealogy's closing clause is the one place it abandons its own formula for Luke's, and the clause that results is a KJV singleton. Note also which names Ether's chain shares with Luke's: Seth at 1:10, Levi at 1:20, and Jared here — three of the antediluvian and Levitical names Luke 3 walks through. Individually each is unremarkable; the switch of syntax at the shared name is what makes the verse worth a row. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold for a quotation and not offered as one.
links.whyNot: Six words, of which five are function words, and the sixth is a proper name the Book of Mormon needs here for its own narrative reasons. A reader could call the agreement an accident of English word order in any 'son of' chain.
links.text: Which was the son of Mathusala, which was the son of Enoch, which was the son of Jared, which was the son of Maleleel, which was the son of Cainan,

pericopes.text: which Jared came forth with his brother and their families, with some others and their families, from the great tower, at the time the Lord confounded the language of the people, and swear in his wrath that they should be scattered upon all the face of the earth; and according to the word of the Lord the people were scattered.

provenance.other: “confound the language” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 11:9; “confound their language” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 11:7. Ether 1:33 has the definite form, 'the Lord confounded the language of the people', which is 11:9's construction with 'of all the earth' replaced by 'of the people'. Genesis 11:9's own scattering clause reads 'scatter them abroad upon the face of all the earth'; Ether does not follow it — see the exclusion register at this verse.
provenance.significance: This is the seam where the Book of Mormon opens onto Genesis and says so. Moroni has just declined to transcribe the record from Adam to the tower because it 'is had among the Jews' (1:3), which is a claim that the reader already owns the previous chapter of this story; the verse then supplies the join in the previous chapter's own words. Read for metalepsis (Hays 2016 on the figure) the borrowing carries more than the event: Genesis 11's tower is a monument built so that its builders should not be scattered, and the scattering is the judgment on it. Ether 1:33 takes the scattering as its starting condition and spends the rest of the chapter obtaining, for one family, an exemption from every clause of it — their language is not confounded (1:35-37), and their dispersion becomes a directed journey to an inheritance (1:38-43).

links.note: 'From the great tower, at the time the Lord confounded the language of the people, and swear in his wrath that they should be scattered upon all the face of the earth; and according to the word of the Lord the people were scattered.' Both halves of Genesis 11:9 are here in Genesis's order — the confounding of the language, then the scattering — and the first half uses the KJV's own collocation, which appears nowhere else in the Bible. The link is not in doubt; what the catalogue can add is where the wording stops following Genesis, which is at the scattering clause.
links.text: Therefore is the name of it called Babel; because the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth: and from thence did the LORD scatter them abroad upon the face of all the earth.

provenance.other: “sware in my wrath” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 95:11 and Hebrews 3:11, and Hebrews 3 is quoting the psalm. tools/mediation-check.py returns one decisive divergence: the psalm continues 'that they should not enter into my rest' and Hebrews turns it into direct speech, 'They shall not enter into my rest.' Ether 1:33 reads 'that they should be scattered', which is the psalm's subordinate 'that they should' and not Hebrews' 'they shall'. The 1830 text reads 'and swear in his wrath'; 1920 emended to 'swore', which moves away from the KJV's 'sware' rather than toward it, so the first edition is the closer witness here even though its verb is ungrammatical.
provenance.significance: Genesis 11 has no oath in it. The LORD deliberates ('Go to, let us go down') and acts, but he does not swear, and no biblical account of Babel says he did. Ether 1:33 supplies one, and supplies it in the words of the one oath in the Psalter that the New Testament made famous — the oath of Psalm 95 barring the wilderness generation from the land: 'Unto whom I sware in my wrath that they should not enter into my rest.' Recover that context and the chapter's shape appears. An oath of exclusion from rest is placed over the whole scattered earth, and the ten verses that follow are a sustained petition to be let out from under it, answered at 1:42-43 with a land 'choice above all the land of the earth' received 'for our inheritance'. The psalm's oath is what Jared's brother is crying against, and the promise of an inheritance is its reversal.

links.note: 'And swear in his wrath that they should be scattered upon all the face of the earth.' The oath is an addition to the Genesis narrative, not a report of it, and its wording is Psalm 95:11's. The construction is the psalm's throughout — the verb 'sware', the phrase 'in my/his wrath', and the subordinate result clause 'that they should' — with only the content of the clause changed, from exclusion from rest to dispersion over the earth. Since Psalm 95:11 is quoted twice in Hebrews (3:11, 4:3), the mediation is worth stating: the Book of Mormon has the Old Testament form.
links.text: Unto whom I sware in my wrath that they should not enter into my rest.

pericopes.text: And the brother of Jared, being a large and a mighty man, and being a man highly favored of the Lord; for Jared his brother said unto him, Cry unto the Lord, that he will not confound us that we may not understand our words.

provenance.other: “confound their language” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Genesis 11:7's purpose clause reads 'that they may not understand one another’s speech'; Ether 1:34 reads 'that we may not understand our words', which is the same clause with the persons turned round and 'speech' exchanged for 'words'.
provenance.significance: The petition is framed as a negation of the divine sentence clause by clause, in the sentence's own vocabulary: Genesis's 'confound' becomes 'not confound us', Genesis's 'that they may not understand' becomes 'that we may not understand'. Jared is not asking for a general mercy; he is asking that one clause of Genesis 11:7 be suspended for two men, and he asks it in the words of the verse. The narrative then grants it in the same words twice over — 'therefore he did not confound the language of Jared' (1:35), 'that they were not confounded' (1:37) — so that the whole intercession is conducted inside a single borrowed clause.

links.note: 'Cry unto the Lord, that he will not confound us that we may not understand our words.' The verb and its purpose clause are Genesis 11:7's and nothing else's in the KJV, taken over with the pronouns reversed. Note that the request is grammatically awkward in the Book of Mormon — 'that he will not confound us that we may not understand' asks God not to do the thing that would produce the result — which is what one gets by negating the head of a KJV sentence and leaving its subordinate clause standing. The awkwardness is itself evidence of the borrowing.
links.text: Go to, let us go down, and there confound their language, that they may not understand one another’s speech.

provenance.other: “highly favoured” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. As at 1 Nephi 1:1 and Mosiah 1:13, the 1830 text spells it 'favored' without the KJV's -our-, so the first edition does not preserve the King James orthography here.
provenance.significance: The corpus has used 'highly favored of the Lord' as a standing epithet since Nephi's first sentence, and it is normally collective — a favored people, a favored nation, revocable if they transgress (the Mosiah 1:13 row makes that case). Ether 1:34 is the one place it returns to Luke's own usage: it is said of a single man, once, at the moment before God speaks to him directly and grants him a request. Gabriel says it to Mary immediately before telling her what God will do through her; Moroni says it of the brother of Jared immediately before the Lord hears him, has compassion on him, and speaks. The formula lands back on the situation it was minted for.
provenance.alternative: The proximate model is arguably not Luke at all but the Book of Mormon's own formula, running from 1 Nephi 1:1 through Mosiah, Alma and here. The `mediation` enum has no value for a New Testament source reaching a verse through an earlier Book of Mormon passage — only `OT-via-earlier-BoM` exists — so this row is recorded as `direct-NT` following the Mosiah 1:13 precedent, and the real route is stated here: Luke 1:28 → KJV → 1 Nephi 1:1 → the corpus formula → Ether 1:34.

links.note: 'Being a man highly favored of the Lord.' The two-word phrase is a KJV singleton and its one occurrence is the angel's greeting. By Ether it is settled Book of Mormon idiom rather than a fresh borrowing, which is why this stays an echo — but it is worth a row rather than an exclusion because the usage here is singular and personal, unlike the collective uses that dominate the corpus, and because a new book is a new hand (ADJUDICATING §4 on repeats across a book boundary). What the KJV says once to one woman on the eve of an annunciation, Ether says of one man on the eve of a theophany.
links.whyNot: An adverb and a participle, and the corpus has used them scores of times without any of those uses being an allusion to Luke. A reader who filed this under the standing formula and pointed back to 1 Nephi 1:1 would be following the register's own practice elsewhere.
links.text: And the angel came in unto her, and said, Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the brother of Jared did cry unto the Lord, and the Lord had compassion upon Jared; therefore he did not confound the language of Jared; and Jared and his brother were not confounded.
Then Jared said unto his brother, Cry again unto the Lord, and it may be that he will turn away his anger from them which are our friends, that he confound not their language.
And it came to pass that the brother of Jared did cry unto the Lord, and the Lord had compassion upon their friends, and their families also, that they were not confounded.

And it came to pass that Jared spake again unto his brother, saying, Go and inquire of the Lord whether he will drive us out of the land; and if he will drive us out of the land, cry unto him whither we shall go. And who knoweth but the Lord will carry us forth into a land which is choice above all the earth. And if it so be, let us be faithful unto the Lord, that we may receive it for our inheritance.

provenance.other: “receive for an inheritance” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “not knowing whither” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — both Hebrews 11:8. The KJV has 'receive' near 'inheritance' in eight verses, but seven of them are the tribal allotments of Numbers and Joshua; the collocation with a call to depart is Hebrews'.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 11:8 has three moving parts — a call to go out, a destination not known, and a land to be received afterwards for an inheritance — and Ether 1:38 has all three in one sentence: 'cry unto him whither we shall go... let us be faithful unto the Lord, that we may receive it for our inheritance.' The interesting thing is what the borrowing changes. Abraham 'went out, not knowing whither he went'; Jared's instruction is to find out whither first. Hebrews makes ignorance the proof of faith; Ether 1 makes inquiry the practice of it, and the chapter is built out of four successive inquiries (1:34, 1:36, 1:38, 1:40). The verse keeps Hebrews' vocabulary of inheritance and faith and reverses its point about not knowing.
provenance.alternative: Hebrews 11:8-9 is already the model for a departure narrative at 1 Nephi 2:3 and for a Red Sea recital at 1 Nephi 4:2, so the proximate model here may be the corpus's own established use of Hebrews 11 rather than Hebrews 11 itself. The `mediation` enum has no value for an NT source reaching a verse via an earlier Book of Mormon passage; `direct-NT` is recorded and the alternative route is stated here.

links.note: 'Go and inquire of the Lord whether he will drive us out of the land... cry unto him whither we shall go... let us be faithful unto the Lord, that we may receive it for our inheritance.' Two KJV singletons stand behind that sentence and both are in the same verse of Hebrews. Note that this is the third time the Book of Mormon builds a migration on Hebrews 11 — 1 Nephi 2 on 11:8-9, 1 Nephi 4:2 on 11:29, and now the Jaredite departure — which is a recurrence worth more than any one of the three: Hebrews 11 is functioning in this corpus as an index to the Old Testament departures it wants to retell.
links.text: By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went.

provenance.route: Joel 2:13-14 and Jonah 3:9 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “who knoweth” occurs in exactly 12 KJV verses; eight are Job, Ecclesiastes or Proverbs asking whether anything can be known, and only Joel 2:14 uses it of God's possible relenting. Its twin is Jonah 3:9, 'Who can tell if God will turn and repent, and turn away from his fierce anger, that we perish not?' — not the same words but the same formula. “turn away his anger” as such stands in no KJV verse; the KJV's idiom is 'turn away his fierce anger' or 'turn away thy wrath'.
provenance.significance: Ether 1:36 and 1:38 reproduce the two halves of the biblical formula of hopeful uncertainty in the biblical order. Jared's first petition is that God 'will turn away his anger' from their friends; his second opens 'And who knoweth but the Lord will carry us forth into a land which is choice.' Joel 2:13-14 runs the same two clauses in the same sequence — God is 'slow to anger, and repenteth him of the evil', therefore 'Who knoweth if he will return and repent, and leave a blessing behind him' — and Jonah 3:9 fuses them into one sentence. The formula is the Old Testament's way of intercession that does not presume, and it is exactly the posture the chapter gives to Jared: four petitions, each phrased as a possibility rather than a claim.

links.note: 'And who knoweth but the Lord will carry us forth into a land which is choice above all the earth.' Taken alone this is two common words. What lifts it is the pairing with 1:36 two verses earlier — 'it may be that he will turn away his anger' — which puts the relenting-of-anger clause and the 'who knoweth' clause in the order Joel 2:13-14 has them and Jonah 3:9 compresses. The chapter's whole intercession is conducted in this register, and Joel and Jonah are where the KJV keeps it.
links.whyNot: No distinctive wording at all: 'who knoweth' is common, 'it may be that' is common, and neither of the two candidate sources shares a rare phrase with the verse. The case is entirely a sequence argument over two verses, and a reader who declined it would be right that nothing here would survive a verbal test.
links.text: Who knoweth if he will return and repent, and leave a blessing behind him; even a meat offering and a drink offering unto the LORD your God?

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the brother of Jared did cry unto the Lord according to that which had been spoken by the mouth of Jared.
And it came to pass that the Lord did hear the brother of Jared, and had compassion upon him, and said unto him,

Go to and gather together thy flocks, both male and female, of every kind; and also of the seed of the earth of every kind, and thy families; and also Jared thy brother and his family; and also thy friends and their families, and the friends of Jared and their families.

provenance.other: “Go to, let us” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Genesis 11:3, 11:4 and 11:7, the whole of the tower narrative and nothing else. As a bare interjection followed by a comma the idiom stands in only five KJV verses altogether: those three, plus Judah's proposition at Genesis 38:16 and the king of Syria's dispatch at 2 Kings 5:5. James's 'Go to now' (4:13, 5:1) is the other New Testament survival. 'Go to and gather together thy flocks' is the phrase's only occurrence in the Book of Mormon.
provenance.significance: Genesis 11's own irony is that the builders and their judge use the same words. 'Go to, let us make brick'; 'Go to, let us build us a city and a tower'; and then, from heaven, 'Go to, let us go down, and there confound their language.' The interjection is the tower story's signature and it belongs to both parties in it. Ether 1:41 gives it a fourth outing — the Lord, speaking to the one man at Babel whose language was not confounded, opening his commission with the builders' own phrase. Everything the builders resolved to do with it is now undone by it: they said 'Go to' to keep from being scattered, and the Lord says 'Go to' to send this family out. Whether the writer heard the echo or not, the KJV places that interjection in exactly one story, and this is a scene in that story.

links.note: 'Go to and gather together thy flocks, both male and female, of every kind.' The divine speech that begins the Jaredite migration opens with the interjection that opens each of the three resolutions in Genesis 11, and with no other KJV passage. The form differs — Ether has 'Go to' plus an imperative rather than 'Go to, let us', which is the construction of Genesis 38:16 and 2 Kings 5:5 — but the setting is Genesis 11's, eight verses after the chapter has quoted Genesis 11:9 outright. Note that the phrase never recurs anywhere else in the Book of Mormon; it appears once, in the one episode where the KJV's own use of it would be audible.
links.text: And they said one to another, Go to, let us make brick, and burn them thoroughly. And they had brick for stone, and slime had they for morter.

provenance.other: Genesis 6:19-21 is the KJV's one inventory for a vessel-borne survival: living creatures 'male and female' (6:19), 'after their kind' three times over (6:20), and food 'gather[ed] to thee' (6:21). Ether 1:41 has the same four elements in the same order — gather, flocks, 'both male and female', 'of every kind', and 'the seed of the earth of every kind'. The exact string “both male and female” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, but that verse is Numbers 5:3 and its sense is opposed; see the exclusion register.
provenance.significance: Ether 1 sits on the seam between Genesis 11 and Genesis 6-8 and takes from both. The chapter has just quoted the tower narrative; the commission that follows is the flood narrative's. Two chapters later the Jaredites will cross the sea in eight sealed, unsteerable, air-holed vessels driven by wind — an ark, told eight times over — and the loading order here is Noah's before the barges exist. The effect is to make one family's exit from Babel into a second flood deliverance: the world's languages are destroyed behind them, and they go out with their beasts by kind and their seed to begin again.

links.note: 'Gather together thy flocks, both male and female, of every kind; and also of the seed of the earth of every kind, and thy families.' No single phrase here is Genesis 6's, which is why this is moderate and why kjvSpecific is uncertain — 'male and female' and 'kind' are the wording of every English Bible at this passage. The argument is the inventory: creatures by sex, creatures by kind, seed for planting, and the household, in Genesis's own order and for the same purpose. Nothing else in the KJV lists those four things together as a command to load.
links.whyNot: The elements are what any migration would need, and a writer preparing a sea crossing might arrive at flocks, seed and families without a source. What keeps the row is the order and the fact that the chapter is demonstrably reading Genesis 11 four verses earlier.
links.text: And of every living thing of all flesh, two of every sort shalt thou bring into the ark, to keep them alive with thee; they shall be male and female.

pericopes.text: And when thou hast done this, thou shalt go at the head of them down into the valley, which is northward. And there will I meet thee, and I will go before thee into a land which is choice above all the land of the earth.

provenance.other: “the head of them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Micah 2:13, where it is the LORD who is at the head. “down into the valley” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 63:14 and Joel 3:2, neither of which is in play here.
provenance.significance: Micah 2:12-13 is the Old Testament's compressed exodus oracle: a flock gathered out of confinement, a breaker going up before them, a gate broken through, a king passing before them and the LORD at their head. Ether 1:41-42 has the same four moves in the same sequence — gather the flocks (1:41), a human leader 'at the head of them' going down into the valley, and the Lord saying 'I will go before thee' into the land. What has happened between the two texts is a swap: in Micah the king passes before the people and the LORD is at their head; in Ether the man is at the head of them and the Lord goes before. The roles are exchanged and the pair is kept intact, which is a more interesting relation than simple borrowing and is the reason for the row.

links.note: 'Thou shalt go at the head of them down into the valley, which is northward. And there will I meet thee, and I will go before thee into a land.' The phrase 'at the head of them' has one home in the KJV and it is the verse where the LORD leads a gathered flock out through a broken gate. Micah's oracle and Ether's commission share the flock, the leader at the head, the going-before, and the movement out of a place where the people had been penned — and Ether 1:41 supplies the gathering of the flock immediately before. Recorded as an echo rather than an allusion because four common words are all the verbal contact there is.
links.whyNot: 'The head of them' is a KJV singleton by arithmetic rather than by distinctiveness — it is an ordinary English phrase the KJV simply had little occasion to write — and it is doing different grammatical work in the two verses. A reader who called the resemblance a shared situation rather than a borrowing would have the better of the verbal argument.
links.text: The breaker is come up before them: they have broken up, and have passed through the gate, and are gone out by it: and their king shall pass before them, and the LORD on the head of them.

pericopes.text: And there will I bless thee and thy seed, and raise up unto me of thy seed, and of the seed of thy brother, and they which shall go with thee, a great nation. And there shall be none greater than the nation which I will raise up unto me of thy seed, upon all the face of the earth. And thus I will do unto thee because of this long time which ye have cried unto me.

provenance.other: “a great nation and I will bless thee” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “make of thee a great nation” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Genesis 12:2, Genesis 46:3 and Exodus 32:10 — of which only Genesis 12:2 attaches the blessing clause. Genesis 12:1-3 is quoted in the New Testament at Acts 7:3 and Galatians 3:8; tools/mediation-check.py against Acts 7:3 shows no contest, because Stephen's quotation stops at 'the land which I shall shew thee' and never reaches the great-nation promise that Ether 1:43 reproduces. The mediation is Old Testament by default rather than by a decided divergence, and it is recorded that way.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's largest claim and it is made entirely by placement. In the King James Bible, Genesis 11 and Genesis 12 are one continuous movement: the tower is confounded, the peoples are scattered, Terah's family leaves Ur, and the LORD says to Abram, get thee out, and I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee. Ether 1 occupies exactly that hinge. It quotes Genesis 11:9 at 1:33, spends nine verses obtaining an exemption from the scattering, and then closes at 1:43 with the promise of Genesis 12:2 given to a second man leaving the same city in the same generation. The Jaredite migration is not merely analogous to Abraham's call; it is narrated in its words, at its point in the story, as though Genesis 12 had two recipients. And the promise is enlarged in the telling — 'there shall be none greater than the nation which I will raise up unto me of thy seed' outbids Genesis 12:2, which promises greatness but not primacy.

links.note: 'And there will I bless thee and thy seed, and raise up unto me of thy seed... a great nation. And there shall be none greater than the nation which I will raise up unto me of thy seed.' The Abrahamic promise is here in Genesis's own terms and in Genesis's order — depart (1:42), a land to be shown (1:42), blessing, seed, a great nation (1:43) — and 1:38 has already supplied the inheritance from Hebrews 11:8. The 1830 reading 'and they which shall go with thee' preserves the KJV's relative 'which' for persons, which 1920 removed. Held at high rather than certain because the individual clauses are the common currency of the patriarchal promises (Genesis 17:7, 22:17, 26:3-4 all supply pieces of it) and no single string is long enough to fix Genesis 12:2 alone; the sequence and the narrative position are what do that.
links.text: And I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and thou shalt be a blessing:

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Jared, and his brother, and their families, and also the friends of Jared and his brother, and their families, went down into the valley which was northward, (and the name of the valley was Nimrod, being called after the mighty hunter,) with their flocks which they had gathered together, male and female, of every kind.

provenance.other: “the mighty hunter” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 10:9, where the epithet is given twice in the one sentence: 'He was a mighty hunter before the LORD: wherefore it is said, Even as Nimrod the mighty hunter before the LORD.' The Book of Mormon supplies the name and the epithet in the same breath — 'the name of the valley was Nimrod, being called after the mighty hunter' — and its parenthesis is a gloss on Genesis, not a fact about a valley.
provenance.significance: Two things the gloss does not say. First, the KJV's epithet is not 'mighty hunter' but 'mighty hunter BEFORE THE LORD', and the valley named for a man defined by his standing before the LORD is where, three verses later, the Lord comes down and stands in a cloud and talks with the brother of Jared. The Jaredites keep the appointment Nimrod's title advertises. Second, Genesis 10:10 makes Babel the beginning of Nimrod's kingdom, and the book this chapter opens is the book of a people leaving Babel: Ether 1 is built on Genesis 11:1-9 and the confounding of the language. So the departure from Babel is staged in the valley of the man who founded it. The etymological parenthesis is doing narrative work — it tells a reader who knows Genesis 10-11 that the Jaredites are not merely leaving a city but walking out of a genealogy.

links.note: The chapter's opening parenthesis is a footnote to Genesis 10. 'Mighty hunter' is a KJV singleton and is not an ordinary description of a man; it is Nimrod's formal title, and the Book of Mormon attaches it to the name Nimrod exactly as Genesis does. Dependence is not seriously deniable and the row is 'certain' on that ground, though the borrowing is three words and stands far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold — it is one of his passages in no sense. What makes it more than an etymology is placement: it is the first of a run of Genesis 6-11 contacts that carries the whole chapter, and the valley it names is where the theophany of 2:4-5 happens.
links.text: He was a mighty hunter before the LORD: wherefore it is said, Even as Nimrod the mighty hunter before the LORD.

pericopes.text: And they did also lay snares and catch fowls of the air; and they did also prepare a vessel, in the which they did carry with them the fish of the waters;

and they did also carry with them deseret, which, by interpretation, is a honey bee; and thus they did carry with them swarms of bees, and all manner of that which was upon the face of the land, seeds of every kind.

provenance.other: “to keep seed alive” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 7:3, and the fuller “seed alive upon the face” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one: 'Of fowls also of the air by sevens, the male and the female; to keep seed alive upon the face of all the earth.' “male and female” occurs in 7 KJV verses, of which Genesis 6:19 and 7:16 are the ark's; “of every sort” occurs in 5, of which Genesis 6:19, 6:20 and 7:14 are the ark's.
provenance.significance: Read the three verses 2:1-3 as one inventory and it is the ark's manifest, item for item and in Genesis's own order: flocks male and female of every kind (Genesis 6:19-20), fowls (7:3), food to be gathered and carried (6:21), and seed for the face of the land (7:3). What Genesis withholds it withholds here too — the Jaredites are not told they are re-enacting the flood, and the text never says so. But the deseret, the swarms of bees, the fish carried alive in a vessel of water are a solution to a problem only an ark has: how a whole biosphere crosses a great water. The chapter will make that explicit at 2:17 and 2:20, where the barges acquire the ark's door and the ark's window. Here the argument is still made only by the packing list.

links.note: The machine proposed nothing at 2:1 or 2:3 and Job 12:7 at 2:2 on 'fowls of the air', which occurs in 13 KJV verses and points nowhere. Read the three verses together, however, and the shared item is not a phrase but a schedule — breeding pairs of livestock, fowls, and seed for replanting a land — which in the KJV exists in exactly one place. The clinching detail is the last one: 'all manner of that which was upon the face of the land, seeds of every kind' against Genesis 7:3's 'to keep seed alive upon the face of all the earth', a KJV singleton that supplies both the seed and the face. The row is 'high' rather than 'certain' because no clause is reproduced; it is an argument about an inventory, and a reader could hold that any migrating people would pack this way. Against that: Genesis is the only text that describes packing this way, and the destination is across a sea in a sealed vessel.
links.text: Of fowls also of the air by sevens, the male and the female; to keep seed alive upon the face of all the earth.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that when they had come down into the valley of Nimrod, the Lord came down and talked with the brother of Jared; and he was in a clowd, and the brother of Jared saw him not.

provenance.route: Numbers 11:25 / Exodus 33:9 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “came down in a cloud” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Numbers 11:25. “talked with Moses” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 33:9, where the cloudy pillar descends and stands at the door of the tabernacle. Numbers 12:5 supplies the third element the Book of Mormon has and neither of the other two does — the Lord comes down in the cloud and STANDS: 'And the LORD came down in the pillar of the cloud, and stood in the door of the tabernacle.' Ether 2:5 has 'as he stood in a cloud'.
provenance.significance: The cloud in the KJV does two different jobs and the Book of Mormon takes both. In Exodus 13 it leads a nation; in Exodus 33-34 and Numbers 11-12 it is what a single man speaks to God through, and specifically it is the medium of a conversation the man is not permitted to see through — 'thou canst not see my face' (Exodus 33:20). Ether 2:4's clause 'and he was in a cloud, and the brother of Jared saw him not' states the Mosaic condition exactly, and states it in a chapter whose whole business is that the brother of Jared will, in the next chapter, see. The cloud is put in place at 2:4 so that Ether 3 can take it away.
provenance.alternative: Exodus 34:5's 'And the LORD descended in the cloud, and stood with him there' is also a KJV singleton for 'descended in the cloud' and holds the descent and the standing in one verse; it is offered here as composite rather than as the source because the Book of Mormon's verb is 'came down', which is Numbers 11:25's and 12:5's, not 'descended'.

links.note: Four words, but they are the four rarest available: 'came down in a cloud' is a KJV singleton and the Book of Mormon has the elements distributed across 2:4 and 2:5 — came down, in a cloud, talked with, stood. No one of the three candidate verses holds all four, which is why the row carries composites rather than claiming a single source; what is not in doubt is that the theophany is built out of the Sinai-and-tabernacle cloud and not out of anything else in the KJV. The machine's top candidate here was Judges 14:7, five words of Samson going down to talk with a woman at Timnath, which is filed in the exclusion register.
links.text: And the LORD came down in a cloud, and spake unto him, and took of the spirit that was upon him, and gave it unto the seventy elders: and it came to pass, that, when the spirit rested upon them, they prophesied, and did not cease.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the Lord commanded them that they should go forth into the wilderness, yea, into that quarter where there never had man been. And it came to pass that the Lord did go before them, and did talk with them as he stood in a cloud, and gave directions whither they should travel.—

provenance.other: Deuteronomy 1:33 reads: 'Who went in the way before you, to search you out a place to pitch your tents in, in fire by night, to shew you by what way ye should go, and in a cloud by day.' “went before them by day” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 13:21; “wherein they should go” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, Nehemiah 9:12 and 9:19, both retellings of it. Deuteronomy 1:33 is the only one of the three that holds the going-before, the showing of the way, the cloud AND the pitching of tents, and Ether has all four across 2:5 and 2:13.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 1:33 is Moses reminding a generation that the guidance they are about to refuse was itemised. Ether 2:5 gives the itemisation and then, at 2:14, the refusal: four years camped at Moriancumer without calling on the name of the Lord, and a three-hour chastening for it. The Jaredite journey is set up as the wilderness journey and then permitted to fail in the wilderness journey's characteristic way — not by rebellion but by forgetting the one who is going before. That the guidance is 'continual' at 2:6 ('being directed continually by the hand of the Lord') makes the four silent years at 2:13 the more pointed.

links.note: 'The Lord did go before them, and did talk with them as he stood in a cloud, and gave directions whither they should travel.' Every clause has a KJV counterpart in the wilderness-guidance formula, and 'gave directions whither they should travel' is the KJV's 'to shew you by what way ye should go' in other words. Two verses later the same source supplies 'they pitched their tents' at 2:13. The row is 'high' and not 'certain' because none of the three candidate verses is reproduced clause for clause; the Book of Mormon paraphrases a formula rather than quoting a verse. Note that Deuteronomy 1:33's guidance is 'in fire by night', which the Lord will explicitly withhold from the Jaredites at 2:23 — see the Exodus 13:21 row there.
links.text: Who went in the way before you, to search you out a place to pitch your tents in, in fire by night, to shew you by what way ye should go, and in a cloud by day.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they did travel in the wilderness, and did build barges, in the which they did cross many waters, being directed continually by the hand of the Lord.

And the Lord would not suffer that they should stop beyond the sea in the wilderness, but he would that they should come forth even unto the land of promise, which was choice above all other lands, which the Lord God had preserved for a righteous people;

provenance.other: “land of promise” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 11:9: 'By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise.' The Old Testament never uses the phrase; it says 'the land which the LORD sware unto thy fathers to give thee'. Every 'land of promise' in the Book of Mormon is therefore an English phrase available only from the New Testament.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 11:9's promised land comes with two qualifications the Book of Mormon keeps and one it inverts. Kept: the promise is held by sojourners who dwell in tents — and Ether 2:13 has the Jaredites dwelling in tents on the seashore for four years before they ever reach it. Inverted: in Hebrews the land is entered 'as in a strange country' and the patriarchs never possess it, whereas Ether 2:7-12 turns the land into a possession governed by a standing condition. The reader who recovers Hebrews 11 finds that the chapter's whole point is that the promise was NOT received (11:13, 11:39), which is a strange foundation for a decree about who shall possess a continent — and a very apt one for a book whose land of promise is twice depopulated.

links.note: A three-word phrase, but a KJV singleton, and a phrase the Book of Mormon uses as a technical term from 1 Nephi onward. The row is written here rather than passed over as an internal formula because Ether is a new book in a different hand — Moroni abridging a record that predates Lehi — and ADJUDICATING §4's ruling is that a phrase re-entering across a book boundary gets its link; the argument for the source was made at 1 Nephi 2:20 and is not restated. What is new here is the use: 1 Nephi applies the phrase to a journey, Ether 2:7-12 makes it the subject of a legal decree.
links.text: By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise:

pericopes.text: and he had sworn in his wrath unto the brother of Jared, that whoso should possess this land of promise, from that time henceforth and forever, should serve him, the true and only God, or they should be swept off when the fulness of his wrath should come upon them.

provenance.route: Psalm 95:11 → Hebrews 4:3 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “sworn in my wrath” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 4:3. The same oath appears twice more and both times in the other form: Psalm 95:11 'Unto whom I sware in my wrath', and Hebrews 3:11 'So I sware in my wrath'. “sworn in his wrath” occurs in 0 KJV verses — the third-person is the Book of Mormon's own adjustment to reported speech.
provenance.significance: The oath in Psalm 95 and in Hebrews 3-4 is an oath of EXCLUSION: God swears that a generation shall not enter his rest, and the whole argument of Hebrews 3-4 hangs on the threat's still being open. Ether 2:8 swears in the same words about entry to a land, and then does something the source does not: it makes the oath conditional and perpetual rather than retrospective, so that the sentence passed on the wilderness generation becomes a standing charter for every nation that possesses this land. Recover the context and the 'righteous people' for whom the land is preserved at 2:7 are standing where the carcases fell in the wilderness (Hebrews 3:17).
provenance.alternative: mediation-check.py run on this verse returns divergences pointing both ways: it scores 'should not' for Psalm 95:11. That point is an artifact and should not be read as evidence — Ether 2:8's 'should' belongs to 'whoso should possess' and 'should serve him', not to entering a rest, and the verse has no rest-clause at all. The one clause genuinely shared is the oath formula, and there the tool's other decisive point stands: the Book of Mormon has 'sworn', which in the KJV is Hebrews 4:3's word alone.

links.note: A four-word contact carrying a real mediation finding. The KJV renders one Hebrew oath three times, twice as 'sware' and once, at Hebrews 4:3, as 'sworn'; the Book of Mormon has 'sworn'. That is the whole of the argument and it is decisive in the way CONVENTIONS §7 asks for — a single word settling which English form was in front of the writer, as 'ruler' not 'prince' does at 1 Nephi 22:20. It also separates this row from the book's other uses of the oath: Alma 12:35 and Jacob 1:7 quote the rest-clause and cannot settle their own mediation, whereas Ether 2:8 quotes only the oath and settles it outright. Below Skousen's threshold and not one of his passages.
links.text: For we which have believed do enter into rest, as he said, As I have sworn in my wrath, if they shall enter into my rest: although the works were finished from the foundation of the world.

pericopes.text: And now we can behold the decrees of God concerning this land, that it is a land of promise, and whatsoever nation shall possess it, shall serve God, or they shall be swept off when the fulness of his wrath shall come upon them. And the fulness of his wrath cometh upon them when they are ripened in iniquity:

for behold, this is a land which is choice above all other lands; wherefore he that doth possess it shall serve God, or shall be swept off; for it is the everlasting decrees of God. And it is not until the fulness of iniquity among the children of the land, that they are swept off.

provenance.other: “iniquity of the Amorites” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 15:16: 'But in the fourth generation they shall come hither again: for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full.' “not yet full” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, Genesis 15:16 and John 7:8. The KJV has no phrase 'fulness of iniquity'; what it has is this single idea, that a people's iniquity has a measure and that dispossession waits on the measure being filled.
provenance.significance: Genesis 15:16 is the verse that reconciles the promise of Canaan with the four hundred years before it is kept: the land is not empty, and the sitting tenants are not yet guilty enough to lose it. Ether 2:9-10 takes that single explanatory clause and makes it the constitution of a hemisphere — 'it is not until the fulness of iniquity among the children of the land, that they are swept off' — and then, at 2:11, turns it on the reader: 'this cometh unto you, O ye Gentiles … that ye may not bring down the fulness of the wrath of God upon you, as the inhabitants of the land hath hitherto done.' The Gentiles are addressed in the position of the Amorites. That is the metalepsis: a verse written to justify a conquest is quoted to warn the conquerors.

links.note: No clause is reproduced; the contact is a doctrine and its distinctive measure-metaphor, which in the KJV belongs to one verse. The row is 'moderate' because 'fulness of iniquity' is not a KJV phrase and a reader could locate the idea instead in the harvest-of-wrath imagery of Joel 3:13 and Revelation 14 — which Ether 2:15 does in fact reach for, in the same speech, with 'fully ripe'. The two are not rivals so much as the two halves of one figure, and I have adjudicated each where its own wording sits. The 1830's plural 'the everlasting decrees of God', singular in 1920, is worth noting: the first edition treats this as a body of law rather than a single ruling, which is what a charter built out of Genesis 15:16 would be.
links.whyNot: The verbal contact is one word ('full'/'fulness') plus a shared metaphor, which is thin enough that a cautious editor would decline it. What holds the row up is context rather than volume: Ether 2:9-11 states, three times in three verses, the exact proposition Genesis 15:16 exists to state, and states it about a land whose inhabitants are to be dispossessed by incomers.
links.text: But in the fourth generation they shall come hither again: for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full.

pericopes.text: And this cometh unto you, O ye Gentiles, that ye may know the decrees of God, that ye may repent, and not continue in your iniquities until the fulness be come, that ye may not bring down the fulness of the wrath of God upon you, as the inhabitants of the land hath hitherto done.

Behold, this is a choice land, and whatsoever nation shall possess it, shall be free from bondage, and from captivity, and from all other nations under Heaven, if they will but serve the God of the land, which is Jesus Christ, which hath been manifested by the things which we have written.

And now I proceed with my record: for behold it came to pass that the Lord did bring Jared and his brethren forth even to that great sea which divideth the lands. And as they came to the sea, they pitched their tents; and they called the name of the place Moriancumer; and they dwelt in tents; and dwelt in tents upon the seashore for the space of four years.

And it came to pass at the end of the four years, that the Lord came again unto the brother of Jared, and stood in a cloud and talked with him. And for the space of three hours did the Lord talk with the brother of Jared, and chastened him because he remembered not to call upon the name of the Lord.

And the brother of Jared repented him of the evil which he had done, and did call upon the name of the Lord for his brethren which were with him. And the Lord said unto him, I will forgive thee and thy brethern of their sins; but thou shalt not sin any more, for ye shall remember that my spirit will not always strive with man; wherefore if ye will sin until ye are fully ripe, ye shall be cut off from the presence of the Lord. And this is my thoughts upon the land which I shall give you for your inheritance; for it shall be a land choice above all other lands.

provenance.other: “strive with man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 6:3: 'And the LORD said, My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh: yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years.' The Book of Mormon has 'my spirit will not always strive with man' — seven words in the KJV's order with 'shall' modernised to 'will'. The 1830 reads lower-case 'my spirit', as the KJV does; 1920 capitalised it to 'my Spirit', which quietly converts a KJV clause into a doctrinal term.
provenance.significance: This is where the chapter's Genesis substructure becomes impossible to miss, because the Lord answers a repentance with the sentence that introduces the Flood. Genesis 6:3 is the verdict; Genesis 6:14-16 is the ark; Genesis 7:16 is the door shut. Ether 2:15 is the verdict, 2:17 is the sealed vessel, 2:17 again is the door shut — in Genesis's order, one verse after another. And the verdict is repurposed: in Genesis the striving ends and the world is drowned, whereas here the same sentence is spoken to the man who is about to be preserved through water, as a condition on his continuing. The brother of Jared is told, in the words that condemned Noah's generation, that he is not yet of that generation.

links.note: Seven words verbatim from a KJV singleton, and the only serious question is whether it is a fresh borrowing or the Book of Mormon reusing its own formula — the clause has already appeared at 1 Nephi 7:14, 2 Nephi 26:11 and Mormon 5:16. ADJUDICATING §4's ruling that a phrase re-entering in a different hand gets its link would be enough on its own, but there is a stronger reason to write it here: at the other three occurrences the clause is cited as a general principle about the withdrawal of the Spirit, and here alone it stands in its own Genesis setting, four verses ahead of an ark. This is the one place in the Book of Mormon where Genesis 6:3 is quoted with Genesis 6-8 around it. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his passages.
links.text: And the LORD said, My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh: yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years.

provenance.route: Jeremiah 26:19 / 2 Samuel 24:16 → KJV → Book of Mormon (1830 only)
provenance.other: “repented him of the evil” occurs in exactly 3 KJV verses — 2 Samuel 24:16, 1 Chronicles 21:15 and Jeremiah 26:19 — and the subject is God in all three. Jeremiah 26:19 is the closest, adding the relative clause the Book of Mormon also has: 'the LORD repented him of the evil which he had pronounced against them' against Ether 2:15's 'repented him of the evil which he had done', a run of six words. The 1830 reads 'repented him of the evil'; 1920 deleted the reflexive pronoun and the modern text reads 'repented of the evil', which is not a KJV construction at all.
provenance.significance: The KJV reserves this reflexive idiom for God relenting of a punishment he had determined — the angel over Jerusalem, the sentence on Micah's Jerusalem — and never uses it of a man repenting of his own sin. Ether 2:15 puts a man in the construction, and does it in the sentence immediately before the Lord says 'I will forgive thee'. Whether that is a solecism or a deliberate reversal cannot be settled from the text; what can be settled is that the KJV's grammar of divine relenting has been transferred to human repentance, and that the transfer is legible only in the first edition.

links.note: A six-word run in a construction the KJV uses three times, all of God. This is a CONVENTIONS §8 row before it is anything else: the borrowing exists in the 1830 and has been edited out of the text most readers have, so the modern 'repented of the evil which he had done' shows no contact with Jeremiah 26:19 at all while the running text of this catalogue shows six words of it. Confidence is 'moderate' rather than higher because the idiom could have been picked up from the KJV's general register rather than from any one of the three verses, and because the sense is genuinely different — God relenting of a judgment is not a man being sorry for a sin.
links.whyNot: If 'repented him' was simply archaic English available to the writer independently of any verse, then the run proves only the register and not a source, and the row should be read as evidence of KJV idiom rather than of Jeremiah 26. Note also that the machine ranked this the chapter's strongest candidate (rarity 2.37) partly because 'which he had' is filler; strip it and the distinctive contact is four words.
links.text: Did Hezekiah king of Judah and all Judah put him at all to death? did he not fear the LORD, and besought the LORD, and the LORD repented him of the evil which he had pronounced against them? Thus might we procure great evil against our souls.

provenance.other: “fully ripe” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 14:18: 'Thrust in thy sharp sickle, and gather the clusters of the vine of the earth; for her grapes are fully ripe.' Joel 3:13, which Revelation is rewriting, has 'put ye in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe' — 'ripe', not 'fully ripe'. The Book of Mormon has the intensified form.
provenance.significance: The vintage of Revelation 14:18-20 ends in a winepress trodden outside the city until blood comes out to the horses' bridles; it is the KJV's most violent image of a judgment that waits on ripeness. Ether 2:15 applies it to a single man's continuing in sin. That compression — an apocalyptic harvest of the nations used as a warning to one repentant person — is what the figure does here, and it ties the private rebuke at Moriancumer back to the public decree of 2:9-10, where the same ripeness governs whether a nation is swept off. The Lord's answer to the brother of Jared restates the land's charter in the second person.

links.note: Two words, but a KJV singleton and the exact point where Revelation intensifies its Old Testament source: 'ripe' is Joel's, 'fully ripe' is John's. The Book of Mormon takes John's form and applies it to a person rather than to the vine of the earth, and it does so in a chapter that has already twice used ripeness as the trigger for dispossession (2:9, 2:10). Confidence is 'moderate' because a two-word contact cannot carry more on its own, and because the metaphor of ripened iniquity is common enough in the Book of Mormon's own idiom that this could be its formula rather than a fresh borrowing — the reason for writing the row anyway is that the formula's distinctive word is available from exactly one KJV verse.
links.text: And another angel came out from the altar, which had power over fire; and cried with a loud cry to him that had the sharp sickle, saying, Thrust in thy sharp sickle, and gather the clusters of the vine of the earth; for her grapes are fully ripe.

pericopes.text: And the Lord said, Go to work and build, after the manner of barges which ye have hitherto built. And it came to pass that the brother of Jared did go to work, and also his brethren, and built barges after the manner which they had built, according to the instructions of the Lord. And they were small, and they were light upon the water, even like unto the lightness of a fowl upon the water;

and they were built after a manner that they were exceeding tight, even that they would hold water like unto a dish; and the bottom thereof was tight like unto a dish; and the sides thereof was tight like unto a dish; and the ends thereof were peaked; and the top thereof was tight like unto a dish; and the length thereof was the length of a tree; and the door thereof, when it was shut, was tight like unto a dish.

provenance.other: “shut him in” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 7:16: 'And they that went in, went in male and female of all flesh, as God had commanded him: and the LORD shut him in.' “pitch it within and without” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 6:14, which is the ark's watertightness and the KJV's only instruction to seal a vessel. “the door of the ark” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 6:16. The Book of Mormon's own “the door thereof” occurs in 0 KJV verses, but 'the side thereof' at Genesis 6:16 and the enumerated 'the top thereof, and the sides thereof' of the tabernacle furniture at Exodus 30:3 are the register it is written in.
provenance.significance: Genesis gives the ark three specifications and Ether 2:17-20 works through all three, changing each. Genesis 6:14 pitches it within and without; Ether makes it 'exceeding tight … that they would hold water like unto a dish', which is the same requirement stated as a test rather than a material. Genesis 6:16 sets the door in the side; Ether puts the door in the enumeration with the top, the bottom and the ends, because a vessel that will be submerged has no side that is not a bottom. And Genesis 7:16 has the LORD shut Noah in from outside — the ark's most theologically loaded sentence, since it means Noah could not have opened it — whereas Ether 2:17's door is shut by the Jaredites and 2:20's air-hole is unstopped by them at need. The Jaredites are sealed in a vessel they can open. That difference is the pivot of the whole episode: they are not passengers but petitioners, which is why the next question they ask gets answered by being handed back.

links.note: No clause is reproduced and the row rests on a construction sequence rather than on wording: seal the vessel, specify the door, shut the door. What makes it more than a general resemblance is that the KJV describes the sealing of a vessel exactly once and the shutting of its door exactly once, both in Genesis 6-7, and that Ether 2:15 has just quoted Genesis 6:3 verbatim two verses earlier. The 1830 is materially better evidence than the modern text here and at 2:20: it enumerates 'the bottom thereof … the sides thereof … the ends thereof … the top thereof … the length thereof … the door thereof', and at 2:20 'a hole in the top thereof, and also in the bottom thereof … unstop the hole thereof … stop the hole thereof', four of which 1920 deleted outright. The KJV's construction idiom — Genesis 6:16's 'the side thereof', Exodus 30:2-3's 'the length thereof … the top thereof, and the sides thereof … the horns thereof' — is thickest in the first edition and has been thinned in the one readers use.
links.text: And they that went in, went in male and female of all flesh, as God had commanded him: and the LORD shut him in.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the brother of Jared cried unto the Lord, saying: O Lord, I have performed the work which thou hast commanded me, and I have made the barges according as thou hast directed me.

provenance.other: “I have performed” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, 1 Samuel 15:13 and Romans 15:28; only the first is a report of obedience made in the Lord's name, and it shares five consecutive words with Ether 2:18 ('Lord, I have performed the'). The composite Deuteronomy 26:13 is the KJV's other avowal-of-compliance formula — 'I have done according to all that thou hast commanded me' — and supplies the Book of Mormon's second clause, 'the work which thou hast commanded me'.
provenance.significance: 1 Samuel 15:13 is the KJV's most famous false report. Saul greets Samuel with 'I have performed the commandment of the LORD' and is answered with 'What meaneth then this bleating of the sheep in mine ears?'; the chapter ends with the kingdom torn from him. Ether 2:18's report is true, and is answered not with an accusation but with the discovery that the obedience was not sufficient — the barges are built exactly as commanded and they are dark and airless. Read against Saul, the interest of the verse is that doing what you were told turns out not to be the end of the matter, which is precisely the lesson Ether 3 will draw out when the Lord refuses to solve the light problem himself.
provenance.alternative: The formula may be the KJV's general idiom of compliance rather than 1 Samuel 15:13 specifically; Deuteronomy 26:13's tithe avowal is the same speech-act without the irony, and is recorded as composite for that reason.

links.note: A five-word run on a two-verse KJV rarity, and the machine's top candidate for the verse. What keeps it at 'moderate' is that 'I have performed the work which thou hast commanded me' is exactly the sentence anyone writing in KJV English would produce for this situation, and the shared context is only the speech-act. What argues for it is that the KJV supplies the speech-act once and once only in these words, and that the Book of Mormon is elsewhere alert to the Saul narrative.
links.whyNot: The senses of the two reports are opposed — Saul is lying and the brother of Jared is not — and this catalogue's own exclusion register is full of entries declining links on exactly that ground. The row is written rather than excluded because the opposition is between the reports' truth-values and not between their meanings: both are a servant telling God the assignment is complete, which is the rarest thing about either verse.
links.text: And Samuel came to Saul: and Saul said unto him, Blessed be thou of the LORD: I have performed the commandment of the LORD.

pericopes.text: And behold, O Lord, in them there is no light, whither shall we steer.— And also we shall perish, for in them we cannot breathe, save it is the air which is in them; therefore we shall perish.

And the Lord said unto the brother of Jared, Behold, thou shalt make a hole in the top thereof, and also in the bottom thereof; and when thou shalt suffer for air, thou shalt unstop the hole thereof, and receive air. And if it so be that the water come in upon thee, behold, ye shall stop the hole thereof, that ye may not perish in the flood.
And it came to pass that the brother of Jared did so, according as the Lord had commanded.

And he cried again unto the Lord, saying, O Lord, behold I have done even as thou hast commanded me; and I have prepared the vessels for my people, and behold, there is no light in them. Behold, O Lord, wilt thou suffer that we shall cross this great water in darkness?

provenance.other: “no light in them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 8:20: 'To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.' The Book of Mormon reproduces six words, 'there is no light in them', and has the same clause in a different order at 2:19 ('in them there is no light'). The clause has already been transcribed at 2 Nephi 18:20 as part of the Isaiah block, so its English was in the record before Moroni abridged Ether.
provenance.significance: Isaiah's darkness is the darkness of consulting the dead instead of the law; the sentence is a judgment on necromancers, and the light that is absent is doctrinal. Ether 2:22 uses the identical clause for the plain fact that sixteen sealed wooden hulls have no windows. That is metalepsis running the other way from the usual: the source's figurative meaning is drained off and its literal one restored. The gain is not in Ether 2 but in Ether 3, where the literal problem is solved by the Lord touching sixteen stones and the man who asked for light sees the finger of God — so the chapter that borrows Isaiah's phrase for want of daylight ends with the most direct revelation in the book. The recovered context supplies the frame: 'to the law and to the testimony' is Isaiah's instruction to consult God rather than the dead, and consulting God directly is exactly what the brother of Jared does.

links.note: Six consecutive words on a KJV singleton, which by the standard of the 1 Nephi 1:14 row is enough to catalogue as a quotation on volume alone; it is kept at 'allusion' because the clause is a natural English sentence for the situation and the writer need not have felt he was citing Isaiah. Rarity settles the source regardless — the KJV says 'no light in them' once. The link is adjudicated here rather than at 2:19, where the same words appear in the inverted order, because 2:22 has the KJV's own word order; 2:19 is cross-referenced in the exclusion register.
links.text: To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.

pericopes.text: And the Lord said unto the brother of Jared, What will ye that I should do that ye may have light in your vessels? For behold, ye cannot have windows, for they will be dashed in pieces; neither shall ye take fire with you, for ye shall not go by the light of fire:

provenance.other: “a window shalt thou make” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 6:16: 'A window shalt thou make to the ark, and in a cubit shalt thou finish it above; and the door of the ark shalt thou set in the side thereof.' The Book of Mormon does not quote it. It denies it: 'ye cannot have windows, for they will be dashed in pieces.' Genesis 8:6 is the window's only other appearance, when Noah opens it to release the raven.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's sharpest gesture and it is made by subtraction. The KJV's one instruction about a window is an instruction to build one, and the ark's window is what makes the end of the Flood narrative possible — Noah opens it, sends out the raven and the dove, and learns that the waters are abated. Take the window away and you take away the ark's only instrument of knowledge; a vessel that cannot be looked out of cannot be navigated, which is why the brother of Jared's first question at 2:19 is 'whither shall we steer'. The Jaredites get Noah's ark with its window removed and its door still shut, and everything that follows — the stones, the touch of the finger, the vision of the premortal Christ — is the compensation for a hole in the roof that Genesis granted and Ether refuses. The refusal is also the tell: it is only worth denying a window to a reader who expects one.

links.note: A negation is harder to catalogue than a borrowing, and the row is written on the grounds that the thing denied is a KJV singleton and that the vessel denying it is otherwise built to Genesis 6's specification (see the Genesis 7:16 row at 2:17). 'Windows' on its own occurs in 26 KJV verses and points nowhere; what points is that this vessel, at this moment, in a chapter that has just quoted Genesis 6:3 verbatim, is told it cannot have the one thing Genesis 6:16 tells an ark-builder to make. Confidence is 'high' rather than 'certain' because the argument is inferential throughout: no words are shared, and a reader who does not grant that the barges are being written against the ark will not grant the row either.
links.text: A window shalt thou make to the ark, and in a cubit shalt thou finish it above; and the door of the ark shalt thou set in the side thereof; with lower, second, and third stories shalt thou make it.

provenance.other: “to give them light” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, Exodus 13:21 and Nehemiah 9:12, and in both the light is given by a pillar of fire so that a travelling people may go by night. Exodus 13:21: 'by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light; to go by day and night.' Nehemiah 9:12: 'in the night by a pillar of fire, to give them light in the way wherein they should go.' The Book of Mormon's clause is 'neither shall ye take fire with you, for ye shall not go by the light of fire' — the same three terms, fire, light, going, in the same relation, negated.
provenance.significance: The Jaredite journey has been built on the wilderness guidance since 2:5, where the Lord goes before them and stands in a cloud. Exodus 13:21-22 gives that guidance two forms, a cloud by day and a fire by night, and Ether has taken the first and is here explicitly refused the second. What is withheld is not merely a lamp but the Exodus's own night-time mode of travel: Israel could 'go by day and night' because it had a fire to go by, and the Jaredites are told they will not. The stones of Ether 3 are then a third thing, neither cloud nor fire — light without burning, which is what a sealed vessel requires and what neither Genesis nor Exodus supplies.
provenance.alternative: The practical reason for the prohibition is obvious — an open flame in a sealed hull — and the verse gives it no scriptural framing. The row claims that the wording is Exodus's, not that the text says so.

links.note: Three shared terms and no shared clause, so this is an argument from the arrangement rather than from volume: the KJV has a formula in which fire gives light so that a people may go, it uses it twice, and Ether 2:23 negates all three of its terms in order. It is kept at 'moderate' for that reason — 'light of fire' occurs in 0 KJV verses, so there is nothing here to count. What raises it above coincidence is the company it keeps: this is the second negated ark-or-exodus provision in one verse, alongside the window of Genesis 6:16, and both are refusals of a precedent the chapter has otherwise been following closely.
links.text: And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of a cloud, to lead them the way; and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light; to go by day and night:

provenance.other: “that I should do unto thee” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 10:51: 'And Jesus answered and said unto him, What wilt thou that I should do unto thee? The blind man said unto him, Lord, that I might receive my sight.' The Book of Mormon's 'What will ye that I should do' takes 'I should do' from Mark and the plural 'will ye' from the same pericope's other half, Mark 10:36 and Matthew 20:32; Matthew's form of the Bartimaeus question is 'What will ye that I shall do unto you' (20:32).
provenance.significance: This is the finding the chapter is worth reading for. The KJV asks 'What wilt thou that I should do unto thee?' twice, and on both occasions the answer is about sight: to Bartimaeus, who says 'that I might receive my sight', and — in the Matthean plural of 20:32-33 — to the two blind men, who say 'that our eyes may be opened'. Ether 2:23 puts that question to a man in the dark, and the Lord's own completion of it is 'that ye may have light in your vessels'. The question the Gospels reserve for the blind is asked here about a hold with no windows, and it is asked, at 2:25, a second time, with the same result Mark's asking has: the petitioner must name what he wants before he can be given it. Recover the context and the theological point of Mark 10:51 comes with it — Jesus does not presume on the need, he requires it to be spoken — which is exactly the pedagogy of Ether 3:2-5, where the brother of Jared must propose the sixteen stones himself.
provenance.alternative: The interrogative is a natural English construction and the Book of Mormon uses it elsewhere (Alma 18:14, 3 Nephi 28:4). What makes this occurrence more than the formula recurring, in the sense of ADJUDICATING §4's Mosiah 29:2 ruling, is the object: alone among the Book of Mormon's uses, this one is answered with sight.

links.note: Five words of a KJV singleton, and the strongest kind of coincidence a catalogue can hope for — a rare interrogative whose two Gospel occurrences both concern the giving of sight, imported into the one Book of Mormon episode about the absence of light. That the Book of Mormon's phrasing fuses Mark's 'I should do' with the plural of Matthew 20:32 is itself evidence of the pericope rather than of a single verse, which is why both are recorded as composite. The row is 'high' and not 'certain' because 'what will ye that I should do' is short and idiomatic enough to have been composed without a source; the rarity count is what argues otherwise. Below Skousen's threshold and not one of his passages.
links.text: And Jesus answered and said unto him, What wilt thou that I should do unto thee? The blind man said unto him, Lord, that I might receive my sight.

pericopes.text: for behold, ye shall be as a whale in the midst of the sea; for the mountain waves shall dash upon you. Nevertheless, I will bring you up again out of the depths of the sea: for the winds have gone forth out of my mouth, and also the rains and the floods have I sent forth.

provenance.other: “as a whale in the” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 32:2: 'thou art like a young lion of the nations, and thou art as a whale in the seas: and thou camest forth with thy rivers, and troubledst the waters with thy feet.' The KJV's only other whales are Genesis 1:21 and Job 7:12, neither of which is a simile. Ether 2:24 reads 'ye shall be as a whale in the midst of the sea'.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one whale-simile is an insult. It is addressed to Pharaoh king of Egypt in a lamentation, and the point of it is that the monster thrashing in the waters will be hauled out in a net and left on the open field for the birds (Ezekiel 32:3-4). Ether 2:24 gives the same simile to the Jaredites as a promise — you will be as a whale, and I will bring you up again out of the depths — so that the figure of a doomed sea-beast becomes the figure of a vessel that submerges and surfaces. The unstated correspondence is drowning: Pharaoh is the KJV's drowned king, the Red Sea is his grave, and the Book of Mormon has already run its Exodus through that drowning at 1 Nephi 4:2. Here the Pharaoh-image is turned inside out and given to the people crossing.

links.note: Four words on a KJV singleton, in a verse where the machine's rarity stream was right for once (Ezekiel 32:2 scored 2.00 and led the verse). The link is secure on rarity; what it does not do is import Ezekiel's argument, and a reader may reasonably hold that 'as a whale in the midst of the sea' is simply the available English for a large thing in deep water. Against that, the KJV offers no other English for it: the noun occurs three times in the Bible and only here in a comparison.
links.text: Son of man, take up a lamentation for Pharaoh king of Egypt, and say unto him, Thou art like a young lion of the nations, and thou art as a whale in the seas: and thou camest forth with thy rivers, and troubledst the waters with thy feet, and fouledst their rivers.

provenance.other: “from the depths of the sea” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 68:22: 'The Lord said, I will bring again from Bashan, I will bring my people again from the depths of the sea.' “bring me up again” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 71:20: 'shalt bring me up again from the depths of the earth.' Ether 2:24's 'I will bring you up again out of the depths of the sea' is the two singletons fused — Psalm 68:22's sea and its first-person divine promise, Psalm 71:20's 'up again'. “depths of the sea” alone occurs in 3 KJV verses (Psalm 68:22, Isaiah 51:10, Micah 7:19).
provenance.significance: Psalm 68:22 is the KJV's one sentence in which the Lord promises, in his own voice, to fetch his people back out of the depths of the sea; the psalm is a march-of-God psalm whose Lord 'went before' his people through the wilderness (68:7), which is what Ether 2:5 has him doing.
