Daniel 12:4 has “seal the book, even to the time of the end” and 12:9 “the words are closed up and sealed till the time of the end”. “the interpretation thereof”, the other half of Ether 4:5, occurs in exactly 16 KJV verses, of which 11 are Daniel and 3 are the Joseph cycle of Genesis 40-41 — it is the King James Bible's phrase for the reading of a sealed or hidden text.
provenance.significance: Ether 4:5 does something no biblical sealing does: it seals the interpretation with the record, and seals up the interpreters as physical objects. Daniel and Revelation both seal words; the interpreter in Daniel is a person, and in Revelation there is no interpreter at all, only a Lamb worthy to open. Recover the context and the difference is the point — the Book of Mormon's sealed book is unreadable not because its meaning is withheld but because its reading instrument is locked away with it, which is the condition Ether 4:6-7 makes contingent on repentance rather than on a heavenly opening.

links.note: “He commanded me that I should seal them up; and he also hath commanded that I should seal up the interpretation thereof; wherefore I have sealed up the interpreters.” Two KJV vocabularies meet in one sentence: the sealing-until-the-end of Daniel 12:4 and 12:9, and the Danielic “interpretation thereof”. Neither supplies a clause, which is why this is an allusion at moderate confidence rather than anything stronger — but the combination of the two, in a verse about a book withheld for a set time, is not likely to be accidental in a chapter that goes on to name the book of Revelation outright at 4:16. Isaiah 29:11's sealed book is the source the Book of Mormon itself has already worked at length (2 Nephi 27), and it is carried here as a composite rather than as the head because Isaiah's man cannot read the book for being unlearned, where Ether 4:5-6 is about a seal with a release condition, which is Daniel's shape.

pericopes.text: For the Lord saith unto me, They shall not go forth unto the Gentiles until the day that they shall repent of their iniquity, and become clean before the Lord;

and in that day that they shall exercise faith in me, saith the Lord, even as the brother of Jared did, that they may become sanctified in me, then will I manifest unto them the things which the brother of Jared saw, even to the unfolding unto them all my revelations, saith Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the Father of the heavens and of the earth, and all things that in them is.

links.text: For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is, and rested the seventh day: wherefore the LORD blessed the sabbath day, and hallowed it.

provenance.route: Exodus 20:11 → KJV Decalogue → Mosiah 13:19 → Book of Mormon creation formula → Ether 4:7
provenance.other: “all that in them is” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 20:11 and Acts 4:24, and Acts 4:24 is itself reciting the fourth commandment. tools/mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence between them: the two verses read identically at every point Ether 4:7 reproduces, so this verse cannot settle its own mediation on internal evidence. What settles it is the corpus — Mosiah 13:19 quotes Exodus 20:11 whole and in Decalogue context (“for in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, and the sea, and all that in them is”), and every later occurrence is a creation formula descending from it.
provenance.significance: The 1830 reading is the evidence. Exodus 20:11's “all that in them is” takes a singular verb because its subject is “all”. The Book of Mormon pluralises the subject to “all things” and keeps the singular verb anyway — “all things that in them is” — at 2 Nephi 2:14, 3 Nephi 9:15, Alma 11:39, Mormon 9:11 and here. A verb that has stopped agreeing with its own subject is a fossil of the clause it was lifted from. The 1920 edition corrected Ether 4:7 to “are”, which is better English and moves the text away from its source; CONVENTIONS §8's point exactly, and running in the opposite direction from the 1 Nephi 1:20 case.

links.note: “Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the Father of the heavens and of the earth, and all things that in them is.” The divine title is built from two KJV phrases: Genesis 2:4's “the heavens and of the earth” (a seven-word run, and the machine's top candidate here) and the Decalogue's merism for the created order. The Decalogue half is the load-bearing one, because it comes with a grammatical fingerprint. Neither the reading nor the borrowing is visible in a modern edition, where the verb agrees; in 1830 the clause is Exodus 20:11's with one word inserted into it. Mediation is recorded as OT-via-earlier-BoM rather than direct-OT because the formula is by this point the Book of Mormon's own standing title for the creator, first set down as an actual Exodus quotation at Mosiah 13:19.

pericopes.text: And he that will contend against the word of the Lord, let him be accursed; and he that shall deny these things, let him be accursed: for unto them will I shew no greater things, saith Jesus Christ, for I am he which speaketh;

links.text: But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.

provenance.other: “let him be accursed” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Galatians 1:8 and 1:9, and they are the same sentence said twice — “As we said before, so say I now again”. Ether 4:8 also says it twice, once for contending against the word and once for denying these things.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the borrowed formula brings its subject with it. Galatians 1:8-9 curses anyone who preaches “any other gospel”; it is the New Testament's one anathema against tampering with a received message, and it is doubled for emphasis. Ether 4:8 doubles it in the same way, and ten verses later the chapter tells its reader to “believe in my Gospel” (4:18). Set beside Revelation 22:18-19, the other canon-guarding curse and the closing words of the book Ether 4:16 names by its author, the chapter turns out to be framed at both ends by the two places in the King James Bible where a text curses those who will not have it: Paul's at the seal, John's at the unsealing.

links.note: “He that will contend against the word of the Lord, let him be accursed; and he that shall deny these things, let him be accursed.” The formula is Paul's and only Paul's — the KJV has it in two verses, both in Galatians 1, and reserves “Anathema” for the other such curse at 1 Corinthians 16:22. The doubling is Paul's too. What is transferred with it is a whole rhetorical situation: an apostle defending a message against those who would set it aside, in the opening paragraph of the letter, before any argument has been made. Moroni is doing exactly that here, at the point where he seals a record and forbids its rejection. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his quotations; the case rests on the rarity of a four-word formula and on the closeness of the situations, not on length.

pericopes.text: and at my command the heavens are opened and are shut; and at my word, the earth shall shake; and at my command, the inhabitants thereof shall pass away, even so as by fire;

links.text: The LORD also shall roar out of Zion, and utter his voice from Jerusalem; and the heavens and the earth shall shake: but the LORD will be the hope of his people, and the strength of the children of Israel.

provenance.other: “the earth shall shake” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Ezekiel 38:20 and Joel 3:16. Only Joel's has the divine voice as the cause — “the LORD also shall roar out of Zion, and utter his voice from Jerusalem; and the heavens and the earth shall shake” — which is the construction Ether 4:9 uses, “and at my word, the earth shall shake”.
provenance.alternative: Hebrews 12:26-29 does the same work in the New Testament and does it in the same order as Ether 4:9: a voice that shakes the earth (12:26), the removing of what is shaken (12:27), and “our God is a consuming fire” (12:29) — against Ether's shaking, passing away, and “even so as by fire”. Hebrews reaches it by quoting Haggai 2:6 rather than Joel, so no single verse can be named as the source, and the head of this link is given to the phrase that actually matches.
provenance.significance: Three verses of the Lord's speech in this chapter (4:8-10) are a demonstration of authority interposed between the curse and the promise, and each clause of 4:9 has a scriptural warrant behind it — opened and shut heavens, a shaken earth, an ending by fire. The point of assembling them here is jurisdictional: the speaker who sealed the record at 4:5 is establishing that the seal is not a librarian's.

links.note: “At my command the heavens are opened and are shut; and at my word, the earth shall shake; and at my command, the inhabitants thereof shall pass away, even so as by fire.” No clause here is a quotation and the case is cumulative rather than verbal. The one phrase rare enough to point anywhere is “the earth shall shake”, in two KJV verses, and the one of those that construes the shaking as the effect of a divine utterance is Joel 3:16 — which is the construction Ether 4:9 repeats twice over with “at my word” and “at my command”. Recorded at moderate under CONVENTIONS §0a as worth putting on the table; a reader who prefers the Hebrews 12:26-29 sequence, which matches the whole verse's order but no single verse's words, is given it in the provenance.

pericopes.text: and he that believeth not my words, believeth not my disciples; and if it so be that I do not speak, judge ye: for ye shall know that it is I that speaketh, at the last day.

But he that believeth these things which I have spoken, him will I visit with the manifestations of my spirit; and he shall know and bear record. For because of my spirit, he shall know that these things are true: for it persuadeth men to do good;

links.text: But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal.

provenance.other: “the manifestation of the Spirit” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 12:7. The Book of Mormon's plural, “the manifestations of my spirit”, occurs in exactly 0 KJV verses; the singular collocation is Paul's alone.
provenance.significance: Read forward and this is the first term of a set. Ether 4:11 promises the manifestation of the Spirit to whoever believes the record; 4:18 promises “signs shall follow them that believe in my name”; and Moroni, the same editor, closes the book by working straight through 1 Corinthians 12's list of gifts at Moroni 10:8-17, where the gifts “are given by the manifestations of the spirit of God” — the same pluralised form of the Pauline singleton that Ether 4:11 uses. The chapter that seals a book and the chapter that hands the reader a test of it are using the same Pauline vocabulary for what a believer is given, seven chapters apart.

links.note: “Him will I visit with the manifestations of my spirit; and he shall know and bear record.” The collocation is a KJV singleton and belongs to the opening of Paul's discussion of spiritual gifts, where “the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal” — given to every man, which is the universality Ether 4:11 also insists on (“he that believeth these things which I have spoken”). Two words carry the link and the syntax is not Paul's, so this is an allusion at moderate rather than anything higher. What raises it above coincidence is that the same verse pairs the manifestation with bearing record, and that seven verses later the chapter quotes Mark 16:17 on signs following believers: Ether 4 is describing a gifts-economy in the New Testament's terms.

pericopes.text: and whatsoever thing persuadeth men to do good, is of me: for good cometh of none, save it be of me. I am the same that leadeth men to all good: he that will not believe my words, will not believe me, that I am; and he that will not believe me, will not believe the Father which sent me. For behold, I am the Father, I am the light, and the life, and the truth of the world.

links.text: Jesus cried and said, He that believeth on me, believeth not on me, but on him that sent me.

provenance.other: “the Father which sent me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 12:49 — five verses after John 12:44, in the same speech. The KJV's usual form is the bare “him that sent me”, which occurs in exactly 17 verses; John 12:49 is the only place the Father is named inside the phrase.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon reads John 12:44 in the negative. John: “He that believeth on me, believeth not on me, but on him that sent me.” Ether: “He that will not believe my words, will not believe me … and he that will not believe me, will not believe the Father which sent me.” Turning a saying about belief into a saying about refusal is what the whole chapter is doing — 4:8 curses the denier, 4:10 answers the man who says the Lord does not speak, 4:15 names the veil of unbelief — and John 12 is the right place to get it from, because John 12:37-40 is itself the Gospel's set-piece on those who “believed not on him” and had their eyes blinded and their heart hardened.

links.note: Two rare things at once. The clause “the Father which sent me” is a King James singleton belonging to John 12:49, and the sentence it sits in is John 12:44's chain of belief run backwards through refusal. Ether 4:12 keeps John's structure — believing (or not believing) the messenger is believing (or not believing) the sender — and keeps the Johannine habit of a three-term chain, adding “my disciples” at 4:10 as the first link, which is John 13:20's move. Note that the 1830 reads “the Father which sent me”, matching John 12:49's relative pronoun exactly; the 1920 modernised it to “who”, erasing the fingerprint.

links.text: Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.

provenance.route: John 14:6 with John 8:12 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 14:6. “the light of the world” occurs in exactly three, Matthew 5:14 and John 8:12 and 9:5, of which the two Johannine ones are self-predications in the mouth of Jesus. “the truth of the world” occurs in exactly 0 KJV verses — the genitive is the Book of Mormon's own addition.
provenance.significance: The chapter's editor is fusing two of John's “I am” sayings into one triad and then attaching a single genitive to all three of them. In John, “of the world” belongs only to the light; here it governs light, life and truth together, so that Christ is not the truth to whom the world may come but the truth of the world itself. That is a stronger claim than either Johannine verse makes, and it is made by a grammatical move rather than by an argument.

links.note: “For behold, I am the Father, I am the light, and the life, and the truth of the world.” Three of the four terms of John 14:6's “I am” saying are here — the truth and the life, with the way replaced by the light of John 8:12 — in a self-predication formula that is otherwise the Fourth Gospel's alone. The replacement is not arbitrary: John 1:4 has already put light and life in apposition (“in him was life; and the life was the light of men”), so the Book of Mormon's triad is assembled out of John's own stock. What is not John's is the closing genitive, which occurs in no KJV verse and which quietly universalises all three predicates at once.

pericopes.text: Come unto me, O ye Gentiles, and I will shew unto you the greater things, the knowledge which is hid up because of unbelief.

Come unto me, O ye house of Israel, and it shall be made manifest unto you how great things the Father hath laid up for you, from the foundation of the world; and it hath not come unto you, because of unbelief.

links.text: Then shall the King say unto them on his right hand, Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world:

provenance.other: “from the foundation of the world” occurs in exactly six KJV verses. What narrows Ether 4:14 to Matthew 25:34 is the dative of advantage attached to it: “the kingdom prepared for you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and Ether 4:14 has “the Father hath laid up for you, from the foundation of the world”. No other KJV occurrence of the phrase says that something was set aside *for* an addressee.
provenance.significance: The verse is addressed to “O ye house of Israel”, and it is Matthew 25:34 that supplies its grammar — the sentence in which the King welcomes the blessed of his Father into what was prepared for them before the world began. Ether 4:14 says the same thing has been laid up for Israel and withheld, “and it hath not come unto you, because of unbelief”. The chapter then closes at 4:19 by quoting the rest of Matthew 25:34 as the promise for whoever is found faithful, so the sheep-and-goats verse frames the second half of this chapter: withheld at 4:14, granted at 4:19.

links.note: “It shall be made manifest unto you how great things the Father hath laid up for you, from the foundation of the world.” The prepositional phrase is common enough in the KJV to prove nothing on its own; the combination with a beneficiary and with the Father as the one who did the laying up is Matthew 25:34's and nothing else's. Moderate rather than high because the verbal overlap is a formula plus a syntactic pattern rather than a clause — the strong version of this link is at 4:19, which reproduces six consecutive words of the same verse, and this row is best read with that one.

pericopes.text: Behold, when ye shall rend that veil of unbelief which doth cause you to remain in your awful state of wickedness, and hardness of heart, and blindness of mind, then shall the great and marvellous things which have been hid up from the foundation of the world from you; yea, when ye shall call upon the Father in my name, with a broken heart and a contrite spirit, then shall ye know that the Father hath remembered the covenant which he made unto your fathers, O house of Israel;

links.text: Afterward he appeared unto the eleven as they sat at meat, and upbraided them with their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they believed not them which had seen him after he was risen.

provenance.other: “unbelief and hardness of heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 16:14, and so does “hardness of heart” on its own — the other KJV instances are “hardness of your hearts” (Matthew 19:8) and “hardness of your heart” (Mark 10:5), which the possessive keeps distinct. Ether 4:15 has both terms in Mark's order inside one clause: “that veil of unbelief which doth cause you to remain in your awful state of wickedness, and hardness of heart, and blindness of mind”.
provenance.significance: This is the finding of the chapter, because it is not one verse but a route. Ether 4 works down the last paragraph of Mark in order: Mark 16:14's unbelief and hardness of heart at Ether 4:15, Mark 16:16 quoted almost whole at Ether 4:18, Mark 16:17's signs following believers in the same verse. Recover Mark 16:14's context and the reason for the choice appears — the risen Christ upbraids the eleven for not believing the witnesses who had seen him, which is precisely the offence Ether 4:10 defines (“he that believeth not my words, believeth not my disciples”) and precisely the situation Moroni is writing into, a record whose readers must believe witnesses they cannot check. Mark's longer ending, the passage whose own canonicity has been argued over since Eusebius, is the scaffolding of the Book of Mormon's charter for believing a sealed book.

links.note: Two of the three terms in Ether 4:15's diagnosis are a King James singleton, and they belong to the resurrection appearance in which unbelief of a testimony is rebuked. The third term, blindness of mind, is not Mark's — it comes from 2 Corinthians 3:14, catalogued separately at this verse — so 4:15 fuses the two New Testament passages about a mind that cannot see what it is being shown. The order matters more than the wording: this is the first of three contacts with Mark 16:14-17 inside four verses, and the last of them (4:18) is a seventeen-word reproduction. A link that would be arguable in isolation is not arguable once the sequence is in view.

links.text: But their minds were blinded: for until this day remaineth the same vail untaken away in the reading of the old testament; which vail is done away in Christ.

provenance.other: “the vail is upon their heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 3:15. “veil of unbelief” and “blindness of mind” each occur in exactly 0 KJV verses; both are the Book of Mormon's coinages, and each is one KJV term away from 2 Corinthians 3:14, whose two halves are “their minds were blinded” and “the same vail untaken away”. The KJV spells Paul's word *vail* throughout 2 Corinthians 3 and spells the temple curtain *veil* at Matthew 27:51; the 1830 reads *veil*, which is the spelling of the verse that supplies the verb.
provenance.significance: Paul's veil has a removal condition — “when it shall turn to the Lord, the vail shall be taken away” (3:16) — and it lies over Israel reading its own covenant. Ether 4:15 keeps the condition, keeps the addressee (“O house of Israel”), and changes the verb: Paul's veil is *taken away* by God, and this one the house of Israel must *rend*. That verb is Matthew 27:51's, where the temple veil is rent from the top downward at the crucifixion. The Book of Mormon has taken Paul's image of covenant blindness and made the reader do to it what the death of Christ did to the temple curtain — and then, in the same sentence, promises that “the Father hath remembered the covenant which he made unto your fathers”, which is what a rent veil in Paul is for.

links.note: “When ye shall rend that veil of unbelief … and blindness of mind, then shall the great and marvellous things which have been hid up from the foundation of the world … then shall ye know that the Father hath remembered the covenant.” Four elements of 2 Corinthians 3:13-16 arrive together: a veil, minds blinded, Israel as the one who cannot see, and a stated condition on which the veil comes off. None of them is a quotation, which is why the evidence scores put vocabulary above syntax, but the cluster is not available anywhere else in the King James Bible, and Romans 11:25's blindness happening to Israel “until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in” is the same argument in the same apostle's hand — which matters here because Ether 4:13-14 has just addressed the Gentiles first and Israel second. The verb “rend” is imported from the passion narrative and does the theological work Paul's passive would not.

links.text: The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.

provenance.route: Psalm 34:18 → KJV → 3 Nephi 9:20 → Book of Mormon formula → Ether 4:15
provenance.other: “broken heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 34:18, which also supplies “contrite spirit” — a phrase occurring in exactly two verses, Psalm 34:18 and Isaiah 66:2. Psalm 51:17, the verse usually named for this idea, crosses the terms the other way: “a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart”. The Book of Mormon consistently follows Psalm 34:18's assignment, heart broken and spirit contrite, never Psalm 51:17's.
provenance.significance: The distribution is the argument. Psalm 34:18 is the only KJV verse that pairs a broken heart with a contrite spirit in that order, and every Book of Mormon occurrence of the phrase — 2 Nephi 2:7, 3 Nephi 9:20, 3 Nephi 12:19, Moroni 6:2, and here — reproduces the pairing exactly. A text drawing loosely on a familiar biblical idea would be expected to drift into Psalm 51:17's more famous crossing at least once in five tries. It never does.

links.note: “When ye shall call upon the Father in my name, with a broken heart and a contrite spirit.” The phrase is by Ether 4 an established Book of Mormon formula, set down in the risen Lord's own mouth at 3 Nephi 9:20 (“ye shall offer for a sacrifice unto me a broken heart and a contrite spirit”) and repeated in the Nephite Beatitudes at 12:19, which is why mediation is recorded as OT-via-earlier-BoM rather than direct-OT: the proximate model is the corpus's own, and Ether 4:15 is the Lord quoting himself to a later editor. Behind the formula stands one KJV verse and not the obvious one — the pairing is Psalm 34:18's, not Psalm 51:17's, and the Book of Mormon never once confuses them.

links.text: That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, saying, I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things which have been kept secret from the foundation of the world.

provenance.other: “kept secret from the foundation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 13:35. Of the six KJV verses carrying “from the foundation of the world”, it is the only one in which what dates from the foundation is something concealed — the others concern a prepared kingdom (Matthew 25:34), shed blood (Luke 11:50), finished works (Hebrews 4:3) and a book of life (Revelation 13:8, 17:8).
provenance.significance: The chapter uses the formula three times and takes a different KJV verse each time: hidden things at 4:15 (Matthew 13:35), things laid up for an addressee at 4:14 and a prepared kingdom at 4:19 (Matthew 25:34). Matthew 13:35's own context is Jesus explaining why he teaches in parables — a deliberate withholding from those outside, quoting Psalm 78:2 — which is the doctrine Ether 4 is built on: 4:13 has the knowledge “hid up because of unbelief”, and 4:7 releases it only to those who exercise faith. The parable theory of Matthew 13 is being applied to a physical book.

links.note: “The great and marvellous things which have been hid up from the foundation of the world.” The formula is too common in the KJV to identify a source by itself, but only one of its six occurrences concerns concealed things, and that verse's concealment is the same kind Ether 4 is describing — teaching withheld from those who will not receive it. An echo rather than an allusion because the shared wording is a stock phrase and the distinctive word differs (Matthew's “kept secret”, the Book of Mormon's “hid up”); the case is that the chapter selects the right verse from a set of six on three separate occasions. Note that 1830 reads *marvellous*, the KJV spelling, which the 1920 edition modernised.

pericopes.text: and then shall my revelations which I have caused to be written by my servant John, be unfolded in the eyes of all the people. Remember, when ye see these things, ye shall know that the time is at hand that they shall be made manifest in very deed;

links.text: The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass; and he sent and signified it by his angel unto his servant John:

provenance.other: “his servant John” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 1:1 — “he sent and signified it by his angel unto his servant John”. The Book of Mormon's “my servant John” makes the possessive first-person because the speaker is the one whose Revelation it is, which is the correction Revelation 1:1's own opening clause invites: “The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him”.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's one uncontestable citation, and it is a citation of a title page. Ether 4:16 does not allude to Revelation; it names the book, its author, its commissioning, and its future publication — “my revelations which I have caused to be written by my servant John, be unfolded in the eyes of all the people”. Set that beside the sealing at 4:5 and the chapter's shape becomes Revelation's: a book written, sealed, and opened at a time the writer does not choose. 1 Nephi 14:27 has already named him — “the name of the Apostle of the Lamb was John, according to the word of the angel” — so the corpus has been pointing at this verse since its fourteenth chapter.

links.note: The whole of the link is in three words that occur together in one King James verse, and they are three words the chapter uses to identify a text rather than to borrow from it. Revelation 1:1's chain of transmission — God to Jesus Christ to an angel to his servant John — is compressed into a single first-person clause in which the second link speaks and the fourth is named. What follows in Ether 4:16 is the promise the sealed record and the Apocalypse share: that the withheld writing will be “unfolded in the eyes of all the people”. Certain, and cited rather than echoed; the interest of the row is in what the naming licenses the rest of the chapter to do.

links.text: And he saith unto me, Seal not the sayings of the prophecy of this book: for the time is at hand.

provenance.other: “the time is at hand” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 1:3 and Revelation 22:10, which is to say it occurs at the opening and the closing of the same book — the book Ether 4:16 has just named in its own first half.
provenance.significance: The metalepsis is sharp enough to be worth stating flatly. Revelation 22:10 reads “Seal not the sayings of the prophecy of this book: for the time is at hand” — the clause Ether 4:16 borrows is, in its source, the reason a book must *not* be sealed. Ether 4:5 seals a book; Ether 4:16 announces that the seal comes off, and gives as its warrant the exact five words with which the angel forbade John to seal. Recover the context and the chapter has arranged itself as the inverse of Revelation's ending: John is told the time is at hand, so do not seal; Moroni seals, and tells his reader that when he sees these things he will know the time is at hand. Daniel 12:4, carried as a composite, is the third term — Daniel is told to seal *until* the time of the end, which is the position the Book of Mormon occupies between the two.

links.note: Within a single verse the chapter names the book of Revelation and then quotes the clause from its last chapter that governs whether such a book may be sealed. That the same five words also close Revelation 1:3 makes the phrase the Apocalypse's own signature rather than a stray idiom, and the second half of Ether 4:16 (“when ye see these things, ye shall know that the time is at hand”) puts it in a knowledge-clause, exactly as Revelation 1:3 puts it in a blessing-clause and 22:10 in a command-clause. The Book of Mormon's sealed record is being positioned inside a canon-closing text's own vocabulary about sealing.

links.text: So likewise ye, when ye see these things come to pass, know ye that the kingdom of God is nigh at hand.

provenance.other: “when ye see these things” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 21:31 — “So likewise ye, when ye see these things come to pass, know ye that the kingdom of God is nigh at hand.” Its Markan parallel reads “when ye shall see these things come to pass” (Mark 13:29), so the Book of Mormon's clause without “shall” follows Luke's wording and not Mark's.
provenance.significance: Ether 4:16 fuses the two ends of the New Testament: an apocalyptic discourse's rule for reading the signs, and the Apocalypse's own clause about the time being at hand. Luke 21:31 supplies the structure — see these things, therefore know — and Revelation 22:10 supplies what is to be known. What Ether 4:16 substitutes for “the kingdom of God is nigh” is the publication of the sealed record, so the sign whose appearance signals the end is, in this chapter, the unsealing of this book.

links.note: “Remember, when ye see these things, ye shall know that the time is at hand.” A five-word King James singleton in the same clause-shape as its source: a temporal clause of seeing, then a main clause of knowing that something is at hand. Ether 4:16 has already used Revelation's words for the second half, so the sentence is a splice, and the seam is visible — Luke's “nigh at hand” about the kingdom becomes Revelation's “at hand” about the time. Moderate rather than high because the shared string, though rare, is ordinary English and the composition is the Book of Mormon's; the argument is that this verse reaches for two different eschatological formulas in one sentence and gets both of them from the King James Bible.

pericopes.text: therefore, when ye shall receive this record, ye may know that the work of the Father has commenced upon all the face of the land.

Therefore, repent all ye ends of the earth, and come unto me, and believe in my Gospel, and be baptized in my name: for he that believeth, and is baptized, shall be saved; but he that believeth not, shall be damned: and signs shall follow them that believe in my name.

links.text: He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved; but he that believeth not shall be damned.

provenance.other: “shall be damned” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 16:16. The reproduced run is seventeen words — “he that believeth, and is baptized, shall be saved; but he that believeth not, shall be damned” — against a KJV verse of nineteen, the only differences being an added comma-bound “and” and nothing else.
provenance.significance: The verse Ether 4:18 reproduces whole is the one that stands three verses after the unbelief-and-hardness-of-heart of 4:15 and immediately before the signs of 4:17 in Mark's own numbering. It is also the verse in the KJV New Testament with the most contested textual standing: Mark 16:9-20 is absent from the two oldest Greek codices and was known to be doubtful long before 1830, so a nineteenth-century printed English Bible is the only text from which this sentence could have been received as the plain word of the risen Christ. The Book of Mormon's charter for baptism, given in the Lord's voice, is a quotation of the longer ending of Mark.

links.note: A seventeen-word reproduction of a nineteen-word verse, in the Lord's own mouth, and above the threshold Skousen uses to define a quotation — though this passage is not one of his identified set and nothing here should be read as claiming it is. Mormon 9:23 quotes the same verse and 3 Nephi 11:33-34 gives its content in other words, so Ether 4:18 is the corpus's third pass at it; what distinguishes this one is that it comes attached to Mark 16:17 in the same sentence and to Mark 16:14 three verses earlier, which is a reading of Mark's ending as a unit rather than three separate borrowings.

links.text: And these signs shall follow them that believe; In my name shall they cast out devils; they shall speak with new tongues;

provenance.other: “signs shall follow them that believe” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 16:17. The Book of Mormon adds four words to it — “signs shall follow them that believe in my name” — which are Mark's next four words read across his semicolon: “them that believe; In my name shall they cast out devils”.
provenance.significance: The addition is the finding. Mark 16:17 puts the signs after a full stop's worth of punctuation and makes “in my name” the instrument of the exorcisms that follow; Ether 4:18 pulls the phrase back across the clause boundary and attaches it to the believing instead, so that what is qualified is the faith rather than the miracle. Mormon 9:24, by the same editor's father, keeps Mark's own division. Two members of the same editorial family quote one verse and divide it differently.

links.note: Six consecutive words of a King James singleton, in the same sentence as the seventeen-word reproduction of Mark 16:16, which is why this is catalogued as a quotation despite its length. The interest is in the join: Ether 4:18 reads Mark's semicolon away and produces “them that believe in my name”, a phrase that exists in the KJV only as two clauses meeting. It is the sort of thing that happens when a text is being recalled as a running sentence rather than copied from a page, and it is evidence about how this chapter's biblical material was carried.

pericopes.text: And blessed is he that is found faithful unto my name, at the last day: for they shall be lifted up to dwell in the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world. And behold, it is I that hath spoken it. Amen.

links.text: Then shall the King say unto them on his right hand, Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world:

provenance.other: “the kingdom prepared for you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:34. Ether 4:19 changes only the pronoun — “the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world” — and in 1830 the pronoun is plural throughout the verse (“they shall be lifted up … prepared for them”), which the 1920 edition changed to “he … him” to agree with the singular “he that is found faithful”.
provenance.significance: The book of Ether ends its editor's charter on the sheep-and-goats verse, and takes both halves of it: the kingdom prepared, and the preparation dated from the foundation of the world. Read with 4:14, which said the same thing was “laid up for you” and had not come because of unbelief, the chapter turns Matthew 25:34 into its own frame — the identical promise withheld from the unbelieving at 4:14 and granted to the faithful at 4:19. And the verb by which the faithful arrive is “lifted up”, the verb that at 4:1 named the crucifixion; the last sentence of the chapter closes the ambiguity John 12:32 opened in its first.

links.note: “They shall be lifted up to dwell in the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world.” Six consecutive words of a King James singleton, altered at one pronoun, in the closing sentence of Moroni's editorial charge. The choice of source is not neutral: Matthew 25:34 is the sentence of acceptance in the last judgment scene, spoken by the King to those on his right hand, and Ether 4:19 gives it to whoever “is found faithful unto my name, at the last day”. The 1830 plural is worth recording — the first edition lets the promise be corporate where the modern text makes it individual, and the 1920 correction is a grammatical tidy that costs the verse its congregation.

pericopes.text: And now I, Moroni, have written the words which was commanded me, according to my memory; and I have told you the things which I have sealed up; therefore touch them not, in order that ye may translate: for that thing is forbidden you, except by and by it shall be wisdom in God.
And behold, ye may be privileged that ye may shew the plates unto those who shall assist to bring forth this work;
and unto three shall they be shewn by the power of God; wherefore, they shall know of a surety that these things are true.

links.text: And when Peter was come to himself, he said, Now I know of a surety, that the LORD hath sent his angel, and hath delivered me out of the hand of Herod, and from all the expectation of the people of the Jews.

provenance.other: “know of a surety” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 15:13 and Acts 12:11. Genesis 15:13 is an imperative spoken to Abram inside a vision; Acts 12:11 is a man's recognition, after the fact, that a divine manifestation he had taken for a vision was real. Ether 5:3 has neither grammatical frame — it is third-person future, ‘they shall know of a surety that these things are true’ — so the rarity count identifies the idiom and the sense decides between the two verses, which is the reverse of how the catalogue's earlier rows on this phrase were argued.
provenance.alternative: The proximate model may not be Acts at all. The idiom has become the Book of Mormon's own by this point — it appears in ten verses of the 1830 text, including the two the catalogue has already adjudicated at 1 Nephi 5:8 and Mosiah 7:14 — so a reader may reasonably hold that Moroni took it from the book he was abridging rather than from the epistle behind it. The `mediation` enum has no value for a New Testament source reaching a verse through an earlier Book of Mormon passage (`OT-via-earlier-BoM` covers only the Old Testament case), so this row is filed `direct-NT` and the route is stated here instead of being encoded. It is flagged for the schema, not adjudicated around.
provenance.significance: Recover Acts 12 and the borrowing acquires the exact epistemological problem the Three Witnesses have. Two verses earlier, Peter walking out of the prison ‘wist not that it was true which was done by the angel; but thought he saw a vision’ (12:9); at 12:11 he comes to himself and knows of a surety. That is the whole difficulty of a testimony given by men who were shown plates by an angel and afterwards had to say whether what they saw was an object or a vision — and the KJV idiom the verse reaches for is the one attached to precisely that transition. Whether the reach was deliberate or not, Acts 12:11 is the Bible's only sentence in which ‘of a surety’ names the moment a suspected vision is ruled real.

links.note: The plates ‘shall be shewn by the power of God’ to three, ‘wherefore, they shall know of a surety that these things are true’. The idiom belongs to two KJV verses and to no others, which is strong evidence on its own; what makes it more than a count is that Acts 12:11 is about the ratification of a doubted sighting and Genesis 15:13 is not. This is a weaker row than the catalogue's other two on the same phrase — 1 Nephi 5:8 and Mosiah 7:14 both reproduce Acts's first-person frame (‘Now I know of a surety that’) and Ether 5:3 does not, having only the bare idiom. Filed here rather than folded into those because Ether is a different book in a different hand (ADJUDICATING §4) and because the context is the one place in the corpus where Acts 12's own problem is also the verse's problem. Four words, far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his thirty-six.

pericopes.text: And in the mouth of three witnesses shall these things be established; and the testimony of three, and this work, in the which shall be shewn forth the power of God, and also his word, of which the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Ghost beareth record; and all this shall stand as a testimony against the world, at the last day.

links.text: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sinneth: at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 19:15 via 2 Corinthians 13:1 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “mouth of three witnesses” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 19:15, and Ether 5:4 reproduces six of its words unbroken — ‘the mouth of three witnesses shall’. One word inside that run is not Deuteronomy's. Deuteronomy reads AT the mouth; the Book of Mormon reads IN the mouth, which is the preposition of the two New Testament citations of the law: “mouth of two or three witnesses” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 18:16 and 2 Corinthians 13:1. Between those two the auxiliary decides. 2 Corinthians has ‘shall every word be established’, Matthew ‘every word may be established’; Ether 5:4 has ‘shall these things be established’, with the auxiliary before the subject as in 2 Corinthians and no ‘may’. (`mediation-check.py` returns 2 Corinthians here too, but its decisive point is an artifact worth naming: it matches 2 Corinthians' ‘every word’ against the ‘and also his word’ further down the Book of Mormon verse, not against ‘these things’. The preposition and the auxiliary are the real evidence.)
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 19:15 is not a devotional verse; it is a rule of court, and its neighbours are the law of the avenger of blood and ‘life shall go for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth’ (19:21). Recover that context and Moroni's sentence stops being a description of a spiritual experience and becomes the constitution of a legal record — which is what its own last clause says it is: ‘all this shall stand as a testimony against the world, at the last day.’ The Three Witnesses are not character references for a book; they are the statutory minimum for a prosecution, and the defendant is named. The New Testament preposition matters for the same reason rather than in spite of it: Matthew 18:16 and 2 Corinthians 13:1 are the two places where the Deuteronomic rule is applied outside a court, to the discipline of a community, and Moroni takes the law in the form the church already had it rather than in the form Moses gave it.

links.note: Six unbroken words of the KJV's one verse containing ‘mouth of three witnesses’, and the single word inside that run which is not Deuteronomy's is the New Testament's preposition. This is the cleanest mediation case in Ether and it turns, as these cases do, on one word: `at` would have made it direct-OT, `in` makes it OT-via-NT, and the auxiliary order then picks 2 Corinthians over Matthew. The object of the establishing is the Book of Mormon's own — ‘these things’, meaning the plates, where the law has ‘the matter’ and the epistles have ‘every word’. Nephi had already made the same fusion twice, at 2 Nephi 11:3 (‘by the words of three, God hath said, I will establish my word’) and 2 Nephi 27:14; what is new here is the length of the run, which is long enough that the choice of preposition can be measured rather than inferred, and the fact that the number three is no longer a legal minimum but a literal count of men. Dependence is not seriously deniable, hence `certain`, though at six words the passage sits well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his thirty-six.
links.whyNot: The one soft point is the dropped ‘two or’. Moroni has three witnesses and no more, so the omission is required by his sense and need not be a reach back past the epistles to Deuteronomy's own ‘three witnesses’. If it is adaptation rather than borrowing, the row reduces to a straightforward use of 2 Corinthians 13:1 and Deuteronomy drops to background — which would not change the mediation call, only the direction of it.

links.text: For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one.

provenance.route: 1 John 5:7 (the Comma Johanneum) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “bear record” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, and only 1 John 5:7 has three named divine subjects doing it: ‘there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one.’ Ether 5:4 has the same three with ‘the Son’ for ‘the Word’ — the substitution the catalogue already recorded at 3 Nephi 11:27, and the one the Comma's own trinitarian reading invites. The 1830 verb is worth the ink: ‘the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Ghost BEARETH record’, a singular under three subjects, which the 1920 edition changed to ‘bear’ — that is, back toward 1 John 5:7's own form. CONVENTIONS §8's second case, and the direction of the correction is the point.
provenance.significance: This is the strongest kjvSpecific claim available anywhere in the corpus, because the source is itself a KJV-tradition reading: the heavenly witnesses of 1 John 5:7 are absent from every Greek manuscript before the fourteenth century, from the critical editions, and from the modern English versions, which read only ‘there are three that bear witness’. A text dependent on this sentence is dependent not on the KJV's English but on the KJV's canon. And the fit here is tighter than at 3 Nephi 11:27, where only the ‘are one’ clause was in play. 1 John 5:7-9 is a passage about witnesses counted in threes — three that bear record in heaven, three that bear witness in earth (5:8), and then ‘if we receive the witness of men, the witness of God is greater’ (5:9). Ether 5:4 is that argument executed: three men on earth see the plates (5:3), and their testimony is under-written by three bearing record in heaven. The chapter does not quote 5:9, but 5:9 is what the chapter is for.

links.note: ‘And the testimony of three, and this work, in the which shall be shewn forth the power of God, and also his word, of which the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Ghost beareth record.’ The three divine subjects bearing record are the Comma Johanneum's, and the Comma is the KJV's alone. What lifts this above a formula — the Book of Mormon uses ‘bear record’ in twenty-six verses — is the count. Moroni does not say that God bears record; he says that three bear record, in a sentence whose first clause has just required three witnesses, and 1 John 5:7-8 is the one biblical passage that pairs a heavenly three with an earthly three for exactly that purpose. The 1830 singular ‘beareth’ is not the KJV's grammar and 1920 restored the KJV's, which is the first edition showing the seam and the later one closing it.

links.text: Take this book of the law, and put it in the side of the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God, that it may be there for a witness against thee.

provenance.other: “for a witness against” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 31:26, and “a witness against thee” occurs in exactly one, the same verse. Ether 5:4 does not use that wording — it reads ‘shall stand as a testimony against the world’ — so the singleton is context, not contact, and the row is filed figural on that account.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 31 is the KJV's one procedure for a written record deposited now so that it can be produced later as evidence against the people who will not keep it. The book of the law goes in the side of the ark (31:26); the song is put in their mouths so that when the evils come it ‘shall testify against them as a witness’ (31:19, 21). Ether 5 is that procedure carried out at a different scale. A record is sealed up and made untouchable until the appointed time (5:1), produced by a fixed number of witnesses (5:3-4), and left to stand ‘as a testimony against the world, at the last day’. Moses' deposit is a witness against Israel at a future apostasy; Moroni's is a witness against the world at the judgment, and the enlargement is the whole distance between the two books.

links.note: The chapter's structure is Deuteronomy 31's, clause for clause and in order: write it, seal it, do not touch it, produce it by witnesses, let it testify against them later. No other biblical passage puts those five moves together, and Ether 5 does nothing else. The row is figural rather than verbal by design — it is offered as a reading of what the chapter is doing, and it is offered because a reader who notices the shape should be told the catalogue noticed it too and where it thinks the shape comes from.
links.whyNot: There is almost no verbal contact. ‘Testimony against’ is not Deuteronomy's phrase — his is ‘witness against’, a KJV singleton at 31:26 — and the four KJV verses that do read ‘for a testimony against’ are the Synoptic dust-shaking sayings, which share nothing else with this verse. The row rests entirely on the shape, and CONVENTIONS §5's Exodus 2:2 case is the standing warning that a typology can pull harder than the wording will bear. A reader who declines it is declining a structure, not a reading of words, and that is a reasonable thing to decline. It is filed as a link rather than an exclusion because the structure runs through the whole chapter rather than one clause of it — 5:1's ‘touch them not’ included.

pericopes.text: And if it so be that they repent and come unto the Father in the name of Jesus, they shall be received into the kingdom of God.

links.text: Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.

provenance.other: “cometh unto the Father” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 14:6. The Book of Mormon's own habit is ‘come unto me’ (thirty-four verses of the 1830 text) or ‘come unto Christ’ (four); ‘come unto the Father’ occurs in the 1830 text exactly here, at Ether 5:5, and nowhere else. So the clause is a departure from Moroni's idiom as well as a reach outside it, which is the main reason for recording it at all. `kjvSpecific` is `uncertain` rather than `yes` because the modern versions render John 14:6 the same way — ‘no one comes to the Father except through me’ — and nothing in the phrasing is distinctively King James.
provenance.significance: John 14:6 is the Bible's one sentence about coming unto the Father, and its whole content is that the coming requires a mediator: ‘no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.’ Ether 5:5 states the condition in the same order and supplies the mediator by name — repent, come unto the Father, in the name of Jesus — and seven verses further down John supplies the operative formula for the second half, ‘whatsoever ye shall ask in my name’ (14:13). What the recovery adds is the negative: John's sentence is exclusive, and Moroni's, read against it, quietly is too. ‘If it so be that they repent’ is the only door in the verse.

links.note: ‘And if it so be that they repent and come unto the Father in the name of Jesus, they shall be received into the kingdom of God.’ Two things make this more than devotional boilerplate. The collocation ‘come unto the Father’ is unique in the Book of Mormon to this verse, against thirty-four instances of the book's usual ‘come unto me’ — a departure from formula is where a borrowing is most likely to show. And the KJV has exactly one verse for the collocation, John 14:6, which supplies not only the phrase but the structure of Moroni's sentence: approach to the Father, licensed by a name. Moderate rather than high because the wording is conjugated rather than reproduced and because ‘in the name of Jesus’ is Acts's formula as much as John's; a reasonable reader could take the whole verse as ordinary Christian idiom and decline the row.

pericopes.text: And now, if I have no authority for these things, judge ye, for ye shall know that I have authority when ye shall see me, and we shall stand before God at the last day. Amen.

links.text: And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works.

provenance.other: “stand before God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 20:12: ‘And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened … and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books.’ The catalogue has filed the same verse repeatedly across the corpus — 2 Nephi 29:11, 3 Nephi 26:4, Mormon 9:13 among others — and in every case at the junction of a written record with the judgment, which is the junction Ether 5:6 makes.
provenance.significance: Moroni answers a challenge to his authority by naming a place where it will be settled: ‘ye shall know that I have authority when ye shall see me, and we shall stand before God at the last day.’ The KJV has one sentence for standing before God, and in it the standing is done by the dead at an assize where books are opened and men are judged out of what is written in them. Moroni has spent five verses manufacturing exactly such a book — 5:4 has already said it ‘shall stand as a testimony against the world, at the last day’. So the verse that settles the question of his authority is the verse in which his record becomes an exhibit and his reader becomes a defendant, and the encounter he promises the reader is a summons rather than a reunion. That the same KJV verse recurs across the corpus wherever a written record meets the judgment is itself a finding: the Book of Mormon's theology of its own text is worked out in the vocabulary of Revelation 20:12.

links.note: Three words, and a KJV singleton — the only verse in the Bible where anyone stands before God. Rarity of that order does most of the work here, but the context does the rest: Revelation 20:12 is a judgment scene organized around opened books, and Ether 5 is a chapter about a book produced in evidence at the judgment. The two halves of Moroni's clause take the two halves of Revelation's — seeing him again, and standing before God — and the chapter's earlier ‘testimony against the world, at the last day’ has already set the scene up. The link is not new to this chapter; the catalogue has it across five books, and the recurrence is part of the argument rather than a reason to suppress the row.

links.text: But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye.

provenance.other: “judge ye” occurs in exactly four KJV verses. Matthew 7:2 is not the idiom (‘with what judgment ye judge’) and Luke 12:57 is negated (‘why even of yourselves judge ye not what is right?’), which leaves two: Acts 4:19 and 1 Corinthians 10:15. Ether 5:6 has the bare imperative in final position, which is Acts 4:19's form; 1 Corinthians 10:15 takes an object, ‘judge ye what I say’.
provenance.alternative: 1 Corinthians 10:15 is the other reading and a reasonable one: an author inviting his readers to judge his own words is Moroni's rhetorical move exactly. The row goes to Acts 4:19 on syntax (bare final imperative) and on subject-matter (a contested claim of authority, Acts 4:7's ‘By what power, or by what name, have ye done this?’), not on the two shared words, which do not by themselves discriminate.
provenance.significance: Acts 4:19 is spoken by two men whose right to say what they are saying has just been challenged by the council, and it answers the challenge by referring it past the challengers: ‘whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye.’ Moroni's sentence does the same two things in the same order — refuses to argue the authority, hands the question to the reader, and then relocates the verdict to God's sight: ‘judge ye … and we shall stand before God at the last day.’ Recovering Acts 4 gives the sentence its posture: the writer is not defending a credential, he is declining to.

links.note: ‘And now, if I have no authority for these things, judge ye, for ye shall know that I have authority when ye shall see me.’ Two words, so the row is an echo and nothing more; but the two words are rare enough to name their verses, the syntax picks one of them, and the situation — an authority publicly challenged, answered by referring the challenger to God — is that verse's situation. It sits immediately beside the Revelation 20:12 row and the two work together: the appeal is handed to the reader, and then withdrawn to a tribunal where the reader will also be standing.
links.whyNot: ‘Judge ye’ is two extremely ordinary English words and the KJV's four instances do not make the collocation distinctive so much as make it countable. Nothing else of Acts 4 is in the verse: no council, no name, no healing, no prohibition. A reader may fairly say that Moroni wrote a natural English imperative and that the resemblance to Acts 4:19 is an accident of a small sample, and the row is recorded at `moderate` because that reader is not obviously wrong.

pericopes.text: And now I, Moroni, proceed to give the record of Jared and his brother.

For it came to pass after that the Lord had prepared the stones which the brother of Jared had carried up into the mount, the brother of Jared came down out of the mount, and he did put forth the stones into the vessels which were prepared, one in each end thereof; and behold, they did give light unto the vessels thereof.
And thus the Lord caused stones to shine in darkness, to give light unto men, women and children, that they might not cross the great waters in darkness.

links.text: For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.

provenance.other: “shine out of darkness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 4:6. “the light shineth in darkness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 1:5. The Genesis creation supplies the light but not the verb: Genesis 1:3 has 'Let there be light', and 'to give light' at Genesis 1:15 and 1:17 is of luminaries set in a firmament, not of light put inside a container.
provenance.significance: The metalepsis is one verse further on than the borrowing. 2 Corinthians 4:6 is Paul reciting the first day of creation as a figure for illumination; 4:7 then says where that light is kept — 'But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us.' Ether 6:2-3 does the thing Paul says figuratively: sixteen stones lit by the finger of the Lord are put into vessels, one in each end, and the vessels give light. Recover the source's next sentence and the Jaredite barges are Paul's earthen vessels carrying a light whose excellency is demonstrably not of the men who made them — which is exactly the argument Ether 3 has just made, where the brother of Jared supplies the stones and can supply nothing else. Neither text says this. The link says it.
provenance.alternative: Genesis 1:2-4 alone, read without the epistle. It accounts for light-in-darkness and for the ordering of the chapter, but not for the verb 'caused ... to shine' or for the vessels.

links.note: 'And thus the Lord caused stones to shine in darkness, to give light unto men, women and children, that they might not cross the great waters in darkness.' Four elements stand in 2 Corinthians 4:6 in this order and in no other KJV verse: God as the agent, a commanding or causing, light made to shine out of darkness, and a purpose clause 'to give the light'. The Book of Mormon has 'caused ... to shine in darkness, to give light'. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his passages; the case rests on the singleton plus the sequence, and on the fact that the preceding verse has already supplied the vessels of 4:7. Ether 6:10's 'they did have light continually, whether it was above the water or under the water' closes the same argument at the far end of the voyage.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that when they had prepared all manner of food, that thereby they might subsist upon the water, and also food for their flocks and herds, and whatsoever beast, or animal, or fowl that they should carry with them: And it came to pass that when they had done all these things, they got aboard of their vessels or barges, and set forth into the sea, commending themselves unto the Lord their God.

And it came to pass that the Lord God caused that there should a furious wind blow upon the face of the waters, towards the promised land; and thus they were tossed upon the waves of the sea before the wind.

links.text: And God remembered Noah, and every living thing, and all the cattle that was with him in the ark: and God made a wind to pass over the earth, and the waters asswaged;

provenance.other: “the face of the waters” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 1:2 and Genesis 7:18 — the Spirit of God moving over the deep, and the ark riding the flood. “made a wind to pass” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 8:1. There is no third biblical place where God sends a wind across floodwaters carrying a vessel.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon has fused the flood's two wind-and-water verses and reversed the function of one of them. In Genesis 8:1 the wind is the end of the ordeal — it passes over the earth and the waters assuage — and in Genesis 7:18 the ark simply goes where the water takes it. In Ether 6:5-8 the same wind is the ordeal and the engine at once: it never ceases to blow, it drives the vessels under, and it is the only reason they arrive. The Jaredite crossing is Noah's flood with the wind moved from the last day to all 344 of them, which is why Ether can say both that they were buried in the deep and that they were never off course.

links.note: 'The Lord God caused that there should a furious wind blow upon the face of the waters, towards the promised land; and thus they were tossed upon the waves of the sea before the wind.' Two Genesis flood phrases in one clause, and the chapter names the source itself two verses later — 6:7's vessels are 'tight like unto the ark of Noah'. The 1830 reads 'that there should a furious wind blow', which 1920 corrected to 'should be'; the first edition's uncorrected syntax is not KJV grammar and is worth recording against any account that treats the borrowing as smooth. Ether 2:17 has already built the barge out of Genesis 6-7 and cross-refers forward to this passage.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they were many times buried in the depths of the sea, because of the mountain waves which broke upon them, and also the great and terrible tempests which were caused by the fierceness of the wind.

And it came to pass that when they were buried in the deep, there was no water that could hurt them, their vessels being tight like unto a dish, and also they were tight like unto the ark of Noah; therefore when they were encompassed about by many waters, they did cry unto the Lord, and he did bring them forth again upon the top of the waters.

links.text: Then they cry unto the LORD in their trouble, and he bringeth them out of their distresses.

provenance.other: Individually the phrases are ordinary — “cry unto the Lord” occurs in exactly seven KJV verses, two of them this psalm's own refrain at 107:19 and 107:28 — so no single count carries the row. What carries it is that “desired haven” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 107:30, and that the psalm is the only KJV passage that runs the whole sequence.
provenance.significance: Psalm 107:23-30 is the Bible's one set-piece of ordinary seafarers in a storm, and Ether 6:3-12 reproduces its programme in order: they that go down to the sea in ships and do business in great waters (6:3-4, crossing the great waters, provisioning, setting forth); he raiseth the stormy wind, which lifteth up the waves thereof (6:5); they mount up to the heaven, they go down again to the depths (6:6, the mountain waves and the burial in the depths of the sea); then they cry unto the LORD in their trouble, and he bringeth them out of their distresses (6:7); he maketh the storm a calm (6:8, the wind that never ceases but no longer drowns them); so he bringeth them unto their desired haven (6:12, the shore of the promised land); and the psalm's answering command, oh that men would praise the LORD for his goodness (6:9, praising all the day long, not ceasing at night). Recover the psalm and the barges are not a miracle story but a liturgy: the Jaredite crossing is the third of Psalm 107's four deliverances performed as narrative.

links.note: 'When they were buried in the deep ... they did cry unto the Lord, and he did bring them forth again upon the top of the waters.' The clause is Psalm 107:28's two halves in Psalm 107:28's order — cry, and be brought out — and the chapter around it walks the psalm's other six stations without repeating any of its distinctive nouns. That is why this is filed as an extended allusion at moderate verbal volume rather than as a quotation: the debt is to a paragraph's structure, and the individual strings would not survive a rarity test on their own. Registered here rather than at 6:5 or 6:12 because 6:7 is the one verse where the psalm's actual grammar surfaces. Note that 6:7's other borrowing, the ark of Noah, is adjudicated at 6:5.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the wind did never cease to blow towards the promised land, while they were upon the waters; and thus they were driven forth before the wind;

and they did sing praises unto the Lord; yea, the brother of Jared did sing praises unto the Lord, and he did thank and praise the Lord all the day long; and when the night came, they did not cease to praise the Lord.

links.text: Sing unto God, ye kingdoms of the earth; O sing praises unto the Lord; Selah:

provenance.other: “sing praises unto the Lord” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 27:6 and Psalm 68:32. “depths of the sea” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Psalm 68:22, Isaiah 51:10 and Micah 7:19. Psalm 68 is the only KJV chapter that holds both.
provenance.significance: The two halves of the Jaredite deliverance are two verses of one psalm. Psalm 68:22 is the KJV's only promise that God will bring his people back out of the sea's depths — 'I will bring again from Bashan, I will bring my people again from the depths of the sea' — and Psalm 68:32 is the summons to sing praises that answers it. Ether 6:6 has the people buried in the depths of the sea and Ether 6:9 has them singing praises unto the Lord; the psalm supplies both clauses and supplies them in that order. This is the same shape as the Psalm 107 reading at 6:7 and does not compete with it: a chapter about being drowned and saved reaches for the two psalms in which that is the plot.

links.note: 'And they did sing praises unto the Lord; yea, the brother of Jared did sing praises unto the Lord, and he did thank and praise the Lord all the day long.' The clause is repeated twice in one verse, which is what raises it above the general devotional register — the Book of Mormon rarely doubles a phrase this way without a source behind it. Moderate rather than high because the collocation is two verses wide and 'all the day long' is spread across thirteen KJV verses, none of which fits; the psalm's proximity to 6:6's depths of the sea is doing as much work as the phrase itself.

pericopes.text: And thus they were driven forth; and no monster of the sea could break them, neither whale that could mar them: and they did have light continually, whether it was above the water or under the water.

links.text: Now the LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.

provenance.route: Jonah 1:17, worded from Matthew 12:40 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “whale” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Job 7:12, Ezekiel 32:2 and Matthew 12:40. Jonah 1:17 does not contain it — the KJV's Jonah has 'a great fish' — so the English word for the animal that swallowed Jonah reaches a reader of the King James Bible only through the Gospel of Matthew. “monster” occurs in no KJV verse at all in the singular. `mediation-check.py` on Ether 6:10 against Jonah 1:17 and Matthew 12:40 reports no decisive divergence, because the candidates share no clause the Book of Mormon reproduces; the mediation here is argued from the single noun and not from the tool.
provenance.significance: This is a denial that only means something if the reader knows what is being denied. Ether 6:7 has just put men inside a sealed vessel, buried them in the deep, had them cry unto the Lord and brought them up again on top of the water — the Jonah plot with the fish removed. Ether 6:10 then removes the fish explicitly: no monster of the sea could break them, neither whale that could mar them. The KJV has one swallowing sea-creature and one man delivered out of the deep after crying to God, and the Jaredite crossing takes the deliverance while ruling out the mechanism. Whether it is deliberate or not, the sentence is legible as an anti-Jonah, and the word it uses to rule the whale out is a word the King James Old Testament never applies to Jonah's fish.
provenance.alternative: Job 7:12 and Ezekiel 32:2, the KJV's other two whales, are both metaphors for a watched or hunted power and neither is a threat to a vessel. Genesis 1:21's 'great whales' are created goods, not hazards.

links.note: 'And thus they were driven forth; and no monster of the sea could break them, neither whale that could mar them.' There is no verbal borrowing — the row is filed on one noun and on the shape of the surrounding narrative, which is why it is moderate and conceptual rather than close-verbal. It is recorded because a reader who has watched Ether 6:7 rehearse Jonah 2 will read 6:10 as an answer to it, and because the mediation is a genuine finding in its own right: the Book of Mormon's word for Jonah's fish is not in the Book of Jonah.

pericopes.text: And thus they were driven forth, three hundred and forty and four days upon the water;

and they did land upon the shore of the promised land. And when they had set their feet upon the shores of the promised land, they bowed themselves down upon the face of the land, and did humble themselves before the Lord, and did shed tears of joy before the Lord, because of the multitude of his tender mercies over them.

links.text: Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness: according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions.

provenance.route: Psalm 51:1 / 69:16 → KJV → 1 Nephi 1:20 → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “multitude of thy tender mercies” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 51:1 and Psalm 69:16; “tender mercies” alone occurs in exactly eleven, so the qualifier is what identifies the source. The 'over' of 'his tender mercies over them' is Psalm 145:9's preposition — 'his tender mercies are over all his works' — which is the verse adjudicated behind 1 Nephi 1:20 and again at Alma 26:37.
provenance.significance: Two psalms have been welded, and the weld is where the corpus's own usage shows. Psalm 51:1 gives 'the multitude of his tender mercies'; Psalm 145:9 gives the preposition that governs them. Nothing in the KJV puts a multitude of tender mercies over anybody. But 1 Nephi 1:20 does — 'the tender mercies of the Lord is over all them whom he hath chosen' — and Ether 6:12 is that formula with Psalm 51's quantifier restored to it. So the psalm reaches Moroni's abridgement of Ether by way of the plates of Nephi, and the sentence records a landing on the promised land in the exact terms in which the corpus's first chapter recorded a deliverance to one.
provenance.alternative: Direct dependence on Psalm 51:1 without the Nephite intermediary. It accounts for the quantifier but not for 'over', which is Psalm 145:9's word and 1 Nephi 1:20's.

links.note: 'They bowed themselves down upon the face of the land, and did humble themselves before the Lord, and did shed tears of joy before the Lord, because of the multitude of his tender mercies over them.' A six-word run from a two-verse KJV collocation, and the whole of the corpus's signature formula on either side of it. 1 Nephi 1:20 reads 'is over all' in the 1830 against the KJV's 'are' and was corrected to 'are' in 1920; Ether 6:12's construction is unaffected by that variant, which is worth saying, since it means the two passages agree on the preposition and not on the grammar. Neither 'tears of joy' nor 'the face of the land' is in the KJV at all.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they went forth upon the face of the land, and began to till the earth.
And Jared had four sons; and they were called Jacom, and Gilgah, and Mahah, and Orihah.
And the brother of Jared also begat sons and daughters.

And the friends of Jared and his brother, were in number about twenty and two souls; and they also begat sons and daughters, before they came to the promised land; and therefore they began to be many.
And they were taught to walk humbly before the Lord; and they were also taught from on high.

links.text: He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?

provenance.other: “walk humbly” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Micah 6:8. The Book of Mormon substitutes 'before the Lord' for Micah's 'with thy God'; 'walk humbly before' is in no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: The substitution is the finding. Micah 6:8's preposition is 'with' — the whole point of the verse in its own context is that what the LORD requires is not sacrifice offered up to him but a manner of going along beside him, and 6:6-7 has just refused burnt offerings, calves of a year old, thousands of rams and a firstborn child. Ether 6:17 changes 'with thy God' to 'before the Lord' and thereby converts a companionship into a posture. It matters where the chapter puts it: the sentence sits between a genealogy and a request for a king, and Ether 6:30 repeats it of Orihah at the moment he becomes one. The KJV's single walking-humbly verse becomes the Jaredite test for monarchy, and the book of Ether will spend twenty-two chapters recording kings who fail it.

links.note: 'And they were taught to walk humbly before the Lord; and they were also taught from on high.' A KJV singleton in a two-word run, which is short, but the phrase has no rival source and is not connective tissue — it is a coined idiom belonging to one prophetic sentence. Far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his passages. Recorded here and cross-referenced rather than repeated at 6:30, where the same phrase returns to describe the first Jaredite king; the recurrence inside one chapter is itself part of the argument, since it frames the kingship request at 6:22-27 on both sides.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they began to spread upon the face of the land, and to multiply and to till the earth; and they did wax strong in the land.

links.text: And God blessed Noah and his sons, and said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth.

provenance.route: Genesis 8-11 as a sequence → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “be fruitful and multiply” occurs in exactly five KJV verses, three of them in the flood narrative's frame (Genesis 8:17, 9:1) and its creation counterpart (Genesis 1:22, 1:28). “overspread” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 9:19, of the whole earth peopled from Noah's three sons — but the Book of Mormon reads 'spread', not 'overspread', so the singleton is context and not evidence. “till the earth” occurs in no KJV verse; the KJV's idiom is 'till the ground' (Genesis 2:5, 3:23), so Ether's phrase is a variation on Genesis's and not a quotation of it.
provenance.significance: Ether 6 is running the back half of Genesis in order, and this is the verse where the order becomes visible rather than the wording. Genesis 7-11 goes: the ark on the face of the waters, the wind, the landing, worship on the new ground, begetting sons and daughters, the earth overspread from three brothers, then Babel and the first kingdom. Ether 6 goes: barges on the face of the waters (6:5), the wind (6:5-8), the landing (6:12), worship on the new ground (6:12), begetting sons and daughters (6:15-16), spreading and multiplying on the face of the land (6:18), then the demand for a king (6:22). Hardy's apparatus points Ether 1:33 to Genesis 11:1-9 and Ether 2:1 to Genesis 10:8-9, which is the same movement one chapter earlier and in the same order; this chapter is the Jaredites doing the Genesis 8-11 sequence a second time, on the far side of a second flood.

links.note: 'They began to spread upon the face of the land, and to multiply and to till the earth; and they did wax strong in the land.' Filed as figural because there is almost nothing verbal to test — 'multiply' is the only content word shared with Genesis 9:1, and the Book of Mormon's 'till the earth' is not the KJV's phrase. What the row records is a sequence, and it is registered because the sequence has already been established for this book by Hardy's own cross-references at 1:33 and 2:1 and by the flood links at 2:17 and 6:5. A reader should be told the catalogue saw the Genesis pattern here; a reader should also be told it will not bear a verbal argument.
links.whyNot: No distinctive shared wording. 'Be fruitful, and multiply' is not reproduced; 'replenish the earth' is not reproduced; 'overspread' is not reproduced. Every element of the case is positional.
