Withdraw the row if the Genesis 8-11 sequence at 6:5, 6:12 and 6:15 is judged to be a general flood-and-settlement pattern rather than this chapter of Genesis in particular.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Ether 1.33 (Genesis 11:1-9), Ether 2.1 (Genesis 10:8-9), and Ether 13.2 (Genesis 8:13-14)

pericopes.text: And the brother of Jared began to be old, and saw that he must soon go down to the grave; wherefore he saith unto Jared, Let us gather together our people, that we may number them, that we may know of them what they will desire of us before we go down to our graves.

links.text: And said unto him, Behold, thou art old, and thy sons walk not in thy ways: now make us a king to judge us like all the nations.

provenance.other: “make us a king” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 8:5; “give us a king” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 8:6; “hearken unto their voice” occurs in exactly two, 1 Samuel 8:9 and 8:22. None of the three is reproduced at Ether 6:19-24 — the Book of Mormon writes 'anoint one of their sons to be a king over them' and 'suffer them that they may have a king'. What is reproduced is the sequence.
provenance.significance: 1 Samuel 8 is the corpus's most heavily worked political chapter — 'the voice of the people' from 8:7 is adjudicated at Mosiah 7:9, Mosiah 29:2, Alma 2:7, Helaman 1:5 and Helaman 5:2 — and Ether 6 is the one place it is used without that phrase. The situation is nevertheless 1 Samuel 8:1-6 step for step: an old ruler at the end of his life (6:19, 'began to be old, and saw that he must soon go down to the grave'; 1 Samuel 8:1, 8:5), a gathering, a question about what the people will desire (6:19), the desire named as a king drawn from the ruler's own sons (6:22; 1 Samuel 8:5), the request found grievous by the man asked (6:23; 1 Samuel 8:6), and the request granted anyway (6:24; 1 Samuel 8:22). Mosiah 29:2 is the same scene with the phrase; Ether 6 is the same scene without it. That the Jaredite version has no 'voice of the people' in it is worth noticing rather than explaining away: the Jaredites are at the start of the sequence 1 Samuel 8 begins and Mosiah 29 ends, and Ether's remaining chapters will supply the captivity.

links.note: 'The brother of Jared began to be old, and saw that he must soon go down to the grave; wherefore he saith unto Jared, Let us gather together our people, that we may number them, that we may know of them what they will desire of us before we go down to our graves.' No clause is reproduced and the row is conceptual for that reason; it is entered at 6:19 rather than 6:22 because this is where the biblical premise is set — a ruler who is old, and a people about to be asked what they want. The 1830 reads 'he saith unto Jared' where 1920 reads 'said', which is the KJV's historic present and one of several places in this chapter where the first edition sounds more like the source than the current text does. “go down to the grave” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Kings 2:6 and Job 21:13; neither is a plausible source and both are recorded here only to show the phrase was tested.

pericopes.text: And accordingly the people were gathered together. Now the number of the sons and the daughters of the brother of Jared were twenty and two souls; and the number of the sons and daughters of Jared were twelve, he having four sons.

And it came to pass that they did number their people; and after that they had numbered them, they did desire of them the things which they would that they should do before they went down to their graves.
And it came to pass that the people desired of them that they should anoint one of their sons to be a king over them.

links.text: The trees went forth on a time to anoint a king over them; and they said unto the olive tree, Reign thou over us.

provenance.other: “anoint a king” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Judges 9:8. “a king over them” occurs in exactly two, Judges 9:8 and Revelation 9:11. The Book of Mormon's clause at 6:22 is 'anoint one of their sons to be a king over them', which contains both. “rule thou over us” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Judges 8:22, and “I will not rule over you” in exactly one, Judges 8:23 — the offer of monarchy and its refusal, already adjudicated in this corpus at 2 Nephi 5:18 and Mosiah 29:3.
provenance.significance: The KJV anoints a king over a people exactly once, and it is a fable told against monarchy. Jotham's trees ask the olive, the fig and the vine to reign over them and each declines — 'Should I leave my fatness ... my sweetness ... my wine?' — until only the bramble is left, and the bramble accepts with a threat of fire. Ether 6:25-27 is that fable as narrative: the firstborn refuses, all the brothers refuse, all the sons of Jared refuse, and the crown is finally taken by the one candidate who will have it. Recover Judges 9 and the reader gets the sequel for nothing — Abimelech, the son who did accept, murders seventy brothers on one stone and dies under a millstone at Thebez, which is the passage this catalogue has already adjudicated at Mosiah 19:5 and 19:20. Ether 6:23 says the thing leads into captivity; the source says it ends in fire between the bramble and the men of Shechem, and the book of Ether ends with both.

links.note: 'The people desired of them that they should anoint one of their sons to be a king over them.' Two KJV singletons inside a single seven-word clause, and both belong to the same verse of Jotham's parable. What makes the row high rather than moderate is that the verses immediately following reproduce the parable's structure and not just its opening: a series of candidates, each declining, until one accepts. 6:25's 'he refused and would not be their king' and 6:26's 'they chose all the brothers of Pagag, and they would not' have no KJV wording behind them, but Judges 9:9-15 is the only biblical passage that has that plot. The 1830 reads 'first born' as two words at 6:25 where 1920 has 'firstborn'; the KJV at Exodus 11:5 spells it both ways in one verse, so the first edition is the closer typographical match without the reading changing.

pericopes.text: And now behold, this was grievous unto them.— But the brother of Jared said unto them, Surely, this thing leadeth into captivity.

links.text: He that leadeth into captivity shall go into captivity: he that killeth with the sword must be killed with the sword. Here is the patience and the faith of the saints.

provenance.other: “leadeth into captivity” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 13:10; the bare “into captivity” occurs in exactly thirty-eight and is formulaic. The distinctive element is the present-tense participle with an unstated object — not led into captivity, but leadeth into captivity — which is what the Book of Mormon has: 'Surely, this thing leadeth into captivity.'
provenance.significance: The chapter of the Bible the phrase comes from is a chapter about a king. Revelation 13 is the beast to whom the dragon gives 'his power, and his seat, and great authority', whom all the world wonders after and worships, who is given a mouth speaking great things and power over all kindreds and tongues and nations; verse 10 is the sentence that tells the saints what to do about it. So the brother of Jared's objection to monarchy — three words long, and the shortest political argument in the Book of Mormon — is worded out of the one KJV verse that answers a demand for a king with a warning about captivity, in the one chapter of the Bible that describes a king as a beast. Neither text says this. The link says it, and the book of Ether then spends chapters 7 through 11 proving the brother of Jared right, with Jaredite kings living out their reigns in captivity in their own kingdoms.
provenance.alternative: Deuteronomy 28:41 and its kin, the covenant curses in which sons and daughters go into captivity. They supply the doctrine and none of the wording; the participial construction is not in them.

links.note: 'But the brother of Jared said unto them, Surely, this thing leadeth into captivity.' Three words reproduced exactly from a KJV singleton, which is far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his passages — the row rests entirely on the rarity of the construction and on the aptness of the source's context. Catalogued as a quotation rather than an allusion because what is shared is a complete predicate lifted intact, not a distinctive vocabulary redeployed. The corpus has used this verse once already, at Mosiah 23:21, where it supplied 'the patience and the faith'; between them the two rows account for the first clause and the last clause of one verse of the Apocalypse, and both arrive in passages about a people about to be put in bondage. The 1830 reads 'But the brother of Jared said' where 1920 reads 'And'; the adversative is the stronger reading and the objection lands harder in the first edition.

pericopes.text: But Jared said unto his brother, Suffer them that they may have a king; and therefore he said unto them, Choose ye out from among our sons a king, even whom ye will.

And it came to pass that they chose even the first born of the brother of Jared; and his name was Pagag. And it came to pass that he refused and would not be their king. And the people would that his father should constrain him; but his father would not; and he commanded them that they should constrain no man to be their king.
And it came to pass that they chose all the brothers of Pagag, and they would not.—

links.text: But the olive tree said unto them, Should I leave my fatness, wherewith by me they honour God and man, and go to be promoted over the trees?

provenance.other: No shared wording; the row is entirely structural. Judges 9:8-15 and Ether 6:25-27 are, as far as this catalogue has found, the only two passages in either book in which a crown is offered to a series of candidates who decline it one after another before it is finally taken.
provenance.significance: Jotham's fable is a theory of who ends up ruling: the good candidates all have something better to do, so the office falls to the one with nothing to lose, and the bramble's acceptance speech is a threat — 'let fire come out of the bramble, and devour the cedars of Lebanon'. Ether 6:25-27 supplies the same sequence and then withholds the fable's verdict. Pagag refuses; his brothers refuse; the sons of Jared refuse; Orihah accepts, and Orihah turns out to be the best king the Jaredites ever have, walking humbly before the Lord at 6:30 and reigning in righteousness. The Book of Mormon has taken the shape of Judges 9 and reversed its conclusion, exactly as 2 Nephi 5:18 took Gideon's refusal and had Nephi neither accept nor refuse. What the fable's polarity does predict is the rest of the book: Orihah's line produces Corihor, Shule, Noah and the captivity that Ether 7 begins.
provenance.alternative: That the refusal sequence is native narrative and not biblical at all. The chapter has a plain reason of its own for the refusals — the brother of Jared has just told them that a king leads to captivity — and a writer who had never read Judges 9 could construct 6:25-27 out of 6:23 alone.

links.note: 'And it came to pass that they chose all the brothers of Pagag, and they would not.' Entered at 6:26 because this is the verse that makes it a series rather than a single refusal, and filed as figural because there is no verbal contact whatever: Judges 9's declining candidates give reasons and quote their own produce, and the Book of Mormon's give none — 'they would not' is the whole speech. The row exists to record that the catalogue saw the type-scene and to say on what terms it is offered. Read with the 6:22 link, where the wording actually is: “anoint a king” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and it is the first verse of this fable, which is what raises 6:26 from a resemblance to a plausible continuation of a borrowing already in progress.
links.whyNot: Nothing verbal survives. The case is the sequence and the sequence alone, and 6:23 supplies an internal motive for the refusals that makes a source unnecessary. Withdraw if the 6:22 link to Judges 9:8 is rejected, since without it there is no reason to expect Judges 9 in this chapter at all.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that neither would the sons of Jared, even all, save it were one; and Orihah, he was anointed to be king over the people.
And he began to reign, and the people began to prosper; and they became exceeding rich.
And it came to pass that Jared died, and his brother also.

And it came to pass that Orihah did walk humbly before the Lord, and did remember how great things the Lord had done for his father, and also taught his people how great things the Lord had done for their fathers.

links.text: Only fear the LORD, and serve him in truth with all your heart: for consider how great things he hath done for you.

provenance.route: 1 Samuel 12:24, in the wording of Mark 5:19 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “how great things” occurs in exactly five KJV verses: 1 Samuel 12:24, Mark 5:19, Mark 5:20, Luke 8:39 and Acts 9:16. Only the first is Old Testament and only the first is about a nation remembering a deliverance. `mediation-check.py` on Ether 6:30 against 1 Samuel 12:24 and Mark 5:19 reports no decisive divergence — the two candidates share no clause the Book of Mormon reproduces in a form that separates them — but at the one slot inside the shared clause where they do differ, 1 Samuel's 'he' against Mark's 'the Lord', the Book of Mormon reads 'the Lord'. So the wording is the gospel's and the situation is Samuel's, and the tool cannot break the tie.
provenance.significance: 1 Samuel 12 is Samuel's farewell address at the making of the monarchy: the king has just been confirmed, Samuel is old, and 12:24 is the standing instruction he leaves the nation — remember what God did for your fathers, now that you have a king. Ether 6:29-30 is that scene without the speech. Jared and his brother die; Orihah, newly anointed, walks humbly before the Lord, remembers how great things the Lord had done for his father, and teaches his people how great things the Lord had done for their fathers. The one KJV verse in which 'how great things' means a national deliverance to be recited after a coronation is the verse that stands behind the first Jaredite king's first recorded act. The catalogue has read the same verse this way at Mosiah 27:16, in another chapter about a king's sons.
provenance.alternative: Mark 5:19 alone, and with it Luke 8:39. The definite article is Mark's, the verse is far the more famous home of the idiom, and the corpus uses it at 1 Nephi 7:11 and Alma 10:7. What Mark cannot supply is the plural fathers and the post-coronation setting: the Gerasene demoniac is told to tell his friends what was done for him, one man, in his own house. Recorded as `uncertain` rather than forced, per CONVENTIONS §7.

links.note: 'Orihah did walk humbly before the Lord, and did remember how great things the Lord had done for his father, and also taught his people how great things the Lord had done for their fathers.' The machine stream ranked Mark 5:19 first in the chapter and it is the right idiom but arguably the wrong verse: what Ether 6:30 does is what 1 Samuel 12:24 commands and what Mark 5:19 does not, namely tell a people to remember a deliverance granted to their fathers under a new king. Filed at moderate because the tie cannot be broken on wording, and the mediation is left `uncertain` for the same reason — see `provenance.other`, which records what the tool actually returned. The verse's other half is the Micah 6:8 phrase adjudicated at 6:17; the two borrowings arrive together, and together they make the founding king of the Jaredites a man defined by the KJV's one command to walk humbly and the KJV's one Old Testament command to remember how great things.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Orihah did execute judgement upon the land in righteousness all his days, whose days were exceeding many.

links.text: In those days, and at that time, will I cause the Branch of righteousness to grow up unto David; and he shall execute judgment and righteousness in the land.

provenance.other: “execute judgment” occurs in exactly 11 KJV verses, so the verb phrase alone points nowhere. What narrows it is the third term: “execute judgment and righteousness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jeremiah 33:15, and its twin at Jeremiah 23:5 supplies the only other member of the pair — “judgment and justice in the” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Ether 7:1 has all three of Jeremiah 33:15's elements: execute, judgment, righteousness, and the land.
provenance.alternative: Jeremiah 21:12's “Execute judgment in the” is also a KJV singleton, but it is an imperative addressed to the house of David about the oppressed, and nothing of its content appears here.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the formula is not a general commendation of good government but the sign of the Davidic Branch: 'I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth.' The Book of Mormon's first Jaredite king — a gentile ruling a gentile people, on the text's own chronology some fifteen centuries before Jeremiah and outside the covenant entirely — is introduced in the King James English reserved for the messianic heir of David, and the sentence that follows him through the chapter (7:11, 7:27) is that same formula. Read metaleptically, the chapter is asserting that the office of the righteous king is not Israel's property: what Jeremiah promises to David, Ether reports as already having happened at Moron.

links.note: 'Orihah did execute judgement upon the land in righteousness all his days.' Three of the four content words of Jeremiah 33:15's closing clause, redistributed but intact — execute, judgement, righteousness, and the land. The redistribution is what keeps this at allusion rather than quotation: Jeremiah has 'execute judgment and righteousness in the land', Ether has 'execute judgement upon the land in righteousness', which is the same lexical stock through a different syntax and well short of Skousen's sixteen-word threshold. The recurrence is the argument's real weight. The formula is not used once and dropped; it opens the chapter at 7:1, marks Shule's accession at 7:11, and closes the chapter at 7:27, so it functions as the chapter's evaluative refrain in the way 'he did that which was right in the sight of the LORD' functions in Kings — but the words chosen for it are Jeremiah's Branch oracle, not Kings'. CONVENTIONS §8 applies to the spelling: 1830 reads 'judgement' at all four occurrences and 1920 changed it to 'judgment', which is the KJV's own spelling, so the later edition moved the text toward its source rather than away.

pericopes.text: And he begat sons and daughters; yea, he begat thirty and one, among whom were twenty and three sons.

links.text: And he had thirty sons that rode on thirty ass colts, and they had thirty cities, which are called Havothjair unto this day, which are in the land of Gilead.

provenance.other: “thirty sons” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Judges 10:4 (Jair) and Judges 12:9 (Ibzan); Judges 12:14 gives Abdon forty. Judges 10:2 supplies the other numeral in play here — Tola 'judged Israel twenty and three years'. Every one of these verses is in the minor-judges notices, and nowhere else in the KJV is a ruler's entire biography a count of his years and a count of his children.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon's account of Orihah gives him two facts and no others: he executed judgment all his days, and he begat a specified number of children of whom a specified number were sons. That is the form of the minor-judges notice and it is a form, not a phrase — which is why this is filed as figural. What the form imports is a theory of succession: in Judges the fertility notice is the whole of a good ruler's record because nothing happened in his time, and Ether 7 immediately falsifies that peace in the next two verses, when Corihor rebels. Orihah is given a judge's obituary and his sons give him a king's civil war.

links.note: 'Whose days were exceeding many. And he begat sons and daughters; yea, he begat thirty and one, among whom were twenty and three sons.' The candidate list offered Numbers 26:62 for 'twenty and three' — a Levite census total — and Genesis 5:4 for 'he begat sons and daughters', neither of which explains why a ruler's reign should be summarised by an offspring count at all. Judges does explain it: Jair had thirty sons and thirty cities, Ibzan thirty sons and thirty daughters, Abdon forty sons and thirty nephews, and Tola judged Israel twenty and three years, which is Ether's other numeral. Ether 7:1-2 reproduces the notice's two components in the notice's order — length of rule, then numbered offspring — and reproduces its silence about everything else.
links.whyNot: The only shared vocabulary is numerals, and numerals are the cheapest coincidence in a corpus that counts as compulsively as the KJV does. 'Thirty and one' and 'twenty and three' are not Judges' numbers; Judges has thirty, forty and seventy. A reader who wants nothing here but a common ancient way of praising a ruler's fruitfulness is not refuted by anything in this row, and the row would be withdrawn if it turned out that the Book of Mormon summarises other reigns this way — it does not; Orihah's is the only such notice in Ether.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he also begat Kib in his old age. And it came to pass that Kib reigned in his stead; and Kib begat Corihor.

links.text: For Sarah conceived, and bare Abraham a son in his old age, at the set time of which God had spoken to him.

provenance.other: “in his old age” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 21:2 and Genesis 21:7, and both are the birth of Isaac. The machine proposed Genesis 37:3, but its wording is “son of his old age”, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse and is a different construction; “her old age” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 1:36, of Elisabeth. The English phrase Ether uses belongs, in the KJV, to Abraham alone.
provenance.significance: The KJV keeps this phrase for the promised son — the heir who arrives after the possibility has closed, 'at the set time of which God had spoken'. Ether 7 uses it three times, and the middle use is the one that matters: 7:7, 'nevertheless Kib begat Shule in his old age, while he was yet in captivity'. The deposed king, imprisoned by one son, fathers in prison the son who will free him. Reading the Isaac context back into it, the Jaredite deliverer is born under the Genesis sign of an impossible birth, and the 'nevertheless' in Ether's sentence is doing the work Genesis 21's 'set time' does — the succession is not broken because a son came when none could.

links.note: Adjudicated at its first occurrence, 7:3, though the argument is carried by 7:7 and the phrase returns a third time at 7:26 when Shule in turn begets in his old age. Three uses of a phrase the King James Bible reserves for Isaac's birth, in a chapter that is about nothing except whether a dynasty can survive its own sons, is more than the ordinary way to say a man was old. What holds the row at 'moderate' rather than higher is that the phrase is short and unremarkable in modern English, so a reader who takes it as plain description rather than borrowing has a case; the reply is that plain description is available in the KJV in half a dozen other forms ('well stricken in years', 'old and full of days') and this is the one that came.

links.text: And Bela died, and Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his stead.

provenance.other: “reigned in his stead” occurs in exactly 63 KJV verses, so no single verse can be named as the source and the row is filed on the formula rather than on a citation. Of those 63, the first seven are Genesis 36:33-39, and they are the only place in the KJV where the formula runs as an unbroken chain outside the regnal histories of Israel and Judah.
provenance.significance: Genesis 36:31 heads that chain: 'these are the kings that reigned in the land of Edom, before there reigned any king over the children of Israel.' It is the King James Bible's one gentile king-list, kept precisely because it is prior to and outside Israel's monarchy, and it is exactly the thing the book of Ether claims to be. Ether 7 does not borrow a verse from it; it borrows the genre, down to the formula that stitches the generations together. Reading the two lists against each other is the interesting result: Genesis 36 records a gentile succession with no evaluation at all, and Ether 7 takes the same form and inserts into it prophets, idolatry, repentance and a curse upon the land — the Deuteronomic machinery that Genesis 36 conspicuously withholds from Edom.

links.note: 'And it came to pass that Kib reigned in his stead.' The formula recurs at 7:10 ('he began to reign in the stead of his father') and at 7:19 ('did build up his kingdom in his stead'), and it is the connective tissue of the whole Jaredite record. Filed as figural rather than allusion because 63 KJV verses cannot be narrowed to one, and no argument here rests on the reader recovering a particular Edomite king. What the row records is that the Book of Mormon's dynastic book is written in the KJV's dynastic English, and that the KJV's model for a dynastic list belonging to a people outside Israel is Genesis 36.
links.whyNot: A formula occurring in 63 verses is close to the boundary CONVENTIONS §5 draws around connective noise, and an adjudicator who filed this as a standing exclusion rather than a link would be applying the rules correctly. The row is written instead because the formula is not connective — it is generic, it marks a genre, and a reader of Ether who is shown nothing at all here has been told there is no borrowing in the Book of Mormon's most conspicuously biblical sentence pattern. Withdraw it if a better-evidenced link to the Kings regnal formula is made at an earlier Jaredite accession, which would displace Genesis 36 as the model.

pericopes.text: And when Corihor was thirty and two years old, he rebelled against his father, and went over and dwelt in the land of Nehor; and he begat sons and daughters; and they became exceeding fair; wherefore Corihor drew away many people after him.

links.text: After this man rose up Judas of Galilee in the days of the taxing, and drew away much people after him: he also perished; and all, even as many as obeyed him, were dispersed.

provenance.other: “drew away” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 5:37, and the clause the Book of Mormon writes is that verse's clause with one word changed: 'drew away much people after him' becomes 'drew away many people after him'. Six words, five of them identical and all six in order, on a phrase the King James Bible uses once.
provenance.significance: Acts 5:37 is not narrative but evidence in an argument. Gamaliel cites Theudas and Judas of Galilee to the council as the two cases proving his rule: a movement that is of men comes to nought of itself, so leave the apostles alone. The King James Bible's only man who 'drew away' a people after him is therefore its type-specimen of the insurrection that fails. Ether 7 gives the sentence to Corihor and then declines Gamaliel's conclusion twice over — Corihor's rising does not come to nought, it succeeds, deposes the king and holds him in captivity for a generation; and Corihor himself does not perish with his followers dispersed but 'repented of the many evils which he had done' and is given power in his brother's kingdom (7:13). The borrowed clause carries Gamaliel's rule into the chapter and the chapter breaks it.

links.note: 'Wherefore Corihor drew away many people after him.' The strongest row in the chapter and the one the candidate list missed entirely — the n-gram stream ranked Judges 6:33 and Matthew 10:35 at this verse and never proposed Acts 5. The evidence is as clean as this catalogue gets: a six-word clause reproduced with a single substitution from a phrase that occurs once in the KJV, in a source whose subject is precisely a man who draws a people away after himself. It falls well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his thirty-six, but by the standard set at 1 Nephi 1:14 — six exact words from a two-verse rarity, catalogued as quotation — the volume here is greater, not less. The construction is the chapter's, not a single verse's accident: Shule arms 'those which he had drew away with him' at 7:9, and Noah 'drew away Cohor his brother' at 7:15. CONVENTIONS §8 bears on the middle one: the 1830 reads 'he had drew away', which is ungrammatical and was corrected to 'drawn' in 1920, so the first edition preserves the verb in a form no KJV verse has while keeping the KJV's phrase.

links.text: Jehoram was thirty and two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem.

provenance.other: “thirty and two years old” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, 2 Kings 8:17, 2 Chronicles 21:5 and 2 Chronicles 21:20, and all three are the same man: Jehoram of Judah, whose age at accession the KJV records three times and no other king's at thirty-two.
provenance.significance: 2 Chronicles 21:4, the verse immediately before, is what makes the number worth a row: 'Now when Jehoram was risen up to the kingdom of his father, he strengthened himself, and slew all his brethren with the sword.' The KJV's one thirty-two-year-old is the king who takes his father's kingdom and destroys his own brothers to hold it, and Ether 7:4 gives that age to the son who rebels against his father and whose brother must later take the kingdom back from him by battle. Neither text mentions the other; the number is doing the work of a marginal cross-reference.

links.note: 'And when Corihor was thirty and two years old, he rebelled against his father.' The machine ranked 2 Chronicles 21:5 here for the run 'thirty and two years old', and the ordinary verdict on a regnal numeral is the one the register gives at Helaman 1:1 — the KJV counts constantly and a shared number is arithmetic, not borrowing. What makes this one different is that the number is not distributed: all three of its KJV occurrences are one king, and that king's defining act is fratricidal usurpation within the father's house, which is the act Ether 7:4 is narrating. Filed as an echo, at moderate, because the verbal contact is a number and nothing else.
links.whyNot: A number is the weakest possible carrier of dependence and the Book of Mormon supplies ages and reign-lengths continually without biblical parallel. Ether 7:4 uses the number for age at rebellion, not age at accession, so even the syntactic frame differs from all three KJV verses. If a reader holds that the coincidence is one in a few dozen and that the chapter's real Jehoram-shaped material is elsewhere, this row does not survive; it is recorded so that a reader who notices the singleton king is told the catalogue noticed too.

pericopes.text: And when he had gathered together an army, he came up unto the land of Moron where the king dwelt, and took him captive, which brought to pass the saying of the brother of Jared, That they would be brought into captivity.

links.text: So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory.

provenance.other: “brought to pass the saying” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and so does the shorter “to pass the saying”. The KJV has many formulas for fulfilment — 'that it might be fulfilled', 'the word of the LORD came to pass' — and this is not one of the common ones; it is Paul's, once.
provenance.alternative: 1 Corinthians 15:54 is itself quoting Isaiah 25:8, so this is a mediation case and tools/mediation-check.py was run on Ether 7:5 against both. It is decisive for the New Testament: the Book of Mormon has 1 Corinthians 15:54's frame ('brought to pass the saying') and not one word of Isaiah 25:8, whose 'He will swallow up death in victory' supplies the content Paul quotes and nothing the Book of Mormon uses. What is borrowed here is the wrapper, not what is inside it.
provenance.significance: This is metalepsis of an unusually exact kind, because the borrowed frame is a slot with a fixed filler. In the King James Bible the one 'saying' that is 'brought to pass' is 'Death is swallowed up in victory' — the abolition of death at the resurrection, the climax of Paul's argument. Ether 7:5 keeps the frame and substitutes the filler: the saying brought to pass is the brother of Jared's, 'That they would be brought into captivity.' Recover the context and the sentence is doing the opposite of what its source does. Paul's formula announces the end of bondage; Ether's announces the beginning of one, and it does so in the first generation of a people who were promised a land of liberty.

links.note: 'Which brought to pass the saying of the brother of Jared, That they would be brought into captivity.' Five consecutive words on a KJV singleton, and the machine ranked it first at this verse for exactly that reason — one of the few places in the chapter where the n-gram stream was right. The row is 'allusion' rather than 'quotation' because what is reproduced is a citation formula and not a proposition: the Book of Mormon is not repeating Paul's saying, it is using Paul's sentence for introducing one. Confidence is 'high' rather than 'certain' on the ground that fulfilment formulas are the kind of language a writer might reconstruct from general familiarity with the KJV without any one verse in view — but the KJV offers a dozen other fulfilment formulas that are far commoner, and this is the rare one.

pericopes.text: Now the land of Moron where the king dwelt, was near the land which is called Desolation by the Nephites.—
And it came to pass that Kib dwelt in captivity, and his people, under Corihor his son, until he became exceeding old; nevertheless Kib begat Shule in his old age, while he was yet in captivity.
And it came to pass that Shule was angry with his brother; and Shule waxed strong, and became mighty, as to the strength of a man; and he was also mighty in judgement.

Wherefore he came to the hill Ephraim, and he did moulten out of the hill, and made swords out of steel for those which he had drew away with him; and after that he had armed them with swords, he returned to the city Nehor and gave battle unto his brother Corihor, by which means he obtained the kingdom, and restored it unto his father Kib.
And now because of the thing which Shule had done, his father bestowed upon him the kingdom; therefore he began to reign in the stead of his father.
And it came to pass that he did execute judgement in righteousness; and he did spread his kingdom upon all the face of the land, for the people had become exceeding numerous.—
And it came to pass that Shule also begat many sons and daughters.
And Corihor repented of the many evils which he had done; wherefore Shule gave him power in his kingdom.
And it came to pass that Corihor had many sons and daughters.— And among the sons of Corihor, there was one whose name was Noah.
And it came to pass that Noah rebelled against Shule, the king, and also his father Corihor, and drew away Cohor his brother, and also all his brethren and many of the people.—
And he gave battle unto Shule, the king, in the which he did obtain the land of their first inheritance; and he became a king over that part of the land.
And it came to pass that he gave battle again unto Shule the king; and he took Shule the king, and carried him away captive into Moron.

links.text: Then they took the king, and carried him up unto the king of Babylon to Riblah in the land of Hamath; where he gave judgment upon him.

provenance.other: “took the king and carried” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The second half of Ether's clause comes from the same deportation vocabulary: “away captive into”, with a place-name following, occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Jeremiah 39:9 and Luke 21:24. tools/mediation-check.py on Ether 7:17 against those two is decisive for Jeremiah — the Book of Mormon has 'carried … away captive into' where Luke has 'led away captive into'.
provenance.alternative: “carried him away” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 15:1 — 'bound Jesus, and carried him away, and delivered him to Pilate' — and the sequence there is the same one Ether has: a king is seized, carried away, and about to be put to death. It is filed in the exclusion register at this verse rather than as a composite, because Jeremiah 52:9 accounts for the whole clause and Mark 15:1 accounts only for three words of it.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 52 is the fall of Jerusalem, and the king taken and carried away is Zedekiah, in whose reign 1 Nephi opens. The Book of Mormon's other deportation sentence, at 1 Nephi 1:13, is the prophecy that Jerusalem should be destroyed 'and many should be carried away captive into Babylon' — the catalogue's flagship rarity. Ether 7:17 writes the fulfilled form of that same sentence for a king in a different hemisphere fifteen centuries earlier, substituting Moron for Babylon. What follows is the point of the substitution. Jeremiah 52:10-11 has Zedekiah's sons slain before his eyes and the king himself kept in prison till the day of his death; Ether 7:18 has the sons of Shule break down the door of the prison and set their father back on his throne. The Jaredite record takes the KJV's worst royal ending and reverses the role of the sons in it.

links.note: 'And he took Shule the king, and carried him away captive into Moron.' The candidate list gave Jeremiah 52:9 for 'took the king and carried' and Mark 15:1 for 'carried him away', and reading the whole verse decides between them: Ether's clause has the object ('the king'), the verb pair ('took … and carried'), the qualifier ('captive') and a named destination, which is Jeremiah's shape entire and Mark's only in part. Set beside 1 Nephi 1:13 this is the same idiom in a different hand and a different book, so CONVENTIONS §4's across-a-book-boundary rule applies: the row is written in full here rather than deferred to its first adjudication, and recurrenceRefs sends the reader back to it.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass as he was about to put him to death, the sons of Shule crept into the house of Noah by night and slew him, and broke down the door of the prison and brought out their father, and placed him upon his throne in his own kingdom;

wherefore the son of Noah did build up his kingdom in his stead; nevertheless they did not gain power any more over Shule the king; and the people which were under the reign of Shule the king, did prosper exceedingly and wax great.
And the country was divided; and there was two kingdoms, the kingdom of Shule, and the kingdom of Cohor, the son of Noah.
And Cohor, the son of Noah, caused that his people should give battle unto Shule, in the which Shule did beat them, and did slay Cohor.

And now Cohor had a son which was called Nimrod; and Nimrod gave up the kingdom of Cohor unto Shule, and he did gain favor in the eyes of Shule; wherefore Shule did bestow great favors upon him, in the which he did do in the kingdom of Shule according to his desires;

links.text: And the beginning of his kingdom was Babel, and Erech, and Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar.

provenance.other: “Nimrod” occurs in exactly four KJV verses: Genesis 10:8, Genesis 10:9, 1 Chronicles 1:10 and Micah 5:6. Of those, Genesis 10:10 is the verse that attaches a kingdom to him, and it is the verse immediately following the two that name him. kjvSpecific is 'no' because a proper name is spelled the same in every English Bible and there is no wording here to test — the rarity is the name itself, not the KJV's rendering of it.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon has already been to Genesis 10 in this book: at Ether 2:1 the Jaredites cross 'the valley of Nimrod, being called after the mighty hunter', which lifts a KJV singleton and is catalogued there as certain. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Genesis 10:8-9 at that verse. What 7:22 adds is the second half of the Genesis notice. Genesis 10:10 says 'the beginning of his kingdom was Babel' — Nimrod is the KJV's first empire-builder, and the tower his kingdom begins with is the tower whose confounding, at Genesis 11, is the founding event of the entire Jaredite record (Ether 1:33). Ether 7:22 then gives the name to a prince who does the one thing the Genesis Nimrod is incapable of: 'Nimrod gave up the kingdom of Cohor unto Shule.' The man whose name means the beginning of a kingdom surrenders one. It is hard to read that as accident in a book that opens at Babel.

links.note: 'And now Cohor had a son which was called Nimrod.' A name and not a phrase, which is why the row is conceptual and why kjvSpecific is 'no'; but a name that occurs four times in the King James Bible, three of them in one genealogy, and which arrives here in a book whose premise is that genealogy's next chapter. The row is written rather than passed over because Ether has demonstrably used Genesis 10 already, at 2:1, where the borrowing is a KJV singleton and the confidence is certain — availability of the source is not in question within this book, only the significance of a second visit. Per CONVENTIONS §4 this is not a narrator reusing his own formula: 2:1 borrows Nimrod's title for a place, 7:22 borrows his name for a person, and the second use argues something the first does not, because the thing this Nimrod does with a kingdom is the reverse of what Genesis 10:10 records of his namesake.

pericopes.text: and also in the reign of Shule there came prophets among the people, which were sent from the Lord, prophesying that the wickedness and idolatry of the people was bringing a curse upon the land, in the which they should be destroyed, if they did not repent.

And it came to pass that the people did revile against the prophets, and did mock them. And it came to pass that king Shule did execute judgement against all those who did revile against the prophets;

links.text: Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake.

provenance.route: Matthew 5:11-12 and 2 Chronicles 36:16 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “revile” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 22:28 and Matthew 5:11; Ether 7:24 uses it twice. Matthew 5:11-12 is the only place in the King James Bible where reviling and prophets stand together — 'when men shall revile you … for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you'. The other verb is the Old Testament's: “mocked the messengers” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “misused his prophets” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both 2 Chronicles 36:16, which is also the only KJV verse in which mocking and prophets stand together.
provenance.alternative: tools/mediation-check.py was run on Ether 7:24 against 2 Chronicles 36:16 and Matthew 5:11 and reports divergences pointing both ways, one decisive point for each — which is the honest result here, not a failure of the tool. Ether 7:24 has the New Testament's rare verb ('revile', twice) applied to the Old Testament's object ('the prophets'), so it is a fusion of the KJV's two treatments of the theme rather than a following of either. Mediation is recorded as 'direct-NT' because the source verse named is Matthew 5:11 and no earlier Book of Mormon passage is the proximate model; the Chronicles half of the fusion is carried in `composite` and argued here.
provenance.significance: Both sources come with an outcome attached and Ether 7 takes neither. 2 Chronicles 36:16 is the epitaph of Judah: they mocked and misused the prophets 'until the wrath of the LORD arose against his people, till there was no remedy', and the next verse is the Chaldeans. Matthew 5:12 tells the disciples to rejoice at the same treatment because it is what the prophets always got. Ether 7:24-26 supplies the remedy that Chronicles says did not exist — the king prosecutes the mockers, legislates the prophets' freedom of movement, and 'the people were brought unto repentance' — and in doing so removes the occasion for the beatitude, since in Shule's kingdom reviling a prophet is a crime rather than a blessing. Note also what this does beside 1 Nephi 1: Lehi is mocked at Jerusalem and must flee, which is Chronicles' outcome; Shule's Jaredites are the counterfactual.

links.note: 'The people did revile against the prophets, and did mock them … king Shule did execute judgement against all those who did revile against the prophets.' The candidate list proposed nothing at this verse, which is a good illustration of CONVENTIONS §9 — the agreement is lexical and split across a clause boundary, exactly what a contiguous n-gram window cannot see. What is there is two rare verbs, each of which the KJV attaches to prophets in exactly one place, arriving in the same sentence. Held at 'moderate' because neither source supplies a clause and the shared material is two words; what carries it above 'low' is that the two words are not synonyms drawn at random from a wide field, but the King James Bible's only two ways of saying what men do to prophets.

pericopes.text: and he did execute a law throughout all the land, which gave power unto the prophets that they should go whithersoever they would; and by this cause the people were brought unto repentance.

And because the people did repent of their iniquities and idolatries, the Lord did spare them, and they began to prosper again in the land. And it came to pass that Shule begat sons and daughters in his old age.

And there was no more wars in the days of Shule; and he remembered the great things that the Lord had done for his fathers in bringing them across the great deep into the promised land; wherefore he did execute judgement in righteousness all his days.

links.text: And there was no more war unto the five and thirtieth year of the reign of Asa.

provenance.other: “no more war” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 15:19. Judges' recurring peace formula is 'the land had rest', which “had rest” shows in exactly 8 KJV verses and which the Book of Mormon does not use here.
provenance.significance: The singleton is the tail of a sequence, and it is the sequence Ether 7:23-27 runs in order. 2 Chronicles 15: a prophet is sent to the king (15:1-7); the king takes courage and 'put away the abominable idols out of all the land' (15:8, itself a KJV singleton); the people enter a covenant to seek the LORD (15:12); they are spared and given rest (15:15); 'and there was no more war' (15:19). Ether 7: 'there came prophets among the people, which were sent from the Lord' about the people's 'wickedness and idolatry' (7:23); the king executes judgment on those who revile them and passes a law protecting them (7:24-25); 'because the people did repent of their iniquities and idolatries, the Lord did spare them, and they began to prosper again in the land' (7:26); 'and there was no more wars in the days of Shule' (7:27). Five stages, same order, closing on the KJV's one occurrence of the closing phrase. Read the other way, the metalepsis cuts: Asa's rest expires at a stated year — 'unto the five and thirtieth year' — and 2 Chronicles 16 has Asa turn on a seer and imprison him. Ether's phrase is bounded by 'in the days of Shule', which does the same work; the peace is dated, and the next chapter is Ether 8's secret combinations.

links.note: 'And there was no more wars in the days of Shule.' A four-word run on a KJV singleton would be a modest row on its own; what makes it a strong one is that the singleton sits at the end of the only reform narrative in the King James Bible with the same five stages in the same order, and the Book of Mormon has just run all five. The verbal contact and the structural contact are pointing at the same chapter, which is the shape ADJUDICATING §3 asks for. CONVENTIONS §8 applies to the grammar: 1830 reads 'there was no more wars' and 1920 corrected it to 'were'. The 1830's singular verb is what the KJV has ('there was no more war'), with the noun pluralised — so the first edition is closer to its source than the current text is, and the 1920 correction moved the sentence away from Chronicles by tidying it.

links.text: And the people served the LORD all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders that outlived Joshua, who had seen all the great works of the LORD, that he did for Israel.

provenance.other: “great works of the LORD” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Judges 2:7, and “seen all the great” occurs in exactly two, Judges 2:7 and Deuteronomy 11:7. The Book of Mormon's noun is 'things' rather than 'works', and the four-word run it does reproduce, “the Lord had done for”, occurs in exactly one KJV verse — 1 Kings 8:66, at the dedication of the temple. The clause here is therefore Judges 2:7's thought in 1 Kings 8:66's words.
provenance.significance: Judges 2:7-10 is the KJV's statement of how a nation forgets: the people served the LORD all the days of Joshua and of the elders who had seen what he did, 'and there arose another generation after them, which knew not the LORD, nor yet the works which he had done for Israel.' Ether 7:27 is the first half of that, exactly — a ruler characterised by remembering a deliverance he did not witness, and the peace lasting his days and being bounded by them. The second half is Ether 8, which opens on Shule's grandson and the secret combinations. The Book of Mormon has put a Judges 2:7 sentence at the last verse of the chapter and then supplied Judges 2:10.

links.note: 'He remembered the great things that the Lord had done for his fathers in bringing them across the great deep into the promised land.' The candidate list offered 1 Kings 8:66 and 2 Kings 8:4 for the run, and 2 Kings 8:4 is the wrong one: 'the great things that Elisha hath done' is Gehazi entertaining a king with prophet stories, with no deliverance and no fathers. 1 Kings 8:66 supplies the exact four-word run but is a crowd going home cheerful after a festival. Judges 2:7 supplies what the Book of Mormon verse actually is — the formula for a generation that keeps faith because it remembers a founding deliverance, framed by 'all the days' of the leader who remembers, which is Ether 7:27's own frame ('all his days'). Held at 'moderate': the closest wording and the closest sense are in two different verses, and a row that has to take one from each is weaker than one that takes both from the same place.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he begat Omer, and Omer reigned in his stead. And Omer begat Jared; and Jared begat sons and daughters.

And Jared rebelled against his father, and came and dwelt in the land of Heth. And it came to pass that he did flatter much people, because of his cunning words, until he had gained the half of the kingdom.

links.text: Then said the king unto her, What wilt thou, queen Esther? and what is thy request? it shall be even given thee to the half of the kingdom.

provenance.route: Esther 5:3 → KJV → Book of Mormon, possibly through Mark 6:23, which is itself an allusion to Esther
provenance.other: “the half of the kingdom” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Esther 5:3, 5:6 and 7:2, and nowhere else; “half of my kingdom” occurs in exactly one, Mark 6:23. Ether 8:2 and 8:3 read “the half of the kingdom”, which is the Esther article, not Mark's possessive.
provenance.alternative: mediation-check.py on Ether 8:2 against Esther 5:3 and Mark 6:23 reports no decisive divergence: the two candidates do not differ at any point Ether actually reproduces, so this verse cannot settle its own route and mediation is left uncertain. What can be said is that the four words Ether has are Esther's exact form, and that the chapter's narrative — a royal feast, a dancing daughter, and a man's head asked as the price — is Mark's. If the phrase came in through Mark 6:23 it was corrected back toward Mark's own Old Testament model on the way.
provenance.significance: The half-kingdom offer is the KJV's formula for a king who has bound himself in advance to a request he has not yet heard, and in both of its biblical settings the request that follows is a death. Esther asks for Haman; Herodias's daughter asks for John's head. Ether 8 splits the formula in two and uses both halves: the half-kingdom is what Jared extorts at 8:2, and the head is what his daughter extorts at 8:10. Read metaleptically, the chapter has taken a single biblical bargain apart and distributed it across a father and a daughter, so that the reader who recovers either source recovers the other.

links.note: 'He did flatter much people, because of his cunning words, until he had gained the half of the kingdom' — repeated at 8:3, 'when he had gained the half of the kingdom'. The phrase is not generic English: 'the half of the kingdom' is Esther's, three times over, and its only other KJV appearance is Mark 6:23's 'unto the half of my kingdom', which is the Herod feast this chapter is about to reproduce in detail. Ether inverts the transaction. In Esther and in Mark the half-kingdom is offered by a king to a woman he wishes to please; here it is taken from a king by a son who flatters a crowd. The 1830 reads 'much people' where 1920 reads 'many people'; the KJV's own idiom is 'much people' (Mark 6:34, in the same chapter as the feast), so the first edition is the more KJV-sounding of the two. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his quotations.

pericopes.text: And when he had gained the half of the kingdom, he gave battle unto his father, and he did carry away his father into captivity, and did make them serve in captivity.
And now in the days of the reign of Omer, he was in captivity the half of his days. And it came to pass that he begat sons and daughters, among whom were Esrom and Coriantumr;

and they were exceeding angry because of the doings of Jared their brother, insomuch that they did raise an army, and gave battle unto Jared. And it came to pass that they did give battle unto him by night.—

And it came to pass that when they had slew the army of Jared, they were about to slay him also; and he plead with them that they would not slay him, and he would give up the kingdom unto his father. And it came to pass that they did grant unto him his life.
And now Jared became exceeding sorrowful because of the loss of the kingdom, for he had set his heart upon the kingdom, and upon the glory of the world.

links.text: Again, the devil taketh him up into an exceeding high mountain, and sheweth him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them;

provenance.other: “kingdoms of the world” occurs in four KJV verses, two of them the temptation (Matthew 4:8, Luke 4:5); “the glory of them” occurs in exactly two, and both are the temptation (Matthew 4:8, Luke 4:6). The pairing of kingdom with glory-of-the-world is therefore the devil's offer and almost nothing else.
provenance.alternative: 1 John 2:16's 'the pride of life' and Psalm 62:10's 'set not your heart upon them' are the other places the KJV warns against exactly this appetite, but neither supplies the two nouns together. Note also that Ether 3:25 already produced a temptation-scene candidate ('shewed unto him all', Luke 4:5) which this catalogue excluded as wrong-sense at that verse; the phrase lands here instead, where the sense fits.
provenance.significance: Metalepsis in the strict sense: the missing half of the source is what the verse is about. Matthew 4:8-9 is not merely a list of what Jared wants, it is a transaction — the kingdoms and the glory are offered, by the devil, at the price of worship. Ether 8 spends the next nine verses showing how that price is paid: the oaths of 8:14 are sworn by heaven, earth and the swearers' own heads, and 8:16 says outright that they 'were kept up by the power of the devil'. The chapter's diagnosis of Jared is that he accepted the offer Christ refused, and the diagnosis is made by lending him the wording of the offer.

links.note: 'He had set his heart upon the kingdom, and upon the glory of the world.' Matthew 4:8 has 'all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them'; Ether has the same two nouns in the same order with 'of the world' moved from the first to the second. The redistribution is what keeps this an allusion rather than a quotation — no clause survives intact — but the lexical stock is the temptation's and the KJV puts that stock nowhere else. What makes the case more than word-counting is that the chapter goes on to name the devil as the sponsor of the arrangement at 8:16 and 8:25, which is Matthew 4's speaker.

pericopes.text: Now the daughter of Jared being exceeding expert, and seeing the sorrows of her father, thought to devise a plan whereby she could redeem the kingdom unto her father.

Now the daughter of Jared was exceeding fair. And it came to pass that she did talk with her father, and saith unto him, Whereby hath my father so much sorrow? Hath he not read the record which our fathers brought across the great deep? Behold, is there not an account concerning them of old, that they by their secret plans did obtain kingdoms and great glory?

And now therefore, let my father send for Akish, the son of Kimnor; and behold, I am fair, and I will dance before him, and I will please him, that he will desire me to wife; wherefore if he shall desire of thee that ye shall give unto him me to wife, then shall ye say, I will give her if ye will bring unto me the head of my father, the king.

links.text: And she, being before instructed of her mother, said, Give me here John Baptist’s head in a charger.

provenance.route: Matthew 14:6-11 / Mark 6:21-28 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “the head of John” occurs in exactly two KJV verses (Mark 6:24, 6:25) and “in a charger” in exactly four, all of them this one story; the KJV has no other narrative in which a head is named as the price of a dance. Ether's 'bring unto me the head of my father, the king' has no KJV phrase-level match — 'bring me the head' occurs in exactly zero KJV verses — so the borrowing here is of the plot, not of a formula.
provenance.alternative: The mother's part is redistributed. In Matthew 14:8 the girl is 'before instructed of her mother' and asks for what her mother wants; in Ether the daughter instructs the father and asks for the father's own enemy. Judith 12-13 is the other ancient beauty-and-a-head story, but it is outside the KJV canon and its head is taken, not asked for.
provenance.significance: The suppressed correspondence is the identity of the victim. In the Gospels the head asked for is a prophet's, and the girl asks for it on her mother's account; in Ether the head asked for is the asker's own grandfather's, and she asks for it on her father's. The Book of Mormon has taken the most notorious murder-by-banquet in the New Testament and made it worse in exactly one respect — the killing is now inside the family — which is the point the chapter needs, because what is being founded here is not a single murder but a hereditary institution of them.

links.note: 'I will dance before him, and I will please him, that he will desire me to wife; wherefore … then shall ye say, I will give her if ye will bring unto me the head of my father, the king.' Four elements of Matthew 14:6-11 arrive in the source's order: a girl who dances, a man pleased by the dance, a promise made on the strength of it, and a head demanded as payment. The verbal contact is concentrated at 8:11 (see the Matthew 14:6 entry there); what 8:10 supplies is the sequence, and the sequence is not otherwise available in the KJV. Note that Ether tells the plan before it happens and then narrates it again at 8:11-12, so the chapter runs the Gospel scene twice — a duplication that is itself evidence, since it is the plan and not merely the event that has to be borrowed.

pericopes.text: And now Omer was a friend to Akish, wherefore when Jared had sent for Akish, the daughter of Jared danced before him, that she pleased him, insomuch that he desired her to wife. And it came to pass that he said unto Jared, Give her unto me to wife.

links.text: But when Herod’s birthday was kept, the daughter of Herodias danced before them, and pleased Herod.

provenance.other: “danced before” occurs in exactly two KJV verses: 2 Samuel 6:14, where David dances before the LORD, and Matthew 14:6. “and pleased” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 14:6 and Mark 6:22, and both are this story. Only Matthew 14:6 has both, and Ether 8:11 has both. “danced before him” as a string occurs in exactly zero KJV verses, so the pronoun is Ether's own.
provenance.alternative: Mark 6:22 supplies the same two verbs but separates them ('came in, and danced, and pleased Herod'); Matthew's 'danced before them, and pleased Herod' is the form Ether reproduces, and Matthew is also the only one of the two to use the preposition.
provenance.significance: The other KJV verse that says 'danced before' is 2 Samuel 6:14, David before the ark — the one dance in scripture that is worship. Set the two occurrences side by side and the King James phrase turns out to cover the whole range: a man dancing before God with all his might, and a girl dancing before a king to get a man killed. Ether 8 takes the second and makes it the founding act of the Jaredite secret combinations, so that the institution which will destroy two civilisations begins, in the KJV's own vocabulary, as the inverse of David's worship.

links.note: 'The daughter of Jared danced before him, that she pleased him, insomuch that he desired her to wife.' Against Matthew 14:6: 'the daughter of Herodias danced before them, and pleased Herod.' The frame is reproduced slot for slot — the-daughter-of-X danced before Y and pleased Y — with every referent substituted, which is precisely why this is catalogued as an allusion and not a quotation under CONVENTIONS §2: no clause survives with its own words intact, only with its own shape. It is well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his quotations. The rarity is what carries it: the KJV uses 'danced before' twice in the whole Bible and 'pleased' after a dance once, and Ether has the one verse that contains both, in a chapter that has just asked for a head and is about to get it.

pericopes.text: And Jared said unto him, I will give her unto you, if ye will bring unto me the head of my father, the king.

And it came to pass that Akish gathered in unto the house of Jared all his kinsfolks, and saith unto them, Will ye swear unto me that ye will be faithful unto me in the thing which I shall desire of you?

links.text: And they said unto him, We are come down to bind thee, that we may deliver thee into the hand of the Philistines. And Samson said unto them, Swear unto me, that ye will not fall upon me yourselves.

provenance.other: “swear unto me that ye will” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Judges 15:12, though 'swear unto me' alone occurs in six. “his kinsfolks” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Kings 16:11 and 2 Kings 10:11, and in both the kinsfolk of a royal house are the ones being exterminated — the opposite of the role Akish's kinsfolk play here, which is why that coincidence is registered rather than catalogued (see the exclusion at 8:13).
provenance.alternative: Genesis 21:23, Joshua 2:12 and 1 Samuel 30:15 are the other KJV oath-extractions, and each is a request for mercy from someone with the upper hand. Judges 15:12 is preferred on the six-word run, which is a KJV singleton.
provenance.significance: The suppressed half of Judges 15:12 is what the oath is for. Samson makes his own tribesmen swear before he lets them bind him, and the content of the oath is that they will not kill him themselves — an oath extracted to guarantee a life. Akish uses the same formula on his own kindred to guarantee deaths, and the penalty clause at 8:14 makes the reversal explicit: whoever breaks this oath forfeits the head that Samson's oath was protecting.

links.note: 'Will ye swear unto me that ye will be faithful unto me in the thing which I shall desire of you?' The six-word run 'swear unto me that ye will' is a KJV singleton, and its one home is Samson's demand of the men of Judah. The machine stream ranked this candidate first for the verse, which is unusual — the n-gram stream is a recall floor and rare boilerplate normally crowds the top (CONVENTIONS §9) — and here the run is not boilerplate: it is an oath formula with a person, a clause of content, and a specified beneficiary, all of which Ether keeps. What Ether adds is the secrecy: Samson states the terms of his oath in the same breath, and Akish will not state his until the swearing is done.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they all sware unto him, by the God of Heaven, and also by the Heavens, and also by the earth, and by their heads, that whoso should vary from the assistance which Akish desired, should lose his head; and whoso should divulge whatsoever thing Akish made known unto them, the same should lose his life.

links.text: Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black.

provenance.other: “by thy head” and “swear by thy head” each occur in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:36. “neither by the earth” occurs in exactly one, James 5:12, and 'by the earth' in exactly two, Matthew 5:35 and James 5:12. Swearing by heaven and by earth is therefore available in two places; swearing by one's head is available in one, and Ether has it.
provenance.alternative: James 5:12 gives heaven and earth in the same breath and is the other KJV prohibition of oaths, but it has no head, and it is the head that carries this verse. Matthew 23:16-22, the other oath passage, swears by the temple, the gold, the altar and heaven — none of which is here.
provenance.significance: Matthew 5:34-36 forbids swearing by heaven, by the earth, by Jerusalem, and by your head, and gives a reason for each: heaven is God's throne, earth his footstool, Jerusalem the great King's city, and your head is not yours — 'thou canst not make one hair white or black.' Ether 8:14 collects three of the four, drops only the one a Jaredite could not use, and then supplies the missing reason itself: the head sworn by is forfeit, 'should lose his head.' The oath Jesus forbids because a man has no power over his own head is here sworn precisely by staking the head, and the head staked is duly collected: at Ether 9:5 the men bound by this oath 'obtained the head of his father-in-law, as he sat upon his throne'. Matthew 5:37's verdict on all such oaths, 'whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil', is what Ether 8:16 restates as doctrine: the oaths 'were kept up by the power of the devil'.

links.note: 'They all sware unto him, by the God of Heaven, and also by the Heavens, and also by the earth, and by their heads.' Four objects of swearing in one clause, three of which are Matthew 5:34-36's in Matthew's own order — heaven, earth, head — with the fourth, Jerusalem, dropped, which is the only one of the four that a Jaredite oath in the New World could not plausibly use. 'By thy head' is a KJV singleton and it is not a natural English idiom that a writer would arrive at independently; the earth-and-heaven pair is available in James 5:12 as well, but the head is available in one verse only. That the chapter should build its oath out of the Sermon on the Mount's prohibition of oaths is the finding: this is the KJV's most explicit condemnation of swearing, quarried for the wording of the most consequential oath in the Book of Mormon. The machine streams did not see it — the shared material is three two-word phrases distributed across a long clause, which contiguous windows cannot reach (CONVENTIONS §9).

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that thus they did agree with Akish. And Akish did administer unto them the oaths which was given by them of old, who also sought power, which had been handed down even from Cain, who was a murderer from the beginning.

links.text: Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do. He was a murderer from the beginning, and abode not in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it.

provenance.other: “a murderer from the beginning” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 8:44. So does “father the devil”, and so does “the father of it”, the phrase Ether reworks at 8:25 into 'the father of all lies'.
provenance.alternative: 1 John 3:12 is the KJV's other verse about Cain as a killer — 'not as Cain, who was of that wicked one, and slew his brother' — and it supplies the theology Ether 8:15 wants, Cain as the devil's man. But it supplies none of the words. Genesis 4:8 supplies the murder and none of the words either.
provenance.significance: In John 8:44 the murderer from the beginning is the devil, and the sentence is Jesus telling opponents who their father is. Ether 8:15 hands the predicate to Cain instead — 'handed down even from Cain, who was a murderer from the beginning' — and then, ten verses later at 8:25, hands it back to the devil, 'that same liar which hath caused man to commit murder from the beginning'. The chapter has split John 8:44's two charges, murderer and liar, between the first human killer and his sponsor, and the split is what lets the chapter claim an unbroken chain of transmission from Eden to the Jaredites to Moroni's own Gentile readers. Whether 'who' at 8:15 refers to Cain or past Cain to the devil is left unresolved by the grammar, and the ambiguity is productive: John 8:44 is the verse that makes both readings the same reading.

links.note: 'Which had been handed down even from Cain, who was a murderer from the beginning.' Five words reproduced exactly from a KJV singleton, in a clause whose subject has been changed from the devil to Cain. Catalogued as a quotation on the CONVENTIONS §2 rule rather than on length — it is far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his thirty-six — because a complete predicate is reproduced verbatim from a verse that is unmistakably its source. The 1830 variant in this verse is elsewhere ('the oaths which was given by them of old', corrected to 'were' in 1920) and does not bear on the judgment. Note what the borrowing does to the chronology: a first-century sentence about the devil, spoken in the temple, is used to date the origin of Jaredite oath-craft to Cain, and the Book of Mormon's own doctrine of secret combinations — carried forward at Helaman 6:26-30 and back to 2 Nephi 2:18 — depends on it.

pericopes.text: And they were kept up by the power of the devil to administer these oaths unto the people, to keep them in darkness, to help such as sought power, to gain power, and to murder, and to plunder, and to lie, and to commit all manner of wickedness and whoredoms.—

And it was the daughter of Jared which put it into his heart to search up these things of old; and Jared put it into the heart of Akish; wherefore Akish administered it unto his kindreds and friends, leading them away by fair promises to do whatsoever thing he desired.
And it came to pass that they formed a secret combination, even as they of old; which combination is a most abominable and wicked above all, in the sight of God:
for the Lord worketh not in secret combinations, neither doth he will that man should shed blood, but in all things hath forbidden it, from the beginning of man.
And now I, Moroni, do not write the manner of their oaths and combinations, for it hath been made known unto me that they are had among all people, and they are had among the Lamanites,
and they have caused the destruction of this people of which I am now speaking, and also the destruction of the people of Nephi;

and whatsoever nation shall uphold such secret combinations, to get power and gain, until they shall spread over the nation, behold, they shall be destroyed, for the Lord will not suffer that the blood of his saints, which shall be shed by them, shall always cry unto him from the ground for vengeance upon them, and yet he avengeth them not;

links.text: And he said, What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground.

provenance.other: “blood crieth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 4:10, and “crieth unto me” in exactly two, of which the other (Exodus 22:27) is about a pledged garment. “from the ground” occurs in four, three of them Ezekiel's temple measurements. On the New Testament side, “avenge our blood” and “How long, O Lord” are each KJV singletons, and both are Revelation 6:10.
provenance.alternative: mediation-check.py against Hebrews 12:24, the New Testament's one re-use of Abel's crying blood, returns a decisive result for Genesis: Ether has 'crieth … from the ground', not 'the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel'. So the Genesis form is direct, even though the second half of the verse is drawing on Revelation.
provenance.significance: Two crying-blood passages stand at the two ends of the Christian canon, and Ether 8:22 fuses them. Genesis 4:10 is God's question to the first murderer; Revelation 6:9-10 is the martyrs under the altar asking how long before their blood is avenged, and receiving the answer that they must wait. Ether takes Abel's ground and Revelation's saints and adds the clause that neither source states outright — 'and yet he avengeth them not' — which is Revelation 6:10's unanswered 'How long' turned into a proposition. Recover both contexts and the verse is claiming that the delay of judgment on a nation that shelters secret combinations is the same delay the martyrs are told to endure: not indifference, but a stay.

links.note: 'The blood of his saints, which shall be shed by them, shall always cry unto him from the ground for vengeance upon them, and yet he avengeth them not.' The spine is Genesis 4:10 — blood, crying, from the ground — in a chapter that has already named Cain at 8:15, so the Abel allusion arrives with its murderer already on the page. The saints and the vengeance are Revelation's: 'blood of the saints' is a KJV singleton at Revelation 17:6, and Revelation 6:10's martyrs cry for exactly the vengeance Ether says is withheld. The 1830 reads 'he avengeth them not' where 1920 reads 'avenge'; the 1830 form is the KJV's own third-person inflection and the later edition moved away from it, the reverse of the direction noted at 1 Nephi 1:20 (CONVENTIONS §8). The formula recurs two verses later — 'they cry from the dust for vengeance' — with 'ground' replaced by the Book of Mormon's own 'dust', which is Isaiah 29:4's word and the book's standing metaphor for its own voice.

pericopes.text: wherefore, O ye Gentiles, it is wisdom in God that these things should be shewn unto you, that thereby ye may repent of your sins, and suffer not that these murderous combinations shall get above you, which are built up to get power and gain, and the work, yea, even the work of destruction come upon you; yea, even the sword of the justice of the eternal God, shall fall upon you, to your overthrow and destruction, if ye shall suffer these things to be;

wherefore the Lord commandeth you, when ye shall see these things come among you, that ye shall awake to a sense of your awful situation, because of this secret combination which shall be among you, or wo be unto it, because of the blood of them which have been slain: for they cry from the dust for vengeance upon it, and also upon those who build it up.

links.text: So ye in like manner, when ye shall see these things come to pass, know that it is nigh, even at the doors.

provenance.other: “when ye shall see these things” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 13:29; “see these things come” in exactly two, Mark 13:29 and Luke 21:31. Matthew 24:33 has the same sentence with 'all these things' and without 'come'. The six-word run Ether reproduces is therefore Mark's alone.
provenance.alternative: Jeremiah 42:18's 'upon you, when ye shall' is a four-word run in a warning of judgment on a people who go down to Egypt, and it is the only Old Testament competitor; it has neither 'these things' nor the sign-recognition structure.
provenance.significance: The suppressed half is the apodosis. In Mark 13:29 the sentence completes itself with 'know that it is nigh, even at the doors' — the sign means the end has arrived at the threshold. Ether 8:24 borrows the protasis and substitutes its own apodosis: when you see these things, 'awake to a sense of your awful situation'. The effect is to install the secret combination in the place the Olivet discourse reserves for the signs of the end, so that a Gentile nation which finds such a thing among itself is being told it is reading an eschatological sign, not a political problem.

links.note: 'When ye shall see these things come among you, that ye shall awake to a sense of your awful situation.' Six words of Mark 13:29 in order, with 'to pass' replaced by 'among you' — a substitution that does real work, since it converts a sign observed at a distance into a condition found at home. The machine stream ranked this candidate first for the verse and was right, which is worth recording because it is not the usual pattern (CONVENTIONS §9). Confidence is held at moderate rather than high because the Olivet formula is common property across three Gospels and the Book of Mormon uses sign-recognition language freely; what points to Mark specifically is only the exact six-word string, and a writer reaching for the discourse from memory could land on it without meaning Mark.

pericopes.text: For it cometh to pass that whoso buildeth it up, seeketh to overthrow the freedom of all lands, nations and countries; and it bringeth to pass the destruction of all people: for it is built up by the devil, which is the father of all lies; even that same liar which beguiled our first parents; yea, even that same liar which hath caused man to commit murder from the beginning; which hath hardened the hearts of men, that they have murdered the prophets, and stoned them, and cast them out from the beginning.

links.text: And the LORD God said unto the woman, What is this that thou hast done? And the woman said, The serpent beguiled me, and I did eat.

provenance.route: Genesis 3:13 → KJV → Book of Mormon, probably by way of 2 Nephi 2:18
provenance.other: “beguiled” occurs in five KJV verses, of which two are the serpent's: Genesis 3:13, where Eve says 'The serpent beguiled me', and 2 Corinthians 11:3, 'as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty'. The other three (Genesis 29:25, Numbers 25:18, Joshua 9:22) are Laban, Peor and the Gibeonites. 'First parents' is not a KJV phrase at all. The KJV-specificity is recorded as uncertain rather than yes for that reason: only one word of this link is King James English, 'beguiled', and at five KJV verses it is too widely distributed to fix a version; the phrase that carries the sense, 'our first parents', is not biblical English at all but the Book of Mormon's own, standing in thirteen of its verses from 1 Nephi 5:11 onward.
provenance.alternative: mediation-check.py against Genesis 3:13 and 2 Corinthians 11:3 finds no decisive divergence — the two candidates do not differ at any word Ether reproduces — so this verse cannot settle its own route.
