The stronger consideration is internal. 2 Nephi 2:18 already reads 'that old serpent, which is the Devil, which is the father of all lies', and Ether 8:25 has 'the devil, which is the father of all lies; even that same liar which beguiled our first parents' — the same two clauses in the same order. Helaman 6:26-29 is closer still: 'that same being who did entice our first parents to partake of the forbidden fruit … that same being who did plot with Cain … and he hath brought it forth from the beginning of man', which is Ether 8:25's whole argument, in the same demonstrative construction ('that same being' / 'that same liar'), attached to the same three items — Eden, Cain, and the transmission of secret murder. 'Our first parents' is itself a Book of Mormon phrase and not a KJV one, standing in thirteen verses from 1 Nephi 5:11 onward. The proximate model is therefore the Book of Mormon's own editorial theology rather than either biblical verse directly, and mediation is recorded as uncertain for that reason. The epithet identifying the serpent as the devil is Revelation 12:9 and 20:2, not Genesis, so that identification also reaches Ether already made.
provenance.significance: Hardy's apparatus cross-references Genesis 3:1-7 here, the temptation narrative itself; the verbal contact is six verses further on, at Genesis 3:13, which is the verse in which the deception is named as deception — and named by its victim. That matters for what Ether 8:25 is doing. The chapter is building a genealogy of the secret combination that runs devil → Eden → Cain → 'them of old' → the Jaredites → the Gentiles, and each stage is attested by a scriptural sentence rather than a narrative: 'beguiled' from Eve's confession, 'a murderer from the beginning' from John 8:44, 'the prophets, and stoned them' from Matthew 23:37. The verse is a chain of citations offered as a chain of custody.

links.note: 'For it is built up by the devil, which is the father of all lies; even that same liar which beguiled our first parents.' The word that carries the link is 'beguiled', which the KJV gives to the serpent twice and to nobody else who matters. Ether generalises Eve's 'beguiled me' to 'beguiled our first parents', which is neither Genesis's singular nor Paul's 'Eve' — a widening that fits the chapter's argument, since what is at stake is the origin of a practice binding on all descendants and not the guilt of one person. Catalogued at moderate: the vocabulary is thin, one word plus a shared referent, and the proximate model is probably 2 Nephi 2:18 and Helaman 6:26-27 rather than either biblical verse (see provenance). Status is 'majority' rather than 'novel' because the association is Hardy's too — his apparatus cross-references Genesis 3 at this verse — and the catalogue's contribution is only to say where in Genesis 3 the wording is. Recorded partly to discharge Hardy's cross-reference to Genesis 3 at this verse, and to say where in Genesis 3 the wording actually is.

links.text: Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do. He was a murderer from the beginning, and abode not in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it.

provenance.route: John 8:44 → KJV → Book of Mormon, with 2 Nephi 2:18 as the likely proximate model for 'the father of all lies'
provenance.other: Three phrases of this one verse are KJV singletons: 'father the devil', 'a murderer from the beginning', and 'the father of it'. Ether 8:25 reproduces the first two and rewrites the third. 'Father of all lies' occurs in exactly zero KJV verses and in exactly two Book of Mormon verses, 2 Nephi 2:18 and here.
provenance.alternative: Revelation 12:9 and 20:2 supply 'that old serpent, which is the Devil', and 2 Nephi 2:18 joins that epithet to 'the father of all lies'; the Book of Mormon's stock phrase is therefore a fusion made before Ether 8, and this verse inherits it. What Ether 8:25 adds on its own account is the murder half, which is John 8:44's and is already in play at 8:15.
provenance.significance: John 8:44 charges the devil with two things in one breath — he was a murderer from the beginning, and he is a liar and the father of it — and Ether 8:25 is the only place in scripture, biblical or Book of Mormon, where both charges are laid in a single sentence and made the explanation of a political institution. The verse reads as an exposition of John 8:44 rather than a quotation of it: the lying accounts for Eden, the murder accounts for Cain, and the combination of the two accounts for a conspiracy that lies in order to kill. Read metaleptically, the suppressed context is Jesus telling his hearers whose children they are — which is exactly the accusation Moroni is about to level at the Gentile reader in 8:23-24.

links.note: The second draw on John 8:44 in ten verses (see 8:15). Here the verse supplies both of its predicates at once: 'built up by the devil, which is the father of all lies' answers 'he is a liar, and the father of it', and 'that same liar which hath caused man to commit murder from the beginning' answers 'he was a murderer from the beginning' — with one telling change, that the devil no longer murders but causes man to murder, which is what a doctrine of transmitted oaths requires. The recurrence is the argument for high confidence: a single distant echo of a famous verse proves little, but a chapter that uses the same verse twice, for two different links in the same chain of descent, is using it deliberately. Note also that 'that same liar' is repeated twice within the verse, a demonstrative anaphora with no antecedent in Ether — the antecedent is John 8:44.

links.text: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!

provenance.route: Matthew 23:37 → KJV → Book of Mormon, but reaching Ether 8:25 through the Book of Mormon's own earlier uses of the formula (1 Nephi 1:20; Helaman 13:25, 13:33; 3 Nephi 8:25) rather than freshly from Matthew
provenance.other: “killest the prophets” and “stonest them” each occur in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 23:37 and Luke 13:34, and nowhere else. The word 'murdered' occurs in exactly zero KJV verses — the King James Bible has 'murder', 'murderer', 'murderers' and 'murders' but never the past participle — so Ether's 'murdered the prophets' is not a KJV phrase at all, and the substitution of 'murdered' for 'killest' is the Book of Mormon's own, made in a chapter whose subject is murder.
provenance.alternative: Acts 7:52-58 is the serious competitor and should be recorded as such: Stephen's speech has the prophets persecuted and slain, calls his hearers 'murderers', and ends four verses later with 'cast him out of the city, and stoned him' — which supplies the third member of Ether's triad, 'cast them out', that Matthew 23:37 does not have. The catalogue prefers Matthew because the two-word sequence 'the prophets, and stoned them' matches Matthew's 'the prophets, and stonest them' exactly in order and in construction, while Acts 7:58's casting out and stoning are done to Stephen and in the reverse order.
provenance.significance: MEDIATION, FLAGGED FOR WILSON. The route here is the shape the enum cannot express: a New Testament source reaching a verse through an earlier Book of Mormon passage. The triad is a fixed Book of Mormon formula before Ether 8 ever uses it — 1 Nephi 1:20, 'the prophets of old, whom they had cast out and stoned and slain'; Helaman 13:25, 'ye would not have slain the prophets; ye would not have stoned them, and cast them out'; Helaman 13:33 and 3 Nephi 8:25, both 'killed the prophets, and stoned them, and cast them out' — and Ether 8:25 is its last occurrence, in Moroni's editorial voice, with the whole record in front of him. Recorded as 'direct-NT' because the ultimate source is Matthew 23:37 and there is no enum value for the actual route; 'uncertain' would understate what is known, which is a great deal. Compare 1 Nephi 4:14, where this catalogue stretched 'OT-via-earlier-BoM' over the same shape and flagged the name as wrong; the two rows should be reconciled when the enum is fixed, and the value wanted in both places is 'via-earlier-BoM'. Metaleptically the borrowing is doing what the formula always does in this book: Matthew 23:37 is a lament over a city about to be destroyed for what it did to its prophets, and every Book of Mormon use of it stands next to a destruction — Jerusalem's at 1 Nephi 1, Zarahemla's at Helaman 13 and 3 Nephi 8, and here the Jaredites' and the Nephites' together, with the Gentile reader named as the next candidate.

links.note: 'Which hath hardened the hearts of men, that they have murdered the prophets, and stoned them, and cast them out from the beginning.' Matthew 23:37 has 'thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee' — the noun, the conjunction and the second verb in Ether's order, from a phrase the KJV uses in two verses only. Ether changes the first verb to 'murdered', a word the King James Bible never uses, and adds a third member, 'cast them out'. Both changes are the Book of Mormon's own and both are older than this verse: the triad is standing formula by Helaman 13, and Moroni is reciting it rather than reaching for Matthew. That is the finding, and it is why the mediation field is flagged rather than answered — see provenance.significance. What the formula contributes to the chapter is its last link: the same devil who lied in Eden and taught Cain to kill is now the author of the killing of prophets, which is the Book of Mormon's standing indictment of the societies it watches collapse.

pericopes.text: Wherefore I, Moroni, am commanded to write these things, that evil may be done away, and that the time may come that satan may have no power upon the hearts of the children of men, but that they may be persuaded to do good continually, that they may come unto the fountain of all righteousness and be saved.

links.text: And God saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.

provenance.route: Genesis 6:5 → KJV → Book of Mormon, if at all
provenance.other: “only evil continually” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 6:5. “do good continually” occurs in exactly zero KJV verses and in five Book of Mormon verses (Mosiah 5:2, Alma 41:14, Alma 63:2, Ether 8:26, Moroni 7:13), two of them Moroni's own.
provenance.alternative: Psalm 14:1 and 53:1, 'there is none that doeth good', are the other KJV sentences that make continual well-doing the thing humanity fails at, but neither has 'continually' and neither is antediluvian.
provenance.significance: If the echo is real it closes the chapter where it opened. Ether 8 traces the secret combinations to Cain and to the devil who taught him, and Genesis 6:5 is the verdict that closes that same antediluvian sequence in Genesis — the wickedness of man was great, and the imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually, which is the sentence that brings the flood. Moroni ends by praying for the opposite of it, hearts free of Satan and men persuaded to do good continually, and the reader who hears Genesis 6:5 underneath hears what the alternative is.

links.note: 'That satan may have no power upon the hearts of the children of men, but that they may be persuaded to do good continually.' The proposal is that this is Genesis 6:5 inverted: the hearts of men, and a moral quality held continually, with 'only evil' turned into 'good'. Recorded at low confidence and openly as a guess.
links.whyNot: 'Do good continually' is Moroni's own idiom and the Book of Mormon's before him — it stands at Mosiah 5:2, Alma 41:14, Alma 63:2 and Moroni 7:13, where Moroni uses it of that which is of God 'inviteth and enticeth to do good continually'. A phrase a writer uses five times across the book is his own vocabulary, and the simplest account of Ether 8:26 is that he reached for it here as he does elsewhere, with no Genesis behind it. Nothing but the adverb is shared with Genesis 6:5, and 'continually' is common in the KJV. A reader who declines this link is not making a mistake.

pericopes.text: And now I, Moroni, proceed with my record. Therefore behold, it came to pass that because of the secret combinations of Akish and his friends, behold they did overthrow the kingdom of Omer;
nevertheless, the Lord was merciful unto Omer, and also to his sons and to his daughters, which were not, or which did not seek his destruction.

links.text: And while he lingered, the men laid hold upon his hand, and upon the hand of his wife, and upon the hand of his two daughters; the LORD being merciful unto him: and they brought him forth, and set him without the city.

provenance.other: “being merciful unto him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 19:16. The looser “merciful unto” is common (Deuteronomy 21:8, Psalm 67:1 and others), but in every other instance it is a petition addressed to God, not a narrator's report that God was merciful to a named man who then left a doomed place.
provenance.significance: Genesis 19:16 is the sentence in which the KJV records a rescue rather than a deliverance: Lot does not escape, he is taken by the hand and set outside a city about to be destroyed, and the clause explaining why is the bare “the LORD being merciful unto him”. Ether 9:1-3 is built on the same asymmetry. The kingdom falls; Omer is not vindicated, restored or avenged; he is simply removed, with his family, before the fire. Recovering Genesis 19 also recovers what the Jaredite record keeps refusing to say — Lot's rescue is the aftermath of an assize in which a city was found to have no righteous men in it, and Ether 9:6 has just reported that the secret society “had corrupted the hearts of all the people”. The one man walked out with his daughters is, in both texts, the whole of what could be saved.

links.note: 'The Lord was merciful unto Omer, and also to his sons and to his daughters, which were not, or which did not seek his destruction.' The Genesis clause is the only place in the King James Bible where mercy is predicated of the LORD toward a single named man in exactly this construction, and it introduces exactly this scene: the departure of a righteous householder, with his sons and daughters, out of a place whose destruction is already settled. Ether 9:2-3 supplies each element in Genesis 19's order — mercy, the family enumerated as sons and daughters, the warning, the departure from the land — and the Jaredite text even preserves Genesis 19's oddity of counting the household by its daughters. What holds the row at moderate rather than higher is that the Book of Mormon uses the ordinary past tense ('was merciful unto') where the KJV has the participle ('being merciful unto'), so the borrowing is of a collocation rather than of a string.

pericopes.text: And the Lord warned Omer in a dream, that he should depart out of the land; wherefore Omer departed out of the land with his family, and travelled many days, and came over and passed hy the hill of Shim, and came over by the place where the Nephites were destroyed, and from thence eastward, and came to a place which was called Ablom, by the seashore, and there he pitched his tent, and also his sons and his daughters, and all his household, save it were Jared and his family.

links.text: And being warned of God in a dream that they should not return to Herod, they departed into their own country another way.

provenance.other: “warned of God in a dream” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 2:12 and Matthew 2:22; the participle 'warned' with a dream occurs nowhere else in the King James Bible. “in a dream” occurs in exactly fourteen KJV verses, so the dream alone would prove nothing — it is the pairing with 'warned' that is Matthean and nothing but Matthean. The trailing clause 'depart out of the land' is not part of this argument: “depart out of the land” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 9:7, of the Exodus, and there is no other contact with it here.
provenance.significance: Matthew 2 is the King James Bible's one sustained account of a dream-warning that saves a life from a king who is killing to secure a succession, and it is a story the Jaredite chapters have been converging on for two chapters: Herod slaughters children to protect a throne, and the dream tells the endangered household to travel and stay away. Ether 9 is that plot with the roles filled by Akish, who has just taken a kingdom by beheading, will starve his own son to death in prison (9:7), and ends by fighting a war against the rest of his sons. Read Matthew back into it and Omer's flight acquires Matthew's shape as well as its wording — the removal is not an escape from the story but a preservation of the line that will be restored (9:13) once the murderer's house has consumed itself. Moroni's phrasing lets the reader see Herod behind Akish without ever naming him.

links.note: 'And the Lord warned Omer in a dream, that he should depart out of the land.' The KJV's verb for a divine dream-warning is confined to Matthew 2, and this is the whole of the King James vocabulary for it; Genesis has God coming to Abimelech and to Laban 'in a dream by night' and saying what he wants, never warning. Matthew 2:12 warns the wise men, Matthew 2:13 sends the household away by the same means, Matthew 2:22 warns Joseph a second time and turns him aside — and each warning is about getting clear of a murderous king. Ether 9:3 compresses all three: a warning, in a dream, to depart, from a court where the king has just been beheaded and the throne taken by the man who did it.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Jared was anointed king over the people, by the hand of wickedness; and he gave unto Akish his daughter to wife.

And it came to pass that Akish sought the life of his father-in-law; and he applied unto those whom he had sworn by the oath of the ancients, and they obtained the head of his father-in-law, as he sat upon his throne, giving audience to his people:

links.text: And immediately the king sent an executioner, and commanded his head to be brought: and he went and beheaded him in the prison,

provenance.other: “his head in a charger” and “gave it to the damsel” each occur in exactly one KJV verse, both Mark 6:28, and neither is echoed here. Ether's own diction at this verse is not the KJV's: “sat upon his throne” occurs in exactly two KJV verses (2 Kings 13:13 and Acts 12:21), and 'obtained the head' is in none.
provenance.significance: Mark's scene turns on the collision of an oath with a request the swearer never anticipated: Herod is 'exceeding sorry', and kills anyway, 'for his oath's sake'. Ether 9:5 is the moment the Jaredite version of that oath comes due, and Moroni has altered it in the one way that makes it worse. In Mark the oath is rash and public and its victim is outside the family; in Ether the oath is a secret combination sworn by kinsfolk (8:13-14), and the head it finally produces is not the one bargained for in chapter 8 but the head of the man who did the bargaining. Herodias's daughter asks for the head of a prophet; Jared's daughter asks for the head of a king, and the mechanism she builds kills her own father with it. Recovering Mark makes the Jaredite sentence a study in what an oath does once it is loose in a family.

links.note: 'He applied unto those whom he had sworn by the oath of the ancients, and they obtained the head of his father-in-law, as he sat upon his throne.' The chapter-8 material is the dance for a head, the pleased king, the promise, and the sworn confederates; 9:5 is the delivery, and it keeps Mark's two structural features — the head is fetched by men the swearer sends rather than by the swearer, and the killing is transacted as the discharge of an oath. Filed as figural because the verbal case for the type-scene sits in chapter 8 ('I will dance before him, and I will please him... bring unto me the head of my father, the king'), not here; 9:5 shares with Mark 6:27 no distinctive string, only the sequence. It is recorded at this verse anyway because this is where the borrowed plot pays out, and a reader who has been shown the dance and not the head has been shown half a borrowing.
links.whyNot: At this verse the case is entirely narrative; every word Ether uses here could have been written by someone who had never read Mark 6. The row stands or falls with the chapter-8 material, and if that is adjudicated to a different source — the daughter's dance has its own claimants — this row should follow it rather than be defended on its own.

pericopes.text: for so great had been the spreading of this wicked and secret society, that it had corrupted the hearts of all the people; therefore Jared was murdered upon his throne, and Akish reigned in his stead.
And it came to pass that Akish began to be jealous of his son, therefore he shut him up in prison, and kept him upon a little or no food, until he had suffered death.
And now the brother of him that suffered death, (and his name was Nimrah,) was angry with his father, because of that which his father had done unto his brother.
And it came to pass that Nimrah gathered together a small number of men, and fled out of the land, and came over and dwelt with Omer.
And it came to pass that Akish begat other sons, and they won the hearts of the people, notwithstanding they had sworn unto him to do all manner of iniquity, according to that which he desired.

links.text: And on this manner did Absalom to all Israel that came to the king for judgment: so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.

provenance.other: “stole the hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 15:6. “hearts of the men of Israel” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Samuel 15:6 and 15:13, both of Absalom. “long war between” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 3:1. The machine's proposal here was Joshua 7:5, on the strength of 'the hearts of the people' — but Joshua's hearts melt in fear, which is the opposite operation.
provenance.significance: The Absalom narrative is the King James Bible's anatomy of a coup mounted from inside a king's own house, and it runs in the order Ether 9:10-13 runs: the sons court the people, the people's hearts go over, the father is driven from his capital, a long war follows, and the father returns to what was his. Ether even reproduces the detail that makes 2 Samuel 15 disturbing — the sons do not seize the kingdom, they are given it, by a people who prefer them. What the borrowing costs Akish is any claim to be an exception: the man who took the throne by an oath sworn on his kinsmen's heads loses it to his own sons doing a milder version of the same thing, and the KJV sentence Moroni reaches for is the one where a beloved son does it to David.

links.note: 'And it came to pass that Akish begat other sons, and they won the hearts of the people.' The KJV has one sentence of this shape, and it is the hinge of Absalom's rebellion. Ether has changed one word — 'won' for 'stole' — and the change is legible: Absalom's theft is a moral verdict the narrator of 2 Samuel passes, while Moroni is describing sons who buy what Absalom took, and who pay for it in the next verse ('the sons of Akish did offer them money'). The sequence continues to track: 2 Samuel 3:1 supplies the KJV's one 'long war between' two houses of a single royal family, and Ether 9:12 has a war between Akish and his sons 'which lasted for the space of many years'; 2 Samuel 19 restores David to his inheritance, and Ether 9:13 restores Omer to his.

pericopes.text: Now the people of Akish were desirous for gain, even as Akish was desirous for power; wherefore the sons of Akish did offer them money, by the which means they drew away the more part of the people after them;

links.text: Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them.

provenance.other: “draw away” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 20:30. “the more part” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 19:32 and Acts 27:12. 'After them' on its own is worthless — it occurs in fifty-seven KJV verses — and the row rests on the verb, not on the preposition.
provenance.significance: Paul's warning to the Ephesian elders is about a specific kind of loss: not persecution from outside, but defection engineered from within, 'of your own selves shall men arise'. Ether 9:10-11 is that sentence turned into narrative and given a price list. Akish's own sons are the men who arise; what they speak is not perverse doctrine but money; and the flock they draw away is the confederacy Akish built by oath. The metaleptic gain is in Acts 20:29, the verse Paul says it in service of — 'grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock'. Moroni's secret combination has no flock and no shepherd, and the wolves are already inside; what Acts contemplates as a danger to a church, Ether reports as the ordinary physics of a conspiracy, which cannot be betrayed because there was never anything in it but appetite.

links.note: 'Wherefore the sons of Akish did offer them money, by the which means they drew away the more part of the people after them.' The construction is Acts 20:30's and no other verse's: to draw away a body of people after oneself. The supporting phrase points the same way — 'the more part' is not ordinary King James English for a majority, and both of its occurrences are in the Acts narrative of Paul's third journey, one of them in the Ephesian riot two chapters before this speech. Ether's substitution of money for 'speaking perverse things' is the chapter's own contribution: Acts imagines a schism made of words, Ether reports one made of purchase, and 9:11's opening clause ('the people of Akish were desirous for gain, even as Akish was desirous for power') is the gloss Moroni supplies for it.

pericopes.text: and there began to be a war between the sons of Akish and Akish, which lasted for the space of many years; yea, unto the destruction of nearly all the people of the kingdom; yea, even all, save it were thirty souls, and they which fled with the house of Omer;
wherefore Omer was restored again to the land of his inheritance.
And it came to pass that Omer began to be old; nevertheless, in his old age he begat Emer; and he anointed Emer to be king to reign in his stead.

And after that he had anointed Emer to be king, he saw peace in the land for the space of two years, and he died, having seen exceeding many days, which were full of sorrow. And it came to pass that Emer did reign in his stead, and did fill the steps of his father.

links.text: So when David was old and full of days, he made Solomon his son king over Israel.

provenance.other: “old and full of days” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Genesis 35:29, 1 Chronicles 23:1 and Job 42:17. The looser “full of days” occurs in exactly six, and 'full of sorrow' in none.
provenance.significance: 'Old and full of days' is the King James Bible's formula of a completed life, and the Chronicler uses it for exactly the transaction Ether 9:14-15 describes: an aged king who, being full of days, makes his son king in his own lifetime. What Ether does with it is a substitution of one word. Omer is not full of days; his days are 'full of sorrow'. Recover the three KJV verses that carry the formula — Isaac buried by the sons who had spent a book at odds, David handing Israel to Solomon, Job at the end of his restoration — and each is a death the text presents as sufficient. Ether withholds exactly that. Omer outlives a usurpation, the murder of his son-in-law's father, the exile of half his household and a war of extermination that leaves thirty souls alive, and Moroni's obituary for him takes the KJV's phrase for a good end and reports that the length was there and the sufficiency was not.

links.note: 'He saw peace in the land for the space of two years, and he died, having seen exceeding many days, which were full of sorrow.' The verbal contact is short and the row is filed at moderate on that account, but the position is exact: 1 Chronicles 23:1 is the only KJV verse in which the formula is the reason a reigning king installs his successor, which is what Ether 9:14-15 has just narrated across two sentences ('Omer began to be old... he anointed Emer to be king to reign in his stead'). Against the alternative that this is plain description, note that the King James Bible offers several plainer ways to say a man was old — 'well stricken in years', 'stricken in age' — and the one that came is the one with 'full of' in it, immediately inverted.
links.whyNot: Nothing here is a string: Ether shares 'full of' and 'days' and inverts the noun that made the phrase a phrase. A reader who takes 'many days, which were full of sorrow' as ordinary English and the resemblance as accidental has a defensible position, and this row is offered as a reading rather than as a demonstration. What would settle it against us is a Jaredite death-notice elsewhere using 'full of' with a third noun, which would show the construction to be Moroni's own habit rather than a KJV inversion.

pericopes.text: And the Lord began again to take the curse from off the land, and the house of Emer did prosper exceedingly under the reign of Emer; and in the space of sixty and two years, they had become exceeding strong, insomuch that they became exceeding rich,
having all manner of fruit, and of grain, and of silks, and of fine linen, and of gold, and of silver, and of precious things,

links.text: And their father gave them great gifts of silver, and of gold, and of precious things, with fenced cities in Judah: but the kingdom gave he to Jehoram; because he was the firstborn.

provenance.other: “and of precious things” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 21:3. “of gold and of silver and” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 11:43. The bare “precious things” occurs in exactly twelve KJV verses and settles nothing by itself.
provenance.significance: The metalepsis here is worth the row on its own. 2 Chronicles 21:3 is the last peaceful sentence of Jehoshaphat's reign: the king distributes silver, gold, precious things and fenced cities among his sons, and gives the kingdom itself to the firstborn. The very next verse is 21:4 — 'Now when Jehoram was risen up to the kingdom of his father, he strengthened himself, and slew all his brethren with the sword.' Ether 9:17 sits four verses after a war between a king and his sons that killed all but thirty people, and eight verses before Heth dethrones his own father and slays him with his own sword. The King James verse whose wealth-catalogue Ether borrows is the KJV's own account of what royal wealth distributed among royal sons produces, and the Jaredite chapter proves the point twice inside twenty verses. Note that 2 Chronicles 21 is already a live source in this book at Ether 7:4.

links.note: 'Having all manner of fruit, and of grain, and of silks, and of fine linen, and of gold, and of silver, and of precious things.' The list as a whole is not the KJV's — 'silks' is in no King James verse, and neither is the animal catalogue that follows in 9:18-19 — but its last three members reproduce 2 Chronicles 21:3's tail exactly, including the repeated 'of' before each item and the closing 'and of precious things', which is a King James singleton. Ether reverses the KJV's order of the metals (silver before gold, where 2 Chronicles has gold before silver) and appends the phrase intact. The competing machine candidate, Daniel 11:43, has the metals in Ether's order but lacks the 'and of precious things' construction, having 'all the precious things of Egypt' instead.

pericopes.text: and also all manner of cattle, of oxen, and cows, and of sheep, and of swine, and of goats, and also many other kind of animals, which were useful for the food of man;
and they also had horses, and asses, and there were elephants, and cureloms, and cumoms; all of which were useful unto man, and more especially the elephants, and cureloms, and cumoms.

And thus the Lord did pour out his blessings opon this land, which was choice above all other lands; and he commanded that whoso should possess the land, should possess it unto the Lord, or they should be destroyed when they were ripened in iniquity: for upon such, saith the Lord, I will pour out the fulness of my wrath.
And Emer did execute judgement in righteousness, all his days; and he begat many sons and daughters; and he begat Coriantum; and he anointed Coriantum to reign in his stead.

And after that he had anointed Coriantum to reign in his stead, he lived four years, and he saw peace in the land; yea, and he even saw the son of righteousness, and did rejoice and glory in his day; and he died in peace.

links.text: But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall.

provenance.other: “sun of righteousness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Malachi 4:2, and “healing in his wings” likewise. Within the Book of Mormon the phrase appears at 2 Nephi 26:9, 3 Nephi 25:2 and here, and in the 1830 edition all three read 'Son'.
provenance.alternative: Direct dependence on Malachi 4:2 cannot be excluded and would be the simpler account if Ether 9:22 shared any of Malachi's other material — the fear of God's name, the wings, the calves. It shares none of it, and shares instead 2 Nephi 26:9's peace, which is why the row is filed as mediated.
provenance.significance: Malachi 4:2 promises that the sun of righteousness will 'arise with healing in his wings' for those that fear God's name, at the head of a verse about the day that shall burn as an oven. What Ether 9:22 does with it is to let one man see, inside his own reign, what Malachi holds out for the last day; and the two things the verse says Emer saw are peace and the son of righteousness, which is 2 Nephi 26:9's pairing, not Malachi's. The 1830 reading is the whole of the interest here. The first edition prints 'the son of righteousness' in lower case, so that the sentence is legible as either the Malachi metaphor or a Christological title and does not decide between them; the 1920 edition capitalises both nouns and decides. A reader of the current text meets a title. A reader of 1830 meets an English homophone of a King James phrase, which is a different fact about the book.

links.note: 'He even saw the son of righteousness, and did rejoice and glory in his day.' The Book of Mormon reads 'Son' where the King James Bible reads 'Sun' throughout — 2 Nephi 26:9, 3 Nephi 25:2 (which is the Malachi block itself, quoting this verse) and here. That is the mediation finding: Ether's proximate model is not Malachi 4:2 in the KJV but the form the phrase already has inside the Book of Mormon, where the substitution has been made and where, at 2 Nephi 26:9, it stands with 'heal them' and 'they shall have peace' — Malachi's healing and a peace Malachi does not mention, both of which Ether 9:22 has. The 3 Nephi quotation also reads 'healings' for the KJV's 'healing' and 'calves in the stall' for 'calves of the stall', so the block is not a clean KJV transcript either.

links.text: Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day: and he saw it, and was glad.

provenance.other: “rejoiced to see my day” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 8:56, and “see my day” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. “and was glad” occurs in exactly three KJV verses. 'Rejoice and glory' occurs in no KJV verse, and 'glory in his day' in none; “go to thy fathers in peace”, which stands behind this verse's closing 'he died in peace', occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 15:15.
provenance.significance: John 8:56 is the King James Bible's one sentence about a man who saw Christ's day before it came and was glad, and the man is Abraham. Ether 9:22 gives Emer the same experience in the same words and adds the third Abrahamic term: he 'died in peace', which is what Genesis 15:15 promised Abraham in the KJV's only 'go to thy fathers in peace'. So the Jaredite king who most conspicuously has nothing to do with the covenant line — a gentile monarch in a book that exists outside Israel's history — is given Abraham's vision and Abraham's death, in Abraham's King James vocabulary, in the space of one verse. That is a considerable claim made entirely by allusion, and Moroni never states it.

links.note: 'And he even saw the son of righteousness, and did rejoice and glory in his day.' Three of the four elements of John 8:56 are present and in John's order: the seeing, the rejoicing, and 'his day'. The Book of Mormon substitutes 'glory' for John's 'was glad', which is the ordinary King James pair for rejoicing (Psalm 64:10, 'the righteous shall be glad in the LORD... and all the upright in heart shall glory'), and supplies the Malachi title as the object John leaves as 'my day'. The verse is doing two borrowings at once, and they cooperate: what Emer sees is Malachi's, and the seeing itself is John's.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Coriantum did walk in the steps of his father, and did build many mighty cities, and did administer that which was good unto his people, in all his days. And it came to pass that he had no children, even until he was exceeding old.

links.text: And the father of circumcision to them who are not of the circumcision only, but who also walk in the steps of that faith of our father Abraham, which he had being yet uncircumcised.

provenance.other: “walk in the steps” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 4:12. “steps of his father” occurs in no KJV verse. The KJV's regnal idiom, “walked in the way of his father”, occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Kings 15:26 and 1 Kings 22:52, and in both it follows 'he did evil in the sight of the LORD' — the King James Bible has no formula at all for a son who walks in a good father's way.
provenance.significance: The choice is what makes this worth recording. A dynastic chronicle written in King James English has a ready-made idiom for a son who governs as his father did — 'he walked in the way of his father', which the books of Kings use of Abijam, Jehoram, Ahaziah and the rest, always as a verdict. Ether declines it. What it uses instead is Paul's phrase from the one passage in the New Testament where walking in someone's steps means inheriting a promise rather than repeating a policy: Romans 4 is about who counts as Abraham's children, and the answer is those who walk in the steps of his faith. Applied to Coriantum, who builds cities and administers what is good, the borrowing quietly assigns the Jaredite succession to the Abrahamic register rather than the Deuteronomic one — which is the same move Ether 9:22 has just made for his father.

links.note: 'Coriantum did walk in the steps of his father.' The phrase is a King James singleton and the Book of Mormon has it verbatim to the preposition. Ether 9:15 has already used a variant of it four sentences earlier ('did fill the steps of his father'), which is why the row is placed here rather than there: 9:23 is where the KJV's own wording appears. Held at moderate because 'walk in the steps of' is unremarkable modern English and a writer could arrive at it without Romans; the reply is that the King James dynastic alternative was available and was not used — and could not have been, since in the KJV it is reserved for sons who do evil, which leaves a chronicler who wants to praise a son with no King James formula and sends him to Paul.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that his wife died, being an hundred and two years old. And it came to pass that Coriantum took to wife, in his old age, a young maid, and begat sons and daughters; wherefore he lived until he was an hundred and forty and two years old.

links.text: Then again Abraham took a wife, and her name was Keturah.

provenance.other: “took to wife” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, Genesis 26:34, Exodus 2:1, 1 Kings 16:31 and 1 Chronicles 7:15. 'A young maid' occurs in no KJV verse; the nearest King James parallel to the situation, 1 Kings 1:2's “a young virgin” sought for the aged David, occurs in exactly one verse and produces no children, which is the point of the Kings scene and the opposite of this one.
provenance.significance: Genesis tells the end of Abraham's life in three notices in a fixed order: Sarah's death with her age given in full (23:1), a second marriage in his old age producing further sons (25:1-4), and his own total age (25:7). Ether 9:24 has all three in the same order in a single verse, and it is the only place in the Jaredite king-list where a queen's age at death is recorded at all. What the borrowing supplies is not wording but a solution to a narrative problem the chapter has stated two sentences earlier: Coriantum 'had no children, even until he was exceeding old'. Genesis is the King James Bible's authority for the proposition that a childless old age is not the end of a line, and Ether 9:23-24 is that proposition run once more, without the covenant that made it meaningful in Genesis and with a young wife instead of a promise.

links.note: 'His wife died, being an hundred and two years old... Coriantum took to wife, in his old age, a young maid, and begat sons and daughters; wherefore he lived until he was an hundred and forty and two years old.' Filed as figural because there is no shared string worth the name — the KJV's “took to wife” occurs in four verses, none of them Abraham's, and Genesis 25:1 reads 'took a wife'. What is shared is the sequence and the peculiar habit of numbering it. The machine offered 2 Chronicles 22:2 here on the strength of 'forty and two years old', which is Ahaziah's age at accession and a coincidence of the numeral; that is not this row's argument and the row would be no weaker if Coriantum had lived to a different age.
links.whyNot: A three-part sequence with no shared vocabulary is close to the limit of what this catalogue will call dependence, and an adjudicator who filed it as an insufficient-verbal exclusion would be applying CONVENTIONS §5 correctly. It is written as a link because the sequence is not generic: recording a wife's age at death is something the King James Bible does exactly once, for Sarah, and Ether does exactly once, here.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he begat Com, and Com reigned in his stead; and he reigned forty and nine years, and he begat Heth; and he also begat other sons and daughters.

And the people had spread again over all the face of the land, and there began again to be an exceeding great wickedness upon the face of the land, and Heth began to embrace the secret plans again of old, to destroy his father.
And it came to pass that he did dethrone his father: for he slew him with his own sword; and he did reign in his stead.

links.text: And it came to pass, as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, that Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword: and they escaped into the land of Armenia. And Esarhaddon his son reigned in his stead.

provenance.route: 2 Kings 19:37 (= Isaiah 37:38) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “with his own sword” occurs in no KJV verse. “reigned in his stead” occurs in exactly sixty-three KJV verses and carries no weight here.
provenance.significance: The King James Bible reports one royal parricide, and reports it twice in identical words, at 2 Kings 19:37 and Isaiah 37:38: sons smite their father with the sword, escape, and another son reigns in his stead. Ether 9:27 has the three elements in the same order and compresses them into one clause. The gain from recovering the context is that Sennacherib is killed in the house of his god, at worship, and the KJV frames the murder as the last instalment of a prophecy against a king who had defied the LORD — the sons are instruments, not agents, and the text shows no interest in them. Ether inverts the theology exactly. Heth kills his father to take the throne and then persecutes the prophets who come to indict him for it (9:28-29), so where 2 Kings has a parricide that fulfils prophecy, Ether has one that provokes it, and the drought of 9:30 is the answer.

links.note: 'He did dethrone his father: for he slew him with his own sword; and he did reign in his stead.' No string is shared beyond 'reigned in his stead', which is worthless on its own — see the standing treatment of that formula at Ether 7:3 — and 'with his own sword' is in no King James verse at all. The row rests on the type-scene, which in the KJV is a singleton and is duplicated verbatim across two books, so it is as prominent a narrative as the King James Bible has for this event. Ether's one addition, that the sword was the father's own, is not in 2 Kings; it belongs to the David-and-Goliath register, and Moroni uses it to make the killing a usurpation of the father's own instrument rather than an assassination from outside.
links.whyNot: Nothing in the wording compels this. A chronicle of a violent dynasty will produce a parricide sooner or later without needing a model, and Ether 9 has already produced several killings that owe nothing to 2 Kings. The row is written because the three elements arrive in the King James order and because the alternative — that the Jaredite record independently reinvented the KJV's only parricide type-scene — is not obviously cheaper. Withdraw it if the wording of the surrounding verses turns out to be drawn from a different regnal narrative.

pericopes.text: And there came prophets in the land again, crying repentance unto them; that they must prepare the way of the Lord, or there should come a curse upon the face of the land; yea, even there should be a great famine, in the which they should be destroyed, if they did not repent.

links.text: For this is he that was spoken of by the prophet Esaias, saying, The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.

provenance.other: “prepare ye the way of the Lord” occurs in exactly four KJV verses: Isaiah 40:3, Matthew 3:3, Mark 1:3 and Luke 3:4. The Book of Mormon's 'prepare the way of the Lord', without the 'ye', occurs in no KJV verse.
provenance.alternative: The 'crying' test identifies the New Testament as the route but cannot identify which Gospel: Mark 1:3 and Luke 3:4 read 'one crying' as Matthew does. Matthew is named as the source because Matthew 3:1-2 alone supplies the arrival of the preacher and the bare imperative 'Repent ye' that Ether's 'crying repentance' answers to — Mark 1:4 and Luke 3:3 have instead 'the baptism of repentance', and there is no baptism here.
provenance.significance: The mediation is the finding. Ether 9:28 sends prophets into a land under a parricide king to demand that the people 'prepare the way of the Lord' or face a curse and a famine — which is Isaiah's oracle of comfort put to a use Isaiah never puts it to, and John the Baptist's use exactly. Matthew 3 attaches the Isaiah verse to a preacher whose message is 'Repent ye', who is refused, and who is killed by a king; Ether 9:28-29 attaches it to prophets whose message is repentance, who are refused, and who are cast into pits by a king. Recovering Matthew therefore recovers the whole of the Jaredite scene and not only its slogan: Moroni is not quoting Isaiah's highway in the desert, he is quoting the Gospel's redeployment of it as a demand made of people who will not meet it.

links.note: 'There came prophets in the land again, crying repentance unto them; that they must prepare the way of the Lord.' `mediation-check.py` returns one decisive divergence between the candidates: the Book of Mormon has the New Testament's participle 'crying' where Isaiah 40:3 has the finite 'him that crieth', against a backbone of five other shared words (voice, wilderness, prepare, way, straight). It is a single word and it should be reported as one, but it is the one word the two forms differ on. The rest of the verse pulls the same way: Matthew 3:1-2 has prophets who 'came... preaching' and whose sermon is 'Repent ye', which is the pair Ether compresses into 'came prophets... crying repentance', and Ether drops Isaiah's second half — the highway, the desert, the God — entirely.

pericopes.text: But the people believed not the words of the prophets, but they cast them out; and some of them they cast into pits, and left them to perish. And it came to pass that they done all these things according to the commandment of the king Heth.

links.text: Therefore also said the wisdom of God, I will send them prophets and apostles, and some of them they shall slay and persecute:

provenance.other: “some of them they” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 11:49, and the fuller “prophets and apostles and some of them they” likewise. The pit is not Luke's: “cast him into a pit” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 37:24, of Joseph, and “into a pit” in exactly three, none of them about a prophet.
provenance.significance: Luke 11:49 is a quotation inside a woe: Jesus tells the lawyers what the wisdom of God said, and the point of quoting it is 11:50-51, 'that the blood of all the prophets, which was shed from the foundation of the world, may be required of this generation'. Ether 9:29 borrows the sentence that carries that indictment and applies it to a generation for whom it is literally true — Moroni has already written, at 8:25, that the adversary behind the secret combinations has 'caused man to commit murder from the beginning' and made men 'murder the prophets, and stone them, and cast them out'. So the Jaredites who cast prophets into pits are being charged in Luke's terms with the offence Luke says will be required of the last generation to commit it, and the famine that follows in 9:30 is the requiring. Nothing in Ether says this; the borrowed clause says it.

links.note: 'But the people believed not the words of the prophets, but they cast them out; and some of them they cast into pits, and left them to perish.' The sequence 'and some of them they' plus a verb of violence is a King James singleton, and Ether reproduces the whole construction including the resumptive pronoun, which is awkward English and survives only because it was copied. Luke's pair of verbs is 'slay and persecute'; Ether's is 'cast them out' and 'cast into pits', and 'cast them out' is the phrase Moroni himself used of the treatment of prophets four verses earlier, at 8:25. The machine found this candidate and ranked it near the bottom of the chapter at 1.10, which is a fair illustration of CONVENTIONS §9 — the rarest construction in the verse scored below a dating formula.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that there began to be a great dearth upon the land, and the inhabitants began to be destroyed exceeding fast, because of the dearth: for there was no rain upon the face of the earth;

links.text: And then the LORD’s wrath be kindled against you, and he shut up the heaven, that there be no rain, and that the land yield not her fruit; and lest ye perish quickly from off the good land which the LORD giveth you.

provenance.other: “that there be no rain” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Deuteronomy 11:17 and 2 Chronicles 7:13. “shut up the heaven” and “yield not her fruit” each occur in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 11:17. 'No rain upon the earth' occurs in no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 11:17 is the covenant curse in its compact form, and it is the only King James verse that puts all three of Ether's terms in one sentence: no rain, a land that yields no fruit, and a people perishing quickly off the land the LORD gives them. Ether 9 has been building the covenant frame since 9:20, where the Lord commands that whoso possesses the land must possess it unto him or be destroyed; Deuteronomy 11:17 is the machinery that clause presupposes, and 9:30 is where it operates. The metaleptic point is in the verse Deuteronomy 11:17 belongs to: 11:16 warns 'that your heart be not deceived, and ye turn aside, and serve other gods'. The Jaredites have not turned to other gods. They have turned to a secret combination and killed the prophets who named it, and Moroni's chapter treats that as the offence for which the KJV's drought-curse is the appointed penalty.

links.note: 'There began to be a great dearth upon the land, and the inhabitants began to be destroyed exceeding fast, because of the dearth: for there was no rain upon the face of the earth.' The two distinctive elements of Deuteronomy 11:17 are both here and both altered in the same direction, toward narration: 'that there be no rain' becomes 'there was no rain', and 'lest ye perish quickly' becomes 'destroyed exceeding fast'. The third element is held back four verses and then supplied at 9:35 — the land yields her fruit again ('there began to be fruit in the north countries'), which is the curse's condition lifted. The machine offered Jeremiah 14:4 here, whose 'there was no rain in the earth' is closer to Ether's tense; that verse is treated in the exclusion register, where the case for Jeremiah 14 as a whole is set out and declined.

links.text: And there stood up one of them named Agabus, and signified by the Spirit that there should be great dearth throughout all the world: which came to pass in the days of Claudius Caesar.

provenance.other: “great dearth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 11:28, and “there should be great dearth” likewise. The bare 'dearth' occurs in exactly seven KJV verses, of which Genesis 41:54 and Acts 7:11 are Joseph's Egyptian famine and 2 Kings 4:38 Elisha's at Gilgal.
provenance.significance: Acts 11:28 is the King James Bible's one instance of a prophet announcing a famine before it happens and the narrative then confirming that it happened — 'signified by the Spirit that there should be great dearth throughout all the world: which came to pass in the days of Claudius Caesar'. Ether 9:28-30 is that two-part structure at two verses' distance, with the prediction in 9:28 and the fulfilment formula in 9:30. What the recovery adds is the use Acts puts its dearth to: it is the occasion of the collection sent from Antioch to Judaea, a famine that produces charity. Ether's produces cannibalised carcasses and repentance under duress. The same King James sentence stands behind both, and the divergence is the reading.

links.note: 'There should be a great famine, in the which they should be destroyed' (9:28), then 'there began to be a great dearth upon the land' (9:30). 'Dearth' is not a word Moroni reaches for elsewhere, and the King James Bible's one 'great dearth' is Agabus's. Ether splits the Acts sentence across the prophecy and its fulfilment, using 'famine' in the prediction and 'dearth' when it arrives — which is also how the verse ends, at 9:35, 'in preserving them from famine'. Filed at moderate because 'great dearth' is two words and the surrounding syntax is Ether's own.

pericopes.text: and there came forth poisonous serpents also upon the face of the land, and did poison many people. And it came to pass that their flocks began to flee before the poisonous serpents, towards the land southward, which was called by the Nephites, Zarahemla.

links.text: And the LORD sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people; and much people of Israel died.

provenance.route: Numbers 21:6-7 (with Deuteronomy 8:15) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “serpents among the people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Numbers 21:6. “fiery serpents” occurs in exactly two, Numbers 21:6 and Deuteronomy 8:15 — and Deuteronomy 8:15 is the only KJV verse in which serpents and drought stand in the same clause. 'Poisonous serpents' occurs in no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Numbers 21:6-7 is the King James Bible's serpent plague and it has a fixed shape: the LORD sends serpents among a people who have spoken against him, the serpents kill, the people say 'we have sinned', and the plague is lifted. Ether 9:31-34 runs it entire, including the confession — 'they began to repent of their iniquities, and cry unto the Lord' — and adds the drought. That addition is what makes the row more than a commonplace. Deuteronomy 8:15 is the only verse in the King James Bible that puts serpents and drought together in one clause, and it does so in a rehearsal of the wilderness that immediately follows Deuteronomy 8:12-14's warning about what happens to a people made rich: 'lest when thou hast eaten and art full... then thine heart be lifted up, and thou forget the LORD thy God.' Ether 9 has spent fifteen verses on exactly that enrichment (9:16-19) and then delivers Deuteronomy 8's two wilderness terrors in order. The chapter is running Deuteronomy 8's argument as narrative.

links.note: 'There came forth poisonous serpents also upon the face of the land, and did poison many people.' The wording is not the KJV's — 'poisonous serpents' is in no King James verse, where the term is 'fiery serpents' — so this is filed as a conceptual allusion and its rarity score reflects the sequence rather than the vocabulary. The mediation test was run against 1 Corinthians 10:9 ('were destroyed of serpents') and returned nothing usable: the tool reports a decisive point on a one-word backbone, which is an artifact, since Ether shares no wording with either candidate. On the evidence the route is direct-OT, and the argument for it is that Ether pairs the serpents with drought, which no New Testament text does and Deuteronomy 8:15 does.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that there were many of them which did perish by the way; nevertheless, there were some which fled into the land southward.

And it came to pass that the Lord did cause the serpents that they should pursue them no more, but that they should hedge up the way, that the people could not pass; that whoso should attempt to pass, might fall by the poisonous serpents.

links.text: Therefore, behold, I will hedge up thy way with thorns, and make a wall, that she shall not find her paths.

provenance.other: “hedge up” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hosea 2:6. “hedge up the way” occurs in no KJV verse; the KJV's object is 'thy way'.
provenance.significance: Hosea 2:6 is the King James Bible's one hedged way, and the point of the hedge is stated in the next verse: she pursues her lovers, cannot reach them, cannot find them, 'then shall she say, I will go and return to my first husband'. The obstruction is not a punishment, it is a device for producing a return. Ether 9:33-34 uses it for precisely that and says so: the Lord stops the serpents pursuing but leaves them barring the road, the people cannot pass, they follow the beasts and eat what falls, and then — the next sentence — 'they began to repent of their iniquities, and cry unto the Lord'. Recovering Hosea supplies the reason the serpents are called off and left in place at the same time, which is otherwise the strangest sentence in the chapter. The wall that stops the flight is what turns the people around.

links.note: 'That they should hedge up the way, that the people could not pass.' 'Hedge up' is a King James singleton, and Ether takes both halves of Hosea's construction — the hedging of a way, and the resulting clause of frustrated passage ('that she shall not find her paths' / 'that the people could not pass'). The machine proposed Ezra 3:13 for the second half on the strength of 'the people could not', which is a shout nobody could distinguish; the exclusion register records it. Note that the metaphor has been literalised: Hosea's thorns become serpents, and Hosea's adulterous wife becomes a nation trying to follow its livestock south.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the people did follow the course of the beasts, and did devour the carcasses of them which fell by the way, until they had devoured them all. Now when the people saw that they must perish, they began to repent of their iniquities, and cry unto the Lord.

And it came to pass that when they had humbled themselves sufficiently before the Lord, the Lord did send rain upon the face of the earth, and the people began to revive again, and there began to be fruit in the north countries, and in all the countries round about. And the Lord did shew forth his power unto them, in preserving them from famine.

links.text: And it came to pass after many days, that the word of the LORD came to Elijah in the third year, saying, Go, shew thyself unto Ahab; and I will send rain upon the earth.

provenance.other: “send rain upon the earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Kings 18:1; the near-identical promise at 1 Kings 17:14 reads 'the LORD sendeth rain upon the earth'. 'Shew forth' occurs in exactly fifteen KJV verses, all but one of them of praise rather than power, so it carries no weight by itself — but the 1830 spelling is the KJV's and 1920's is not.
provenance.significance: 1 Kings 17-18 is the King James Bible's drought narrative and Ether 9:28-35 has its whole armature: a king who does evil, prophets he will not hear and who are hunted, a drought declared by prophetic word, and the rain restored only when the people turn. 1 Kings 18:1 is the sentence that ends it, and Ether 9:35 has both of that verse's distinctive words. The 1830 reading is what makes the row visible. The first edition reads 'the Lord did send rain upon the face of the earth' and 'the Lord did shew forth his power'; 1920 changed the first 'the Lord' to 'he' and modernised 'shew' to 'show', so the current text names the Lord once where 1830 names him twice, and loses the King James spelling. In 1830 the verse is doing what 1 Kings 18:1 does — the LORD says 'I will send rain upon the earth' and tells Elijah to shew himself — and the borrowing is legible on the page.

links.note: 'The Lord did send rain upon the face of the earth... And the Lord did shew forth his power unto them, in preserving them from famine.' 'Send rain upon the earth' is a King James singleton and Ether has it with one interpolated phrase. `mediation-check.py` was run against James 5:18, the New Testament's account of the same drought, and the result should be read with care: it reports a decisive point for 1 Kings, but on a zero-word backbone, which is an artifact of the two candidates having almost nothing in common. The honest statement is that James's distinctive wording ('the heaven gave rain', 'the earth brought forth her fruit') is absent and 1 Kings 18:1's is present, so the route is direct-OT — and that the tool did not establish this, the singleton did.

links.text: If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.

provenance.other: “humbled themselves” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, 2 Chronicles 12:6, 12:7 and 30:11. “heal their land” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 7:14. “that there be no rain” occurs in exactly two, 2 Chronicles 7:13 and Deuteronomy 11:17.
provenance.significance: 2 Chronicles 7:13-14 is the King James Bible's one statement of the whole cycle Ether 9:28-35 narrates, and it states it in the same order: God shuts up heaven so that there is no rain; if the people humble themselves and pray and turn, he hears and heals their land. Ether supplies each stage as event — the drought at 9:30, the humbling and the crying at 9:34-35, the rain and the returning fruit at 9:35 — and adds one word that is its own: 'sufficiently'. That word is the chapter's verdict on the sequence. Solomon's prayer contemplates a people who turn from their wicked ways; Ether's people repent because they have run out of carcasses to eat, and Moroni measures their humbling by whether there was enough of it. Recovering the Chronicler makes the Jaredite repentance look transactional in a way the text never says outright.

links.note: 'When they had humbled themselves sufficiently before the Lord, the Lord did send rain upon the face of the earth... and there began to be fruit in the north countries.' Filed as conceptual because the verbal contact is a two-word phrase, 'humbled themselves', which the KJV uses in three verses, all in Chronicles and two of them (12:6-7) in the closest possible situation — a people under a declared judgment who humble themselves and are told 'they have humbled themselves; therefore I will not destroy them'. The strength of the row is positional rather than lexical: it is the only King James passage that binds a rain-drought to a humbling and to the healing of a land, and Ether binds the same three.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Shez, which was a descendant of Heth, for Heth had perished by the famine, and all his household, save it were Shez; wherefore Shez began to build up again a broken people.

And it came to pass that Shez did remember the destruction of his fathers, and he did build up a righteous kingdom, for he remembered what the Lord had done in bringing Jared and his brother across the deep; and he did walk in the ways of the Lord, and he begat sons and daughters.

links.text: And the days of Adam after he had begotten Seth were eight hundred years: and he begat sons and daughters:

provenance.route: Genesis 5:4 (and the Genesis 5 / Genesis 11 genealogical formula) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “And he begat sons and daughters” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 5:4 and 2 Chronicles 24:3. Dropping the leading conjunction, “begat sons and daughters” occurs in eighteen, and seventeen of those eighteen are the two genealogies of Genesis 5 (Adam to Noah) and Genesis 11 (Shem to Terah); the remaining two are 2 Chronicles 24:3 and Jeremiah 29:6. The phrase is, in the King James Bible, almost the private property of the primeval genealogies.
provenance.significance: Genesis 11 is the chapter the book of Ether begins from — the confusion of tongues and the scattering, which Ether 1:33 rehearses. Genesis 11:10-26 is what immediately follows the tower: the surviving genealogy, generation after generation, each man living so many years and begetting sons and daughters. Ether 10 is that same list resumed on the other side of the ocean. The Jaredite dynastic chapter is not merely set after Babel; it is written in the formula the King James Bible uses for the descendants of Babel, so that the Jaredite kings take their place in the sentence-shape reserved in scripture for the sons of Shem.

links.note: 'And he did walk in the ways of the Lord, and he begat sons and daughters.' The formula returns at 10:14 ('he begat sons and daughters in captivity'), 10:16 and 10:29, four times in one chapter, and it is doing the same structural work Genesis 5 and 11 do: it marks the passage of a generation and licenses the narrative to move on. Filed as an allusion rather than a quotation because no single verse can be named as the source — the argument is about a formula with seventeen occurrences in two chapters of Genesis, not about Genesis 5:4 in particular, which is cited here as the formula's first instance. What makes the row worth writing is where the formula is used: 10:14 fuses it with captivity ('he begat sons and daughters in captivity'), which is a thing Genesis 5 and 11 never say, and the chapter's last dynastic movement (10:30-31) is nothing but this formula run through four generations of prisoners.

pericopes.text: And his eldest son, whose name was Shez, did rebel against him; nevertheless, Shez was smitten by the hand of a robber, because of his exceeding riches, which brought peace again unto his father.

And it came to pass that his father did build up many cities upon the face of the land, and the people began again to spread over all the face of the land. And Shez did live to an exceeding old age; and he begat Riplakish, and he died. And Riplakish reigned in his stead.

And it came to pass that Riplakish did not do that which was right in the sight of the Lord, for he did have many wives and concubines, and did lay that upon men’s shoulders which was grievous to be borne; yea, he did tax them with heavy taxes; and with the taxes he did build many spacious buildings.

links.text: For they bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men’s shoulders; but they themselves will not move them with one of their fingers.

provenance.other: “men's shoulders” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 23:4. “grievous to be borne” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 23:4 and Luke 11:46, which are the same saying in the two gospels. Ether 10:5 has both phrases, and the only KJV verse that has both is Matthew 23:4. Running the two gospel forms against the Book of Mormon returns two decisive points, both for Matthew: Luke has ‘ye lade men with burdens’ where Matthew and Ether have the burden laid on shoulders, and Luke drops the shoulders altogether.
provenance.significance: Matthew 23:4 is the second of the woes against the scribes and Pharisees, and its charge is precisely hypocrisy of imposition: they bind the burden and 'will not move them with one of their fingers'. Ether 10:5-7 takes that sentence out of the synagogue and puts it in a treasury. Riplakish lays on men's shoulders what is grievous to be borne, and the next two verses say exactly what Matthew's finger-clause implies — the burden purchases the burden-layer's own comfort: an exceeding beautiful throne, many spacious buildings, and fine gold refined by prisoners. The metalepsis is that Matthew's woe supplies the moral verdict the Jaredite chronicle never pronounces in its own voice; Ether 10:8 simply reports that the people rebelled and killed him.

links.note: 'He did have many wives and concubines, and did lay that upon men's shoulders which was grievous to be borne; yea, he did tax them with heavy taxes.' Two KJV phrases, one of them a singleton, drawn from a single verse and reassembled around a relative pronoun: Matthew's 'lay them on men's shoulders' and 'grievous to be borne' become 'lay that upon men's shoulders which was grievous to be borne'. The shared run is well under Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and this is not one of his passages; what carries it is the rarity, not the length. The transposition is itself evidence of use rather than coincidence — the clauses are in Matthew's order but joined by a construction Matthew does not have.

links.text: Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away: neither shall he greatly multiply to himself silver and gold.

provenance.other: “multiply wives” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 17:17. But the Book of Mormon's own phrase is 'many wives and concubines', which occurs in no KJV verse at all; 'many wives' occurs in three (Judges 8:30 of Gideon, 1 Chronicles 7:4, 2 Chronicles 11:23 of Rehoboam), and none of them is Deuteronomy. There is no verbal contact here, and the row is filed on the catalogue of offences rather than on any phrase.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 17:14-20 is the law of the king: he shall not multiply horses, nor wives, nor 'greatly multiply to himself silver and gold', and he shall write himself a copy of the law that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren. Riplakish's régime in 10:5-7 is that list read as an indictment — many wives and concubines, heavy taxation, spacious buildings, and fine gold refined in prison — and the chapter has already announced the Deuteronomic verdict in the same sentence ('did not do that which was right in the sight of the Lord'). Read against Deuteronomy 17, the forty-two years and the rebellion that ends them are not a political accident but the sanction the law attaches to the offence.

links.note: Filed because a reader who knows Deuteronomy 17 will see it here and the catalogue should say whether it saw it too. The chapter is a king-list judged by a Deuteronomic standard, and the specific sins it charges to its worst king are the specific things Deuteronomy 17:16-17 forbids a king. But the wording is not Deuteronomy's at any point, so this is a figural row and nothing more: the evidence is the coincidence of a catalogue, not of an English phrase.
links.whyNot: No verbal contact whatever. 'Many wives and concubines' is Solomon's profile in 1 Kings 11:3 rather than Deuteronomy's diction, and a chronicler describing a bad ancient king has few other sins available; polygamy, taxation and monumental building are what tyranny looks like in almost any source. A reader may reasonably decline the row and read Ether 10:5 as an independent catalogue of vices.

links.text: Twenty years old was Ahaz when he began to reign, and reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem, and did not that which was right in the sight of the LORD his God, like David his father.

provenance.route: The Deuteronomistic regnal-evaluation formula (2 Kings / 2 Chronicles) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “that which was right in the sight of the Lord” occurs in exactly fifteen KJV verses, every one of them in 2 Kings or 2 Chronicles and every one of them an evaluation of a reigning king. The negative form Ether 10:5 uses, “did not that which was right”, occurs in exactly two, 2 Kings 16:2 and 2 Chronicles 28:1, which are the two accounts of Ahaz. The chapter's other formula, 'did that which was good in the sight of the Lord' (10:17, 10:19), occurs in no KJV verse: the King James Bible's regnal verdicts are 'right' or 'evil', never 'good'.
provenance.significance: The formula is the machinery by which Kings turns a chronicle into a theodicy: reign-length, succession, and one clause saying whether the reign was approved. Ether 10 has adopted the whole apparatus — nine kings evaluated in thirty-four verses, alternating good and wicked, each verdict attached to a consequence in the next sentence. What the row records is that a book which claims to predate the Israelite monarchy entirely writes its own monarchy in the monarchy's own retrospective idiom. The variation is the interesting part: 'good in the sight of the Lord' is not a King James regnal formula, and its two KJV occurrences (Deuteronomy 6:18, Malachi 2:17) are not regnal at all, so at 10:17 and 10:19 the chapter is improvising on a form it otherwise reproduces exactly.

links.note: Adjudicated at 10:5, the formula's first appearance in the chapter and the one that reproduces a King James clause verbatim. It recurs at 10:13 (in the substitute form 'did not reign in righteousness'), 10:16 ('did that which was right in the sight of the Lord', the fifteen-verse formula exactly), and 10:17 and 10:19 in the non-biblical 'good' variant. 2 Kings 16:2 is named as source because it is one of only two verses carrying the negative form Ether 10:5 has, not because Ahaz is in view; like the Genesis 36 king-list row at Ether 7:3, this is a borrowing of a genre's connective tissue rather than of a verse, and it is filed figural for that reason.

pericopes.text: And he did erect him an exceeding beautiful throne, and he did build many prisons, and whoso would not be subject unto taxes, he did cast into prison; and whoso were not able to pay taxes, he did cast into prison; and he did cause that they should labor continually for their support; and whoso refused to labor, he did cause to be put to death;

wherefore he did obtain all his fine work; yea, even his fine gold he did cause to be refined in prison, and all manner of fine workmanship he did cause to be wrought in prison. And it came to pass that he did afflict the people with his whoredoms and abominations;

and when he had reigned for the space of forty and two years, the people did raise up in rebellion against him, and there began to be war again in the land, insomuch that Riplakish was killed, and his descendants were driven out of the land.

And it came to pass after the space of many years, Morianton, (he being a descendant of Riplakish,) gathered together an army of outcasts, and went forth and gave battle unto the people; and he gained power over many cities; and the war became exceeding sore, and did last for the space of many years, and he did gain power over all the land, and did establish himself king over all the land.
And after that he had established himself king, he did ease the burden of the people, in the which he did gain favor in the eyes of the people, and they did anoint him to be their king.

links.text: Thy father made our yoke grievous: now therefore ease thou somewhat the grievous servitude of thy father, and his heavy yoke that he put upon us, and we will serve thee.

provenance.route: 2 Chronicles 10:3-4 (parallel at 1 Kings 12:3-4) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “ease thou somewhat the grievous” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 10:4; the parallel at 1 Kings 12:4 reads 'make thou the grievous service ... lighter'. Ether's word is 'ease'. “the burden of the people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Numbers 11:17, where the seventy elders are to bear it with Moses.
provenance.significance: 1 Kings 12 / 2 Chronicles 10 is the King James Bible's one narrative about taxation and succession, and Ether 10:5-10 distributes its roles across two reigns. Riplakish is Solomon and Rehoboam at once — spacious buildings, forced labour, a heavy yoke — and 10:8's rebellion is 1 Kings 12:18-19 with the outcome carried to its end: Rehoboam escapes in his chariot, Riplakish is killed. Morianton then does what Rehoboam refused to do, eases the burden, and receives what Rehoboam lost. Recovering the Chronicles context makes 10:11 the sting of the row: the king who granted the petition Rehoboam denied is nevertheless 'cut off from the presence of the Lord', so the Jaredite chronicle grants the political lesson of the schism narrative and then withholds its theological reward.

links.note: 'He did ease the burden of the people, in the which he did gain favor in the eyes of the people.' The verbal contact is one word, and it is the word on which the two King James accounts of the same speech differ: Kings has the people ask Rehoboam to make the yoke 'lighter', Chronicles has them ask him to 'ease' it. Ether has Chronicles' verb. Set against that, 'the burden of the people' is a King James singleton belonging to Numbers 11:17, a verse about sharing a burden rather than lifting one; the phrase is listed as composite because it is where the English comes from, not because Numbers 11 is in view.
links.whyNot: The whole weight of the source identification rests on a single common verb. 'Ease' is an unremarkable word for the action being described, and a writer with no text in front of him would very likely reach for it. What keeps the row at moderate rather than lower is the narrative sequence around it — heavy taxes, corvée, rebellion, a new king who lightens the load and is acclaimed — which is 1 Kings 12 in order.

links.text: To morrow about this time I will send thee a man out of the land of Benjamin, and thou shalt anoint him to be captain over my people Israel, that he may save my people out of the hand of the Philistines: for I have looked upon my people, because their cry is come unto me.

provenance.other: “anoint him to be” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 9:16, where the LORD tells Samuel to anoint Saul 'to be captain over my people Israel'. Every other King James anointing is phrased otherwise — 'anointed him king', 'anointed David king over Israel', 'anoint unto me him whom I name unto thee'.
provenance.significance: The one King James verse with this construction is careful about its noun.
