Israel had demanded a king (1 Samuel 8:5, which the catalogue adjudicates at Ether 6:19); what God authorises Samuel to anoint is a captain, and the withholding of the word 'king' is the point of the sentence. Ether 10:10 supplies the word: 'they did anoint him to be their king'. The Jaredite people, having been warned in Ether 6:23 that kings lead into captivity, perform the anointing 1 Samuel 9:16 declines to name and get, four verses of chronicle later, the captivity of 10:30-31. Ether 6 borrows Israel's demand; Ether 10 completes it with the formula Israel's own text would not use.

links.note: 'And they did anoint him to be their king.' A four-word run that occurs once in the King James Bible, in the commission to anoint Saul, and it arrives at the end of a verse whose other borrowing (the eased burden) is also from the monarchy narratives. The strength of the row is that the Book of Mormon's substitution is the one substitution the King James verse is structured to refuse; the weakness is that four short words is a small thing to hang it on, and 'anoint him to be their king' is an obvious way to say what the sentence says.

pericopes.text: And he did do justice unto the people, but not unto himself, because of his many whoredoms; wherefore he was cut off from the presence of the Lord.

And it came to pass that Morianton built up many cities, and the people became exceeding rich under his reign, both in buildings, and in gold, and in silver, and in raising grain, and in flocks, and herds, and such things which had been restored unto them.

links.text: And when thy herds and thy flocks multiply, and thy silver and thy gold is multiplied, and all that thou hast is multiplied;

provenance.other: The individual pairs are widely distributed — “gold and in silver” occurs in four KJV verses, all of them craft inventories — so the row rests on the catalogue rather than on a phrase. Deuteronomy 8:12-13 is the King James Bible's warning-list in this order: houses built and dwelt in, herds and flocks multiplied, silver and gold multiplied, 'and all that thou hast is multiplied'.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 8 supplies both halves of this chapter's economy and it supplies them in Deuteronomy's order. The mineral wealth of 10:23 is Deuteronomy 8:9, and the accumulation of 10:12 is Deuteronomy 8:12-13; what stands between them in Deuteronomy is 8:11, 'beware that thou forget not the LORD thy God', and what follows is 8:14, 'then thine heart be lifted up, and thou forget the LORD thy God, which brought thee forth out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage'. Ether 10 says the first half aloud at 10:28 — 'never could be a people more blessed ... and more prospered by the hand of the Lord' — and then, without a word of comment, gives 10:30-31: the kingdom taken away, and four generations who dwelt in captivity all their days. The house of bondage is the term Deuteronomy uses and the outcome Ether narrates.

links.note: 'The people became exceeding rich under his reign, both in buildings, and in gold, and in silver, and in raising grain, and in flocks, and herds.' The machine ranked Exodus 35:32, Exodus 31:4 and 2 Chronicles 2:7 here for the run 'in gold, and in silver, and in', and all three are craftsmen's commissions with brass as the third metal; Ether's third item is grain, and its fourth and fifth are flocks and herds, which is Deuteronomy's list and not Exodus's. The clinching consideration is that the chapter uses the Exodus craft vocabulary eleven verses later, at 10:23 and 10:27, where 'work' and 'brass' actually appear — so the two sources are both present in the chapter and each sits where its own words are.

pericopes.text: And Morianton did live to an exceeding great age, and then he begat Kim; and Kim did reign in the stead of his father; and he did reign eight years, and his father died. And it came to pass that Kim did not reign in righteousness, wherefore he was not favored of the Lord.

links.text: Behold, a king shall reign in righteousness, and princes shall rule in judgment.

provenance.other: “reign in righteousness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 32:1: 'Behold, a king shall reign in righteousness, and princes shall rule in judgment.' The unqualified phrase “shall reign in” occurs in three (Isaiah 24:23, Isaiah 32:1, Romans 5:17), only one of which has a human king as its subject.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 32:1 is the King James Bible's single sentence defining what a good reign is, and Isaiah 32:2 tells what such a king is for: 'a man shall be as an hiding place from the wind, and a covert from the tempest; as rivers of water in a dry place, as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land'. Ether 10:13 negates the sentence — Kim 'did not reign in righteousness' — and the next verse gives Isaiah 32:2's inverse: not shelter but captivity, and a man who begets sons and daughters in prison and dies there. The chapter has, in three words, measured a Jaredite king against the only standard the King James Bible states positively for kingship, and recorded the shortfall.

links.note: 'Kim did not reign in righteousness, wherefore he was not favored of the Lord.' A three-word King James singleton, and the chapter's one departure from the Kings-and-Chronicles evaluation formula it uses everywhere else (10:5, 10:16, 10:17, 10:19). That departure is the argument: where the chapter wants the standard formula it uses the standard formula, and here it reaches instead for the prophetic phrase, which is what the reader should notice. Filed at moderate because three words are three words, and a writer could compose 'reign in righteousness' without Isaiah.

pericopes.text: And his brother did raise up in rebellion against him, in the which he did bring him into captivity; and he did remain in captivity all his days; and he begat sons and daughters in captivity; and in his old age he begat Levi, and he died.

And it came to pass that Levi did serve in captivity after the death of his father, for the space of forty and two years. And he did make war against the king of the land, in the which he did obtain unto himself the kingdom.

And after that he had obtained unto himself the kingdom, he did that which was right in the sight of the Lord; and the people did prosper in the land, and he did live to a good old age, and begat sons and daughters; and he also begat Corom, whom he anointed king in his stead.

links.text: And he died in a good old age, full of days, riches, and honour: and Solomon his son reigned in his stead.

provenance.other: “good old age” occurs in exactly four KJV verses: Genesis 15:15 and 25:8 (Abraham), Judges 8:32 (Gideon), and 1 Chronicles 29:28 (David). Only one of the four attaches the phrase to a royal succession — 1 Chronicles 29:28, 'and he died in a good old age, full of days, riches, and honour: and Solomon his son reigned in his stead'. “king in his stead” occurs in four KJV verses, all of them 2 Kings or 2 Chronicles.
provenance.significance: 1 Chronicles 29:28 is the King James Bible's model royal death: long life, wealth, honour, and an uncontested succession to a son the father himself had made king. Ether 10:16 assembles the same four elements for Levi — the kingdom obtained, the reign approved, the good old age, and a son anointed king in his stead — and it does so immediately after 10:14-15, two verses of dynastic imprisonment. Reading David's death notice into it makes the chapter's alternation legible: the chronicle is not merely listing good and bad kings, it is placing the King James Bible's best royal ending next to its own account of a king who spent forty-two years in captivity.

links.note: 'He did live to a good old age, and begat sons and daughters; and he also begat Corom, whom he anointed king in his stead.' The machine ranked Judges 8:32 for 'a good old age', which is Gideon's death notice, and Gideon is displaced here on the succession: Judges 8:33-9:5 is a succession by fratricide and Ether 10:16-17 is a peaceful one to a son who then also does what is good in the sight of the Lord. 1 Chronicles 29:28 is the King James verse that puts 'good old age' and a son succeeding into one sentence.
links.whyNot: 'Good old age' is a natural English phrase and the chapter is full of long-lived kings (10:4, 10:13); a chronicler saying a man died old and left a successor need have no verse in mind. There is no distinctive shared wording beyond the four-word phrase itself, and the succession language differs — Chronicles has the son reign in his stead, Ether has the father anoint him.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Corom did that which was good in the sight of the Lord, all his days; and he begat many sons and daughters; and after that he had seen many days, he did pass away, even like unto the rest of the earth; and Kish reigned in his stead.
And it came to pass that Kish passed away also, and Lib reigned in his stead.

And it came to pass that Lib also did that which was good in the sight of the Lord. And in the days of Lib the poisonous serpents were destroyed; wherefore they did go into the land southward, to hunt food for the people of the land; for the land was covered with animals of the forest. And Lib also himself became a great hunter.—

links.text: He was a mighty hunter before the LORD: wherefore it is said, Even as Nimrod the mighty hunter before the LORD.

provenance.other: “mighty hunter” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 10:9, where it occurs twice. “great hunter”, which is Ether's phrase, occurs in none. The noun 'hunter' is confined in the King James Bible to Nimrod (Genesis 10:9) and to Esau, 'a cunning hunter, a man of the field' (Genesis 25:27); it is not otherwise a description the Bible gives a man, and it is never elsewhere given a king.
provenance.significance: Nimrod is not an incidental figure for this book. Genesis 10:8-10 makes him the first man to be mighty in the earth and gives him Babel as the beginning of his kingdom, which is where the Jaredites come from; the Jaredite migration in Ether 2:1 passes through 'the valley which was northward ... called Nimrod, being called after the mighty hunter'. So when Ether 10:19 says of a righteous king that he 'also himself became a great hunter', it is reaching back past nine chapters to the one name the record has already borrowed from Genesis 10. The metalepsis runs both ways. Recover Genesis 10 and Lib's hunting is a Babel inheritance surfacing in a good reign; read Ether 10:19-21 forward and the inheritance has been domesticated — Nimrod hunted before the LORD and founded a kingdom, Lib hunts to feed the people and sets aside the land southward as a game preserve.

links.note: 'And Lib also himself became a great hunter.' The wording is not the King James Bible's — 'great' for 'mighty' — and that is why the row is an allusion rather than a quotation; what carries it is that the King James Bible has exactly one hunter-king, that the book of Ether has already named him and named a valley after him, and that the sentence's redundant 'also himself' marks the clause as an addition the chronicle wanted to make rather than a detail it needed. The immediate occasion is the destruction of the poisonous serpents of Ether 9:31-33, which reopens the land southward; hunting is what the reopening is for.

pericopes.text: And they built a great city by the narrow neck of land, by the place where the sea divides the land.
And they did preserve the land southward for a wilderness, to get game. And the whole face of the land northward was covered with inhabitants;
and they were exceeding industrious, and they did buy and sell, and traffic one with another, that they might get gain.

links.text: Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain:

provenance.other: “buy and sell” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “get gain” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is the same verse: James 4:13, 'ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain'. Ether 10:22 has both. The Book of Mormon's third term, 'traffic', is King James vocabulary too — 'traffick' occurs in five verses, of which 1 Kings 10:15 (Solomon's revenue from the spice merchants) and Ezekiel 28:5 ('by thy traffick hast thou increased thy riches, and thine heart is lifted up because of thy riches') are the commercial ones.
provenance.significance: James 4:14 is the next sentence: 'Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.' The two King James singletons that make up Ether 10:22 are lifted from the one biblical passage whose entire point is that a trading people does not know how long it has. They are placed at the head of the chapter's prosperity sequence, six verses before 'never could be a people more blessed than were they' — and nine verses before the kingdom is taken away, in a book that ends with the extinction of the nation. Nothing in Ether says this. James 4:14 says it, and the borrowing puts it there.
provenance.alternative: Ezekiel 28:5, of Tyre: 'By thy great wisdom and by thy traffick hast thou increased thy riches, and thine heart is lifted up because of thy riches.' This supplies 'traffick' and the theological verdict, but neither of the two singletons, and it cannot account for 'buy and sell' or 'get gain'.

links.note: 'They were exceeding industrious, and they did buy and sell, and traffic one with another, that they might get gain.' Two King James singletons from a single verse, in that verse's order, with the Book of Mormon's own word inserted between them. The run is short and well below Skousen's threshold; what makes it a strong row is that neither phrase has any other King James home, and that James 4:13 is the Bible's only sentence about buying, selling and getting gain as one continuous activity. Ezekiel 28:5 is recorded as an alternative because its rebuke of Tyre's traffick and lifted-up heart is the closest Old Testament analogue, and because the chapter's other main source, Deuteronomy 8:14, uses the same 'heart be lifted up'.

pericopes.text: And they did work in all manner of ore, and they did make gold, and silver, and iron, and brass, and all manner of metals; and they did dig it out of the earth; wherefore they did cast up mighty heaps of earth for to get ore, of gold, and of silver, and of iron, and of copper. And they did work all manner of fine work.

links.text: A land wherein thou shalt eat bread without scarceness, thou shalt not lack any thing in it; a land whose stones are iron, and out of whose hills thou mayest dig brass.

provenance.other: “whose stones are iron” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “dig brass” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is the same verse: Deuteronomy 8:9, 'a land whose stones are iron, and out of whose hills thou mayest dig brass'. It is the only place in the King James Bible where metal is dug out of the ground at all.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 8:7-10 is the description of the promised land, and mineral wealth is its last item before the warning that follows: eat and be full, bless the LORD for the good land, and then 'beware that thou forget not'. Ether 10:23 takes the one King James verse that puts iron and brass under the hills of a promised land, and Ether 10:28 takes its conclusion — 'they were in a land that was choice above all lands, for the Lord had spoken it'. What the chapter does not take is Deuteronomy 8:11-14, and it does not need to: the reader who recovers the context has already been told what comes after the mining, and Ether 10:30 supplies it without argument.

links.note: 'They did work in all manner of ore ... and they did dig it out of the earth; wherefore they did cast up mighty heaps of earth for to get ore, of gold, and of silver, and of iron, and of copper.' The machine offered Daniel 11:43 and Exodus 31:5 for the metal-list runs, and both are inventories; neither has anything dug. Deuteronomy 8:9 is the King James Bible's only mining verse, it names two of Ether's four metals as the products of that mining, and it is the promised-land passage this chapter reaches for again five verses later. Note that Ether's fourth metal is copper, which does not appear in Deuteronomy 8:9 — nor, as a mined metal, anywhere in the King James Bible.

links.text: And to devise curious works, to work in gold, and in silver, and in brass,

provenance.route: Exodus 31:3-5 and 35:31-35 (the commission of Bezaleel) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “curious works” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 35:32, 'And to devise curious works, to work in gold, and in silver, and in brass'; its near-twin at Exodus 31:4 reads 'cunning works'. “in gold, and in silver, and in” occurs in four KJV verses, three of which (Exodus 31:4, Exodus 35:32, 2 Chronicles 2:7) are commissions to a named master craftsman. Exodus 35:35 supplies 'to work all manner of work'.
provenance.significance: Exodus 31 and 35 are the King James Bible's account of Bezaleel, filled with the spirit of God 'in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship', to devise curious works for the tabernacle. It is sacred manufacture, commissioned for one building, and it is the vocabulary Ether 10:23-27 uses for a secular boom — ore, metals, cloth, ploughs, and weapons of war. The chapter that names no temple and no priesthood describes its industry entirely in the diction the King James Bible reserves for building the sanctuary, and the last item on the list (10:27, 'all manner of weapons of war ... all manner of work of exceeding curious workmanship') is the one thing Bezaleel was never commissioned to make.

links.note: 'And they did work in all manner of ore ... and they did work all manner of fine work', continued at 10:27, 'they did work all manner of work of exceeding curious workmanship'. Three separate Bezaleel formulae — working in gold and in silver, curious work, and all manner of work — in five verses of a chapter about commerce. Adjudicated here at their first occurrence; 10:27, where 'curious' and 'all manner of work' both appear and the machine ranked Exodus 35:35, is recorded in recurrenceRefs rather than given its own row. Filed at moderate because each formula on its own is common enough that a reader may take the cluster as the ordinary King James way to describe skilled making.

pericopes.text: And they did have silks, and fine twined linen; and they did work all manner of cloth, that they might clothe themselves from their nakedness.

links.text: And a mitre of fine linen, and goodly bonnets of fine linen, and linen breeches of fine twined linen,

provenance.route: Exodus 26-39 (the tabernacle and the priestly vestments) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “fine twined linen” occurs in exactly twenty KJV verses, and every one of them is in Exodus 26-39: the curtains, the veil, the hangings of the court, the ephod, the breastplate, and the linen breeches. The phrase has no other home in the King James Bible — it never appears in a description of ordinary clothing, wealth, or trade. Exodus 39:28 is the verse that makes the breeches of it, and Exodus 28:42 says what they are for: 'linen breeches to cover their nakedness', which is a King James singleton.
provenance.significance: The two halves of Ether 10:24 are the two halves of Exodus 28:42 and 39:28, and in the same relation: fine twined linen, and the covering of nakedness. In Exodus the covering is priestly and the nakedness is a ritual danger — the breeches are ordered so that the priests 'bear not iniquity, and die'. Ether 10:24 has the phrase supply clothes for a whole trading population, 'that they might clothe themselves from their nakedness', which is the language of Genesis 3:21 doing the work of an economy. The recovery is that the chapter has dressed a commercial nation in the fabric the King James Bible manufactures only for the sanctuary and its priests.

links.note: 'And they did have silks, and fine twined linen; and they did work all manner of cloth, that they might clothe themselves from their nakedness.' Twenty occurrences is too many to name a verse, so the row is filed on the phrase's exclusive location rather than on Exodus 39:28 in particular; 39:28 is named because it is the occurrence that puts fine twined linen into a garment whose stated purpose, four chapters earlier, is covering nakedness. Set beside 10:23's Bezaleel formulae, the tabernacle vocabulary in this chapter is not one phrase but a register.

links.text: The merchandise of gold, and silver, and precious stones, and of pearls, and fine linen, and purple, and silk, and scarlet, and all thyine wood, and all manner vessels of ivory, and all manner vessels of most precious wood, and of brass, and iron, and marble,

provenance.other: “and silk” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Ezekiel 16:13 and Revelation 18:12; 'silk' in any form occurs in four (adding Proverbs 31:22 and Ezekiel 16:10), and Ether's plural 'silks' occurs in none. Of the two, only Revelation 18:12 is a list of merchandise, and only Revelation 18:12 also contains gold, silver, fine linen, brass and iron — five of the six commodities Ether 10:23-24 names.
provenance.significance: Revelation 18 is the fall of Babylon, and 18:11-13 is its cargo manifest, recited by merchants who weep because no man buys their merchandise any more. The book of Ether is, by its own account, the record of the people who came out of Babel (Ether 1:33). Ether 10:22-24 gives that people its commercial summit — buying, selling, getting gain, working every metal, wearing silk and fine linen — and the passage sits six verses before the kingdom is taken away and four generations pass their lives in captivity, in a book that will end with the nation destroyed to the last man. If the register of Revelation 18 is in play here, the chapter has written Babel's descendants a Babylon inventory and put it immediately before the fall.
provenance.alternative: Ezekiel 16:13, 'thy raiment was of fine linen, and silk, and broidered work', which pairs silk with fine linen in one clause as Ether does, and ends 'thou didst prosper into a kingdom' — but it is a bridal adornment, not commerce.

links.note: 'And they did have silks, and fine twined linen.' Silk is a King James rarity and its only merchant-catalogue occurrence is Revelation 18:12, whose surrounding list matches Ether 10:23-24 commodity for commodity in a different order. The reading is offered as the chapter's largest risk and is filed as an echo at moderate for that reason: the argument is the coincidence of a whole catalogue plus one rare word, not of a phrase. It is recorded separately from the Exodus row above because the verse's two nouns point to two different places in the King James Bible, and the catalogue should say so rather than choose.
links.whyNot: No shared run of more than two words, and the order of the commodities does not match. A people that mines metals and weaves cloth will produce a list resembling any other such list, and Revelation 18:12's distinctive items — pearls, thyine wood, ivory, marble, the souls of men — are all absent from Ether. Ezekiel 16:13, the other 'and silk' verse, is at least as good a home for silk beside fine linen and gold and silver, though it is not a merchant's list.

pericopes.text: And they did make all manner of tools to till the earth, both to plough and to sow, to reap and to hoe, and also to thrash.
And they did make all manner of tools in the which they did work their beasts.
And they did make all manner of weapons of war. And they did work all manner of work of exceeding curious workmanship.
And never could be a people more blessed than were they, and more prospered by the hand of the Lord. And they were in a land that was choice above all lands, for the Lord had spoken it.
And it came to pass that Lib did live many years, and begat sons and daughters; and he also begat Hearthom.

And it came to pass that Hearthom reigned in the stead of his father. And when Hearthom had reigned twenty and four years, behold the kingdom was taken away from him. And he served many years in captivity; yea, even all the remainder of his days.

And he begat Heth, and Heth lived in captivity all his days. And Heth begat Aaron, and Aaron dwelt in captivity all his days; and he begat Amnigaddah, and Amnigaddah also dwelt in captivity all his days; and he begat Coriantum, and Coriantum dwelt in captivity all his days; and he begat Com.

And it came to pass that Com drew away the half of the kingdom. And he reigned over the half of the kingdom forty and two years; and he went to battle against the king Amgid, and they fought for the space of many years, in the which Com gained power over Amgid, and obtained power over the remainder of the kingdom.
And in the days of Com there began to be robbers in the land; and they adopted the old plans, and administered oaths after the manner of the ancients, and sought again to destroy the kingdom.
Now Com did fight against them much; nevertheless, he did not prevail against them.

And there came also in the days of Com many prophets, and prophesied of the destruction of that great people, except they should repent and turn unto the Lord, and forsake their murders and wickedness.

links.text: But shewed first unto them of Damascus, and at Jerusalem, and throughout all the coasts of Judaea, and then to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, and do works meet for repentance.

provenance.other: “should repent and turn” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 26:20. The bare pair “repent and turn” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Ezekiel 14:6, Ezekiel 18:30, Jonah 3:9 and Acts 26:20 — and of the four only Acts carries the modal. Ether's continuation, “turn unto the Lord”, occurs in exactly four KJV verses (Deuteronomy 30:10, 2 Chronicles 15:4, Psalm 22:27, Joel 2:13) where Acts reads 'turn to God'; the substitution is the one point at which the Book of Mormon leaves the singleton.
provenance.significance: Recover Acts 26 and the borrowing acquires a sequel. Acts 26:20 is Paul before Agrippa summarising his entire prophetic commission in one sentence; Acts 26:21 is what it cost him — 'For these causes the Jews caught me in the temple, and went about to kill me.' Ether 11:1 gives the Jaredite prophets that commission in that sentence, and Ether 11:2 gives them Acts 26:21: 'the prophets were rejected by the people … for the people sought to destroy them.' Two consecutive verses of Ether reproduce two consecutive verses of Acts in their order, the second of them (see 11:2) on a second KJV singleton.

links.note: 'Many prophets, and prophesied of the destruction of that great people, except they should repent and turn unto the Lord, and forsake their murders and wickedness.' The five-word run is a KJV singleton and it opens the chapter, which matters because everything that follows in Ether 11 is the working out of a refusal to do what those five words ask. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and so no candidate for his list, but the run is exact and its source is not in doubt: no other KJV verse puts 'should' in front of 'repent and turn'. The Jaredite prophets are given the terms of Paul's commission, and — as the next verse shows — its consequences.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the prophets were rejected by the people, and they fled unto Com for protection, for the people sought to destroy them;

links.text: And he taught daily in the temple. But the chief priests and the scribes and the chief of the people sought to destroy him,

provenance.other: “the people sought to destroy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 19:47. The shorter “sought to destroy” occurs in exactly two, Esther 3:6 and Luke 19:47, and Esther's subject is Haman planning a pogrom, not a rejected prophet.
provenance.significance: Luke 19:47 sits four verses after the lament over Jerusalem — 'they shall lay thee even with the ground, and thy children within thee … because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation' (19:44) — which is the King James Bible's fullest statement that a city's destruction follows from its refusal of the one sent to it. That is the whole argument of Ether 11, and the chapter has borrowed the sentence that stands next to it. The suppressed correspondence is what Luke gives as the reason the people cannot act: 'and could not find what they might do: for all the people were very attentive to hear him.' In Ether the restraint is not popular attention but a king — the prophets 'fled unto Com for protection' — and when the protecting king dies (11:4) his successor's brother kills them all (11:5).

links.note: 'And it came to pass that the prophets were rejected by the people, and they fled unto Com for protection, for the people sought to destroy them.' A second KJV singleton in consecutive verses, and the pair is the argument: 11:1 has Acts 26:20's commission and 11:2 has the persecution that Acts 26:21 reports as its result, in Luke's words rather than Paul's. Note what the Book of Mormon does to the grammar. In Luke the destroyers are 'the chief priests and the scribes and the chief of the people'; Ether drops the leadership and leaves the people, then inverts the Bible's usual arrangement by making the ruler the prophets' shelter. The verse is running on a KJV phrase and reversing the KJV's politics with it.

pericopes.text: and they prophesied unto Com many things: and he was blessed in all the remainder of his days.
And he lived to a good old age, and begat Shiblom; and Shiblom reigned in his stead. And the brother of Shiblom rebelled against him; and there began to be an exceeding great war in all the land.

links.text: And Gideon the son of Joash died in a good old age, and was buried in the sepulchre of Joash his father, in Ophrah of the Abiezrites.

provenance.other: “a good old age” occurs in exactly four KJV verses: Genesis 15:15 (the promise to Abram), Genesis 25:8 (Abraham's death), Judges 8:32 (Gideon's) and 1 Chronicles 29:28 (David's).
provenance.significance: Of the four, only Judges 8:32 is followed by what Ether 11:4 is followed by. Gideon dies in a good old age and is buried in his father's sepulchre; Judges 9 opens immediately with Abimelech murdering his seventy brethren to take the kingdom, and the land falls into a civil war that ends with a city burned and its ruler killed by a woman's millstone. Ether 11:4 reads: Com dies in a good old age, begets Shiblom, 'and the brother of Shiblom rebelled against him; and there began to be an exceeding great war in all the land.' The catalogue already reads Ether 6:22-26 out of Jotham's parable in Judges 9:8-9 — the speech that answers Abimelech's coup — so the book's Judges 9 material is on the record before this verse arrives at its first clause. The phrase is doing the work of a stage direction: it marks the end of the last good reign and the death that releases the fratricide.

links.note: 'And he lived to a good old age, and begat Shiblom; and Shiblom reigned in his stead. And the brother of Shiblom rebelled against him.' The four-word run is not rare enough to fix a source by itself; what fixes it is the sequel. Three of the four KJV holders of the phrase close a patriarch's life with nothing following, and the fourth closes a judge's life and is followed at once by a brother-killing usurpation and a general war, which is what Ether 11:4 puts in its second half. Com's whole characterisation in 11:1-3 — blessed, sheltering prophets, dying old — is also Gideon's arc read charitably, and Ether has already mined Judges 9 for the coup that answers it.
links.whyNot: Four verses is not a singleton, and Genesis 25:8's Abraham is by a wide margin the phrase's most familiar occurrence. The row rests on the sequence rather than on the phrase, and a reader who declines the Judges 9 reading of Ether 6 will want to decline this one too.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the brother of Shiblom did cause that all the prophets which prophesied of the destruction of the people, should be put to death;

links.text: That the blood of all the prophets, which was shed from the foundation of the world, may be required of this generation;

provenance.other: “all the prophets which” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 11:50. tools/mediation-check.py run against the Matthean parallel, Matthew 23:35, is decisive for Luke: the Book of Mormon has Luke's 'prophets, which was shed from the foundation', not Matthew's 'righteous blood'. Where the two Synoptic forms of one woe diverge, Ether 11:5 has Luke's.
provenance.significance: Luke 11:49-51 is Wisdom's oracle: 'I will send them prophets and apostles, and some of them they shall slay and persecute: that the blood of all the prophets, which was shed from the foundation of the world, may be required of this generation.' Ether 11:5-6 is that sentence executed and its bill presented in the next breath — the prophets are put to death, and 'there was great calamity in all the land: for they had testified that a great curse should come upon the land.' Luke's 'required of this generation' and Ether's great destruction are the same accounting, and Ether has kept Luke's causal order: the killing first, the reckoning immediately after.

links.note: 'The brother of Shiblom did cause that all the prophets which prophesied of the destruction of the people, should be put to death.' The four-word run is a KJV singleton and it is the one place in the Bible where 'all the prophets' are counted as a body of the murdered. CONVENTIONS §8 bears directly: the 1830 text reads 'all the prophets which prophesied' and the 1920 edition corrected 'which' to 'who', which removes the string that identifies the source — the borrowing is legible in the first edition and invisible in the modern one. The chapter's method is now clear enough to name: 11:1 takes Acts 26:20, 11:2 takes Luke 19:47, 11:5 takes Luke 11:50, and the Jaredite decline is being narrated in the vocabulary the KJV reserves for a covenant people that kills the prophets sent to it.

pericopes.text: and there was great calamity in all the land: for they had testified that a great curse should come upon the land, and also upon the people, and that there should be a great destruction among them, such an one as never had been upon the face of the earth; and their bones should become as heaps of earth upon the face of the land, except they should repent of their wickedness.

links.text: And at that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince which standeth for the children of thy people: and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time: and at that time thy people shall be delivered, every one that shall be found written in the book.

provenance.route: Daniel 12:1 → KJV → Book of Mormon, possibly by way of Matthew 24:21
provenance.other: “such as never” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 12:1. tools/mediation-check.py against Matthew 24:21 — which is Daniel 12:1's own New Testament reuse — returns one decisive point, and it favours Daniel: the Book of Mormon has 'never', where Matthew reads 'such as was not since the beginning of the world'.
provenance.alternative: Mediation is left `uncertain` on purpose. The decisive word is Daniel's; the sequence around it is Matthew's. Ether 11:7's 'famines and pestilences' is Matthew 24:7's phrase (see the row on that verse), and Matthew 24 puts its unparalleled tribulation after its famines and pestilences exactly as Ether 11:6-7 puts its unparalleled destruction after its. So one test points to direct dependence on Daniel and the other to an OT-via-NT route in which Matthew 24 supplies the frame and Daniel supplies the word; the evidence does not presently choose, and the enum's `OT-via-NT` would assert more than we can show.
provenance.significance: Daniel 12:1's time of trouble ends in a deliverance: 'at that time thy people shall be delivered, every one that shall be found written in the book.' Ether takes the trouble and not the deliverance. What survives the Jaredite destruction is only the book itself — Ether writing in the cavity of a rock — and it is found by a people who are not his. The unstated half of the borrowing is the half Ether 11 cannot have.

links.note: 'A great destruction among them, such an one as never had been upon the face of the earth', repeated at 11:7 as 'such an one as never had been known'. The unparalleled-calamity formula is common enough in substance — Exodus 9:18, Joel 2:2, Mark 13:19 — but only one KJV verse builds it on 'never', and that verse is Daniel 12:1. The doubling within two verses is what raises this above an echo: the writer has a form of words and uses it twice, and the form is a form the KJV supplies once.

links.text: And they shall spread them before the sun, and the moon, and all the host of heaven, whom they have loved, and whom they have served, and after whom they have walked, and whom they have sought, and whom they have worshipped: they shall not be gathered, nor be buried; they shall be for dung upon the face of the earth.

provenance.other: “dung upon the face of the earth” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Jeremiah 8:2 and Jeremiah 16:4, and they are the Bible's two pictures of a nation's dead left lying unburied on open ground. “upon the face of the earth” by itself occurs in exactly twelve KJV verses and settles nothing.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 8:1 itemises whose bones are meant: 'the bones of the kings of Judah, and the bones of his princes, and the bones of the priests, and the bones of the prophets, and the bones of the inhabitants of Jerusalem.' The prophets are on the list. Ether 11:5 has just made the prophets into bones, and 11:6 is the sentence their killers earn: the land that took the prophets' bodies will be covered with everyone else's. Ether 14:21-23, where the dead are left unburied because there is nobody to bury them and 'the scent thereof went forth upon the face of the land', is where the promise is kept.

links.note: 'And their bones should become as heaps of earth upon the face of the land, except they should repent of their wickedness.' The image is not a Book of Mormon invention and it is not generic: unburied bones lying on the surface of the ground is a specific covenant curse with a specific home in the KJV, Jeremiah 8:1-2 and its doublet at 16:4. Ether substitutes 'heaps of earth' for Jeremiah's 'dung' and 'land' for 'earth', so there is no run to quote; what carries the row is that the picture, the cause (a people that would not hear) and the position in the sentence are all Jeremiah's.
links.whyNot: Not one distinctive string is shared. “heaps of earth” is in no KJV verse at all, and the phrase Ether does share, 'upon the face of the earth', is among the commonest in the Bible. This is a picture rather than a phrase, and a reader who requires verbal contact should decline it.

pericopes.text: And they hearkened not unto the voice of the Lord, because of their wicked combinations; wherefore there began to be wars and contentions in all the land, and also many famines and pestilences, insomuch that there was a great destruction, such an one as never had been known upon the face of the earth: and all this came to pass in the days of Shiblom.

links.text: But it shall come to pass, if thou wilt not hearken unto the voice of the LORD thy God, to observe to do all his commandments and his statutes which I command thee this day; that all these curses shall come upon thee, and overtake thee:

provenance.other: “hearken unto the voice of the Lord” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, Deuteronomy 15:5, 28:2, 28:15 and 30:10 — three of them in the blessing-and-curse chapter and its coda. The negative form the Book of Mormon actually uses, “hearkened not unto the voice”, occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Samuel 2:25 and Psalm 106:25, and Psalm 106:25's clause — 'and hearkened not unto the voice of the LORD' — is Ether 11:7's word for word.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 28:15 is not one curse among many; it is the protasis on which the whole catalogue of curses depends, and the pestilence, the sword and the consuming famine follow it at 28:21-25. Ether 2:8-12 has already put the Jaredites under a land covenant of exactly this Deuteronomic shape — serve the God of the land or be swept off. Ether 11:7 is that covenant's curse clause discharging, compressed from fourteen verses of Deuteronomy into one sentence and given in Deuteronomy's own order: the failure to hearken, then war, then famine and pestilence, then destruction.

links.note: 'And they hearkened not unto the voice of the Lord, because of their wicked combinations; wherefore there began to be wars and contentions in all the land, and also many famines and pestilences.' The sentence has two sources and the machine test says so out loud: tools/mediation-check.py run on Deuteronomy 28:15 against Matthew 24:7 returns divergences pointing both ways — one decisive point for Deuteronomy on the conditional clause, two for Matthew on the disaster list. That is a composite, not an ambiguity, and the register carries a row for each half. This row is the frame: the covenant conditional, the causal 'wherefore', and the Deuteronomic logic by which not hearkening is itself the cause of the war. Compare Hays on thematic coherence — the chapter has been building a covenant argument since 11:1, and the Deuteronomy 28 frame is what the argument needs.

links.text: For nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom: and there shall be famines, and pestilences, and earthquakes, in divers places.

provenance.other: “famines and pestilences” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 24:7 and Luke 21:11, and both are the Olivet discourse. It is also a hapax in the Book of Mormon: Ether 11:7 is the only verse in the entire book where the pair occurs.
provenance.significance: Matthew 24 runs wars and rumours of wars (24:6), then famines and pestilences (24:7), then a tribulation 'such as was not since the beginning of the world' (24:21). Ether 11:7 runs wars and contentions, then famines and pestilences, then 'a great destruction, such an one as never had been known upon the face of the earth' — three stages in one sentence in Matthew's order. The metalepsis is what stands immediately before the discourse. Matthew 23:34-37 is the woe on those who kill the prophets sent to them, ending 'O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets'; the Olivet prediction of the city's fall follows it directly. Ether 11 has the same two things in the same relation: the prophets are put to death at 11:5, and the wars, famines and pestilences arrive at 11:7.

links.note: 'Wars and contentions in all the land, and also many famines and pestilences, insomuch that there was a great destruction.' Two KJV verses hold 'famines and pestilences' and both are the same discourse; the Book of Mormon uses the pair once in 6,000 verses and uses it here. What makes the row more than a two-word coincidence is that the words arrive inside their source's sequence: Ether 11:5-7 kills the prophets, then gives wars, then famines and pestilences, then an unparalleled destruction, which is Matthew 23:34-24:21 in order. Taken with 11:1 (Acts 26:20), 11:2 (Luke 19:47) and 11:5 (Luke 11:50), the chapter's controlling register is the New Testament's judgment-on-a-prophet-killing-people material, laid over a Deuteronomy 28 frame — and the mediation test at 11:7 confirms the two are welded rather than alternatives.

pericopes.text: And the people began to repent of their iniquity; and inasmuch as they did, the Lord did have mercy on them.
And it came to pass that Shiblom was slain, and Seth was brought into captivity; and he did dwell in captivity all his days.

And it came to pass that Ahah, his son, did obtain the kingdom; and he did reign over the people all his days. And he did do all manner of iniquity in his days, in the which he did cause the shedding of much blood; and few were his days.

links.text: Let his days be few; and let another take his office.

provenance.other: “his days be few” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 109:8, and so does “let another take his office”. tools/mediation-check.py against Acts 1:20, where Peter cites this psalm of Judas, returns two decisive points for the psalm: the Book of Mormon has 'days' and 'few', where Acts reads 'habitation' and 'desolate'. Acts quotes the psalm's second clause only and drops the first — and the first is precisely the clause Ether has.
provenance.significance: Psalm 109:8's two clauses arrive in Ether in order and one verse apart. 'Let his days be few' is Ether 11:10, 'and few were his days'; 'and let another take his office' is Ether 11:11, 'And Ethem, being a descendant of Ahah, did obtain the kingdom.' Psalm 109 is an imprecation against a man of blood — 109:16, 'he persecuted the poor and needy man, that he might even slay the broken in heart' — and Ether 11:10 has just said that Ahah 'did cause the shedding of much blood'. What the psalm prays for, Ether reports as having happened; the curse is delivered as an annal.

links.note: 'And he did do all manner of iniquity in his days, in the which he did cause the shedding of much blood; and few were his days.' The clause is a KJV singleton in inverted order — Ether has 'few were his days' where the psalm has 'let his days be few' — which is what a borrowing looks like when a petition is turned into a report. The clinching evidence is the next verse. Psalm 109:8 is a two-clause line and the Book of Mormon has both clauses in sequence: the shortened reign at 11:10, the successor taking the office at 11:11. The mediation test is worth stating plainly, since Psalm 109:8 is one of the most heavily mediated verses in the Bible: Ether has the psalm's own form and not the New Testament's, and it has the half of the verse the New Testament never quotes.

links.text: And in his estate shall stand up a vile person, to whom they shall not give the honour of the kingdom: but he shall come in peaceably, and obtain the kingdom by flatteries.

provenance.other: “obtain the kingdom” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 11:21. Ether 11:10 is its first appearance anywhere in the Book of Mormon; the chapter then uses it three more times (11:11, 11:16, 11:18) and the book once more at 13:24.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one man who obtains a kingdom is 'a vile person, to whom they shall not give the honour of the kingdom: but he shall come in peaceably, and obtain the kingdom by flatteries' — a usurper taking what was not granted him, in the chapter of Daniel that reads history as a sequence of kings displacing kings. Ether 11 is that chapter in miniature, and it uses the phrase as Daniel's context licenses: Moron regains by force a kingdom rebellion took from him (11:16), and an unnamed descendant of the brother of Jared overthrows Moron and takes it (11:18). The Jaredite king-list has borrowed Daniel 11's one verb for coming by a throne, and by the fourth use it has arrived at Daniel's sense.

links.note: 'And it came to pass that Ahah, his son, did obtain the kingdom.' A three-word KJV singleton is not much on its own; four occurrences of it in nine verses, in a passage about thrones changing hands by war, is a different kind of evidence — the writer has a phrase for the transaction and the KJV supplies it once. The four uses also chart the chapter's decline: it enters on a lawful succession, and by 11:18 it describes a man with no claim at all overthrowing a king and putting him in captivity for life. ADJUDICATING §4 asks for the adjudication at first use, so the row sits at 11:10 and the register sends a reader from 11:18 back here.
links.whyNot: The first use is a son succeeding his father, which is not Daniel 11:21's case, so if the borrowing is real the chapter took the phrase before it took the sense. A reader could hold that 'obtain the kingdom' is unremarkable English and that its single KJV occurrence is an accident of how rarely the KJV needs to say it.

pericopes.text: And Ethem, being a descendant of Ahah, did obtain the kingdom; and he also did do that which was wicked in his days.

And it came to pass in the days of Ethem, there came many prophets and prophesied again unto the people; yea, they did prophesy that the Lord would utterly destroy them from off the face of the earth, except they repented of their iniquities.

links.text: Behold, the eyes of the Lord GOD are upon the sinful kingdom, and I will destroy it from off the face of the earth; saving that I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob, saith the LORD.

provenance.other: “from off the face of the earth” occurs in exactly five KJV verses: Genesis 7:4, Deuteronomy 6:15, 1 Kings 13:34, Jeremiah 28:16 and Amos 9:8. Only Amos 9:8 also carries 'utterly destroy', and only Amos 9:8 attaches an exception to the threat.
provenance.alternative: The catalogue adjudicates the same clause at Mosiah 12:8, in Abinadi's mouth, as Deuteronomy 6:15 with the common idiom 'utterly destroy' welded onto it. That reading is sound for Abinadi and the phrase certainly carries Deuteronomy 6:15's exact six-word run. Amos 9:8 is preferred here because Ether 11:12 keeps all three of Amos's elements in one sentence — utter destruction, from off the face of the earth, and a stated exception — and because Amos 9:7 turns up again nine verses later at Ether 11:21.
provenance.significance: Amos 9:8's exception is unconditional and it saves: 'saving that I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob.' Ether 11:12's exception is conditional — 'except they repented of their iniquities' — and it is not met. The Jaredites are the case Amos rules out. Read with Ether 11:21, the pair Amos 9:7-8 appears to be open in front of this chapter: 9:8 supplies the destruction at 11:12, and 9:7's question about God bringing up other nations as he brought Israel supplies the substitute people at 11:21.

links.note: 'They did prophesy that the Lord would utterly destroy them from off the face of the earth, except they repented of their iniquities.' Five KJV verses hold the six-word run and one of them holds the whole sentence-shape. ADJUDICATING §4 governs the relation to Mosiah 12:8: a phrase re-entering across a book boundary in a different hand gets the link rather than an exclusion, and Moroni abridging a Jaredite record is not Abinadi before Noah's priests. What the two rows disagree about is worth leaving on the record rather than harmonising — the Mosiah row reads a Deuteronomy verse plus an idiom, this one reads a single Amos verse that already contains both, and the tiebreak offered here is the return of Amos 9:7 at the end of the same chapter.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the people hardened their hearts, and would not hearken unto their words; and the prophets mourned and withdrew from among the people.

links.text: And yet they would not hearken unto their judges, but they went a whoring after other gods, and bowed themselves unto them: they turned quickly out of the way which their fathers walked in, obeying the commandments of the LORD; but they did not so.

provenance.other: “would not hearken unto their” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Judges 2:17, where the object is 'judges' and Ether's is 'words'.
provenance.significance: This catalogue already reads Ether 7:27 out of Judges 2:7-10 — the KJV's account of how a nation forgets, the generation that served the LORD all the days of Joshua and the generation after it that knew him not. Ether 11:8-13 turns out to be the rest of the same paragraph, in order. Judges 2:18, 'it repented the LORD because of their groanings by reason of them that oppressed them', stands behind Ether 11:8, 'the people began to repent of their iniquity; and inasmuch as they did, the Lord did have mercy on them'; Judges 2:17's refusal to hearken stands behind 11:13; and Judges 2:19's 'corrupted themselves more than their fathers' is the movement of the chapter as a whole, each reign worse than the last. What was found at Ether 7 as one verse's model is the template the book's decline is built on.

links.note: 'The people hardened their hearts, and would not hearken unto their words; and the prophets mourned and withdrew from among the people.' The four-word run is a KJV singleton, and its verse is the pivot of the Judges cycle — the sentence that explains why deliverance never holds. The Book of Mormon has substituted 'words' for 'judges', which is the substitution Ether needs: the Jaredites have no judges, they have prophets, and it is the prophets' words that go unheard. The row is offered at moderate rather than high because the run alone would not carry it; what carries it is that the surrounding verses take the surrounding verses of Judges 2, and that the catalogue reached Judges 2 independently four chapters earlier.
links.whyNot: The object of the verb is different, and refusal-to-hearken language is spread thickly through the prophets — Ezekiel 20:8's 'they rebelled against me, and would not hearken unto me' is nearly as close and has no Judges cycle behind it. The case is the chapter-length sequence, not the phrase.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Ethem did execute judgement in wickedness all his days; and he begat Moron. And it came to pass that Moron did reign in his stead; and Moron did do that which was wicked before the Lord.

links.text: Thus saith the LORD; Execute ye judgment and righteousness, and deliver the spoiled out of the hand of the oppressor: and do no wrong, do no violence to the stranger, the fatherless, nor the widow, neither shed innocent blood in this place.

provenance.route: Jeremiah 22:3 → KJV → Book of Mormon (entering the book at Ether 9:21)
provenance.other: “execute judgment” occurs in exactly eleven KJV verses, and in the royal ones it is invariably the king's covenant duty: Jeremiah 22:3 commands the house of David to 'Execute ye judgment and righteousness', and Jeremiah 23:5 promises a king who 'shall execute judgment and justice in the earth'. The KJV never once predicates the phrase of wickedness.
provenance.significance: The formula enters Ether at 9:21, where Emer 'did execute judgement in righteousness, all his days' — which is Jeremiah 22:3's pairing intact. Ether 11:14 keeps the frame and substitutes its opposite: Ethem 'did execute judgement in wickedness all his days'. The Jaredite king-list is being scored against the Davidic job description, and this is the verse where the score turns over. ADJUDICATING §4's default would file a second use within one book as a repeat; it is written as a link because the second use is the argument — the phrase is not recurring, it is being inverted, and the inversion is only visible because the earlier verse said the other thing.

links.note: 'Ethem did execute judgement in wickedness all his days.' CONVENTIONS §8 applies twice over. The 1830 text spells the word 'judgement'; the KJV spells it 'judgment' in all eleven of its occurrences, and the 1920 edition changed the Book of Mormon to match — a case where a later edition moved the text toward its source rather than away from it, and worth recording as such. The link itself is an echo and nothing stronger: eleven KJV verses is not rarity, and 'execute judgment' was ordinary legal English in 1830 independent of the Bible. What makes it worth a row is the antithesis with Ether 9:21 and the fact that the King James Bible reserves the phrase for the thing a righteous king does.
links.whyNot: No rare string, no run longer than two words, and a phrase in general English use at the time of dictation. If Ether 9:21 did not exist the row would not be written.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that there arose a rebellion among the people, because of that secret combination which was built up to get power and gain; and there arose a mighty man among them in iniquity, and gave battle unto Moron, in the which he did overthrow the half of the kingdom; and he did maintain the half of the kingdom for many years.
And it came to pass that Moron did overthrow him, and did obtain the kingdom again.
And it came to pass that there arose another mighty man; and he was a descendant of the brother of Jared.
And it came to pass that he did overthrow Moron and obtain the kingdom; wherefore Moron dwelt in captivity all the remainder of his days; and he begat Coriantor.
And it came to pass that Coriantor dwelt in captivity all his days.

And in the days of Coriantor there also came many prophets, and prophesied of great and marvellous things, and cried repentance unto the people, and except they should repent, the Lord God would execute judgement against them to their utter destruction;
and that the Lord God would send or bring forth another people to possess the land, by his power, after the manner which he brought their fathers.

links.text: Are ye not as children of the Ethiopians unto me, O children of Israel? saith the LORD. Have not I brought up Israel out of the land of Egypt? and the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Syrians from Kir?

provenance.other: “another people” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Deuteronomy 28:32, 1 Chronicles 16:20 and Psalm 105:13; “to possess the land” occurs in exactly seven, every one of them Deuteronomic or in Joshua and Judges. Neither phrase appears in Amos 9:7 — the contact here is conceptual, and the row says so.
provenance.significance: Amos 9:7 is the one place in the King James Bible where God says the exodus was not unique: 'Have not I brought up Israel out of the land of Egypt? and the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Syrians from Kir?' Other nations get their own bringing-out, at the same hand, and it does not make them chosen. Ether 11:21 says exactly that about the land the Jaredites are about to forfeit — the Lord 'would send or bring forth another people to possess the land, by his power, after the manner which he brought their fathers.' The proposal is made because Amos 9:8, the very next verse, is the best source for Ether 11:12 nine verses earlier: if that row stands, this chapter has Amos 9:7-8 open in front of it and is taking the destruction from one verse and the replacement exodus from the other. Metaleptically the reading is heavy, because the 'another people' turns out to be Lehi's, and the Book of Mormon's own second exodus is thereby licensed by the verse that says God does this sort of thing for the Philistines too.

links.note: 'That the Lord God would send or bring forth another people to possess the land, by his power, after the manner which he brought their fathers.' The Deuteronomic vocabulary is real but diffuse — 'possess the land' is Joshua's standing phrase and 'another people' sits, suggestively, in the curse chapter that stands behind Ether 11:7. What the verse actually asserts, though, is not a Deuteronomic dispossession but a second exodus for a second people, by the same power and after the same manner, and the KJV states that doctrine once. This is filed as `figural` because there is no wording to test, and at moderate because it is proposed on the strength of a neighbouring verse rather than on its own.
links.whyNot: There is no verbal contact with Amos 9:7 whatsoever — not one distinctive shared word. The row rests entirely on the theology and on the adjacency of Amos 9:8 at 11:12, and it should be withdrawn if that row is withdrawn.

pericopes.text: And they did reject all the words of the prophets, because of their secret society and wicked abominations.

links.text: But they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and misused his prophets, until the wrath of the LORD arose against his people, till there was no remedy.

provenance.other: “misused his prophets” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 36:16, and so does “no remedy”. The Book of Mormon has neither string; the shared content is 'prophets' and 'words' against Chronicles' 'his prophets' and 'his words'.
provenance.significance: 2 Chronicles 36:15-16 is the King James Bible's own closing verdict on a nation, and the offence it names is this one and no other: God sent to them by his messengers, rising up betimes, 'but they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and misused his prophets, until the wrath of the LORD arose against his people, till there was no remedy.' Nebuchadnezzar arrives in the next verse. Ether 11:22 occupies the same position exactly — it is the last thing said of the Jaredites before Ether is born and the terminal war begins, and it too puts the rejection of the prophets, not the murders and not the abominations, in the operative clause.

links.note: 'And they did reject all the words of the prophets, because of their secret society and wicked abominations.' The verbal contact is thin and the row says so; what is not thin is the placement. Both sentences are one-line verdicts, both make prophet-rejection the ground of the sentence rather than one item in a list, and both stand immediately before the destroying army enters the narrative. The chapter has spent twenty-two verses assembling the KJV's prophet-rejection vocabulary — Acts 26:20, Luke 19:47, Luke 11:50, Judges 2:17 — and it closes on the frame of the verse the KJV uses to close a kingdom.
links.whyNot: One shared content word. A reader could reasonably say that any summary of prophet-rejection will resemble 2 Chronicles 36:16 because 2 Chronicles 36:16 is the paradigm, and that resemblance to a paradigm is not dependence on a verse.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Coriantor begat Ether, and he died, having dwelt in captivity all his days.
And it came to pass that the days of Ether was in the days of Coriantumr; and Coriantumr was king over all the land.—

And Ether was a prophet of the Lord; wherefore Ether came forth in the days of Coriantumr, and began to prophesy unto the people, for he could not be constrained because of the spirit of the Lord which was in him:

for he did cry from the morning, even until the going down of the sun, exhorting the people to believe in God unto repentance, lest they should be destroyed, saying unto them, That by faith all things are fulfilled;

wherefore, whoso believeth in God, might with surety hope for a better world, yea, even a place at the right hand of God, which hope cometh of faith, maketh an anchor to the souls of men, which would make them sure and steadfast, always abounding in good works, being led to glorify God.

links.text: Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil;

provenance.other: Hebrews 6:19 is a verse made almost entirely of KJV singletons. “anchor of the soul” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “sure and stedfast” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “within the veil” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. All three are the same verse, and Ether 12 has all three.
provenance.significance: This is the structural key to the chapter, and it is missed if the verse is read only for its anchor image. Hebrews 6:19 says three things in sequence: hope is an anchor of the soul, it is sure and stedfast, and it enters within the veil. Ether 12:4 takes the first two — “hope … maketh an anchor to the souls of men, which would make them sure and steadfast” — and then holds the third in reserve for fifteen verses, until 12:19-21, where those whose faith is exceeding strong “could not be kept from within the veil” and the brother of Jared “could no longer be kept without the veil.” Moroni has distributed one KJV verse across the two halves of his discourse, and the veil that closes the argument is the veil the anchor of the opening sentence was already entering. Compare Hays on metalepsis: the reader who recovers Hebrews 6:19 finds that Moroni's veil was promised at the start.

links.note: “Whoso believeth in God, might with surety hope for a better world … which hope cometh of faith, maketh an anchor to the souls of men, which would make them sure and steadfast.” The KJV's one anchor-of-the-soul verse supplies the image, the plural “souls of men” for its singular “soul”, and the doublet “sure and stedfast” intact. Moroni's one substantive change is doctrinal rather than verbal: Hebrews says hope is the anchor, and Moroni adds a derivation, “which hope cometh of faith”, subordinating hope to the faith that is his subject. The link falls well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his thirty-six; what carries it is three singletons from one verse, not length.

links.text: But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city.

provenance.other: “better country” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The comparative-plus-place construction for the object of hope is Hebrews', not the Old Testament's.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 11:16 is the hinge of the faith chapter Moroni is about to recite: the patriarchs' faith is redescribed as desire for a better country which God has prepared. Ether 12:4's “hope for a better world” takes the construction, and the preparation motif Hebrews attaches to it (“he hath prepared for them a city”) then governs the end of Moroni's discourse, where the object of hope is four times “the place which thou hast prepared” (12:32, 12:34, 12:37). So the chapter's opening hope and its closing inheritance are held together by one verse of Hebrews 11 that Moroni never quotes outright.

links.note: “Might with surety hope for a better world, yea, even a place at the right hand of God.” The KJV has exactly one comparative country-of-hope, and it is in the chapter Ether 12 is built on. Moroni substitutes “world” for “country” and glosses it with a location at God's right hand — a substitution rather than an independent coinage, since nothing else in the KJV licenses hoping for a better anything.

links.text: Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.

provenance.other: “always abounding” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Paul's phrase is “always abounding in the work of the Lord”, singular; Ether 12:4 has “always abounding in good works”, plural.
provenance.significance: Ether 12:4 fuses two exhortation-endings that are not related in the Bible. “Sure and steadfast” is Hebrews 6:19's; “steadfast … always abounding” is 1 Corinthians 15:58's; the word steadfast is the seam, and it belongs to both. The result is a sentence in which Paul's resurrection peroration and Hebrews' anchor of hope are welded at their one shared adjective. This is the pattern of the whole chapter — Moroni composes out of Hebrews and the Corinthian letters simultaneously — and 12:4 is where it is easiest to see.

links.note: “Which would make them sure and steadfast, always abounding in good works, being led to glorify God.” The second half of the clause is 1 Corinthians 15:58's, in Paul's order: steadfast, then always abounding. Moroni's “good works” for Paul's “work of the Lord” is the ordinary Book of Mormon substitution, and the sequence steadfast → always abounding is what makes the borrowing visible rather than the individual words.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Ether did prophesy great and marvellous things unto the people, which they did not believe, because they saw them not.

And now I, Moroni, would speak somewhat concerning these things: I would shew unto the world that faith is things which are hoped for and not seen; wherefore, dispute not because ye see not, for ye receive no witness until after the trial of your faith:

links.text: Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.

provenance.other: “things hoped for” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “things not seen” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Hebrews 11:1 and Hebrews 11:7, both in the same chapter. Both of Moroni's phrases are therefore Hebrews 11's, and they are in Hebrews 11:1's order.
provenance.significance: Moroni's version drops precisely the two abstract nouns — substance, evidence — and keeps the two phrases they govern, which is the reading the rest of the chapter needs: not a definition of what faith IS but a rule about what may be seen. The verse that follows makes the excision do work: “dispute not because ye see not, for ye receive no witness until after the trial of your faith.” Hebrews 11:1 is a definition; Ether 12:6 is a procedure derived from it. The same verse is quoted at Alma 32:21 with a different excision (“ye hope for things which is not seen, which are true”) and read backwards at Ether 3:19, where the brother of Jared's sight ends his faith — three uses of one verse, none of them the same use.

links.note: “I would shew unto the world that faith is things which are hoped for and not seen.” This is the chapter's programmatic sentence and it is Hebrews 11:1 with the copular nouns removed: faith is [the substance of] things which are hoped for and [the evidence of things] not seen. The 1830 “shew” for the current “show” preserves the KJV spelling and is worth noting under CONVENTIONS §8; it is not itself evidence of this link, but it is evidence that the passage was composed in KJV English. Everything from 12:7 to 12:22 is the working-out of this verse, and Hebrews 11 is the model for that working-out as well.

links.text: That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ:

provenance.other: “trial of your faith” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. James 1:3 has the same idea in different English — “the trying of your faith worketh patience” — which is the comparison that shows how specific Moroni's wording is: he has Peter's noun, not James's gerund.
provenance.significance: 1 Peter 1:7 is about a trial that vindicates faith at the appearing of Jesus Christ; Moroni turns it into an epistemic rule — no witness until after the trial. The transposition is the interesting part. Peter's trial is suffering; Moroni's is the period of not-seeing that 12:6 has just defined faith as. Recovering Peter's context supplies what Moroni's sentence leaves out, namely that the withheld witness is finally given, and given at an appearing.

links.note: “Ye receive no witness until after the trial of your faith.” Four words shared with the KJV's one occurrence of the phrase, and the surrounding argument is not Peter's, which is why this is an allusion and not a quotation. The formula recurs as the governing structure of 12:7-18, where the pattern “he shewed not himself … until after they had faith” is stated five times.

pericopes.text: for it was by faith that Christ shewed himself unto our fathers, after that he had risen from the dead; and he shewed not himself unto them, until after they had faith in him; wherefore it must needs be that some had faith in him, for he shewed himself not unto the world.

But because of the faith of men, he has shewn himself unto the world, and glorified the name of the Father, and prepared a way that thereby others might be partakers of the heavenly gift, that they might hope for those things which they have not seen;

links.text: For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost,

provenance.other: “heavenly gift” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The exact string “partakers of the heavenly gift” occurs in no KJV verse: Hebrews 6:4 reads “tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost”, so Moroni has fused the two halves of one verse, attaching Hebrews' participle to Hebrews' other noun.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 6:4 and Hebrews 6:19 are fifteen verses apart and Ether 12:4 and 12:8 are four verses apart; the same page of Hebrews supplies the anchor of hope and the heavenly gift. Hebrews 6 is the chapter that warns it is impossible to renew apostates to repentance; Moroni takes its vocabulary and reverses its polarity, so that partaking of the heavenly gift is opened to “others” on the condition of faith rather than closed against them. What Hebrews uses to describe what is lost, Ether uses to describe what is available.

links.note: “He has shewn himself unto the world, and glorified the name of the Father, and prepared a way that thereby others might be partakers of the heavenly gift.” The distinctive noun phrase is a KJV singleton, and the participle Moroni attaches to it is the one Hebrews 6:4 uses two clauses later. The fusion is the evidence: an independent writer reaching for 'heavenly gift' would not also reach for 'partakers'. The 1830 “shewn” preserves the KJV spelling here as at 12:6, 12:7, 12:12, 12:21, 12:27, 12:28 and 12:31 — eight instances in one chapter, all modernized in 1920.

pericopes.text: wherefore ye may also have hope, and be partakers of the gift, if ye will but have faith.
Behold, it was by faith that they of old were called after the holy order of God;

links.text: For by it the elders obtained a good report.

provenance.other: “the elders obtained” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “obtained a good report” occurs in exactly two, Hebrews 11:2 and Hebrews 11:39, the opening and closing frames of the faith catalogue.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 11 runs definition (11:1), then a summary claim about the ancients (11:2), then the catalogue (11:4-31). Ether 12 runs definition (12:6), then a summary claim about the ancients (12:10), then the catalogue (12:13-21). The order is what argues here, not the vocabulary: Moroni is not merely quoting Hebrews 11, he is reproducing its architecture, and 12:10 is the joint where that becomes checkable.

links.note: “It was by faith that they of old were called after the holy order of God.” Moroni's “they of old” answers Hebrews' “the elders”, and both sentences do the same structural job — a one-line claim that the ancients' standing came by faith, placed between the definition and the roll-call. The wording is not close enough for more than moderate: Moroni supplies a different predicate, the holy order, from the Book of Mormon's own Melchizedek material rather than from Hebrews 5 and 7. Recorded because the position in the argument is the evidence.

pericopes.text: wherefore, by faith, was the law of Moses given. But in the gift of his Son, hath God prepared a more excellent way; and it is by faith that it hath been fulfilled:

links.text: But covet earnestly the best gifts: and yet shew I unto you a more excellent way.

provenance.other: “more excellent way” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Hebrews 8:6 has “a more excellent ministry”, which is the nearest competitor and is not the phrase.
provenance.significance: This is the best metalepsis in the chapter. 1 Corinthians 12:31 is not a saying about excellence in general: it is the sentence with which Paul leaves the subject of spiritual gifts and introduces 1 Corinthians 13, so that in the King James Bible “a more excellent way” means, and can only mean, charity. Moroni writes it at 12:11 while discussing the law of Moses and the gift of the Son, and then his discourse arrives, seventeen verses later, exactly where Paul's does: at faith, hope and charity (12:28), at charity as the condition of inheritance (12:34), and at a prayer for charity (12:36). Moroni announces a more excellent way and then walks Paul's way. Whether the design is the writer's or the reader's, the phrase carries its destination with it.

links.note: “But in the gift of his Son, hath God prepared a more excellent way; and it is by faith that it hath been fulfilled.” The KJV has one more excellent way and it is Paul's introduction to the charity hymn. Two of the verse's other words are also in Moroni's neighbourhood — Paul's “gifts” beside Moroni's “gift of his Son”, Paul's “shew I unto you” beside Moroni's repeated “I will shew unto them” at 12:27-28. The phrase then reappears in Moroni's own mouth at 12:32 as “a more excellent hope”, which is a use no biblical verse licenses and which shows the phrase had become his.

pericopes.text: for if there be no faith among the children of men, God can do no miracle among them; wherefore he shewed not himself until after their faith.
Behold, it was the faith of Alma and Amulek that caused the prison to tumble to the earth.

links.text: And what shall I more say? for the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae; of David also, and Samuel, and of the prophets:

provenance.other: There is little shared vocabulary and the link is not proposed on vocabulary. It is proposed on form: an anaphoric catalogue of exemplars, each introduced by the same faith-formula, running from named individuals to a rapid closing list.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 11 names its worthies in pairs and clusters as the recitation accelerates — Gedeon and Barak, Samson and Jephthae, David and Samuel. Ether 12:13-15 does the same in the same place in the argument: Alma and Amulek, Nephi and Lehi, Ammon and his brethren. The Book of Mormon has written its own eleventh of Hebrews, with its own worthies substituted at every slot, and then, at 12:16, generalized in Hebrews' manner — “all they which wrought miracles, wrought them by faith” — before returning to a single extended exemplum, the brother of Jared, as Hebrews returns to none but instead to the sufferings of 11:35-38. The one place Moroni does not follow the model is the ending, and that is because his exemplum, unlike Hebrews', saw.

links.note: “Behold, it was the faith of Alma and Amulek that caused the prison to tumble to the earth.” The anaphora that runs 12:13, 12:14, 12:15, 12:17, 12:18, 12:19 and 12:20 is Hebrews 11's device — “By faith Abel … By faith Enoch … By faith Noah” — inflected into the Book of Mormon's own idiom, “Behold, it was the faith of X.” The catalogue is keyed here, at its first member, and the note covers the whole run rather than repeating at each verse. Note that the closest formal match is not the opening of Hebrews 11 but its summation at 11:32, where the names come in pairs and the writer says he has no more room; Moroni's equivalent is 12:16's “yea, and even all they which wrought miracles.”

pericopes.text: Behold, it was the faith of Nephi and Lehi, that wrought the change upon the Lamanites, that they were baptized with fire and with the Holy Ghost.

links.text: I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance. but he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire:

provenance.other: “baptize you with the Holy Ghost” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Matthew 3:11, Mark 1:8 and Luke 3:16 — the same saying of John the Baptist in three Gospels. In all three the Holy Ghost is named before the fire; Ether 12:14 reverses the order.
provenance.alternative: The proximate model is not the KJV but the Book of Mormon's own earlier form of the phrase. 3 Nephi 9:20 reads “him will I baptize with fire and with the Holy Ghost”, inverting the KJV's order of the two elements, and Ether 12:14 has the inverted order — “baptized with fire and with the Holy Ghost.” The `mediation` enum has no value for an NT source reaching a verse through an earlier Book of Mormon passage; `OT-via-earlier-BoM` is the wrong shape because the source is not Old Testament. Recorded here as `uncertain` and flagged rather than resolved by inventing a value.
