provenance.significance: The inversion is the finding. Every Gospel that has the saying has the Holy Ghost first and fire second (Matthew 3:11, Luke 3:16); the Book of Mormon consistently reverses it, and Ether 12:14 — a book presented as older than any of them, written last by Moroni — carries the reversed order. So the phrase reaches Ether not from the Bible directly but through a form the Book of Mormon has already standardized on.

links.note: “That they were baptized with fire and with the Holy Ghost.” Both nouns and the baptism verb are the KJV's, in an order no KJV verse has. The machine proposed Acts 13:52 (“filled with joy, and with the Holy Ghost”) on the strength of five contiguous words; that is the wrong verse, because Acts 13:52 has no fire and no baptism. Moderate rather than high because the phrase is by this point a Book of Mormon formula, and formulae are poor evidence of a particular act of borrowing.

pericopes.text: Behold, it was the faith of Ammon and his brethren, which wrought so great a miracle among the Lamanites;
yea, and even all they which wrought miracles, wrought them by faith, even those which were before Christ, and also them which were after.
And it was by faith that the three disciples obtained a promise that they should not taste of death; and they obtained not the promise until after their faith.

links.text: Verily I say unto you, There be some standing here, which shall not taste of death, till they see the Son of man coming in his kingdom.

provenance.other: “taste of death” occurs in exactly four KJV verses: Matthew 16:28, Mark 9:1, Luke 9:27 and John 8:52. Three of the four are the same saying, and it is the saying about disciples standing here who will not taste of death.
provenance.alternative: The proximate model is again an earlier Book of Mormon passage rather than the Bible: 3 Nephi 28:7 grants the three disciples that they “shall never taste of death”, and Ether 12:17 refers back to that grant explicitly (“the three disciples obtained a promise”). As at 12:14 the enum has no value for an NT source arriving through an earlier Book of Mormon text; recorded `uncertain` and explained rather than forced.
provenance.significance: The KJV's not-tasting-death saying is spoken to disciples standing in front of Jesus and is left, in all three Synoptics, unexplained — the interpretive crux of the passage is what it means that some of them did not die. The Book of Mormon answers it: three disciples, in another hemisphere, who did not. Moroni's contribution here is to make faith the mechanism (“they obtained not the promise until after their faith”), which neither the Gospels nor 3 Nephi 28 says.

links.note: “It was by faith that the three disciples obtained a promise that they should not taste of death.” The idiom is the KJV's and the situation is the KJV saying's, transposed. Note the second half of the verse, “they obtained not the promise until after their faith”, which is Hebrews 11:39's clause — “these all, having obtained a good report through faith, received not the promise” — with the negation moved: Hebrews' worthies did not receive it, Moroni's did, once their faith was in place. Two verses of Hebrews 11 (33's “obtained promises”, 39's “received not the promise”) sit under one sentence.

links.text: And these all, having obtained a good report through faith, received not the promise:

provenance.other: “obtained promises” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 11:33; “obtained a good report” occurs in exactly two, Hebrews 11:2 and 11:39. Moroni's sentence has both halves of the collocation — obtained a promise, and did not obtain it until faith — and the verb is Hebrews' throughout.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 11:39 is the closing sentence of the faith catalogue and its point is deferral: the worthies obtained a report but not the promise, because God provided some better thing for us. Moroni's catalogue closes the same way and reverses the verdict — his exemplars do obtain, and what stands between them and the obtaining is only the interval before faith. The chapter's whole polemic against not-seeing is aimed at that interval.

links.note: “And they obtained not the promise until after their faith.” The clause is Hebrews 11:39's, minus the deferral. Moderate rather than high because 'obtain the promise' is not by itself distinctive English and the case rests on the position in a catalogue that is already Hebrews 11's.

pericopes.text: And neither at any time hath any wrought miracles until after their faith; wherefore they first believed in the Son of God.

And there were many whose faith was so exceeding strong even before Christ came, which could not be kept from within the veil, but truly saw with their eyes the things which they had beheld with an eye of faith, and they were glad.

links.text: Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil;

provenance.other: “within the veil” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Hebrews 10:20 has “through the veil”, Exodus and Leviticus have “within the vail” of the tabernacle in a different spelling that `kjv-rarity` does not conflate; the phrase as spelled here belongs to Hebrews 6:19 alone.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 6:19's veil is entered by hope; Ether 12:19's is a barrier that strong faith cannot be kept outside of, and 12:21's is one the brother of Jared can no longer be kept without. The Book of Mormon has taken a metaphor of access and made it a threshold in a narrative — the veil is now a thing a man stands on one side of and then does not. This is where the anchor of 12:4 arrives, and the two verses should be read together.

links.note: “Many whose faith was so exceeding strong even before Christ came, which could not be kept from within the veil.” The phrase is a KJV singleton and its verse is the one already standing behind 12:4, which makes recurrence rather than volume the argument: one verse of Hebrews supplies the opening image of the discourse and the pivot of its climax. Note the 1830 relative “which” for persons, corrected to “who” in 1920 — the KJV's own usage, and one more sign of the register the chapter is composed in.

links.text: Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day: and he saw it, and was glad.

provenance.other: “and was glad” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Esther 8:15, Psalm 97:8 and John 8:56 — and only John 8:56 predicates it of a man before Christ who saw Christ. The sequence saw-it-and-was-glad is that verse's.
provenance.significance: John 8:56 is the New Testament's own statement of the problem Ether 12:19 exists to solve: how a believer who lived before Christ nevertheless saw him. Jesus asserts it of Abraham without explaining it; Moroni generalizes it to a class — 'many whose faith was so exceeding strong even before Christ came' — and supplies the mechanism, the eye of faith becoming sight. Read the two together and Moroni is answering the Jews' objection in John 8:57, that a man not yet fifty years old cannot have been seen by Abraham.

links.note: “But truly saw with their eyes the things which they had beheld with an eye of faith, and they were glad.” The clause closes on John 8:56's three words in John 8:56's order, and the whole verse is about the one thing John 8:56 claims: pre-Christian sight of Christ, ending in gladness. The middle of the verse belongs to Hebrews 11:13 — “having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them” — so the sentence looks through Hebrews' distant sight to John's actual seeing. Moderate because “and they were glad” is short and the shared vocabulary with John is thin; what raises it above an echo is that the subject matter is identical and rare.

pericopes.text: And behold, we have seen in this record, that one of these was the brother of Jared: for so great was his faith in God, that when God put forth his finger, he could not hide it from the sight of the brother of Jared, because of his word which he had spoken unto him, which word he had obtained by faith.

And after that the brother of Jared had beheld the finger of the Lord, because of the promise which the brother of Jared had obtained by faith, the Lord could not withhold any thing from his sight; wherefore he shewed him all things, for he could no longer be kept without the veil.
And it is by faith that my fathers have obtained the promise that these things should come unto their brethren through the Gentiles; therefore the Lord hath commanded me, yea, even Jesus Christ.

And I said unto him, Lord, the Gentiles will mock at these things, because of our weakness in writing: for Lord, thou hast made us mighty in word by faith, whereunto thou hast not made us mighty in writing: for thou hast made all this people that they could speak much, because of the Holy Ghost which thou hast given them;

links.text: And Moses said unto the LORD, O my LORD, I am not eloquent, neither heretofore, nor since thou hast spoken unto thy servant: but I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.

provenance.other: There is almost no shared wording and the link is not offered on wording; “am not eloquent” is a KJV singleton but Moroni does not use it. The case is the scene.
provenance.significance: The commissioning objection is a fixed Old Testament form: the prophet protests his inadequacy of utterance, and God answers by asserting who made the mouth. Moroni runs it with one substitution that is the whole point — the medium is writing rather than speech. “Thou hast made us mighty in word by faith, whereunto thou hast not made us mighty in writing”; “thou hast made us that we could write but little, because of the awkwardness of our hands.” The Lord's reply at 12:26-27 is the Exodus 4:11-12 reply in Pauline vocabulary: not I will be with thy mouth, but my grace is sufficient and weakness is given on purpose. A book that presents itself as a written record has taken scripture's standing scene about speech and converted it into a scene about the hand.

links.note: Recorded as figural and flagged as such: the wording will not bear more, and CONVENTIONS §5's Exodus 2:2 'goodly' entry is the warning against pressing typology past the words. What justifies a link rather than an exclusion is that Moroni's objection is not a general complaint but the specific commissioning-objection form, made in the second person to God, answered by God in the next sentence, and answered with a statement about how God makes people — which is Exodus 4:11's “who hath made man's mouth?” The Jeremiah 1:6 objection (“I cannot speak: for I am a child”) is the same form and would serve equally; Exodus 4:10 is named because it is the fullest.
links.whyNot: Not one distinctive word is shared. A reader who requires verbal contact should decline this link; it is proposed on the shape of the scene and on the fact that the divine answer at 12:27 addresses the objection in the terms Exodus 4:11 does.

pericopes.text: and thou hast made us that we could write but little, because of the awkwardness of our hands. Behold, thou hast not made us mighty in writing like unto the brother of Jared, for thou madest him that the things which he wrote, were mighty even as thou art, unto the overpowering of man to read them.

Thou hast also made our words powerful and great, even that we cannot write them; wherefore, when we write, we behold our weakness, and stumble because of the placing of our words; and I fear lest the Gentiles shall mock at our words.
And when I had said this, the Lord spake unto me, saying, Fools mock, but they shall mourn; and my grace is sufficient for the meek, that they shall take no advantage of your weakness:

links.text: And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.

provenance.other: “my grace is sufficient” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The frame is reproduced with it: Paul writes “And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee”, Moroni writes “the Lord spake unto me, saying … my grace is sufficient for the meek.” Both are first-person reports of a divine answer to a complaint about weakness, and in both the answer is that same sentence.
provenance.significance: The borrowing is not of a phrase but of an entire rhetorical situation, and the situation is 2 Corinthians 12's: an apostle boasting reluctantly, conscious of a weakness he has asked to have removed, receiving in reply a refusal that is also a promise. Moroni's weakness is his prose; Paul's is unspecified. What Moroni adds is a change of addressee — Paul's “for thee” becomes “for the meek”, then at 12:27 “for all men that humble themselves before me” — turning a private oracle into a general law, which is exactly what the chapter has been doing to Hebrews 11:1 since 12:6.

links.note: “Fools mock, but they shall mourn; and my grace is sufficient for the meek, that they shall take no advantage of your weakness.” The KJV's one grace-is-sufficient verse, reported in the same words and in the same frame — a divine answer, quoted, to a complaint about weakness. This is one of the least deniable New Testament borrowings in the Book of Mormon, and the chapter goes on to build its distinctive weak-things-made-strong doctrine out of the rest of the verse at 12:27. The machine also proposed Ezekiel 39:10 for “they shall take no”; see the exclusion register.

links.text: Fools make a mock at sin: but among the righteous there is favour.

provenance.other: “make a mock” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The collocation of fools with mocking as their characteristic act is otherwise Proverbs 1:22-26's, where Wisdom promises to laugh at the calamity of the scorners.
provenance.significance: Moroni has been afraid of mockery for three verses — “the Gentiles will mock at these things”, “I fear lest the Gentiles shall mock at our words.” The Lord's answer opens with a proverb-shaped antithesis of exactly the KJV's kind: fools mock, but they shall mourn. The reversal of laughter into mourning is the sapiential move of Proverbs 1:26 and of James 4:9; naming Proverbs 14:9 is naming the KJV's only verse that makes mocking the defining act of fools.

links.note: “Fools mock, but they shall mourn.” Four words, in the antithetical form the King James Proverbs uses constantly, with the KJV's one fools-and-mocking verse behind them. Moderate: 'fool' and 'mock' are common words and the sentence could be composed without a source. It is recorded because it stands at the head of a divine reply and because it is the one clause in the chapter whose register is Wisdom rather than Paul.

pericopes.text: and if men come unto me, I will shew unto them their weakness. I give unto men weakness, that they may be humble; and my grace is sufficient for all men that humble themselves before me: for if they humble themselves before me, and have faith in me, then will I make weak things become strong unto them.

links.text: But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;

provenance.other: “weak things” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “confound the wise” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The Book of Mormon's most quoted single sentence about weakness therefore rests on a phrase found nowhere else in the King James Bible.
provenance.significance: Recover 1 Corinthians 1 and the fit is closer than the phrase alone suggests. Paul's argument is that the preaching of the cross is foolishness to them that perish, that the Greeks seek after wisdom and count it folly, and that God chose the foolish and weak things of the world to shame the wise and mighty. Moroni's situation, four verses earlier, is that “the Gentiles will mock at these things, because of our weakness in writing.” The Gentiles who mock a weak text are Paul's Greeks; the answer given to Moroni is Paul's answer, that the weak thing is chosen on purpose. And it is chosen, in Paul, to confound precisely those who mock. Moroni's oracle does not say this. 1 Corinthians 1:27 says it for him.

links.note: “I give unto men weakness, that they may be humble … then will I make weak things become strong unto them.” The two-word phrase is a KJV singleton and the doctrine built on it is the chapter's most famous sentence. Note what Moroni changes: Paul's weak things are chosen to confound the mighty and remain weak; Moroni's are made strong. The change is doctrinally substantial and verbally minimal, which is the signature of a borrowing rather than a coincidence — an independent writer reaching for this idea in English would be very unlikely to reach for these two words.

links.text: Quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens.

provenance.other: “out of weakness were made strong” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and that verse is inside the faith catalogue Ether 12 has been reciting since 12:13.
provenance.significance: This is the finding that makes the second half of the chapter cohere with the first. Moroni's weak-things-made-strong doctrine is usually read as a development of 2 Corinthians 12:9, and it is; but the actual proposition — that weakness is turned into strength — is stated in the King James Bible in exactly one place, and that place is Hebrews 11, four verses after the catalogue Moroni has just finished imitating. So the oracle at 12:27 is not a departure from the chapter's Hebrews 11 programme; it is the programme's next line. Moroni recites Hebrews 11's worthies at 12:13-21, and Hebrews 11's own summary of what faith did for them — out of weakness were made strong — becomes the promise made to him at 12:27 and kept to him at 12:37, “because thou hast seen thy weakness, thou shalt be made strong.”
provenance.alternative: 2 Corinthians 12:9-10 is the other candidate and is certainly also present in the passage (see the link at 12:26). The two are not alternatives so much as a fusion: Paul supplies the grace-is-sufficient frame and the vocabulary of glorying in weakness; Hebrews 11:34 supplies the actual weak-to-strong transformation, which Paul does not state — his strength is made perfect in weakness, which is not the same claim.

links.note: “Then will I make weak things become strong unto them”, and at 12:37, “because thou hast seen thy weakness, thou shalt be made strong.” The KJV's only weakness-to-strength clause is Hebrews 11:34's, and Moroni uses the transformation twice, ten verses apart, in a discourse otherwise built on Hebrews 11 from end to end. Below any quotation threshold on length; the argument is rarity plus the chapter's established dependence on the source's immediate context.

links.text: If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.

provenance.other: “humble themselves” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Moroni has it twice in one sentence — “all men that humble themselves before me: for if they humble themselves before me” — and the sentence, like 2 Chronicles 7:14, is a conditional promise in the divine first person.
provenance.significance: 2 Chronicles 7:14 is the KJV's classic if-then oracle: if my people humble themselves, then will I hear. Ether 12:27 has the same grammar with different conditions and a different apodosis — if they humble themselves and have faith in me, then will I make weak things become strong. The Old Testament formula supplies the syntax into which the Pauline and Hebraic material of the verse is poured, which is worth noticing: the doctrine is New Testament, the sentence-shape is Chronicles.

links.note: “My grace is sufficient for all men that humble themselves before me: for if they humble themselves before me, and have faith in me, then will I make weak things become strong unto them.” A KJV singleton verb-phrase, doubled, inside a then-will-I conditional. Moderate rather than high because 'humble themselves' is unremarkable English and the doubling may be Moroni's own emphasis rather than an echo; recorded because the conditional structure matches as well as the phrase.

pericopes.text: Behold, I will shew unto the Gentiles their weakness, and I will shew unto them that faith, hope, and charity, bringeth unto me the fountain of all righteousness.

links.text: And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.

provenance.other: “faith, hope, charity” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Moroni's “faith, hope, and charity” inserts the conjunction; the triad and its order are the KJV's, and 'charity' rather than 'love' is the King James translators' choice at this verse and not the choice of most English versions before or since.
provenance.significance: The triad is the culmination of a discourse that has run through faith (12:3-22) and hope (12:4, 12:9, 12:32) in order, and it arrives with the third term unannounced. That is Paul's shape too: 1 Corinthians 13 is introduced by 12:31's 'more excellent way' — the phrase Moroni used at 12:11 — and ends on the triad. Moroni's discourse enters Paul's chapter at its door and leaves by its window. The word charity is then repeated at 12:34, 12:35, 12:36 and 12:37, so a chapter that began by defining faith ends by making charity the condition of inheritance, which is 1 Corinthians 13:2's judgment exactly.

links.note: “I will shew unto them that faith, hope, and charity, bringeth unto me the fountain of all righteousness.” The KJV's one occurrence of the triad, in its order, with the King James word for the third term. What Moroni adds is a destination — the triad brings men to God — where Paul only ranks the three. The 1830 “shew”, modernized in 1920, is the KJV's spelling; the machine proposed Daniel 2:24 for “I will shew unto the” and that is a formula, not a source (see the exclusion register).

pericopes.text: And I, Moroni, having heard these words, was comforted, and said, O Lord, thy righteous will be done, for I know that thou workest unto the children of men according to their faith:
for the brother of Jared said unto the mountain Zerin, Remove, and it was removed. And if he had not had faith, it would not have moved; wherefore thou workest after that men have faith:

links.text: And Jesus said unto them, Because of your unbelief: for verily I say unto you, If ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to yonder place; and it shall remove; and nothing shall be impossible unto you.

provenance.other: “remove hence” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 17:20; “remove mountains” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 13:2. Moroni's construction — a man speaking to a named mountain, the imperative 'Remove', and the mountain removing — is Matthew 17:20's alone; Mark 11:23 has 'Be thou removed, and be thou cast into the sea', a different imperative.
provenance.significance: The metalepsis is worth stating plainly. In the King James Bible, faith that removes mountains occurs twice: once as Jesus' promise (Matthew 17:20) and once as Paul's example of a faith that is worthless without charity (1 Corinthians 13:2, “though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing”). Ether 12 cites the mountain at 12:30 and arrives at charity at 12:34, where the verdict is that without charity men “cannot inherit that place.” Moroni has, without quoting Paul, reproduced Paul's sequence and Paul's judgment on it. Whoever composed the chapter had 1 Corinthians 13 in view — 12:11 and 12:28 prove that independently — and the mountain of 12:30 is the example that chapter itself uses.

links.note: “The brother of Jared said unto the mountain Zerin, Remove, and it was removed.” The bare imperative to a mountain, and the mountain's obedience, is Matthew 17:20's sentence with the mountain named. That the Book of Mormon supplies a proper name where the Gospel says 'this mountain' is characteristic: the promise is turned into an event, as the not-tasting-death saying was at 12:17 and as John 8:56's Abraham was at 12:19. Three times in this chapter an unexplained New Testament claim is given a narrative that discharges it.

pericopes.text: for thus did thou manifest thyself unto thy disciples. For after that they had faith, and did speak in thy name, thou didst shew thyself unto them in great power;

and I also rememberest that thou hast said that thou hast prepared a house for man; yea, even among the mansions of thy Father, in the which man might have a more excellent hope; wherefore man must hope, or he cannot receive an inheritance in the place which thou hast prepared.

links.text: In my Father’s house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you.

provenance.other: “mansions” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “prepare a place” occurs in exactly two, John 14:2 and 14:3, consecutive verses of the same saying. Ether 12:32 has both — a prepared house, among the mansions of the Father — and so has all of John 14:2's distinctive vocabulary in one sentence.
provenance.significance: The King James translators' 'mansions' for μοναί is a choice no modern version keeps (rooms, dwelling places), so a text depending on the word depends on the KJV and on nothing earlier or later. What Moroni does with it is to make it the terminus of the hope he defined at 12:4: hope is an anchor, hope is for a better world, and here at last the better world is named, and named in John's words. The verse also completes 12:11's phrase — “a more excellent way” has become “a more excellent hope” — so the two Pauline and Johannine strands of the chapter meet in one sentence.

links.note: “Thou hast prepared a house for man; yea, even among the mansions of thy Father, in the which man might have a more excellent hope; wherefore man must hope, or he cannot receive an inheritance in the place which thou hast prepared.” House, mansions, Father, prepared, place — the whole content of John 14:2, redistributed. Hardy's apparatus cross-references John 14:2 here and the reference is exactly right. The 1830 reads “in the which”, a KJV relative construction the 1920 edition simplified to “which”, and the same formula appears at Enos 1:27 (“a place prepared for you in the mansions of my Father”), so the phrase is one the Book of Mormon has used before; the recurrence strengthens rather than weakens the case, since the source of both is the same singleton.

pericopes.text: And again I remember that thou hast said that thou hast loved the world, even unto the laying down of thy life for the world, that thou mightest take it again to prepare a place for the children of men.

links.text: Therefore doth my Father love me, because I lay down my life, that I might take it again.

provenance.other: “take it again” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 10:17 and John 10:18 — the same saying, twice. “lay down my life” occurs in exactly three, John 10:15, 10:17 and 13:37. Moroni's clause “even unto the laying down of thy life for the world, that thou mightest take it again” has both halves of John 10:17 in John 10:17's order.
provenance.significance: The laying down and taking again is a Johannine formula with no Synoptic parallel, and Moroni reproduces the causal structure as well as the words: in John the Father loves the Son BECAUSE he lays down his life to take it again; in Ether the Son's love of the world is expressed AS the laying down of his life to take it again. The direction of the love has moved from Father-to-Son to Son-to-world, which is John 3:16's direction. So one sentence holds John 10's formula inside John 3:16's proposition and ends in John 14:2's prepared place — three Johannine sayings in a row, in the order a reader of John would meet them.

links.note: “Thou hast loved the world, even unto the laying down of thy life for the world, that thou mightest take it again to prepare a place for the children of men.” Hardy cross-references John 10:17-18 at this verse and the wording bears it out precisely. The final clause returns to John 14:2's “prepare a place”, which is why 12:32 and 12:33 have to be read as one movement; and the purpose Moroni assigns to the resurrection — that Christ took his life again in order to prepare a place — is a joining of the two Johannine sayings that neither text makes.

links.text: For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.

provenance.other: “so loved the world” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Moroni does not have the intensifier — he writes “thou hast loved the world” — which is why this is moderate rather than high; loved-the-world without 'so' is not a KJV string.
provenance.significance: John 3:16's proposition is that God's love of the world took the form of a gift, and the gift is the Son. Ether 12:33 makes the same proposition with the Son as the subject rather than the object, and specifies the gift as his own life. Held next to the John 10 borrowing in the same verse, the effect is that the Book of Mormon has said what John 3:16 says using John 10:17's vocabulary — which is not what either verse says on its own, and is the reason 12:34 can then identify that love as charity.

links.note: “That thou hast loved the world.” The clause is short and the argument is contextual: this is the only KJV proposition about God loving the world, it is the best-known verse in the English Bible, and Moroni immediately draws from it the conclusion that this love “is charity” (12:34). Recorded as moderate because the intensifier is absent and 'love the world' has a different and opposed sense at 1 John 2:15, which the exclusion register notes.

pericopes.text: And now I know that this love which thou hast had for the children of men, is charity; wherefore, except men shall have charity, they cannot inherit that place which thou hast prepared in the mansions of thy Father.

links.text: And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.

provenance.other: “remove mountains” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and it is this one; the mountain of Ether 12:30 stands four verses earlier. The conditional 'have not charity, therefore nothing' is 1 Corinthians 13:1-3's refrain, stated three times there and once here.
provenance.significance: Paul's argument is that the greatest exercises of faith are void without charity. Moroni's chapter has spent thirty verses arguing that faith moves prison walls, changes Lamanites, opens the veil and removes mountains — the exact list Paul discounts — and then concludes that without charity none of it secures the inheritance. Read as a whole, Ether 12 is a defence of faith that ends by subordinating faith to charity, which is the structure of 1 Corinthians 12:31-13:13 and of nothing else in scripture.

links.note: “Except men shall have charity, they cannot inherit that place which thou hast prepared in the mansions of thy Father.” The condition is Paul's, with an inheritance substituted for Paul's 'I am nothing'. Confidence is high on the strength of the chapter's other two demonstrable contacts with the same Pauline unit — 12:11's KJV-singleton 'more excellent way', which is 1 Corinthians 12:31, and 12:28's KJV-singleton triad, which is 13:13 — so this verse is not being read into Paul from a distance; it sits between two verses that are certainly his.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, I know by this thing which thou hast said, that if the Gentiles have not charity, because of our weakness, that thou wilt prove them, and take away their talent, yea, even that which they have received, and give unto them which shall have more abundantly.

links.text: Take therefore the talent from him, and give it unto him which hath ten talents.

provenance.other: “take therefore the talent” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “unto every one that hath shall be given” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:29. Moroni's “take away their talent, yea, even that which they have received, and give unto them which shall have more abundantly” has the talent and the transfer of Matthew 25:28 and the that-which-they-have of 25:29.
provenance.alternative: Moroni's closing phrase is “more abundantly”, and Matthew 25:29 reads “he shall have abundance” while the parallel logion at Matthew 13:12 reads “he shall have more abundance” — a KJV singleton. `mediation-check.py` on Ether 12:35 against Matthew 25:29 and Matthew 13:12 finds no decisive divergence, because Moroni reproduces neither verse's surrounding clause; so the comparative cannot be pressed. It is recorded because Hardy's cross-reference is to Matthew 25 alone, and the one word Moroni adds beyond Matthew 25's wording happens to be the word Matthew 13:12 has.
provenance.significance: The parable of the talents is a story about a servant judged for what he did with what he received; Moroni applies it to the Gentiles who receive his record. That is a substantial reassignment — the talent is now a book, the servant is now a readership, and the condition of forfeiture is charity rather than industry. Note that the parable then supplies the chapter's own conclusion two verses later: 'thou hast been faithful' at 12:37 is the lord's commendation at Matthew 25:21, so the same parable both threatens the Gentiles and acquits Moroni.

links.note: “That thou wilt prove them, and take away their talent, yea, even that which they have received, and give unto them which shall have more abundantly.” Hardy cross-references Matthew 25:28-29 here; the wording supports it, with 'talent' as the decisive term — it is a unit of weight nowhere else in the Book of Mormon and its only KJV life as a thing given and taken away is this parable. The 1830 relative 'which' for persons is again the KJV's usage, corrected in 1920.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that I prayed unto the Lord that he would give unto the Gentiles grace, that they might have charity.

And it came to pass that the Lord said unto me, If they have not charity, it mattereth not unto thee, thou hast been faithful; wherefore thy garments shall be made clean. And because thou hast seen thy weakness, thou shalt be made strong, even unto the sitting down in the place which I have prepared in the mansions of my Father.

links.text: His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.

provenance.other: “thou hast been faithful” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Matthew 25:21, Matthew 25:23 and Luke 19:17. Two of the three are the parable of the talents, whose other end Moroni has just quoted at 12:35; the third is its Lucan cousin.
provenance.significance: This is our own addition to Hardy's row, and it is what makes his row larger than it looks. Hardy cross-references Matthew 25:28-29 at 12:35, the parable's judgment on the unprofitable servant. Two verses later Moroni receives the parable's blessing on the profitable one, in the parable's own words, from the Lord speaking directly to him: 'thou hast been faithful.' The whole of the chapter's ending is therefore staged inside Matthew 25 — the Gentiles in the place of the servant who buried the talent, Moroni in the place of the servant commended — and the reward Matthew promises, 'enter thou into the joy of thy lord', becomes 'the sitting down in the place which I have prepared in the mansions of my Father.' Neither Hardy's apparatus nor the verse itself says this; the pair of quotations says it.

links.note: “If they have not charity, it mattereth not unto thee, thou hast been faithful.” Four words shared with a parable already demonstrably in view two verses earlier, spoken in the same voice (a lord commending a servant) and to the same effect (the servant is admitted where the other is dispossessed). What raises this above coincidence is the pairing: a chapter that quotes Matthew 25:28 and then Matthew 25:21 has read the parable, not remembered a phrase from it.

links.text: Behold, I send an Angel before thee, to keep thee in the way, and to bring thee into the place which I have prepared.

provenance.other: “the place which I have prepared” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Ether 12:37 has it word for word, in the divine first person, as Exodus does.
provenance.alternative: Exodus 23:20 has a New Testament quotation — Matthew 11:10, Mark 1:2 and Luke 7:27 all cite 'Behold, I send my messenger before thy face' — so the mediation question is real. `mediation-check.py` on Ether 12:37 against Exodus 23:20 and Matthew 11:10 returns one decisive point: the entire clause Moroni reproduces, 'to bring thee into the place which I have prepared', is absent from the Gospel form, which stops at the messenger and replaces the destination with 'shall prepare thy way before thee'. The Book of Mormon has the Old Testament form. Mediation is `direct-OT` on that evidence.
provenance.significance: The prepared place of Ether 12:32-37 has been Johannine for five verses — the mansions of the Father — and here, in the one clause where it is God who has prepared and God who is speaking, the words are Exodus'. Exodus 23:20's prepared place is Canaan and the promise is escorted arrival; Moroni's is heaven and the escort is his own faithfulness. That the two frames are welded without seam is characteristic of the chapter, which does the same thing at 12:4 with Hebrews and Corinthians.

links.note: “Even unto the sitting down in the place which I have prepared in the mansions of my Father.” Seven words identical to a KJV singleton, inside a sentence whose other half is John 14:2's. Moderate rather than high because the component words are all common and the string could in principle be assembled independently from 'prepare a place' in John 14:2 — which is why the mediation check matters: the exact string, with 'which I have', exists in the KJV once, and Moroni has it.

pericopes.text: And now I, Moroni, bid farewell unto the Gentiles, yea, and also unto my brethren whom I love, until we shall meet before the judgement seat of Christ, where all men shall know that my garments are not spotted with your blood;

links.text: But why dost thou judge thy brother? or why dost thou set at nought thy brother? for we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ.

provenance.other: “judgment seat of Christ” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 14:10 and 2 Corinthians 5:10, and nowhere else; the KJV's other judgment seats belong to Pilate, Gallio and Herod. The 1830 spells it 'judgement seat' and the 1920 hyphenates, 'judgment-seat'.
provenance.alternative: The phrase is by Moroni's point in the record a Book of Mormon formula (Jacob 6:13, 2 Nephi 33:11, Moroni 10:34 all use it in the same farewell posture), so the proximate model may be the Book of Mormon's own earlier farewells rather than Paul. The enum has no value for an NT source reaching a verse through an earlier Book of Mormon passage; the link is recorded `direct-NT` because Romans 14:10 and 2 Corinthians 5:10 are the only English source the formula can have, and the route through the earlier farewells is stated here rather than encoded.
provenance.significance: Both Pauline verses put the judgment seat at the end of an argument about how Christians treat one another — Romans 14 about not judging a brother, 2 Corinthians 5 about persuading men. Moroni's farewell is doing both: he has just been told that the Gentiles' failure of charity is not chargeable to him, and he takes leave of the Gentiles and of his brethren in one sentence. The tribunal is invoked as the place where the reckoning he has been relieved of will nevertheless be made.

links.note: “Until we shall meet before the judgement seat of Christ, where all men shall know that my garments are not spotted with your blood.” Four words shared with a phrase the KJV uses twice, in the posture Paul uses it in. The 1830 spelling 'judgement' is the older form and was regularized in 1920; it is orthographic rather than substantive, but it belongs in the record under CONVENTIONS §8.

links.text: Wherefore I take you to record this day, that I am pure from the blood of all men.

provenance.other: “pure from the blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The garment half of Moroni's image is Jude 1:23's, “the garment spotted by the flesh” — the KJV's only spotted garment outside Jacob's flocks in Genesis 30, where 'spotted' means piebald cattle and has nothing to do with defilement.
provenance.significance: Moroni's sentence fuses two verses that the Bible keeps apart: Paul's declaration of innocence of his hearers' blood (Acts 20:26, spoken as a farewell at Miletus, exactly the situation here) and Jude's spotted garment. Neither has both terms. The Book of Mormon does this fusion repeatedly — Jacob 1:19 and 2 Nephi 9:44 both shake the garments clean of blood — so the compound is by Moroni an inherited idiom, and this verse is its last use in the book.
provenance.alternative: As at 12:38's judgment seat, the proximate model is likely the Book of Mormon's own earlier formula rather than the KJV; `direct-NT` records the ultimate English source, and the intermediate route is stated here because the enum has no value for it.

links.note: “Where all men shall know that my garments are not spotted with your blood.” The declaration of blood-innocence at a farewell is Acts 20:26's and the spotted garment is Jude 1:23's, and the sentence needs both. Moderate: no long verbal run, and the compound is a Book of Mormon formula by this point, which makes it evidence of the book's habits rather than of a fresh act of borrowing at this verse.

pericopes.text: and then shall ye know that I have seen Jesus, and that he hath talked with me face to face, and that he told me in plain humility, even as a man telleth another in mine own language, concerning these things;

links.text: And the LORD spake unto Moses face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend. And he turned again into the camp: but his servant Joshua, the son of Nun, a young man, departed not out of the tabernacle.

provenance.other: “face to face” occurs in exactly eleven KJV verses and is not by itself distinctive. What is distinctive is the two-part construction: face to face, followed immediately by an as-a-man simile. “as a man speaketh unto his friend” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and Exodus 33:11 is therefore the only KJV verse that has both halves — 'face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend' — and Ether 12:39 has 'face to face, and that he told me in plain humility, even as a man telleth another in mine own language.' The machine's proposal of Numbers 14:14 catches the common phrase and misses the construction; see the exclusion register.
provenance.significance: Exodus 33:11 is the KJV's charter text for the highest grade of prophetic access, and Deuteronomy 34:10 makes it the criterion by which no prophet since has equalled Moses. Moroni claims it, in Moses' own construction, in the last words of his book — and then adds a clause Moses does not have, 'in mine own language', which converts the simile into a claim about translation and about the very inadequacy of writing he complained of at 12:23-25. The chapter that began by protesting the awkwardness of Moroni's hands ends with the Lord speaking to him as a man speaks to his friend, in his own language.

links.note: “He hath talked with me face to face, and that he told me in plain humility, even as a man telleth another in mine own language.” The KJV's face-to-face-plus-simile construction occurs once, at Exodus 33:11, and Moroni reproduces both halves with his own substitutions in the simile (telleth another for speaketh unto his friend). Deuteronomy 34:10, 'whom the LORD knew face to face', is the verse that makes the claim exclusive to Moses and is worth reading beside it. High rather than certain because the individual phrase is common; the construction is what carries it.

links.text: Am I not an apostle? am I not free? have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord? are not ye my work in the Lord?

provenance.other: “seen Jesus” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Elsewhere the KJV writes 'seen the Lord' (John 20:18, 20:25, 1 Corinthians 9:1 aside) or names him otherwise; the bare collocation is Paul's here alone.
provenance.significance: 1 Corinthians 9:1 is Paul authenticating his apostleship against people who dispute it, and the ground he offers is that he has seen Jesus. Moroni, having spent the chapter fearing that the Gentiles will mock his writing, offers the same credential in the same words and to the same end: 'then shall ye know that I have seen Jesus.' Given that the chapter demonstrably has 1 Corinthians 1, 12 and 13 in view, the Corinthian correspondence's own self-defence formula appearing at the point where Moroni defends himself is at least worth recording.

links.note: “And then shall ye know that I have seen Jesus.” Three words, one of them the KJV's only 'seen Jesus'. Filed as an echo, not an allusion: the phrase is short, the situation supplies most of the case, and a writer could reach these words without a source. Recorded because the chapter's Pauline density makes the coincidence worth a reader's attention rather than silence.

pericopes.text: and only a few have I written, because of my weakness in writing.

And now I would commend you to seek this Jesus of whom the prophets and apostles have written, that the Grace of God the Father, and also the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Ghost, which beareth record of them, may be, and abide in you forever. Amen.

links.text: For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one.

provenance.other: “three that bear record” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Ether 12:41 names the same three in the same order — the Father, the Lord Jesus Christ (for 'the Word'), and the Holy Ghost — and attaches to the third of them the same verb, 'which beareth record'.
provenance.significance: This is the strongest `kjvSpecific` claim in the chapter, and it is strong for a reason that has nothing to do with rarity counts. 1 John 5:7 as printed here is the Johannine Comma: it is absent from every Greek manuscript before the sixteenth century, absent from the Vulgate's oldest witnesses, and present in the King James Bible because Erasmus admitted it under pressure into his third edition. A text dependent on this verse cannot be dependent on any Greek New Testament; it can only be dependent on the Latin-and-Erasmus tradition that the KJV transmits. Availability, in Hays's sense, does not merely fail on the Book of Mormon's own chronology here — it fails on the text-critical history of the source itself.
provenance.alternative: The triadic form is also the shape of 2 Corinthians 13:14's benediction and of Matthew 28:19's baptismal formula, both of which are ordinary KJV text; if the resemblance is to a generic trinitarian triad rather than to this verse, the argument above does not apply. What weighs against the generic reading is the verb: Matthew and 2 Corinthians have no bearing of record, and 1 John 5:7 is the only KJV verse in which the three are said to bear record.

links.note: “That the Grace of God the Father, and also the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Ghost, which beareth record of them, may be, and abide in you forever. Amen.” The three persons, in order, with 'bear record' predicated of the Holy Ghost — 1 John 5:7's content in a benediction's grammar. The benediction's own frame is 2 Corinthians 13:14's, 'the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all. Amen', including the closing Amen; the two are fused, as Hebrews and Corinthians were fused at 12:4 and John 10 and John 3 at 12:33. That the last sentence of Moroni's discourse should rest on the KJV's most famous interpolated verse is a fact the catalogue should state plainly rather than leave to a footnote.

links.text: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all. Amen.

provenance.other: The KJV's apostolic benedictions are numerous but only 2 Corinthians 13:14 names all three persons, begins with grace, and ends 'Amen'. “abide in you” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 15:7 and 1 John 2:24, which supply Moroni's closing verb.
provenance.significance: Moroni ends his farewell with the form in which the Pauline letters end, which is consistent with a chapter that has been reading 1 and 2 Corinthians since 12:11. The one alteration is that Paul's benediction wishes the three to be WITH the reader and Moroni's wishes them to ABIDE IN him — a Johannine verb, from the discourse the chapter has already drawn on at 14:2. The last sentence of Ether 12 is therefore a Pauline benediction with Johannine content, which is a fair description of the whole discourse.

links.note: “May be, and abide in you forever. Amen.” The tripartite grace-benediction with its closing Amen. Moderate: benedictions are formulaic by nature and the individual words are unremarkable, so the case rests on the completeness of the match — three persons, grace first, Amen last — rather than on any rare string.

pericopes.text: And now I, Moroni, proceed to finish my record concerning the destruction of the people of which I have been writing.—

For behold, they rejected all the words of Ether: for he truly told them of all things, from the beginning of man; and how that after the waters had receded from off the face of this land, it became a choice land above all other lands, a chosen land of the Lord; wherefore the Lord would have that all men should serve him, which dwelleth upon the face thereof;

provenance.other: “the waters were abated” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Genesis 8:3, 8:8 and 8:11, all of the flood; “from off the face of” occurs in exactly six, of which only Genesis 8:8 puts the waters and that preposition together. Genesis 8:13, which the study apparatus cites here, reads ‘the waters were dried up from off the earth’ — the right event, the wrong preposition. “receded” occurs in no KJV verse; it is the Book of Mormon's own word.
provenance.significance: Ether's opening chapter took its people out of Genesis 11, the tower and the confounded language, and this verse takes the land they arrive at out of Genesis 8, the receding flood. The two halves of the primeval history frame the book: Moroni has Ether preach 'all things, from the beginning of man', and the sequence he preaches is the sequence of Genesis — creation, flood, dispersion — with the New World inserted at the point where the waters go down and dry land appears. The chosen land is, in the logic of the borrowing, the first land the flood uncovers.

links.note: 'How that after the waters had receded from off the face of this land, it became a choice land above all other lands.' The verb is not the King James Bible's but the prepositional phrase is, and it is the flood's: of the six KJV verses reading 'from off the face of', five are destructions and one, Genesis 8:8, is the dove sent out to see whether the waters had abated. The dependence is on the episode rather than on a clause — hence 'moderate', not higher — but it is not a general flood allusion: Ether 13:2 is describing the moment Genesis 8:8-13 describes, the uncovering of ground, and it reaches for Genesis's own preposition to describe it. Note that the promise attached to the land here ('the Lord would have that all men should serve him, which dwelleth upon the face thereof') is the same decree Ether 2:10 states, so the verse is folding the book's own land-covenant into the flood narrative.
links.text: Also he sent forth a dove from him, to see if the waters were abated from off the face of the ground;

pericopes.text: and that it was the place of the New Jerusalem, which should come down out of Heaven, and the Holy Sanctuary of the Lord.

provenance.other: “New Jerusalem” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 3:12 and 21:2, and nowhere in the Old Testament. “cometh down out of heaven” occurs in exactly one, Revelation 3:12; Revelation 21:2 reads 'coming down from God out of heaven' and 21:10 'descending out of heaven from God'. Ether 13:3's relative clause — 'which should come down out of heaven' — has Revelation 3:12's shape without 'from God', which is the half of the phrase 3:12 also omits.
provenance.significance: The catalogue has already recorded the name at 3 Nephi 20:22 and 21:23, where the risen Christ uses it. What Ether 13:3 adds is the descent, and the descent is what makes the anachronism total: a Jaredite prophet who lives before Babel's dispersion has finished is given a term coined in the last book of the New Testament, together with the clause Revelation attaches to it. Recover Revelation 3:12's context and the borrowing gathers a second meaning — the promise there is made to a church told 'thou hast a little strength, and hast kept my word, and hast not denied my name', which is precisely the posture Moroni assigns to Ether in this chapter: a prophet whose word is kept and whose people 'esteemed him as nought' (13:13).

links.note: 'And that it was the place of the New Jerusalem, which should come down out of heaven, and the holy sanctuary of the Lord.' Two of the three elements are traceable to one verse. Revelation 3:12 is one of only two KJV verses to name the new Jerusalem and the only one whose relative clause reads 'which cometh down out of heaven'; Ether 13:3 keeps the relative construction and shifts the tense to the future the prophecy needs. The third element, 'the holy sanctuary of the Lord', is not from Revelation — 'sanctuary of the LORD' occurs in exactly five KJV verses and none of them is eschatological — and it is what makes the sentence a Jaredite one rather than a Johannine one: the city descends and it is a temple. The chapter then does something Revelation does not, which is to give the descending city an address on a continent.
links.text: Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out: and I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, which is new Jerusalem, which cometh down out of heaven from my God: and I will write upon him my new name.

pericopes.text: Behold, Ether saw the days of Christ, and he spake concerning a New Jerusalem upon this land;

and he spake also concerning the house of Israel, and the Jerusalem from whence Lehi should come; after that it should be destroyed, it should be built up again a holy city unto the Lord; wherefore it could not be a New Jerusalem, for it had been in a time of old, but it should be built up again, and become a holy city of the Lord; and it should be built up unto the house of Israel;

provenance.other: “the holy city” occurs in exactly nine KJV verses — Nehemiah 11:1 and 11:18, Isaiah 48:2 and 52:1, Matthew 4:5 and 27:53, Revelation 11:2, 21:2 and 22:19. Only one of them addresses Jerusalem as the holy city in a promise of restoration after destruction, and that is Isaiah 52:1. “put on thy strength” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 52:1-2 is quoted outright elsewhere in the Book of Mormon, at 3 Nephi 20:36 and again in Moroni's last chapter; it is the passage the book uses for Jerusalem's rebuilding. So this verse's 'built up again a holy city unto the Lord' is not reaching for a fresh source but for the one the corpus has already settled on, and the argument of Ether 13:4-8 is built by setting it against Revelation's city: the old Jerusalem gets Isaiah's promise, the new one gets John's, and verse 5 exists to say that the two are not the same city.

links.note: 'The Jerusalem from whence Lehi should come; after that it should be destroyed, it should be built up again a holy city unto the Lord.' The verbal contact is one phrase widely spread across the KJV, so the row is recorded at moderate and not above. What earns it is the discrimination the verse is performing: Moroni has just used Revelation's 'New Jerusalem' and now stops to rule out the obvious misreading — 'wherefore it could not be a New Jerusalem, for it had been in a time of old'. The old city he keeps is Isaiah's, the KJV's one address to Jerusalem as a holy city to be raised after ruin, and the Book of Mormon quotes that address at length in two other books. Recorded so that a reader who arrives here from 3 Nephi 20:36 is told the catalogue saw the same passage standing behind the phrase.
links.whyNot: 'Holy city' is nine KJV verses and 'built up' is common; nothing in Ether 13:5 reproduces a clause of Isaiah 52:1, and the sentence can be accounted for as the Book of Mormon's own idiom for restoration. The row rests on which of the nine verses fits, not on the words themselves.
links.text: Awake, awake; put on thy strength, O Zion; put on thy beautiful garments, O Jerusalem, the holy city: for henceforth there shall no more come into thee the uncircumcised and the unclean.

pericopes.text: and that a New Jerusalem should be built up upon this land, unto the remnant of the seed of Joseph, for the which things there has been a type:

for as Joseph brought his father down into the land of Egypt, even so he died there; wherefore the Lord brought a remnant of the seed of Joseph out of the land of Jerusalem, that he might be merciful unto the seed of Joseph, that they should perish not, even as he was merciful unto the father of Joseph, that he should perish not;

provenance.route: Genesis 46:1-7 and 49:33 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “brought his father” and “he died there” occur in no KJV verse; there is no clause here to count. Genesis 46:4 is the single verse of the descent narrative that contains both halves of Ether's sentence — the going down into Egypt and the death there, the latter in the idiom 'Joseph shall put his hand upon thine eyes'. Genesis 49:33 is where Jacob actually dies.
provenance.significance: The text announces its own figure — 'for the which things there has been a type' — which is unusual enough to be worth saying plainly: this is one of the few places in the Book of Mormon where a typological reading is not the catalogue's inference but the text's instruction. The type is exact in its structure and inverted in its direction. Joseph brings his father down into a foreign land and the father dies there, and the mercy consists in his not perishing before he arrives; the Lord brings a remnant of Joseph's seed out of Jerusalem to a foreign land, and the mercy is the same word twice, 'that they should perish not'. Genesis's descent preserves a family in exile; Ether's exodus preserves a family for an inheritance. The New Jerusalem of verses 6 and 8 is what the antitype gets that the type did not.

links.note: 'For as Joseph brought his father down into the land of Egypt, even so he died there; wherefore the Lord brought a remnant of the seed of Joseph out of the land of Jerusalem.' No clause is reproduced and none needs to be: the verse is a declared typology, marked as such in verse 6, and it is adjudicated as figural on the strength of its structure rather than its wording. Genesis 46:4 is the verse that holds the whole of the type in one sentence, God's promise to Jacob that he will go down with him into Egypt and that Joseph will close his eyes there. Note that our extract of the study apparatus keys Genesis 46:1-7 to this verse but drops the second half of its own note, which reads 'Gen 46.1–7; 49.33' on the page — and 49:33 is the verse that supplies 'even so he died there'. Recorded at high because the text asserts the figure and the figure holds at every point.
links.text: I will go down with thee into Egypt; and I will also surely bring thee up again: and Joseph shall put his hand upon thine eyes.

pericopes.text: wherefore the remnant of the house of Joseph shall be built upon this land; and it shall be a land of their inheritance; and they shall build up a holy city unto the Lord, like unto the Jerusalem of old; and they shall no more be confounded, until the end come, when the earth shall pass away.

provenance.other: “confound” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, of which Genesis 11:7 and 11:9 are the tower; “did there confound” occurs in exactly one, Genesis 11:9. The passive 'confounded' is common in the KJV — 47 verses — and almost always means 'put to shame', which is not what it means here. The sense required at Ether 13:8 is Genesis 11's active one, and it is the sense Ether 1:33-35 has already established for the book.
provenance.significance: This is the book closing its own circle, and the circle is a KJV one. Ether opens at Genesis 11: Jared and his brother come 'from the great tower, at the time the Lord confounded the language of the people', and 1:35 records that 'Jared and his brother were not confounded'. Thirteen chapters later the same verb returns in the promise that the seed of Joseph 'shall no more be confounded, until the end come'. The Jaredites are, by their own founding story, the people who escaped the confounding once; the prophecy Ether is given is that the confounding ends for good in a city built on the land they were brought to. Genesis 11:9's second half — 'from thence did the LORD scatter them abroad upon the face of all the earth' — is the sentence Ether 1:33 also borrows for the scattering, so both halves of Babel are in the book's first chapter and both are answered in its thirteenth.

links.note: 'And they shall build up a holy city unto the Lord, like unto the Jerusalem of old; and they shall no more be confounded, until the end come, when the earth shall pass away.' “shall no more be confounded” occurs in no KJV verse, and read as ordinary King James English 'confounded' would mean put to shame — which is how it reads to anyone who has not been through Ether 1. Read against the book's own opening it means the other thing. The mediation field carries the argument: the proximate model is not Genesis 11:9 directly but Ether 1:33-35, which is where Genesis 11's active 'confound' enters this book, and 13:8 is answering that verse rather than the chapter of Genesis. Recorded at moderate because the single shared word is doing all the work; what makes it worth a row is that no other reading of the word makes sense of the sentence.
links.whyNot: One word, and a common one in the KJV in a different sense. A reader may reasonably take 'confounded' here as Isaiah 45:17's 'ye shall not be ashamed nor confounded world without end', which fits the eschatological frame and requires no Babel at all.
links.text: Therefore is the name of it called Babel; because the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth: and from thence did the LORD scatter them abroad upon the face of all the earth.

pericopes.text: And there shall be a new heaven and a new earth; and they shall be like unto the old, save the old have passed away, and all things have become new.

provenance.route: Isaiah 65:17 → Revelation 21:1 (with 2 Corinthians 5:17) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.mt: Isaiah 65:17 reads plural throughout — 'I create new heavens and a new earth' — and its second clause is 'the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind'.
provenance.other: “a new heaven” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 21:1. “new heavens and a new earth” occurs in exactly two, Isaiah 65:17 and 2 Peter 3:13, both plural. “old things are passed away” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “all things are become new” occurs in exactly one, and they are the same verse, 2 Corinthians 5:17.
provenance.alternative: tools/mediation-check.py returns two decisive points and both favour Revelation 21:1 over Isaiah 65:17: the Book of Mormon has the singular 'heaven' where Isaiah has 'heavens', and it has the passing-away clause where Isaiah has 'the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind'. 2 Peter 3:13 is ruled out on the same singular/plural test.
provenance.significance: The verse is a seam between two New Testament passages that are not otherwise joined, and the seam is visible in one sentence. Its first half is Revelation 21:1, the cosmological new creation seen by a seer; its second half is 2 Corinthians 5:17, where the new creation is a person — 'if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new'. Both of Paul's clauses are KJV singletons and both are here. What the fusion produces is a doctrine neither verse states: that the new heaven and new earth 'shall be like unto the old, save the old have passed away', a continuity Revelation 21:1 explicitly denies by adding 'and there was no more sea'. The Book of Mormon has taken John's cosmos and Paul's grammar of renewal and used the second to soften the first.

links.note: 'And there shall be a new heaven and a new earth; and they shall be like unto the old, save the old have passed away, and all things have become new.' Seven words in order from a KJV singleton, then both surviving clauses of a second. The mediation is the finding. Isaiah 65:17 is the ultimate source and the Book of Mormon does not have Isaiah's form of it: Isaiah writes 'new heavens' and the singular 'a new heaven' occurs in exactly one KJV verse in the whole Bible. Since the verse is transmitted through the New Testament it is recorded as OT-via-NT rather than direct-OT, which is the same test that decided 1 Nephi 22:20 and 3 Nephi 5:24. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his quotations, but the fusion is tighter than a threshold measures — three of the four elements are KJV singletons.
links.text: And I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away; and there was no more sea.

pericopes.text: And then cometh the New Jerusalem; and blessed are they which dwell therein, for it is they whose garment are white through the blood of the Lamb; and they are they which are numbered among the remnant of the seed of Joseph, which were of the house of Israel.

provenance.other: “white in the blood of the Lamb” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “washed their robes” occurs in exactly one, both Revelation 7:14. “the blood of the Lamb” occurs in exactly two, Revelation 7:14 and 12:11. “blessed are they” occurs in exactly twelve, of which Revelation 19:9 — 'Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb' — is the one that pairs the formula with the Lamb.
provenance.alternative: The mediation is genuinely unsettled and the enum has no value for its likeliest shape. Revelation 7:14 reads 'made them white IN the blood of the Lamb'; Ether 13:10 reads 'white THROUGH the blood of the Lamb', which is not the KJV's preposition but is the Book of Mormon's — Alma 13:11, 'their garments were washed white, through the blood of the Lamb', and Alma 5:21, 'through the blood of him of whom it hath been spoken'. So the proximate model is probably an earlier Book of Mormon passage rather than the KJV page, exactly as with an OT source reaching a verse through an earlier Nephite quotation. The schema offers OT-via-earlier-BoM and nothing for a New Testament source arriving the same way, so this row is filed direct-NT and the route is stated here rather than in a sixth invented value. Flagged for the schema, not resolved by it.
provenance.significance: Revelation 7:13-14 is a dialogue in which an interlocutor asks who the white-robed are and the seer is told: 'These are they which came out of great tribulation.' The Book of Mormon has been answering that question in its own terms since 1 Nephi 12:11, and Ether 13:10-11 gives the answer a geography. The white-robed of the New Jerusalem are 'numbered among the remnant of the seed of Joseph'; the white-robed of the old Jerusalem, one verse later, are the scattered of Israel gathered back. John's undifferentiated multitude out of every nation has been sorted into two cities, and the sorting principle is descent.

links.note: 'For it is they whose garment are white through the blood of the Lamb; and they are they which are numbered among the remnant of the seed of Joseph.' Revelation 7:14 supplies both halves of the identification: the whitened garments in the Lamb's blood, which is a KJV singleton, and the demonstrative formula for naming who the whitened are. The 1830 reading is the singular 'garment', corrected to 'garments' in 1920 — which is worth flagging because 'garments' is the KJV's word and the first edition does not have it. The preposition is likewise not Revelation's: 'through' rather than 'in', which is the Book of Mormon's own settled form of the phrase by Alma 13:11 and is why the mediation note above is unresolved.
links.text: And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.

pericopes.text: And then also cometh the Jerusalem of old; and the inhabitants thereof, blessed are they, for they have been washed in the blood of the Lamb; and they are they which were scattered and gathered in from the four quarters of the earth, and from the north countries, and are partakers of the fulfilling of the covenant which God made with their father Abraham.

provenance.route: Genesis 22:18 → Acts 3:25 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “the covenant which God made” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 3:25. Genesis has no such phrase: at 17:7 the covenant is 'established', at 15:18 the LORD 'made a covenant with Abram', and neither wording is this one.
provenance.alternative: tools/mediation-check.py returns one decisive point: the Book of Mormon stops where Acts 3:25 stops and does not carry Genesis 22:18's closing clause, 'because thou hast obeyed my voice'. The relative construction with 'God' as subject is Acts's and not Genesis's.
provenance.significance: Acts 3:25 is Peter telling the men of Israel in Solomon's porch that they are the children of the covenant, and the catalogue has recorded the Book of Mormon reaching for that verse three times before, always for the Abrahamic promise to a scattered Israel. Ether 13:11 is the strangest of the four contexts, because the speaker is not an Israelite: Moroni is reporting a Jaredite prophecy about the old Jerusalem, and the covenant language he uses for it is a Petrine sermon's. Recover the context and the metalepsis is sharper still — Peter's next words are the promise that God will send Jesus Christ 'whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things', which is what Ether 13:9-11 has just spent three verses describing.

links.note: 'And are partakers of the fulfilling of the covenant which God made with their father Abraham.' Seven consecutive words — 'of the covenant which God made with' — reproducing a KJV singleton, and the singleton is a New Testament verse quoting Genesis. That makes it a mediation case rather than a straightforward Old Testament borrowing, and the diff decides it cleanly: Acts 3:25 ends the promise at the blessing of the kindreds of the earth, Genesis 22:18 continues 'because thou hast obeyed my voice', and the Book of Mormon has Acts's shorter form. Below Skousen's threshold and not one of his quotations.
links.text: Ye are the children of the prophets, and of the covenant which God made with our fathers, saying unto Abraham, And in thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed.

provenance.other: “the four quarters of the earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 20:8. Isaiah 11:12, the gathering prophecy this sentence is otherwise reciting, reads 'the four corners of the earth'; Jeremiah 49:36 has 'the four quarters of heaven'.
provenance.significance: By Ether the phrase is a Book of Mormon idiom and the row is calibrated accordingly — the argument for it was made at 1 Nephi 19:16 and again at 3 Nephi 5:24, and it is not remade here. What the recurrence adds is its reach: the same KJV singleton, taken from the mustering of Gog and Magog and used for the gathering of Israel, has now appeared in four books and three hands. A borrowing that survives that many redactional layers is either the corpus's own formula or a habit of the English behind all of them, and the catalogue cannot tell those apart from inside the text.

links.note: 'And they are they which were scattered and gathered in from the four quarters of the earth.' The link is written rather than excluded because Ether is a new book and a reader who meets the phrase here should be told where it comes from; the argument itself belongs to 1 Nephi 19:16, where the substitution of Revelation's 'quarters' for Isaiah 11:12's 'corners' was first adjudicated. Recorded at moderate, as at 3 Nephi 20:13, on the ground that 'gathered in from the four quarters' is by this point a standing Book of Mormon idiom and the verse can be accounted for without any KJV page open.
links.whyNot: The phrase has become the corpus's own; five words shared with Revelation 20:8 prove dependence somewhere in the book's history but not at this verse. The contexts are also opposed — Revelation 20:8 gathers the nations to battle, Ether 13:11 gathers Israel to a covenant.
links.text: And shall go out to deceive the nations which are in the four quarters of the earth, Gog, and Magog, to gather them together to battle: the number of whom is as the sand of the sea.

provenance.route: Jeremiah 31:8 (with 16:15 and 23:8) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “north countries” occurs in no KJV verse; the King James Bible has the singular “the north country” in exactly eight, six of them Jeremiah. “the coasts of the earth” occurs in exactly three, of which Jeremiah 31:8 is the one that pairs it with the north country and a gathering. Jeremiah 23:8 supplies the other half of Ether's clause, 'the seed of the house of Israel out of the north country, and from all countries whither I had driven them'.
provenance.alternative: The printed study apparatus keys 'the lost tribes; see Jer 15.16; 31.8' to this verse. Jeremiah 15:16 is 'Thy words were found, and I did eat them' and has no contact with a gathering from the north at any point; Jeremiah 16:15 is 'The LORD liveth, that brought up the children of Israel from the land of the north', which is exactly what the note says it is citing. The likeliest account is a transposition of digits in the printed apparatus — 16.15 for 15.16 — of the same class as the 2 Nephi 17:17 citation already recorded in data/hardy-corrections.json. Separately, our own extract of the note dropped its second reference, 31.8, keeping only the first; that is a fact about our parser, and the same truncation shows at Ether 13:7.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 31 is the new-covenant chapter, and verse 8 is the gathering that precedes it: 'I will bring them from the north country, and gather them from the coasts of the earth, and with them the blind and the lame.' Ether 13:11 sets that gathering beside the covenant with Abraham in a single sentence, so the old Jerusalem's restoration is given both of the Bible's covenants at once — the one made with the father and the one Jeremiah says will be new. Neither text says this; the sentence does.

links.note: 'And from the north countries' — the Book of Mormon's plural against the King James Bible's consistent singular, which is why this is an echo and not an allusion. The referent is not in doubt: a gathering of Israel from the north is Jeremiah's subject at 16:15, 23:8 and 31:8, and 31:8 is the only one that also gathers from the ends of the earth, which is what Ether's preceding clause does. Recorded so that the study apparatus's cross-reference here is discharged with a verse that actually bears it; see the exclusion register at 13:11 for why the printed citation cannot be right.
links.whyNot: No clause is shared and the one distinctive noun is in the wrong number. A reader may fairly say the Book of Mormon has a general biblical idea of the northern captivity and no particular verse of Jeremiah in view.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Ether 13.11 (the lost tribes; Jer 15.16; 31.8)
links.text: Behold, I will bring them from the north country, and gather them from the coasts of the earth, and with them the blind and the lame, the woman with child and her that travaileth with child together: a great company shall return thither.

pericopes.text: And when these things come, bringeth to pass the Scripture which saith, There are they which were first, which shall be last; and there are they which were last, which shall be first.

provenance.other: “which shall be last” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “which shall be first” occurs in exactly one, and they are the same verse, Luke 13:30. Matthew 19:30 and Mark 10:31 read 'many that are first shall be last'; Matthew 20:16 reads 'So the last shall be first, and the first last'. Only Luke has the relative pronoun, and only Luke has the existential 'there are'.
provenance.alternative: tools/mediation-check.py returns one decisive point for Luke over Matthew 19:30, but the evidence is genuinely split and the split is worth stating. The syntax is Luke's twice over — 'there are they which ... which shall be' reproduces Luke 13:30's construction, and both of its halves are KJV singletons. The ORDER is not Luke's: Luke runs last-then-first, and Ether 13:12 runs first-then-last, which is Matthew 19:30's and Mark 10:31's sequence. So the verse has Luke's words in Matthew's arrangement, and the row is filed at Luke because the words are the harder evidence.
provenance.significance: 'And when these things come, bringeth to pass the Scripture which saith' — a Jaredite prophecy is here said to fulfil 'the scripture', and the scripture in question is a saying of Jesus recorded in Luke, in wording that did not exist in English until 1611. This is the availability criterion failing in the most concentrated form the catalogue has met in Ether: not an echo that could be unconscious but an explicit citation formula pointing at a text that, on the book's own chronology, is two thousand years in its future. The metalepsis is worth recovering as well. Luke 13:30 closes the passage about the strait gate, where many will seek to enter and shall not be able, and where those who come 'from the east, and from the west, and from the north, and from the south' sit down in the kingdom while the householder's own acquaintances are shut out — which is precisely the sorting Ether 13:10-11 has just performed between the seed of Joseph and the Jerusalem of old.

links.note: 'There are they which were first, which shall be last; and there are they which were last, which shall be first.' Two KJV singletons in one sentence, and both belong to Luke 13:30. The catalogue has adjudicated the same saying once before, at 1 Nephi 13:42, where the wording was Matthew 20:16's most regular English form; this is a different form of the same logion and the difference is diagnostic — Ether has the relative pronouns and the existential that only Luke has. The 1830 text reads 'which' at all four points where 1920 reads 'who', which preserves the KJV's own relative and makes the borrowing plainer in the first edition than in the current one. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his quotations.
