bibliography: Hardy MSI at Ether 13.12 (Matt 19.30; Mark 10.31; Luke 13.30)
links.text: And, behold, there are last which shall be first, and there are first which shall be last.

pericopes.text: And I was about to write more, but I am forbidden; but great and marvellous were the prophecies of Ether, but they esteemed him as nought, and cast him out, and he hid himself in the cavity of a rock by day, and by night he went forth viewing the things which should come upon the people.

provenance.other: “I was about to write” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 10:4. The catalogue has already used that verse at Ether 4:5, but for its second half — 'seal up those things' — rather than its first; this is where the first half arrives, verbatim.
provenance.significance: Revelation 10:4 is the seer stopped mid-transcription: the seven thunders speak, John lifts his pen, and a voice from heaven forbids him to write what he heard. Moroni's chapter does the same thing at the same point in its own argument, and the parallel is structural, not just verbal — both prohibitions fall immediately after a vision of the new Jerusalem and immediately before the seer turns to the destruction of a people. The prohibition is also the book's own recurring gesture: Ether 4:5 sealed a record up, Ether 12:24 confessed the weakness of writing, and here the writing simply stops. Compare 3 Nephi 26:11, where Mormon reports the same interdiction — but the 1830 text there reads 'Behold I were about to write them all ... but the Lord forbid it', and 'I were' is in no KJV verse. Moroni's clause is the one that matches the singleton exactly.

links.note: 'And I was about to write more, but I am forbidden.' Six words reproducing a KJV singleton, and the situation reproduced with them: a seer interrupted in the act of writing by a prohibition he does not explain. The Book of Mormon's version compresses Revelation's — John hears a voice and is told what not to write, Moroni simply says he is forbidden — but the compression keeps the one clause that is unique to Revelation 10:4 in the whole English Bible. Recorded as an allusion rather than a quotation because the reproduced run stops at six words and the rest of the verse goes its own way; below Skousen's threshold and not one of his quotations.
links.text: And when the seven thunders had uttered their voices, I was about to write: and I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Seal up those things which the seven thunders uttered, and write them not.

provenance.other: “great and marvellous” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 15:1 and 15:3, and in no Old Testament verse in that form. The 1830 text preserves the KJV's double-l spelling, 'marvellous'; 1920 modernized it to 'marvelous', so the borrowing is visible on the page of the first edition and not on the page of the current one.
provenance.significance: The pairing entered the Book of Mormon at 1 Nephi 1:14, where Lehi's praise reproduces six words of Revelation 15:3 and the catalogue reads the echo metaleptically — Revelation labels those words 'the song of Moses ... and the song of the Lamb'. Here at the far end of the corpus the same adjective pair is spent not on God's works but on a rejected prophet's prophecies, and immediately before the sentence that says his hearers 'esteemed him as nought, and cast him out'. Revelation 15:1's great and marvellous sign is the seven angels with the seven last plagues; Ether's great and marvellous prophecies are followed in this book by the annihilation of a nation. Neither text draws that line.

links.note: 'But great and marvellous were the prophecies of Ether, but they esteemed him as nought, and cast him out.' The phrase occurs in exactly two KJV verses, both in one chapter of Revelation, and the 1830 spelling is the King James one. Recorded at moderate and as an echo rather than an allusion, because by Ether the pair is a standing Book of Mormon formula and the row is written for a reader of this book rather than to re-argue what was settled at 1 Nephi 1:14. What is worth noticing is the reversal: the corpus's first use praises God with it, its last narrative use applies it to a prophet nobody listened to.
links.whyNot: Two ordinary adjectives in a common conjunction, and one of the most-used formulas in the Book of Mormon by this point in the text. Nothing else of Revelation 15 is present at this verse.
links.text: And I saw another sign in heaven, great and marvellous, seven angels having the seven last plagues; for in them is filled up the wrath of God.

pericopes.text: And as he dwelt in the cavity of a rock, he made the remainder of this record, viewing the destructions which came upon the people by night.

And it came to pass that in that same year which he was cast out from among the people, there began to be a great war among the people, for there were many which rose up who were mighty men, and sought to destroy Coriantumr by their secret plans of wickedness, of which hath been spoken.
And now Coriantumr, having studied himself in all the arts of war, and all the cunning of the world, wherefore he gave battle unto them which sought to destroy him;

but he repented not, neither his fair sons nor daughters; neither the fair sons and daughters of Cohor; neither the fair sons and daughters of Corihor; and in fine, there was none of the fair sons and daughters upon the face of the whole earth, which repented of their sins;

wherfore it came to pass that in the first year that Ether dwelt in the cavity of a rock, there was many people which was slain by the sword of those secret combinations fighting against Coriantumr, that they might obtain the kingdom.
And it came to pass that the sons of Coriantumr fought much, and bled much.

And in the second year, the word of the Lord came to Ether, that he should go and prophesy unto Coriantumr, that if he would repent, and all his household, the Lord would give unto him his kingdom, and spare the people,

otherwise they should be destroyed, and all his household, save it were himself, and he should only live to see the fulfilling of the prophecies which had been spoken concerning another people receiving the land for their inheritance; and Coriantumr should receive a burial by them; and every soul should be destroyed save it were Coriantumr.

And it came to pass that Coriantumr repented not, neither his household, neither the people; and the wars did cease not; and they sought to kill Ether, but he fled from before them, and hid again in the cavity of the rock.
And it came to pass that there arose up Shared, and he also gave battle unto Coriantumr; and he did beat him, insomuch that in the third year he did bring him into captivity.
And the sons of Coriantumr, in the fourth year, did beat Shared, and did obtain the kingdom again unto their father.
Now there began to be a war upon all the face of the land, every man with his band, fighting for that which he desired.

provenance.other: “every man did that which was right in his own eyes” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Judges 17:6 and 21:25; “no king in Israel” occurs in exactly four, all of them Judges. Ether 13:25 shares none of that wording: it reads 'every man with his band, fighting for that which he desired'. The row is filed as figural for that reason and not as a verbal link.
provenance.significance: Judges' refrain is the King James Bible's one formula for a society that has come apart because there is no king, and it is spoken over a book that ends in civil war between the tribes of Israel. Ether 13-15 is the same shape run to its end: the kingdom is contested by Coriantumr, Shared, and after them Gilead, Lib and Shiz; the land divides into bands; and by 15:2 two million have fallen. The difference is the one the catalogue should not smooth over. Judges says there was no king, and Ether's anarchy is caused by there being too many claimants to one — the verse before this records the kingdom changing hands twice in two years. Ether 13:31's 'there was none to constrain them' is the closest the chapter comes to Judges' diagnosis, and it names an absent restraint rather than an absent king.

links.note: 'Now there began to be a war upon all the face of the land, every man with his band, fighting for that which he desired.' No clause is shared and the row is written as figural on that basis. What it records is that the King James Bible has exactly one way of narrating a nation dissolving into private violence — the Judges refrain, twice at 17:6 and 21:25 and echoed at 18:1 and 19:1 — and that Ether 13:25 constructs the same sentence out of its own vocabulary: a distributive 'every man', a private object of desire, and no authority in the frame. Recorded at moderate because the pattern is strong and the wording will not carry it; a reader who sees Judges here should be told the catalogue saw it too and declined to call it verbal dependence.
links.whyNot: Not one distinctive word is shared, and civil collapse narrated as 'every man' doing as he pleases is available to any English writer without Judges. If the wording is the test, this row fails it; it is kept because the exclusion register would lose the observation.
links.text: In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.

pericopes.text: And there was robbers, and in fine, all manner of wickedness upon all the face of the land.

And it came to pass that Coriantumr was exceeding angry with Shared, and he went against him with his armies, to battle; and they did meet in great anger; and they did meet in the valley of Gilgal; and the battle became exceeding sore.—
And it came to pass that Shared fought against him for the space of three days. And it came to pass that Coriantumr beat him, and did pursue him until he came to the plains of Heshlon.
And it came to pass that Shared gave him battle again upon the plains; and behold, he did beat Coriantumr, and drove him back again to the valley of Gilgal.
And Coriantumr gave Shared battle again in the valley of Gilgal, in the which he beat Shared, and slew him.

And Shared wounded Coriantumr, in his thigh, that he did not go to battle again for the space of two years, in the which time all the people upon all the face of the land were a shedding blood, and there was none to constrain them.

provenance.other: “and there was none to” occurs in exactly five KJV verses — Deuteronomy 22:27, 2 Samuel 14:6, Psalm 79:3, Psalm 107:12 and Isaiah 63:5. Only one of them completes the clause with a burial, and only one has blood shed in the same sentence: Psalm 79:3, “Their blood have they shed”, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “none to bury” occurs in exactly three, Psalm 79:3 among them. The 1830 text reads 'constrain' where 1920 reads 'restrain'; neither is the Psalm's word.
provenance.significance: Ten verses earlier the Lord has told Coriantumr that everyone he knows will die and that he alone will live 'to see the fulfilling of the prophecies ... and Coriantumr should receive a burial by them' — by another people, because his own will not be there to do it. Psalm 79 is the one place in the King James Bible where those two facts stand in a single verse: blood shed like water round about Jerusalem, and no one left to bury the dead. The chapter's closing sentence and its central prophecy are the two halves of Psalm 79:3, split across ten verses, and the book spends its last two chapters demonstrating them. Ether 15:33 is where the demonstration finishes: Coriantumr alone, and a people he cannot bury.

links.note: 'All the people upon all the face of the land were a shedding blood, and there was none to constrain them.' The construction is the KJV's — a clause of slaughter closed by 'and there was none to' plus an infinitive — and of the five verses that use it, Psalm 79:3 is the only one whose slaughter is a shedding of blood and whose missing office is burial. The Book of Mormon substitutes restraint for burial, which is why this is an echo rather than an allusion; but it has already supplied the burial itself at 13:21, in a prophecy that exists to say who will not be alive to perform one. Recorded at moderate: the shared frame is real, the shared words are five and ordinary.
links.whyNot: The one distinctive element of Psalm 79:3, 'none to bury them', is not in this verse, and the five-word frame that is shared is common enough that Isaiah 63:5 or Psalm 107:12 would serve as well if the sense did not decide it. The argument rests on 13:21 supplying what 13:31 lacks, which is a reading of the chapter rather than of the clause.
links.text: Their blood have they shed like water round about Jerusalem; and there was none to bury them.

pericopes.text: And now there began to be a great curse upon the land, because of the iniquity of the people, in the which, if a man should lay his tool or his sword upon the shelf, or upon the place whither he would keep it, and behold, upon the morrow, he could not find it, so great was the curse upon the land.

Wherefore every man did cleave unto that which was his own, with his hands, and would not borrow, neither would he lend; and every man kept the hilt of his sword thereof, in his right hand, in the defence of his property and his own life, and they of his wives and children.

links.text: They which builded on the wall, and they that bare burdens, with those that laded, every one with one of his hands wrought in the work, and with the other hand held a weapon.

provenance.alternative: The curse itself is the Book of Mormon's own 'slippery treasures' motif (Helaman 13:31-36, Mormon 1:18), and nothing in Nehemiah is behind that; only the posture of verse 2 is at issue here.
provenance.significance: Nehemiah 4 is the one place in the King James Bible where a man holds a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other, and it is a scene of a community building itself: the builders keep their swords on because of enemies outside the wall, and Nehemiah's charge is to 'fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses'. Ether 14:1-2 holds the same two objects — 'his tool or his sword' — and the same never-ungirded sword, and empties the scene of everything that made it Nehemiah's. The enemy is not outside; the neighbour is the enemy. Nobody lends, nobody borrows, nobody builds. Read against Nehemiah, the Jaredite collapse is not merely a war, it is the exact reversal of a restoration: the armed builder becomes the armed hoarder, and what he defends is 'his property and his own life' before it is his wives and children.

links.note: 'Every man did cleave unto that which was his own, with his hands … and every man kept the hilt of his sword thereof, in his right hand.' The wording is not the argument and should not be pretended to be: the shared words are sword, hand, wives and children, all common. What is not common is the tableau. The tool-and-weapon pairing of Ether 14:1-2 occurs once in the KJV, at Nehemiah 4:17-18, and the Jaredite verse reproduces its physical detail (the sword never released, the man never disarmed even at work) while inverting its social content point for point. Proposed as figural because there is no clause to trace; kept at moderate because the inversion is complete enough to be a reading rather than a coincidence, and offered so a reader who sees Nehemiah here is told the catalogue saw it too and decided it was worth recording.

pericopes.text: And now after the space of two years, and after the death of Shared, behold, there arose the brother of Shared, and he gave battle unto Coriantumr, in the which Coriantumr did beat him, and did pursue him to the wilderness of Akish.
And it came to pass that the brother of Shared did give battle unto him in the wilderness of Akish; and the battle became exceeding sore, and many thousands fell by the sword.

And it came to pass that Coriantumr did lay siege to the wilderness, and the brother of Shared did march forth out of the wilderness by night, and slew a part of the army of Coriantumr, as they were drunken.
And he came forth to the land of Moron, and placed himself upon the throne of Coriantumr.
And it came to pass that Coriantumr dwelt with his army in the wilderness, for the space of two years, in the which he did receive great strength to his army.
Now the brother of Shared, whose name was Gilead, also received great strength to his army, because of secret combinations.
And it came to pass that his High Priest murdered him as he sat upon his throne.

And it came to pass that one of the secret combinations murdered him in a secret pass, and obtained unto himself the kingdom; and his name was Lib; and Lib was a man of great stature, more than any other man among all the people.

links.text: And there was yet a battle in Gath, where was a man of great stature, that had on every hand six fingers, and on every foot six toes, four and twenty in number; and he also was born to the giant.

provenance.other: “a man of great stature” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — 2 Samuel 21:20, 1 Chronicles 20:6 (its parallel) and 1 Chronicles 11:23. The first two are the giants of Gath, Goliath's kin; the third is the Egyptian with the weaver's-beam spear whom Benaiah kills. The second half of the Jaredite clause is a different verse's: “higher than any of the people” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Samuel 9:2 and 10:23, both of Saul.
provenance.significance: Lib is assembled out of the King James Bible's two ways of saying a man is too big. From the Philistine side he takes the fixed phrase for the champions of Gath; from the Israelite side he takes Saul's measurement, the height that made a man look like a king and did not make him one. That combination is the whole of the Jaredite endgame in one sentence: Lib obtains the kingdom by assassination in a secret pass, and what the record gives as his qualification is his body. The Anakim tradition behind the Gath giants is the same one the chapter reaches for again eight verses later, when the cry against Lib's brother is Deuteronomy 9:2's cry against the children of Anak — so this is not an isolated borrowing but the opening of a giant-terror frame the chapter sustains, on down to two armies encamped on facing high ground with a valley between them (14:28) in the posture of 1 Samuel 17:3.

links.note: 'Lib was a man of great stature, more than any other man among all the people.' Five words reproduced exactly from a three-verse KJV phrase, followed immediately by a paraphrase of a two-verse KJV phrase describing a different giant. Neither is a formula the Book of Mormon uses elsewhere: “man of great stature” occurs nowhere else in the Book of Mormon, so this is not the text reusing its own stock. The dossier's own top candidate here was 1 Samuel 14:39 for the connective run 'man among all the people', which is the n-gram stream ranking boilerplate above the borrowing beside it — CONVENTIONS §9's failure mode, in miniature. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not to be counted among his thirty-six.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that in the first year of Lib, Coriantumr came up unto the land of Moron, and gave battle unto Lib.

And it came to pass that he fought with Lib, in the which Lib did smite upon his arm, that he was wounded; nevertheless, the army of Coriantumr did press forward upon Lib, that he fled to the borders upon the seashore.
And it came to pass that Coriantumr pursued him; and Lib gave battle unto him upon the seashore.
And it came to pass that Lib did smite the army of Coriantumr, that they fled again to the wildernsss of Akish.
And it came to pass that Lib did pursue him until he came to the plains of Agosh. And Coriantumr had taken all the people with him, as he fled before Lib, in that quarter of the land whither he fled.

And when he had come to the plains of Agosh, he gave battle unto Lib, and he smote upon him until he died; nevertheless, the brother of Lib did come against Coriantumr in the stead thereof, and the battle became exceeding sore, in the which Coriantumr fled again before the army of the brother of Lib.

Now the name of the brother of Lib was called Shiz. And it came to pass that Shiz pursued after Coriantumr, and he did overthrow many cities, and he did slay both women and children, and he did burn the cities thereof;
and there went a fear of Shiz throughout all the land; yea, a cry went forth throughout the land: Who can stand before the army of Shiz? Behold, he sweepeth the earth before him!

links.text: A people great and tall, the children of the Anakims, whom thou knowest, and of whom thou hast heard say, Who can stand before the children of Anak!

provenance.other: “who can stand before” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Deuteronomy 9:2, Psalm 147:17 ('who can stand before his cold?') and Nahum 1:6 ('who can stand before his indignation?'). Only Deuteronomy 9:2 asks it of a human enemy, and only Deuteronomy 9:2 gives it as a quoted popular cry — 'of whom thou hast heard say'. The phrase occurs nowhere else in the Book of Mormon.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the borrowing turns argumentative. Deuteronomy 9:2 quotes the cry only to overrule it: the very next verse is 'Understand therefore this day, that the LORD thy God is he which goeth over before thee … so shalt thou drive them out, and destroy them quickly, as the LORD hath said unto thee.' The saying is the report of the spies, the fear that cost Israel forty years, and Moses cites it as the thing faith answers. Ether 14:18 puts that cry in the mouth of a whole land and lets it stand. Nobody overrules it; the next verses are the people flocking into the two armies that will annihilate each other. The Jaredites are given Israel's sentence of terror at the precise moment there is no Moses to finish it — and the man they are terrified of is the brother of the man the chapter has just described in the Anakim's own phrase.

links.note: 'A cry went forth throughout the land: Who can stand before the army of Shiz?' Five words in sequence, in the same syntactic slot — an anonymous popular saying about an enemy too big to face, introduced as something the whole land is heard to say. The tie to 14:10 is what makes the case: the chapter has already called Lib 'a man of great stature', which is the KJV's phrase for the giants of Gath, and Numbers 13:32-33 puts 'men of a great stature' and 'the sons of Anak' in consecutive verses of the report Deuteronomy 9:2 is quoting back. Two contacts with one tradition, eight verses apart, on the two brothers in turn. The 1830 punctuation keeps the cry as direct speech, which is how Deuteronomy 9:2 carries it.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the people began to flock together in armies, throughout all the face of the land.
And they were divided, and a part of them fled to the army of Shiz, and a part of them fled to the army of Coriantumr.—
And so great and lasting had been the war, and so long had been the scene of bloodshed and carnage, that the whole face of the land was covered with the bodies of the dead;

and so swift and speedy was the war, that there was none left to bury the dead, but they did march forth from the shedding of blood, to the shedding of blood, leaving the bodies of both men, women and children, strewed upon the face of the land, to become a prey to the worms of the flesh;

links.text: Their blood have they shed like water round about Jerusalem; and there was none to bury them.

provenance.other: “none to bury them” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 79:3 and Jeremiah 14:16; “the dead bodies of” occurs in exactly three. Psalm 79:2-3 is the only place in the KJV that holds all three of Ether 14:21-22's elements in one breath — dead bodies given to the beasts, blood shed like water, and nobody left to bury.
provenance.alternative: Alma 16:11 describes the corpses of Ammonihah 'heaped up upon the face of the earth' and is the Book of Mormon's own precedent for the scene, including the word 'scent' that Ether 14:23 uses twice. But Alma 16:11's dead are buried, under 'a shallow covering', and the distinctive thing about Ether 14:22 — that there is nobody left to bury them at all, and the bodies feed something — is Psalm 79's and not Alma's.
provenance.significance: Psalm 79 is a communal lament over Jerusalem sacked: it is spoken by survivors, to God, and it asks a question ('How long, LORD?') on the strength of the unburied dead. Ether 14 borrows the scene and cancels the speaker. There is nobody to lament, because both parties to the slaughter are the wicked, and the verse that answers 'how long' is 14:25 — 'the Lord did visit them in the fulness of his wrath'. The psalm's unburied bodies are evidence against God's enemies; the Jaredites' unburied bodies are evidence against themselves.

links.note: 'There was none left to bury the dead … leaving the bodies of both men, women and children, strewed upon the face of the land, to become a prey to the worms of the flesh.' Three of Psalm 79:2-3's four elements in Psalm 79's order, with one substitution: the psalm's corpses are eaten by the fowls of heaven and the beasts of the earth, the Jaredites' by worms. That substitution is worth its own line — carrion birds and beasts are what the KJV always supplies here (Jeremiah 16:4, 34:20, Ezekiel 39:4), and worms in the KJV belong to a man's own grave, not a battlefield (Job 21:26, Isaiah 14:11). The Book of Mormon has moved the image from the field to the tomb, which is what makes the next verse's stench a problem for the living rather than a portent. Offered at moderate because no clause is reproduced; the case rests on the co-occurrence, which is rare, and on the sequence, which is exact.

pericopes.text: and the scent thereof went forth upon the face of the land, even upon all the face of the land; wherefore the people became troubled by day and by night, because of the scent thereof;

nevertheless, Shiz did not cease to pursue Coriantumr, for he had sworn to avenge himself upon Coriantumr of the blood of his brother, which had been slain, and the word of the Lord which came to Ether, that Coriantumr should not fall by the sword.

links.text: For I will surely deliver thee, and thou shalt not fall by the sword, but thy life shall be for a prey unto thee: because thou hast put thy trust in me, saith the LORD.

provenance.other: “fall by the sword” occurs in twenty-four KJV verses and is pure formula; the negated form is not. “not fall by the sword” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jeremiah 39:18, which is the oracle to Ebed-melech the Ethiopian on the day Jerusalem falls.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 39:18 and its twin at 45:5 are the King James Bible's survivor oracles: in the middle of a national annihilation one named man is told he personally will come through it, and is given his own life 'for a prey' — kept, but as spoil salvaged from a wreck. Ether 13:20-21 gave Coriantumr exactly that oracle in exactly that setting, and 14:24 is where the record states it in Jeremiah's words. The difference is the ground. Ebed-melech survives 'because thou hast put thy trust in me'; Coriantumr survives so that he can watch, and be buried by strangers. The Book of Mormon has taken the KJV's one promise of personal deliverance out of a total judgment and made it a sentence.

links.note: 'And the word of the Lord which came to Ether, that Coriantumr should not fall by the sword.' The five-word negated formula is a KJV singleton and the situation around it is the singleton's own: a besieged nation, a prophet, and one man exempted by name. The oracle itself is delivered at Ether 13:20-21, which words it as 'he should only live to see' and has no contact with Jeremiah; per CONVENTIONS §6a the link is filed where the wording is. Note also the second-hand framing — 'the word of the Lord which came to Ether' — which is Jeremiah's own superscription formula (Jeremiah 46:1 and some fifty others) and was the dossier's highest-scoring run on this verse; that half is boilerplate and is not part of the claim.

links.text: And when Abner was returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside in the gate to speak with him quietly, and smote him there under the fifth rib, that he died, for the blood of Asahel his brother.

provenance.other: “the blood of his brother” occurs in no KJV verse, and “avenge himself” in none; the verbal contact is limited to 2 Samuel 3:27's closing clause 'for the blood of Asahel his brother' and the institution it invokes, the revenger of blood of Numbers 35:19.
provenance.significance: The Israelite blood-feud narrative is not a duel but a chain, and Ether 14 runs the chain in Samuel's order. Coriantumr kills Lib in the field (14:16); Lib's brother is thereby made the goel, sworn to take the killer's blood, and he pursues him without stopping until one of them is dead. That is 2 Samuel 2:18-3:30, where Abner kills Asahel in the field and Asahel's brother Joab hunts him to Hebron and kills him 'for the blood of Asahel his brother' — and where the narrator, like Moroni, treats the vengeance as a thing that ruins the avenger's house as surely as the enemy's. What the Jaredite version removes is the city of refuge. Numbers 35's whole apparatus exists to bound blood-vengeance; Ether 14 has an oath, a pursuit and a land with no boundaries left in it, and the feud consumes the population.

links.note: 'He had sworn to avenge himself upon Coriantumr of the blood of his brother, which had been slain.' There is one clause of contact and it is a real one — the KJV's way of naming a motive, 'for the blood of X his brother' — but the case is structural rather than verbal and is filed as figural for that reason. Recorded because Shiz's motive is stated once, in this verse, and stated in the grammar of an institution the record's compiler knew; a reader who takes 'sworn to avenge himself' as generic bloodthirst has missed that the text is describing a legal office. Kept at moderate: the shape is Samuel's, the words are mostly not.

pericopes.text: And thus we see that the Lord did visit them in the fulness of his wrath, and their wickedness and abominations had prepared a way for their everlasting destruction.

links.text: Who shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power;

provenance.route: 2 Thessalonians 1:9 → KJV → Book of Mormon, but very probably not directly into this verse; see alternative
provenance.other: “everlasting destruction” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Thessalonians 1:9. It occurs in nine Book of Mormon verses, the earliest at Alma 5:7 and Alma 12:6, and Ether 14:25 is the last of them.
provenance.alternative: The mediation is genuinely undecided and the field is set to 'uncertain' to say so. The phrase is a KJV singleton, so its ultimate source is not in doubt; what is in doubt is whether Pauline text stands behind THIS verse at all, or whether Moroni is reaching for a formula the Book of Mormon has used eight times already — in which case the borrowing happened in Alma and Ether 14:25 merely inherits it. The schema has no value for an NT source arriving through an earlier Book of Mormon passage: 'OT-via-earlier-BoM' covers the Old Testament case only, and the gap is flagged here rather than filled by inventing a sixth value. If the enum gains an 'NT-via-earlier-BoM', this row should take it.
provenance.significance: 2 Thessalonians 1:9 defines everlasting destruction as exclusion — 'from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power' — and Ether 14:25 arrives at it by the opposite motion: 'the Lord did visit them in the fulness of his wrath.' Being visited and being shut out are the same sentence in this book. Coriantumr, the one man exempted at 14:24, is the exception that states the rule: he alone will be present to see, which is what the everlasting destruction of everyone else consists in.

links.note: 'Their wickedness and abominations had prepared a way for their everlasting destruction.' Two words, a KJV singleton, in the summary sentence Moroni uses to close the chapter's carnage — and the same two words carry Alma's whole doctrine of the state of the soul between death and judgment (Alma 12:6, 12:17, 12:36). Recorded at moderate because the rarity is absolute and the theological weight is real, and flagged rather than pressed because the proximate model is very likely internal. The rest of the sentence is not Paul's and is not anyone's: 'prepared a way' occurs in no KJV verse and is the Book of Mormon's own idiom (1 Nephi 17:41, Ether 12:8).
links.whyNot: By the time Ether is written 'everlasting destruction' has been standard Book of Mormon vocabulary for eight previous verses across three books. A phrase that common inside the corpus cannot show that its ninth user had 2 Thessalonians open; the honest claim is that the phrase entered the Book of Mormon from 2 Thessalonians 1:9, not that it entered here.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Shiz did pursue Coriantumr eastward, even to the borders by the seashore, and there he gave battle unto Shiz for the space of three days;

and so terrible was the destruction among the armies of Shiz, that the people began to be frightened, and began to flee before the armies of Coriantumr; and they fled to the land of Corihor, and swept off the inhabitants before them, all they that would not join them;

links.text: And so terrible was the sight, that Moses said, I exceedingly fear and quake:)

provenance.other: “and so terrible was the” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 12:21, and the construction occurs nowhere else in the Book of Mormon. Hebrews 12:21 is itself a rendering of Sinai, glancing at Deuteronomy 9:19; but Deuteronomy 9:19 has none of these words ('For I was afraid of the anger and hot displeasure'), so the English clause is the epistle's own and the Book of Mormon has the epistle's form. tools/mediation-check.py returns this as decisive.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 12:18-21 is arguing that Christians have not come to Sinai — to the mountain that burned, the blackness, the trumpet, and the voice the people begged to stop. The clause Ether borrows is the peak of that terror, and the epistle's point in reciting it is that this is precisely what the reader has been spared. Ether 14:27 gives the Jaredites Sinai's terror with no mountain and no voice in it: what is 'so terrible' is a body count, and the effect is not repentance but a stampede in which the fleeing army sweeps off everyone who will not join it. The chapter has already used Deuteronomy 9:2's cry at 14:18; the same chapter of Deuteronomy stands behind Hebrews 12:21, so the two loudest sentences of Jaredite terror both come out of Moses' account of the two things Israel was most afraid of — the giants and the mountain.

links.note: 'And so terrible was the destruction among the armies of Shiz, that the people began to be frightened.' Five words reproduced exactly, in the same construction — 'so terrible was the X, that' plus the resulting fear — from the only KJV verse that has them. The substituted noun is the whole of the argument: Hebrews' terrible thing is a sight shown by God, Ether's is a destruction inflicted by men, and the fear it produces is not Moses' quaking before God but a rout. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six. The dossier ranked this candidate at 2.00, its joint highest for the chapter, and here the n-gram stream was right.

pericopes.text: and they pitched their tents in the valley of Corihor. And Coriantumr pitched his tents in the valley of Shurr. Now the valley of Shurr was near the hill Comnor; wherefore Coriantumr did gather his armies together, upon the hill Comnor, and did sound a trumpet unto the armies of Shiz, to invite them forth to battle.

And it came to pass that they came forth, but were driven again; and they came the second time; and they were driven again the second time. And it came to pass that they came again the third time, and the battle became exceeding sore.
And it came to pass that Shiz smote upon Coriantumr, that he gave him many deep wounds. And Coriantumr having lost his blood, fainted, and was carried away as though he were dead.
Now the loss of men, women and children, on both sides, were so great that Shiz commanded his people that they should not pursue the armies of Coriantumr; wherefore they returned to their camp.
And it came to pass that when Coriantumr had recovered of his wounds, he began to remember the words which Ether had spoken unto him:

He saw that there had been slain by the sword already nearly two millions of his people, and he began to sorrow in his heart; yea, there had been slain two millions of mighty men, and also their wives and their children.

He began to repent of the evil which he had done; he began to remember the words which had been spoken by the mouth of all the prophets, and he saw them that they were fulfilled, thus far, every whit; and his soul mourned, and refused to be comforted.

provenance.other: “refused to be comforted” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Genesis 37:35 (Jacob for Joseph), Psalm 77:2, and Jeremiah 31:15 (Rachel for her children). Only Psalm 77:2 makes the soul the subject of the refusal — “my soul refused to be comforted” — against Ether's “his soul mourned, and refused to be comforted”. Jeremiah 31:15 is quoted at Matthew 2:18, which reads “would not be comforted”; tools/mediation-check.py finds that divergence decisive for the Old Testament form, so wherever in the trio the phrase came from, it did not come through Matthew.
provenance.alternative: Jeremiah 31:15, which supplies the chapter's other two elements (see the link at 15:11) but not the soul as subject.
provenance.significance: Recover Psalm 77 and the metalepsis is exact. It is the psalm of a man who cannot be comforted and who therefore *remembers*: “I will remember the works of the LORD” (77:11), “I have considered the days of old” (77:5), “I call to remembrance my song in the night” (77:6). Ether 15:3 puts the remembering in the same clause as the refusal — Coriantumr “began to remember the words which had been spoken by the mouth of all the prophets” and his soul “refused to be comforted”. The difference is where the remembering leads. Psalm 77 ends by recalling the Red Sea and the flock led by Moses and Aaron; the memory is a comfort withheld only for a night. Coriantumr remembers the prophets and finds that what he remembers is his own destruction, “fulfilled, thus far, every whit”. The psalm's structure is borrowed and its consolation removed.

links.note: “And his soul mourned, and refused to be comforted.” This is the hinge of the chapter: the king who has killed two million people repents, four verses before the killing resumes and finishes the nation. The KJV gives the sentence its words. “refused to be comforted” belongs to three verses of the Bible and to no other English idiom of grief, and the one of the three that attaches the refusal to the soul rather than to the mourner is Psalm 77:2. The verse also carries “every whit”, which occurs in exactly four KJV verses (Deuteronomy 13:16, 1 Samuel 3:18, John 7:23, John 13:10) and which the Book of Mormon has used once before at 1 Nephi 4:19 — in the other beheading scene this chapter is going to reproduce. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold, and not a quotation: five words, but five words the King James Bible almost never says.
links.text: In the day of my trouble I sought the Lord: my sore ran in the night, and ceased not: my soul refused to be comforted.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he wrote an epistle unto Shiz, desiring him that he would spare the people, and he would give up the kingdom for the sake of the lives of the people.

And it came to pass that when Shiz had received his epistle, he wrote an epistle unto Coriantumr, that if he would give himself up, that he might slay him with his own sword, that he would spare the lives of the people.

And it came to pass that the people repented not of their iniquity; and the people of Coriantumr were stirred up to anger against the people of Shiz; and the people of Shiz were stirred up to anger against the people of Coriantumr; wherefore the people of Shiz did give battle unto the people of Coriantumr.—
And when Coriantumr saw that he was about to fall, he fled again before the people of Shiz.

And it came to pass that he came to the waters of Ripliancum, which, by interpretation, is large, or to exceed all; wherefore, when they came to these waters, they pitched their tents; and Shiz also pitched his tents, near unto them; and therefore, on the morrow, they did come to battle.
And it came to pass that they fought an exceeding sore battle, in the which Coriantumr was wounded again, and he fainted with the loss of blood.

And it came to pass that the armies of Coriantumr did press upon the armies of Shiz, that they beat them, that they caused them to flee before them; and they did flee southward, and did pitch their tents in a place which was called Ogath.
And it came to pass that the army of Coriantumr did pitch their tents by the hill Ramah; and it was that same hill where my father Mormon did hide up the records unto the Lord, which were sacred.—

provenance.other: The name is spelled Ramah in the KJV Old Testament and Rama in the KJV New Testament (Matthew 2:18); the Book of Mormon's hill is Ramah. Ramah as a place name is common in the KJV and proves nothing by itself — the argument here is the cluster, not the name. What is testable is that both of the other elements Jeremiah 31:15 supplies appear in this chapter in the Old Testament's wording: “refused to be comforted” at 15:3 (Matthew reads “would not be comforted”), and “lamentation” at 15:16.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 31:15 holds four things in one sentence: Ramah, a lamentation, weeping for children, and a refusal to be comforted ‘because they were not’. Ether 15 holds all four, distributed — Coriantumr's soul refusing comfort at 15:3, the hill Ramah at 15:11, the howling and lamentation for the slain at 15:16 and again at 15:17, and at 15:2 the reason for all of it, two millions slain ‘and also their wives and their children’. This is metalepsis in Hays's sense working across a chapter rather than within a phrase: the fragmentary echoes are unremarkable one at a time, and the verse they all came from is the Bible's single sentence about a mother at Ramah who will not be comforted because her children are not. The chapter is Jeremiah 31:15 acted out at national scale, and the verse itself is never quoted.

links.note: “The army of Coriantumr did pitch their tents by the hill Ramah; and it was that same hill where my father Mormon did hide up the records unto the Lord.” The name is doing two jobs. Internally it identifies the Jaredite battlefield with Cumorah, where Mormon will lose his own nation (Mormon 6:11) — the same hill, twice emptied. Externally it is a KJV place name, and the KJV verse that made Ramah famous is the one where a voice is heard in Ramah, lamentation and bitter weeping, and the weeper refuses to be comforted because the children are not. Ether 15 has already used that verse's refusal at 15:3 and will use its lamentation at 15:16. A reader may reasonably decline this: Ramah is a real toponym with a plain Hebrew sense, and no single verse of Ether 15 quotes Jeremiah. The catalogue records it because the three elements are the three elements of one biblical sentence and they occur nowhere else together.
links.text: Thus saith the LORD; A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they did gather together all the people, upon all the face of the land, which had not been slain, save it were Ether.

provenance.other: “gather them together to battle” is a KJV singleton, Revelation 20:8. The nearest competitor, “gathered together to battle”, occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Samuel 23:9 and 1 Chronicles 11:13, both of them ordinary Philistine musters. The Book of Mormon's clause is “they did gather together all the people”, resumed at 15:14 as “four years, gathering together the people” and completed at 15:15 as “when they were all gathered together … they did march forth one against another, to battle”.
provenance.significance: Revelation 20:8's gathering is the last one in the Bible: Gog and Magog fetched from the four quarters of the earth, ‘the number of whom is as the sand of the sea’, mustered for a battle that ends the world's history rather than a war. Ether 15:12-15 is the only muster in the Book of Mormon with that shape — not an army raised but a population collected, everyone left alive on the face of the land, four years spent doing it, women and children included, and no survivor contemplated on either side. The scale is what makes the echo audible: nobody gathers *all the people* to a battle except at the end of the world.

links.note: “They did gather together all the people, upon all the face of the land, which had not been slain, save it were Ether.” The apocalyptic register the chapter has been reaching for since 15:2 arrives here, and its KJV home is Revelation. The verbal contact is modest and I record it as such — the shared run is ‘gather’ plus ‘together’ plus ‘to battle’ spread over four verses, not a clause — but the collocation belongs to exactly one verse of the King James Bible, and the situation belongs to exactly one biblical episode. Note what the chapter does with the hill: Revelation 16:16 gathers its armies ‘into a place called in the Hebrew tongue Armageddon’, a Hebrew name for a hill; Ether 15:11 gathers its armies at a hill with a Hebrew name.
links.text: And shall go out to deceive the nations which are in the four quarters of the earth, Gog, and Magog, to gather them together to battle: the number of whom is as the sand of the sea.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Ether did behold all the doings of the people; and he beheld that the people which were for Coriantumr, were gathered together to the army of Coriantumr; and the people which were for Shiz, were gathered together to the army of Shiz;

wherefore they were for the space of four years, gathering together the people, that they might get all which were upon the face of the land, and that they might receive all the strength which it were possible that they could receive.

And it came to pass that when they were all gathered together, every one to the army which he would, with their wives, and their children; both men, women and children being armed with weapons of war, having shields, and breast-plates, and head-plates, and being clothed after the manner of war, they did march forth one against another, to battle; and they fought all that day, and conquered not.

And it came to pass that when it was night they were weary, and retired to their camps; and after that they had retired to their camps, they took up a howling and a lamentation for the loss of the slain of their people; and so great were their cries, their howlings and lamentations, that it did rend the air exceedingly.

provenance.other: “an howling” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Jeremiah 25:36 and Zephaniah 1:10, and ‘howling’ in any form in exactly five. “take up a lamentation” occurs in exactly six KJV verses — Jeremiah 7:29 and Ezekiel 26:17, 27:2, 27:32, 28:12 and 32:2 — and every one of the six is a prophetic dirge raised over a nation or a king under sentence. The Book of Mormon fuses the two: ‘they took up a howling and a lamentation’.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 25 is the chapter of the cup of the LORD's fury, and it is the chapter Ether 15 is living inside. The nations drink and ‘be moved, and be mad, because of the sword that I will send among them’ (25:16); they are told to ‘drink ye, and be drunken … and fall, and rise no more, because of the sword’ (25:27); the howling of 25:36 follows; and at 25:33 ‘the slain of the LORD shall be at that day from one end of the earth even unto the other: they shall not be lamented, neither gathered, nor buried’. Ether 15 supplies each in turn — the drunkenness at 15:22, the falling by the sword and rising no more at 15:23, the howling here — and Moroni has already reported at 14:22 that there was none left to bury the dead. The one thing Jeremiah 25:33 denies the slain is lamentation, and the lamentation is the one thing Ether 15 gives them.

links.note: “They took up a howling and a lamentation for the loss of the slain of their people; and so great were their cries, their howlings and lamentations, that it did rend the air exceedingly.” Both nouns are KJV prophetic-dirge vocabulary and neither is ordinary English for grief: taking *up* a lamentation is the formula that opens an oracle against a nation, six times in Jeremiah and Ezekiel, and 'an howling' is the noun in only two verses. What the Book of Mormon has done is put the oracle in the mouths of the condemned. In Jeremiah and Ezekiel the prophet takes up the lamentation over Tyre or Pharaoh or Jerusalem; here the doomed army raises it over itself, twice, on two successive nights, and then goes back to the field in the morning. ‘Rend the air’ is not biblical — the KJV rends garments and hearts (Joel 2:13) — and I do not claim it.
links.text: A voice of the cry of the shepherds, and an howling of the principal of the flock, shall be heard: for the LORD hath spoiled their pasture.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that on the morrow they did go again to battle, and great and terrible was that day; nevertheless they conquered not, and when the night came again, they did rend the air with their cries, and their howlings, and their mournings, for the loss of the slain of their people,
And it came to pass that Coriantumr wrote again an epistle unto Shiz, desiring that he would not come again to battle, but that he would take the kingdom, and spare the lives of the people.

But behold, the spirit of the Lord had ceased striving with them, and satan had full power over the hearts of the people, for they were given up unto the hardness of their hearts, and the blindness of their minds, that they might be destroyed; wherefore they went again to battle.

provenance.other: “strive with man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 6:3. But Genesis reads ‘My spirit’, in God's own mouth, and Ether 15:19 reads ‘the spirit of the Lord’ in the third person — which is the form already fixed inside the Book of Mormon at 1 Nephi 7:14, 2 Nephi 26:11, Mormon 5:16 and Moroni 8:28. 2 Nephi 26:11 is the proximate model and it is nearly exact: ‘for the spirit of the Lord will not always strive with man. And when the spirit ceaseth to strive with man, then cometh speedy destruction.’ Ether 15:19 has both halves — the ceasing, and then ‘that they might be destroyed’.
provenance.alternative: Direct dependence on Genesis 6:3. Possible, but it does not account for the third-person ‘spirit of the Lord’ or for the destruction clause, both of which 2 Nephi 26:11 supplies and Genesis does not.
provenance.significance: Genesis 6:3 is the sentence God says immediately before the Flood — the announcement that the restraint on human violence is being lifted, and the last words before ‘the earth was filled with violence’ and every living thing is destroyed. The Book of Ether opened from the other end of that same story, at the tower after the waters (Ether 1:33, 13:2), and it closes by pronouncing the Flood's own formula over a second annihilation. The Jaredites came out of the world's first universal destruction and go into their own by the same sentence.

links.note: “The spirit of the Lord had ceased striving with them.” The clause has one biblical home, and it is the verse God speaks with the Flood in view. What makes this a mediation case rather than a plain Genesis borrowing is the wording: Genesis has ‘My spirit shall not always strive with man’, and the Book of Mormon has been saying ‘the spirit of the Lord’ since 1 Nephi 7:14, with 2 Nephi 26:11 stating the whole rule — cessation, then speedy destruction — in the form Ether 15:19 reproduces. So the source is Genesis and the model is Nephi. Moroni is writing the last chapter of a book whose own scriptures have already made Genesis 6:3 into a law of national history, and he applies the law.
links.text: And the LORD said, My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh: yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years.

provenance.other: “the blindness of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 4:18 (‘the blindness of their heart’); Ether 15:19 has ‘the blindness of their minds’. “hardness of their hearts” likewise occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 3:5. Ether 15:19 has both nouns in one clause, and Ephesians 4:19 continues ‘who being past feeling have given themselves over unto lasciviousness’, which is the giving-up the Book of Mormon's ‘they were given up unto’ reproduces; compare Romans 1:28, ‘God gave them over to a reprobate mind’.
provenance.significance: Ether 15:19 swaps Paul's organs. Ephesians 4:18 darkens the understanding and blinds the *heart*; the Book of Mormon hardens the *hearts* and blinds the *minds*, taking Mark 3:5's phrase for the one and Ephesians' for the other and crossing them. The effect is to make the two KJV singletons into a single formula for a nation that can no longer be reached, which is precisely the state Genesis 6:3 has just been invoked to describe in the same verse.

links.note: “They were given up unto the hardness of their hearts, and the blindness of their minds, that they might be destroyed.” Two phrases, each of which the King James Bible uses once. Neither is a natural English collocation and both are Pauline in origin — Ephesians 4:18 for the blindness, Mark 3:5 for the hardness — and the passive ‘given up’ is the verb of Romans 1:24-28, where God's abandonment of a people to its own mind is itself the judgment. The verse is doing in six words what Romans 1 does in five: the destruction is not an event that befalls them, it is the handing-over.
links.text: Having the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart:

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they fought all that day, and when the night came they slept upon their swords;
and on the morrow they fought even until the night came;
and when the night came they were drunken with anger, even as a man which is drunken with wine; and they slept again upon their swords;

provenance.route: Isaiah 49:26 → KJV → 1 Nephi 21:26 / 2 Nephi 6:18 / 1 Nephi 22:13 → Ether 15:22
provenance.other: “drunken with” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Isaiah 49:26 (‘drunken with their own blood, as with sweet wine’), Lamentations 3:15 (‘drunken with wormwood’) and Revelation 17:6 (‘drunken with the blood of the saints’). Only Isaiah 49:26 has the full construction Ether 15:22 uses — drunken with a thing that is not wine, followed by an ‘as with’ comparison to wine. Isaiah 49:26 is quoted verbatim twice earlier in the Book of Mormon, at 1 Nephi 21:26 and 2 Nephi 6:18, and glossed at 1 Nephi 22:13: ‘they shall war among themselves, and the sword of their own hands shall fall upon their own heads, and they shall be drunken with their own blood.’ “drunken with wine” is not a KJV phrase at all; in the Book of Mormon it occurs exactly twice, at 1 Nephi 4:7 and here.
provenance.alternative: Direct dependence on Isaiah 49:26, or on Isaiah 29:9 / 51:21 (‘drunken, but not with wine’). The Isaiah 29/51 idiom is the nearer paraphrase of the *sense*; Isaiah 49:26 is the nearer match of the *syntax*, and it is the verse the Book of Mormon has already made its own.
provenance.significance: 1 Nephi 22:13 is the Book of Mormon's own reading of Isaiah 49:26, and it reads it as mutual annihilation: a people who war among themselves until their own sword falls on their own heads and they are drunk with their own blood. Ether 15 is that reading executed. The men are drunken — with anger, not wine; they fight until every one of them has fallen by the sword (15:23), the last two by each other's hand; and three times in the chapter (15:9, 15:27, 15:29) a man faints ‘with the loss of blood’. Isaiah's oracle promised that oppressors would be made to consume themselves; the Jaredites do it. The second echo is nearer home. The Book of Mormon says ‘drunken with wine’ in exactly one other place — 1 Nephi 4:7, of Laban, lying in the street before Nephi takes his sword and smites off his head. Eight verses later this chapter's survivor smites off the head of Shiz. The book's first killing and its last are both introduced by the same phrase.

links.note: “They were drunken with anger, even as a man which is drunken with wine.” The simile is not decorative; it is the King James Bible's own figure for a nation under judgment, and the Book of Mormon has spent four earlier passages establishing it. The syntax is Isaiah 49:26's — drunken with X, as with wine — and the substance Isaiah names is blood, which is what this chapter's men keep losing. Note the direction of the borrowing: the proximate model is not the KJV Isaiah but the Book of Mormon's own Isaiah, quoted at 1 Nephi 21:26 and interpreted at 1 Nephi 22:13 as a prophecy of a people destroying itself by its own sword. Ether 15 is where that interpretation is cashed.
links.text: And I will feed them that oppress thee with their own flesh; and they shall be drunken with their own blood, as with sweet wine: and all flesh shall know that I the LORD am thy Saviour and thy Redeemer, the mighty One of Jacob.

pericopes.text: and on the morrow they fought again; and when the night came they had all fallen by the sword, save it were fifty and two of the people of Coriantumr, and sixty and nine of the people of Shiz.
And it came to pass that they slept upon their swords that night, and on the morrow they fought again, and they contended in their mights with their swords, and with their shields, all that day;
and when the night came there was thirty and two of the people of Shiz, and twenty and seven of the people of Coriantumr.
And it came to pass that they ate and slept, and prepared for death on the morrow. And they were large and mighty men, as to the strength of men.

provenance.other: There is almost no shared wording and I do not claim any: ‘on the morrow’ is KJV boilerplate the Book of Mormon uses five times in this chapter alone. The contact is the scene — a doomed king, told he will die tomorrow, with no strength left in him because he has not eaten, made to eat a meal and then rising to go out to the battle that kills him.
provenance.significance: The Saul-at-Gilboa reading is what holds this end of the chapter together, and its verbal evidence sits four verses later at 15:30, where ‘leaned upon his sword’ reproduces the KJV's only occurrence of ‘leaned upon his’ — 2 Samuel 1:6, Saul on Mount Gilboa leaning on his spear. Read backwards from there, 15:26 is the night before Gilboa: 1 Samuel 28:20 has Saul with ‘no strength in him; for he had eaten no bread all the day’, 28:22-25 has him eat, 28:25 has them rise and go away that night, and 28:19 has the sentence ‘to morrow shalt thou and thy sons be with me’. Ether 15:26 compresses all of it into eleven words, and 15:28 supplies the missing half of 28:20 — ‘when the men of Coriantumr had received sufficient strength, that they could walk’.

links.note: “They ate and slept, and prepared for death on the morrow.” The sentence has no scriptural wording in it, which is why this is filed as figural and at moderate rather than high. What it has is a scriptural scene, and only one: the King James Bible's single night-before-the-last-battle, where a king who already knows the verdict is fed a meal he does not want and goes out in the morning to die. I record it because the chapter's next mention of a leaning king (15:30) is verbally Saul's, and because a reader who has seen that will want to know whether the catalogue noticed the meal. It did.
links.text: Moreover the LORD will also deliver Israel with thee into the hand of the Philistines: and to morrow shalt thou and thy sons be with me: the LORD also shall deliver the host of Israel into the hand of the Philistines.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they fought for the space of three hours, and they fainted with the loss of blood.

And it came to pass that when the men of Coriantumr had received sufficient strength, that they could walk, they were about to flee for their lives, but behold, Shiz arose, and also his men, and he swore in his wrath that he would slay Coriantumr, or he would perish by the sword;

provenance.route: Psalm 95:11 → KJV → Book of Mormon, or Psalm 95:11 → Hebrews 3:11 / 4:3 → KJV → Book of Mormon; the verse cannot settle it
provenance.other: “sware in my wrath” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 95:11 and Hebrews 3:11, and Hebrews 4:3 has ‘As I have sworn in my wrath’ — so the collocation of swearing and wrath belongs, in the whole King James Bible, to one oath quoted three times. tools/mediation-check.py on Ether 15:28 against Psalm 95:11 and Hebrews 3:11 reports no decisive divergence: the two candidates differ only at ‘Unto whom’/‘So’ and ‘should’/‘shall’, and Ether 15:28 reproduces neither point. Mediation is therefore recorded as uncertain rather than guessed. The one straw, and it is only a straw, blows the other way from the default: Ether reads ‘swore’, and the KJV's ‘sware’ is the Old Testament and Hebrews 3:11 form while Hebrews 4:3's is ‘sworn’.
provenance.alternative: That there is no dependence at all and ‘swore in his wrath’ is ordinary narrative English. Possible; against it, the King James Bible never once uses the collocation for a human oath.
provenance.significance: The oath in Psalm 95 has exactly one content: that they shall not enter into my rest. It is the sentence on the wilderness generation, the whole nation excluded from the land for unbelief, and Hebrews takes it up twice to argue that a rest remains for the people of God. Ether 15:28 gives the oath to Shiz, who swears in his wrath that he will kill Coriantumr or die, and thereby denies rest to the only men left alive — his own, who had just ‘received sufficient strength, that they could walk’ and were ‘about to flee for their lives’. The chapter grants rest once, two verses later: ‘when Coriantumr had leaned upon his sword, that he rested a little, he smote off the head of Shiz.’ The only man who enters into rest in Ether 15 does so leaning on a sword, and uses it to behead the man who swore.

links.note: “He swore in his wrath that he would slay Coriantumr, or he would perish by the sword.” In the King James Bible, swearing in wrath is not something men do. The collocation occurs twice and is God's, both times, and both times it is the same oath — the exclusion of a whole generation from rest. Putting it in Shiz's mouth at the moment when the last survivors could have walked away is the chapter's sharpest single stroke, and it is the reason his men do not get to flee. I leave mediation open: the OT verse and its NT quotation are worded too nearly alike at the points Ether reproduces for this verse to decide between them, and I would rather say so than pick.
links.text: Unto whom I sware in my wrath that they should not enter into my rest.

pericopes.text: wherefore he did pursue them, and on the morrow he did overtake them; and they fought again with the sword. And it came to pass that when they had all fallen by the sword, save it were Coriantumr and Shiz, behold, Shiz had fainted with loss of blood.
And it came to pass that when Coriantumr had leaned upon his sword, that he rested a little, he smote off the head of Shiz.

provenance.route: 2 Samuel 1:6 → KJV → Book of Mormon, with Judges 5:26 fused in the second clause
provenance.other: “leaned upon his” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 1:6 — ‘behold, Saul leaned upon his spear; and, lo, the chariots and horsemen followed hard after him’, the Amalekite's report of the end of Saul on Mount Gilboa. “smote off” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Judges 5:26, where Jael smites off Sisera's head after his army has been destroyed to the last man, and Matthew 26:51, where a disciple smites off an ear; only Judges 5:26 is a beheading, and it too is a killing done by the survivor of an annihilation to a commander too spent to resist. “with his own sword”, which Shiz demands at 15:5, occurs nowhere in the KJV and three times in the Book of Mormon before this verse: 1 Nephi 4:18, 4:19 and Ether 9:27.
provenance.significance: The verse is an inclusio for the whole Book of Mormon. Its first killing is 1 Nephi 4: Laban lying in the street ‘drunken with wine’ (4:7), and Nephi taking the man's own sword and smiting off his head (4:18-19). Its last killing is this one: men ‘drunken with anger, even as a man which is drunken with wine’ (15:22), and Coriantumr smiting off the head of Shiz. ‘Drunken with wine’ occurs in the Book of Mormon at those two places and nowhere else, and ‘smote off’ a head at those two places and nowhere else. Recover 2 Samuel 1 and a third layer opens: the man leaning on his weapon in that chapter is a king at the end of his people, who asks to be killed and is, and whose death is reported to the man who will inherit what is left. Coriantumr will be the one carried to a new people (Omni 1:21). Ether 15:30 makes him Saul and Jael at once — the doomed king leaning on the weapon, and the hand that takes the head.

links.note: “When Coriantumr had leaned upon his sword, that he rested a little, he smote off the head of Shiz.” Two of the KJV's rarest verbs of violence in eighteen words. ‘Leaned upon his’ is a King James singleton and belongs to Saul on Gilboa, wounded and about to die; ‘smote off’ is used twice, and the beheading of the two is Jael's of Sisera in the Song of Deborah, after the army that was to have destroyed Israel has itself been destroyed to a man. The chapter has taken the last posture of one doomed king and the last stroke of one annihilated general and put them in the same sentence, in the same hand. Under Skousen's threshold and not a quotation; four words, but four words that the King James Bible spends only three verses on.
links.text: And the young man that told him said, As I happened by chance upon mount Gilboa, behold, Saul leaned upon his spear; and, lo, the chariots and horsemen followed hard after him.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that after he had smote off the head of Shiz, that Shiz raised upon his hands and fell; and after that he had struggled for breath, he died.
And it came to pass that Coriantumr fell to the earth, and became as if he had no life.

And the Lord spake unto Ether, and said unto him, Go forth. And he went forth, and beheld that the words of the Lord had all been fulfilled; and he finished his record; (and the hundredth part I have not written,) and he hid them in a manner that the people of Limhi did find them.

provenance.route: John 21:25 → KJV → Jacob 3:13 / 3 Nephi 5:8 and the corpus formula → Ether 15:33
provenance.other: “the hundredth part” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Nehemiah 5:11, where it is a rate of interest on money and has nothing to do with writing; the King James Bible's actual too-much-to-write formula is John 21:25. Inside the Book of Mormon the fraction is a house idiom by the time Moroni uses it — Jacob 3:13, Words of Mormon 1:5, Helaman 3:14, 3 Nephi 5:8 and 3 Nephi 26:6 — and 3 Nephi 5:8 is the one that keeps John's own verb: ‘this book cannot contain even a hundredth part’, against John's ‘the world itself could not contain the books’.
provenance.alternative: That the formula is wholly internal to the Book of Mormon and owes the KJV nothing. Against that: the KJV has a formula of exactly this shape in exactly one place, and it stands in exactly this position, at the close of a book, one verse before the last.
provenance.significance: The mediation enum has no value for this shape — a New Testament source reaching a verse through earlier Book of Mormon passages rather than through the Bible — so the route is written out here instead. ‘direct-NT’ records where the phrase came from and understates how it arrived. What John 21:24-25 supplies is not the fraction but the colophon: a witness named, his record declared finished and true, the remainder declared unwritable, and Amen. Ether 15:33-34 is that colophon exactly — the record finished, the hundredth part unwritten, the last words of the witness, Amen — with the difference that Moroni is quoting a colophon inside a colophon, since these are Ether's last words reported by Moroni at the end of Moroni's own abridgement.

links.note: “He finished his record; (and the hundredth part I have not written,) and he hid them in a manner that the people of Limhi did find them.” The parenthesis is Moroni's, and it is the fifth time the Book of Mormon has said it. Its biblical model is the last sentence of John's Gospel, the one place in the King James Bible where a writer closes by saying that what he has left out would not fit — and the Book of Mormon's nearest form of it, 3 Nephi 5:8, keeps John's verb, 'contain'. The link is filed at moderate because the wording has been through the corpus rather than coming straight off the page: Moroni is writing in a formula his own scriptures gave him. That the formula reaches the reader at the end of the last book Moroni abridged, four verses from the end of Jaredite history, is the point of putting it here at all.
links.text: And there are also many other things which Jesus did, the which, if they should be written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written. Amen.

pericopes.text: Now the last words which are written by Ether, are these: Whether the Lord will that I be translated, or that I suffer the will of the Lord in the flesh: It mattereth not, if it so be that I am saved in the kingdom of God. Amen.

provenance.other: “translated” occurs in exactly two KJV verses: Hebrews 11:5, where Enoch ‘was translated that he should not see death’, and Colossians 1:13, where God ‘hath translated us into the kingdom of his dear Son’. “was translated” is a KJV singleton, Hebrews 11:5. Both of the KJV's two verses stand inside Ether 15:34's one sentence — the translation that avoids death, and the being translated into a kingdom — and the sentence ends ‘if it so be that I am saved in the kingdom of God’. In the Book of Mormon ‘translated’ appears four other times (Mosiah 8:12, 28:11, 28:13) and always means rendering a language; this is the only occurrence in the Enoch sense in the whole book.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 11:5 does not only supply the verb. It says that before his translation Enoch ‘had this testimony, that he pleased God’ — and Ether 15:34 is a testimony, introduced as ‘the last words which are written by Ether’, the closing witness of a prophet who has watched his nation destroy itself from a cave. The whole of Hebrews 11 is the chapter of witnesses who died without receiving the promises, and the Book of Mormon has quarried it before at 1 Nephi 2 and 1 Nephi 4:2. Ether's last sentence takes Hebrews 11's one man who did not die, and declines to care which of the two he gets.

links.note: “Whether the Lord will that I be translated, or that I suffer the will of the Lord in the flesh: It mattereth not.” The King James Bible uses ‘translated’ twice, and Ether's closing sentence contains both uses — Enoch's escape from death and Colossians' being carried into a kingdom — with ‘the kingdom of God’ four words later. Nothing else in the Book of Mormon uses the word this way. For a book that has just annihilated a civilization, the last word is a shrug about the writer's own body, and it is a KJV shrug: the only two verses in the English Bible that could have furnished it, both used at once.
links.text: By faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death; and was not found, because God had translated him: for before his translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God.

provenance.other: “in the flesh” occurs in 28 KJV verses and settles nothing on its own; the case is the structure, not the phrase. Philippians 1:21-24 is the King James Bible's one passage in which a writer sets two possible ends for himself side by side — departing, or abiding ‘in the flesh’ — declares himself ‘in a strait betwixt two’, and refuses to prefer either. 2 Corinthians 12:2-3 supplies the other half of the form, ‘whether in the body, or out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth’, and it is the KJV's account of a man caught up to the third heaven, which is the state Ether's first alternative names.
provenance.significance: Read against Philippians the indifference formula changes character. Paul cannot choose because both outcomes are good and one of them serves the church; Ether cannot choose because there is no church left — his people are dead to the last man but one, and his record is hidden in a rock for strangers to find. ‘It mattereth not’ is Paul's strait betwixt two with nothing on either side of it but God. Compare the other closing testimonies in the corpus: Moroni 10:34 knows exactly what is coming and describes it in detail; Ether 15:34, which is the older book and the earlier civilization, ends by saying the question is not worth asking.

links.note: “Whether the Lord will that I be translated, or that I suffer the will of the Lord in the flesh: It mattereth not, if it so be that I am saved in the kingdom of God. Amen.” The sentence is built on a Pauline form — whether X or Y, it makes no difference, so long as the one thing that matters holds — and Paul uses it twice about precisely this question, at Philippians 1:21-24 about staying in the flesh or departing, and at 2 Corinthians 12:2-3 about being in the body or out of it. ‘Suffer the will of the Lord in the flesh’ is Philippians 1:24's ‘to abide in the flesh’ with the resignation made explicit. I record it at moderate: the vocabulary is common and the argument rests on the shape of the sentence rather than on a rare phrase.
links.text: But if I live in the flesh, this is the fruit of my labour: yet what I shall choose I wot not.
